lessons.plain: Designing a structure for the flow of work means deciding how a team moves a change from an idea to running software: who picks up a task, where the code is changed, how it gets checked, and when it reaches users. GitHub Flow is one common answer. Everyone makes changes on short-lived side copies of the code, asks for a review when a change is ready, and then merges it into one main line that is always meant to be safe to release. Think of a shared kitchen where each cook prepares a dish on a separate board, a second cook tastes it, and only then does it go on the menu.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of five developers each works for three weeks on a private copy of the code and merges everything at the end of the sprint. What is the most likely problem with this, and what would you change?
lessons.teach:
A branch is a named, separate line of changes in a version control system such as Git. The main branch is the line the team treats as the official, releasable version of the code. A pull request, on GitHub, is a request to merge one branch into another. It gives reviewers a place to comment and lets automated checks run on the proposed change first. Continuous integration (CI) means that every change is automatically built and tested as it is proposed, rather than at the end. A work item is a tracked unit of work, such as a task or a bug, recorded in a tool like Azure Boards or as a GitHub issue.

GitHub Flow works because it keeps main always releasable, keeps each branch small so merges are easy, and makes every change pass review and tests before it joins main.

Worked example. Work item 412 says the position API client needs a timeout. Step 1: create a branch named after the item, such as feature/412-api-timeout, from the current main. Step 2: make a small change and commit it. Step 3: open a pull request and put the work item number in its title so the change can be traced back to the ticket. Step 4: CI builds the branch and runs the tests. Step 5: a teammate requests a change, and you push a fix to the same branch. Step 6: once approved and green, merge into main and delete the branch. Main now holds a tested, reviewed change that the pipeline can deploy.

Common mistake: letting a branch stay open for weeks. It drifts away from main, and the final merge produces large conflicts that nobody has tested in pieces. Committing straight to main has the same flaw, because nothing is checked before it lands.

In a running system the consequence is concrete. The deployment pipeline ships from main, so a long-lived branch that merges late and breaks main can stop releases or put a faulty build in front of customers.

questions.prompt: A logistics software team at a freight company takes work item 2291, which says the label printer client should retry a failed print job once. Follow the steps and fill the gap. Step 1: create a branch named bug/2291-label-retry from the current main. Step 2: commit a small change that adds the single retry. Step 3: this step is missing. Step 4: CI builds the branch and runs the printer client tests. Step 5: a reviewer asks for a clearer log message, and the developer pushes a fix to the same branch. Step 6: after approval and green checks, the branch is merged into main and deleted. Which step belongs in the gap?
choices: Open a pull request with 2291 in its title so the change traces back to the work item
Create a second branch from the first branch and leave both open
Wait three weeks so the branch collects more changes before review
Commit the change straight to main so the retry ships sooner
questions.why: Step 3 opens a pull request with the work item number in its title, which is what lets CI run on the proposed change and keeps it traceable to the ticket, while the other options skip review or let branches drift.

questions.prompt: In GitHub Flow, what is the main branch meant to hold?
choices: Every experimental idea the team has tried, kept for reference
The official, releasable version of the code that the team treats as trusted
Only the changes a developer is still writing and has not shared
A copy of the last release archive that nobody changes
questions.why: The teaching text defines main as the line the team treats as the official, releasable version of the code, which is the idea behind keeping it always releasable.

questions.prompt: A developer on a retail team wants a change checked by a colleague and by automated tests before it reaches the release line. Which practice fits GitHub Flow?
choices: Open a pull request from a small branch so reviewers can comment and CI builds and tests the proposed change
Email the changed files to the release manager for manual copying
Push the change directly to main so it is available immediately
Create a long-lived branch and merge it only after the next quarter
questions.why: A pull request gives reviewers a place to comment and lets CI run on the proposed change before it joins main, which is how GitHub Flow makes every change pass review and tests first.

questions.prompt: A team at a travel booking company keeps a branch open for five weeks. When it finally merges into main, the merge causes many conflicts that nobody has tested in pieces. Why is this a risk for the running system?
choices: Git stores the branch in a separate archive, so nothing reaches main at all
Conflicts only affect the developer's laptop and never reach the servers
Long branches automatically delete the work items they are linked to
The deployment pipeline ships from main, so a late merge that breaks main can stop releases or put a faulty build in front of customers
questions.why: The teaching text explains that the pipeline ships from main, so a long-lived branch that merges late and breaks main can halt releases or expose customers to a faulty build.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how GitHub Flow carries one change from a work item to production, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: GitHub Flow keeps one main branch that is always in a releasable state. For each work item, you create a short-lived branch from main, commit small changes to it, and open a pull request so reviewers can comment and automated tests can run on the proposed change. When the review passes and the checks are green, you merge into main, and the pipeline deploys from main. The main tradeoff is that it assumes main is safe to release after every merge, so it depends on solid automated tests and on merging often. A team with slow tests or infrequent releases may need an extra release branch on top, and pull requests left open for days can make reviewers a bottleneck.
rubricPoints: Describes the steps: short-lived branch from main, commits, pull request, review and CI, merge into main
Explains that main stays releasable and the deployment pipeline ships from it
Names a real limit, such as dependence on good automated tests or frequent merging
Notes that long-lived branches or slow reviews cause drift, conflicts or bottlenecks

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying a branching structure for a team scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation.

lessons.plain: A feedback cycle is the loop that tells people how their work is doing: a failed build, a bug report, a question about a change. The faster and more clearly the right person hears about it, the sooner they can act. A feedback strategy decides which events matter, who should hear about them, through which channel, and how much noise is acceptable. GitHub Issues are one place where feedback is recorded as a trackable item, and notifications are the messages that pull people back to it. Too few signals and problems go unseen; too many and people mute everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team receives about 200 notification emails a day and quietly stops reading them. Before any teaching, what would you change first, and why would that help?
lessons.teach:
A feedback cycle is the time between an action and the moment someone learns its result. A feedback strategy decides which events deserve a signal, who receives it, where it arrives, and what happens next.

An issue is a numbered record of a piece of work, a bug, or a question, kept in a GitHub repository. It has a title, a description, labels for category, an assignee for the owner, and a state of open or closed. A notification is a message sent when something happens to an item you are subscribed to, such as a comment, an @mention of your name, or a status change. Watching a repository or an issue controls how much of this reaches you. A webhook is an automatic HTTP message a service sends to another address when an event occurs. That is how a chat channel or a dashboard can learn about activity without someone checking by hand.

Why it works: feedback that arrives close to the action, and reaches the person who can fix it, gets acted on. Linking closes the loop. If a pull request description contains a closing keyword such as 'Closes #42', merging that pull request into the default branch closes issue 42 automatically, so the record matches reality without manual upkeep.

Worked example: a bug is reported as issue #42 and labelled 'bug' and 'checkout'. The checkout owner is assigned. A developer opens a pull request whose description says 'Closes #42'. A reviewer is @mentioned. When the pull request merges to the default branch, issue #42 closes, and the subscribed team channel receives one event instead of a stream of comments.

Common mistake: sending every event to everyone. People mute the channel, and the one urgent failure is lost. Route by label or owner instead.

Consequence: if a failed production deploy emails only a release manager who is on leave, the team learns about the outage from customers hours later.

questions.prompt: A payments team at another company keeps issue #317, labelled 'incident' and 'payments' and assigned to Priya, to track a retry bug. Priya opens a pull request into the default branch whose description reads 'Fixes #317', and a reviewer is @mentioned in a comment. The labelling, assignment, closing keyword and mention are all in place. The one step still missing is: the pull request must be ____ so that issue #317 closes automatically. Which completes the chain?
choices: given the label 'incident' as well
moved to the Done column of a project board
approved by two reviewers before anyone reads the description
merged into the default branch
questions.why: A closing keyword in a pull request description closes its linked issue only when that pull request merges into the default branch, so the merge is the missing step.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a webhook in the context of GitHub activity?
choices: A personal email that arrives each time someone comments on your issue
A label that marks an issue as belonging to a particular component
An automatic HTTP message a service sends to another address when an event occurs
A setting that closes stale issues automatically after a fixed number of days
questions.why: A webhook is defined as an automatic HTTP message sent to another address when an event happens, which lets other tools learn about activity without a person checking.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants a team dashboard to refresh whenever a pipeline run in one of their repositories fails, without anyone checking by hand. Which mechanism fits best?
choices: Configure a webhook from the repository events to the dashboard's receiving address
Subscribe the team lead to every notification in the organisation
Assign every failed run to the dashboard maintainer as an issue owner
Add a 'failed' label to each run and rely on people to filter for it
questions.why: A webhook is the mechanism that lets a service push events automatically to another address, which removes the need for manual checking.

questions.prompt: A release manager is the only person subscribed to deployment failure notifications for a service, and that manager is on leave when a production deploy fails. Customers report the outage hours later. What change best addresses this failure?
choices: Wait for customers to raise a support ticket, because they will report real outages quickly
Route failure events by label or owner to an on-call owner and to a shared team channel
Email the whole company about every deployment event so that someone is bound to notice
Mute the deployment channel so that the release manager is not disturbed by routine events
questions.why: Routing by label or owner sends the urgent failure to someone who can act and to a shared place, so a single absence does not hide the signal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up issue tracking and notifications so that a failed production deploy reaches the right person quickly without flooding everyone. Name one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the signal narrow. A failed production deploy should create or reopen a GitHub issue labelled 'deploy-failure' and assign the on-call owner. The pull request or release that caused it should reference that issue with a closing keyword, so the link is recorded and closing it on merge is automatic. Only that label routes to the team channel through a Microsoft Teams subscription. General activity stays in the repository for people who choose to watch it, and everyone else keeps default settings so they still see mentions and their own items. The tradeoff is that a narrow route makes anything unlabelled quieter, so a failure with the wrong label can be missed. The design only works if labels are applied consistently, whether by people or by automation.
rubricPoints: Names GitHub Issues as the recorded item, with labels and an assignee for routing.
Routes notifications by label or owner rather than broadcasting every event.
Links the causing change to the issue so closing it happens automatically on merge.
States a real tradeoff, such as missed alerts when labelling is inconsistent.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about who should hear what and explaining the tradeoff back, which a read-only lookup would not build.

lessons.plain: Work tracking integration means connecting the place where a team plans its work (a list of tasks, bugs, and requests) with the place where the code lives. Without a link, a bug report and the code change that fixed it are two separate stories that someone has to match by memory. With a link, you can move from a task to its code and from a code change back to the reason it exists. Think of a library catalogue that points to each book's shelf, while each book carries a note pointing back to its catalogue entry. The design questions are which link to use, where to put it, and what should happen automatically when it changes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer merges a code change that fixes bug 412, but the bug stays open on the team board. What single piece of information, if the two tools were connected, would let the board know which bug the change fixed, and where would you expect that information to appear?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A work item is a tracked unit of planned work, such as a task, bug, or user story. A repository (repo) is the stored history of source code. A commit is one saved change in that history. A pull request (PR) is a proposed set of commits that a reviewer checks before they are merged into the main line of code. A work-tracking tool, such as Azure Boards or GitHub Projects with GitHub Issues, holds work items and their status. Integration means a defined link between these systems, so that an identifier in one place points to a record in the other.

Why it works. A tool cannot infer that a commit relates to a bug. Teams make the relationship explicit by putting a work item's ID into the commit message or PR title, or by linking the item from the PR side. The tracker then shows the code activity attached to the item, and the code host shows which item the change serves. Some integrations also apply status rules, so that when a PR merges the linked item is marked done.

Worked example. Bug 412 reads 'positions API returns stale data'. Step 1: a developer creates the branch fix/412-stale-positions. Step 2: they commit with the message 'Fix cache invalidation, refs 412'. Step 3: they open a PR titled 'Fix stale positions (412)'. Step 4: the tracker shows the PR against bug 412. Step 5: the PR merges and the status rule marks the bug resolved, leaving a trail from bug to change to reviewer.

Common mistake. Teams assume that because two tools are connected, every commit is linked automatically. If the ID is missing from the message or PR title, the link is silently absent and the board shows a bug with no code behind it. Test the link on a real item before relying on it.

Consequence. In a running system, a missing link means an incident fix ships with no record of which bug it closed, so release notes and audit trails come out incomplete.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company has work item 3310, 'label printer queue stalls'. Their commits do not contain any work item ID. Here is how the change moves through the process. Step 1: a developer pushes a branch with three commits, none mentioning 3310. Step 2: the developer opens a pull request titled 'Clear stalled print queue'. Step 3: [MISSING STEP: the developer or a teammate with access to the item adds a link from the pull request to work item 3310]. Step 4: the tracker shows the pull request attached to item 3310. Step 5: the pull request merges and the status rule marks item 3310 resolved. Which action completes the missing step 3?
choices: Create a second work item for the pull request so the tracker can match the two by count.
Nothing is needed, because the tracker links the pull request automatically when the branch and pull request live in the same repository.
Close work item 3310 manually before the pull request is opened, so the status rule has nothing left to do.
Add a link from the pull request to work item 3310, so the tracker shows the code change against that item.
questions.why: The teaching text says a tool cannot infer that a change relates to a work item, so the link must be made explicitly, and linking from the pull request side is one valid way to do that.

questions.prompt: In a work-tracking integration, what is a work item?
choices: A stored history of source code that records every saved change over time.
A reviewer's approval recorded on a proposed set of changes.
A single saved change to the code, identified by a hash.
A tracked unit of planned work, such as a task, bug, or user story.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a work item as a tracked unit of planned work, such as a task, bug, or user story.

questions.prompt: A team's last release contained six fixes, and none of their commit messages or pull request titles mention a work item ID. What will the work-tracking board most likely show for the bugs those fixes were meant to close, and what does that mean for release notes?
choices: The bugs will show no code behind them, so release notes and audit trails for those fixes will be incomplete.
The bugs will be merged into one combined work item, so the release notes will list them once.
The bugs will be reopened on every commit, so the release notes will show duplicate entries.
The bugs will be marked resolved automatically, so the release notes are complete.
questions.why: Without an ID in the commit message or pull request title, the link is absent, so the board shows the bugs with no linked code and the release record cannot show which fixes closed them.

questions.prompt: A developer at a different company writes the commit message 'fixes the timeout bug' on a change that was meant to close work item 1177. The pull request merges. What is the most likely result?
choices: Work item 1177 is closed, because merging a pull request always closes every open item in the same repository.
Work item 1177 is closed, because the tracker reads plain-language phrases such as 'fixes' and matches them to the nearest open bug.
Work item 1177 stays open, because the tracker did not receive the identifier it needs to link the change to that item.
Work item 1177 is split into two items, one for the commit and one for the pull request.
questions.why: The tracker needs the work item's ID in the message or title to form the link, and a phrase without the ID leaves the item unlinked and open.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used one tool how you would link a bug on your team's board to the code change that fixes it, and name one limit of that link.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the bug's ID in the branch name, the commit message, and the PR title, so the tracker and the code host can both find the match. The tracking tool then shows the PR on the bug, and if the integration has a status rule, merging the PR can close the bug. The main limit is that the link is only as good as the text someone typed. If the ID is missing or wrong, nothing fails loudly; the bug just looks untouched and the code has no record of what it fixed. Another limit is that the status rule only fires on the events the integration understands, so a fix pushed directly to the main branch may never update the bug. Before trusting the setup, I would test it with a throwaway item and check both sides show the link.
rubricPoints: Names a concrete linking mechanism, such as an ID in the commit message, branch name, or PR title.
Explains that the tracker and code host each show the other side of the link.
States a limit: a missing or mistyped ID silently breaks the link.
Mentions that automatic status changes depend on what the integration recognises, and suggests testing the link.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission practises work-item linking, so the core skill here is explaining the link and its limits in your own words.

lessons.plain: Traceability means being able to follow a thread between what was asked for, the code written to answer it, the build that tested that code, and the release that shipped it. If a customer reports a bug, you want to walk backwards: which change caused it, why that change was made, and which tests covered it. Teams make this possible by linking their tracking items (tasks, bugs, requirements) to the source changes, builds, and releases that relate to them. Without those links, every investigation starts from memory and guesswork.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer reports a bug in last Tuesday's release. Without relying on anyone's memory, what would you need to be able to find, and in what order, to learn which code change caused the bug and why that change was made?
lessons.teach:
A work item is a tracked record of something to do or a problem to fix, such as a user story, a task, or a bug. A commit is a saved set of code changes with a short message describing them. A pull request (PR) is a proposal to merge a branch of changes into the main line after review. A build is an automated run that compiles and tests the code, and a release is a deployment of a build to an environment. A link is a recorded connection between two of these items, so the tool can show it from either end.

Traceability works because links are stored once and can be followed in both directions. In Azure Boards, putting the token AB# followed by a work item number into a commit message or PR title creates a link to that work item. In GitHub, a PR description with a closing keyword such as Fixes #12 links the PR to issue 12 and closes it when merged. Builds record which commits they contain, and releases record which build they deployed, so the chain can be walked from a production release back to the work item that asked for the change.

Worked example. Bug 412 says positions on the dispatch map are stale. Step 1: open bug 412 and find the fix linked to it. Step 2: the fix commit a1f9 has the message 'Cache positions for 30s AB#398', so it is linked to story 398 and to PR 88. Step 3: build 2201 lists a1f9 among its changes, with its test results attached. Step 4: release 57 deployed build 2201 to production. Release 57 therefore carried the change that caused the staleness, and story 398 explains why the change was made.

Common mistake: a commit message such as 'fix stuff' has no work item number, so the chain breaks at the first link and the investigation falls back to searching logs by date.

In a running system, a broken chain costs time during an incident, because you cannot quickly decide which release to roll back. Traceability of quality works the same way: test results and defects are linked to the builds they came from, so you can see whether a defect escaped past testing.

questions.prompt: Harbor Bakery tracks orders in GitHub Issues. A customer reports that coupon codes are accepted twice. Work through the chain, then fill in the missing step. Step 1: open issue 57, 'Coupon codes accepted twice'. Step 2: PR 203 has the description 'Fixes #57', so PR 203 is linked to issue 57 and will close it when merged. Step 3: PR 203 contains commits 4fa2 and c81e. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: release 31 deployed build 778 to production. Which statement correctly fills step 4?
choices: Issue 57 is linked directly to release 31, so no build needs to be checked.
Build 778 is checked for commit c81e, since a build records which commits it contains, and that build is the one the release deployed.
Build 778 is searched for in the PR 203 description, which lists the release number.
The closing keyword 'Fixes #57' changes release 31 so it is marked as containing the fix.
questions.why: A build records its commits and a release records its build, so finding the build that contains commit c81e connects the fix to release 31.

questions.prompt: A team writes 'AB#812' at the start of a commit message on a branch that will later be merged. What does that token do?
choices: It marks work item 812 as complete once the commit is pushed.
It stores the commit's test results inside work item 812 as attachments.
It creates a recorded link from the commit to work item 812, so the tool can show the connection from either end.
It deploys the commit to the test environment automatically.
questions.why: The AB# token followed by a work item number creates a link to that item, which can be followed from both the commit and the work item.

questions.prompt: A developer pushes a commit with the message 'minor tweaks' and no work item number, and the commit later ships to production. A defect appears in production. What is the most likely result for the investigation?
choices: The tool links the commit to the nearest work item by timestamp, so tracing still works.
The build fails automatically, which shows exactly which commit caused the defect.
The release record is cleared, so the defect cannot be traced to any build.
The chain from the release back to a work item breaks at the commit, so the team has to fall back to searching logs by date.
questions.why: Without a work item number the link from commit to work item is missing, so the chain breaks and the investigation becomes a manual search by date.

questions.prompt: A team stores test results as attachments on each build. A regression appears in production, and the team wants to know whether it got past testing. Which check answers that question?
choices: Count how many work items are open in the backlog for the sprint.
Look at the build that the production release deployed and see whether its linked test results and defects show the problem was already caught or missed.
Check whether the production environment has enough memory to run the release.
Compare the release date with the date the developer last logged in.
questions.why: Test results and defects are linked to the build they came from, so the build that was deployed shows whether the defect was already visible in testing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined how a bug reported by a customer can be traced back to the work item that justified the change that caused it. Name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the bug and follow the links the team recorded at each step. The bug links to the fix or its source; the fix commit or pull request names the work item it implements, usually through the AB# token or a closing keyword on a GitHub issue; the build that produced the release lists the commits it contains; and the release record shows when that build reached production. That gives us the change, the reason for it, and the tests that ran against it. The limit is that the chain is only as complete as the links people wrote. A commit without a work item number, or a bug fixed outside the normal flow, breaks the trail, so we have to fall back to searching history by date and author. Traceability tells us where to look quickly; it does not prove the change was correct.
rubricPoints: Starts from the bug and follows recorded links backward through the fix or commit, the build, and the release.
Names how links are created, such as the AB# token in commits or PRs, or a closing keyword on a GitHub issue.
Says what the trail gives: the change, its reason or requirement, and the tests run on it.
States a limit: links are only as good as the discipline behind them, and gaps force a manual search.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where the learner must decide which link to follow and where the trail breaks adds more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A flow-of-work dashboard is one screen that shows how fast finished changes reach users and how fast the team recovers when something breaks. Lead time measures how long a request takes from being asked for until it is live. Cycle time measures how long active work takes from the moment someone starts it until it is done. Time to recovery measures how long a service stays broken after a failure begins. Together these numbers show whether work is slowing down, getting stuck, or being repaired quickly. Picture a bakery that tracks how long an order waits in the queue, how long baking takes, and how long a burnt batch keeps customers waiting.
lessons.guessPrompt: A request was logged on Monday, started on Thursday, and went live the following Tuesday. Roughly how many days is its lead time, and why might that number differ from how long the coding itself took?
lessons.teach:
Lead time is the elapsed time from when a request is created until the change is running in production. Cycle time is the elapsed time from when work is started (the item moves into an active state) until it is finished. Time to recovery, sometimes called time to restore, is the elapsed time from when a failure in production starts until service works again. Each tool defines its start and end points slightly differently, so a good dashboard states which points it uses on the page itself.

Why these three together? Lead time includes waiting, so it reveals queues that cycle time hides. Cycle time shows how long active work takes once someone is really on it. Time to recovery shows how well the team can respond when production breaks, which matters as much as how often it breaks.

Worked example. A work item is created Monday 09:00, moved to Active Tuesday 10:00, its code is deployed to production Thursday 11:00, and the item is closed Thursday 11:30. Lead time runs from creation to deployment: Monday 09:00 to Thursday 11:00, which is 3 days and 2 hours. Cycle time runs from Active to closed: Tuesday 10:00 to Thursday 11:30, which is 2 days and 1.5 hours. A production incident starts Friday 14:00 and service is restored at 14:45, so that incident's time to recovery is 45 minutes.

Common mistake: averaging these durations with a plain mean. One item that waited two months can drag the average far from what most work experiences, so show the median and a high percentile instead.

Consequence: if the lead time tile is wrong, a team can look fast while requests quietly sit in a queue for weeks, and nobody sees the delay on the dashboard.

questions.prompt: A request was created Monday 10:00 and its change reached production Friday 15:00. Step 1 is done: lead time is the elapsed time from creation until the change is running in production, so the start is Monday 10:00 and the end is Friday 15:00. Step 2 is missing: convert the elapsed time between those two points into days and hours. What is the result of step 2?
choices: 4 days 5 hours
5 days 5 hours
4 days 6 hours
3 days 5 hours
questions.why: From Monday 10:00 to Friday 10:00 is exactly 4 days, and Friday 10:00 to Friday 15:00 adds 5 hours, giving 4 days 5 hours.

questions.prompt: A production failure starts Tuesday 22:10 and the service is working again at Wednesday 00:40. What is the time to recovery for this failure, where time to recovery is the elapsed time from when a production failure starts until service works again?
choices: 2 hours 10 minutes
2 hours 40 minutes
3 hours 30 minutes
2 hours 30 minutes
questions.why: Time to recovery runs from the failure start (22:10) to restoration (00:40), which is 2 hours 30 minutes.

questions.prompt: A team's dashboard shows the median of its lead times as 3 days, but the mean of the same five items is 14 days because one item waited about two months. Which dashboard design best follows the guidance for reporting flow durations?
choices: Show the longest item, 60 days, so the worst case is visible
Show the median of 3 days plus a high percentile, with the start and end points of each measure stated on the page
Show the mean of 14 days, because every item counts equally in the average
Show only the median of 3 days, since a percentile adds noise
questions.why: Plain means are distorted by a single long item, so the median and a high percentile describe typical and tail experience, and the page should state the measurement points.

questions.prompt: A team wants a dashboard figure for how long active work takes once someone is really working on an item, leaving out the time the item sat waiting in the backlog. Which measure fits?
choices: Cycle time, measured from the moment the item moves into an active state until it is finished
Time to recovery, measured from the start of a production failure until service works again
Queue depth, measured as the number of items waiting in the backlog
Lead time, measured from the moment the request is created until the change is in production
questions.why: Cycle time measures only the active period from start to finish, which excludes waiting, whereas lead time includes the waiting time and the other options measure different things.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would define and choose the lead time, cycle time and time-to-recovery tiles for a team dashboard, and name one limit or tradeoff of these numbers.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first agree on start and end points and write them on the dashboard: lead time from request creation to production deployment, cycle time from the item becoming active to done, and time to recovery from when a production failure starts to when service is restored. I would show medians and a high percentile rather than averages, so one stuck item does not hide the typical experience. The main limit is that these numbers depend on how carefully the team updates work item states. If people leave items in Active after they stop working, cycle time looks worse than the real work, and if they close items before deployment, lead time looks better than it is. Teams should treat the tiles as prompts for conversation, not as scores for individuals.
rubricPoints: Defines lead time as creation (or request) to production, and cycle time as started to done
Explains that time to recovery runs from failure start to restoration
Recommends medians or percentiles instead of plain averages
Names a limit, such as dependence on accurate state updates or outlier distortion

suggested.rationale: Choosing which flow metrics fit a team's situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with trade-offs.

lessons.plain: Project planning metrics are numbers that show how a team's planned work is actually moving: how much effort is left in a sprint, how much is waiting, how much is finished. A query is a saved question you ask a work-tracking tool, such as 'show me every open bug in the payments area created in the last two weeks'. Together they let a team plan from evidence instead of memory. This lesson covers which measure answers which planning question, and how to write the filter that produces it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has finished 15 of 18 work items in a sprint, but only about half the estimated effort is done. Which single measure would reveal this gap, and why might simply counting finished items hide it?
lessons.teach:
A work item is a tracked unit of work, such as a user story, a task or a bug. Each one has a state (for example New, Active or Closed), belongs to an iteration (the team's name for a time-boxed sprint), and sits in an area path (a label that groups work by team or component). A query is a filter over work items. In Azure Boards you write it in WIQL, the Work Item Query Language, which reads like a simple SQL statement: choose fields from work items where conditions hold. Planning metrics are computed from those filtered sets. A burndown shows remaining effort in the current iteration against an ideal straight line. Velocity is the effort a team completed in past iterations, used to forecast the next one. A cumulative flow diagram stacks the count of items in each state over time; a widening band means work is piling up in one state.

Why it works: a metric is only as good as its scope. Filtering by iteration and area path lets you compare like with like.

Worked example: a 10-day sprint plans 40 story points, so the ideal remaining effort at day 5 is 20. On day 5, a query for Remaining Work across stories in this iteration whose state is not Closed returns 26. The team is 6 points behind the ideal line. The next step is to find which items are stuck, not to announce a late sprint.

Common mistake: counting work items instead of effort, so one large story and one small task look equal. Consequence: a team that reports 'fifteen of eighteen items done' may still be far behind on the effort that determines the release date.

The right planning metric is chosen by the question you need answered, not by habit.

questions.prompt: A support tooling team has a 9-day iteration with 36 story points planned, so the ideal remaining effort falls by 4 points each day. On day 6 the ideal line therefore sits at 12 points (36 minus 4 times 6). The team runs a WIQL query for Remaining Work across items in this iteration, area path Support Tooling, whose state is not Closed, and it returns 17. Step 3 is missing: compare the actual 17 with the ideal 12 to find how far the team is off the line. Step 4 is to find which items are stuck.
choices: The team is 5 points behind the ideal line, so the next step is to find which items are stuck.
The team is on track, because 17 is still below the 36 planned points.
The team is 5 items behind, so the next step is to count open items against the ideal.
The team is 17 points behind, because the query result is the gap.
questions.why: The gap is the actual remaining effort minus the ideal remaining effort (17 minus 12 = 5 points), and the teaching text says the next move is to find stuck items rather than to count items or assume the sprint is late.

questions.prompt: A product group wants to estimate how much work to plan for its next iteration by looking at the effort it finished in its last four iterations. Which planning metric fits this need?
choices: Burndown, the remaining effort in the current iteration against an ideal line
Velocity, the effort completed in past iterations used to forecast the next one
A WIQL query that counts all work items with state Closed in any iteration
Cumulative flow diagram, the count of items in each state over time
questions.why: Velocity is defined in the teaching text as the effort a team completed in past iterations, used to forecast the next one, which matches the forecasting need.

questions.prompt: A team reports that it closed 20 of 22 items in its sprint and calls the sprint nearly finished. Two of the open items are very large stories, and the closed items were mostly small tasks. What is the core flaw in the team's report?
choices: The team used a WIQL query, which cannot measure closed items accurately
The area path should have been set to the team's name instead of the sprint name
The team should have used a burndown instead of a cumulative flow diagram
The team counts items instead of effort, so one large story and one small task look equal
questions.why: The teaching text names counting work items instead of effort as the common mistake, because it treats a large story and a small task as equal, which hides how much effort remains.

questions.prompt: Over three months, a bug-fix team wants to see whether bugs are building up in its Testing state while moving steadily through New and Active. Which chart best shows this?
choices: A velocity figure averaged over the last two iterations
A count of Closed bugs from one WIQL query run today
A cumulative flow diagram, where a widening band in one state means work is piling up there
A burndown for the current iteration only
questions.why: The teaching text says a cumulative flow diagram stacks the count of items in each state over time, and a widening band shows work piling up in one state, which is the pattern the team is asking about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would choose between a burndown and a cumulative flow diagram for reviewing a team's sprint, and name one limit of the measure you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a burndown when the question is whether the team will finish the sprint, because it compares remaining effort with an ideal line for each day of the iteration. I would use a cumulative flow diagram when the question is where work is getting stuck, because it shows how many items sit in each state over time, and a widening band means a bottleneck. The burndown has a real limit: it only tracks effort that someone has estimated and updated. If items are added mid-sprint without new estimates, or left with stale remaining values, the line looks healthier than the team really is. So before trusting either chart, I check the query scope and whether the estimates have been kept current.
rubricPoints: Burndown measures remaining effort against an ideal line for a single iteration.
Cumulative flow shows work count per state over time and reveals bottlenecks.
Choice of metric follows the planning question being asked.
Any metric is limited by scope and by how current the estimates are.

suggested.rationale: The objective is mainly catalogue knowledge of which Boards charts and WIQL query fields apply, and no listed mission or planned engine makes the learner build planning queries.

lessons.plain: A development metric is a number calculated from recorded events, such as how long a change waits for review or how often builds pass. A query is a saved question that selects which items or events count, such as every open bug in one area that has not been touched for two weeks. Designing metrics and queries means choosing the right question first, then picking the field, filter, and chart that answers it honestly. Done well, the numbers guide decisions. Done badly, they reward the wrong behaviour. This lesson shows how to match a requirement to a specific measure and where that measure comes from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to know whether code reviews are slowing them down. Without any further teaching, what is one specific thing you would measure, and where would the start and end of that measurement come from?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number calculated from recorded events, and a query is the saved filter that decides which items or events are included. Work-tracking tools such as Azure Boards and GitHub Projects store each item with fields (state, assignee, area, and any custom fields you add) and keep timestamps for changes. GitHub also records pull request events such as opened, review requested, approved, and merged, and build systems record when each run started and ended. Because this history is stored, you can ask timing questions afterwards, as long as you choose a start event and an end event. This works because most development metrics are subtraction over stored timestamps, grouped and filtered by a query. Worked example: the question is how long pull requests wait for a first review in one repository over the last 30 days. Step one: choose the start event, the pull request being marked ready for review. Step two: choose the end event, the first review being submitted. Step three: subtract to get hours for each pull request. Step four: filter to that repository and to pull requests closed in the last 30 days. Step five: report the median rather than the average, because a few very old pull requests distort an average. Common mistake: measuring what is easy to count, such as commits per developer, instead of what the question actually asks. The consequence in a running team is that people split work into tiny commits to look busy, the chart rises, and real delivery slows. A good metric is tied to a decision the team will make from it.

questions.prompt: A retail app team wants to know how long bugs stay blocked before someone clears them. Bugs in the Payments area path get the tag Blocked when work stops and the tag is removed when work resumes. The team has these steps. Step one: query work items in the Payments area path that carried the Blocked tag at any point in the last 90 days. Step two: for each item, take the timestamp when the Blocked tag was added and the timestamp when it was removed. Step three: subtract the two timestamps to get the blocked time in hours. Step four: filter to items whose Blocked tag was added in the last 90 days. Step five is missing. Some items are still Blocked today, so they have a start timestamp but no end timestamp. What should the team do with those items in the blocked-time calculation?
choices: Average them together with the finished items as if they had a duration
Use today's date as the end timestamp so they count toward the median like the others
Leave them out of the duration calculation and report their count separately
Set their blocked time to zero so they do not raise the median
questions.why: An item still Blocked has no end event, so no duration can be subtracted for it, and it should be excluded from the duration statistic and counted on its own; using today's date, zero, or a mixed average would misstate how long finished waits took.

questions.prompt: In this course, what is a metric?
choices: A saved filter that decides which work items appear on a board
A rule that blocks a pull request from merging until a review is submitted
A number calculated from recorded events, such as timestamps of changes
A list of every field stored on a work item, such as state and assignee
questions.why: The teaching text defines a metric as a number calculated from recorded events, while a query is the saved filter that selects which items or events are included.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether reviewers respond quickly to pull requests that are ready for review. A manager suggests counting how many approvals each reviewer gives per week. Why is this a poor choice for the question being asked?
choices: It is impossible to count approvals in GitHub because approval events are not stored
Weekly counts always produce an average that hides outliers, which is the only problem
It is fine because any count of review events is a valid response time
It measures how much reviewers act, not how long pull requests wait, so it cannot answer the speed question and can be gamed
questions.why: The question is about waiting time, which needs a start event such as review requested and an end event such as the first review submitted, and an approval count does not measure that interval.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know how long their build runs take on the main branch over the last two weeks. Which approach fits the question?
choices: Count the number of builds that ran on any branch in the last two weeks
Report the number of work items closed during the two weeks
Average the number of commits per developer on the main branch
For each build on main from the last two weeks, subtract the run start time from the run end time, then report the median
questions.why: Build systems store when each run started and ended, so the duration is a subtraction over those timestamps, filtered to the branch and time window, with a median to limit distortion from a few very long runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would build a metric and query to answer the question how long does a bug stay open, and name one limit or tradeoff of the measure you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by defining the start and end events precisely. The start would be when the bug item moves to an active state, and the end would be when it moves to closed or resolved, using the state history that the tracker keeps. I would subtract the two timestamps for each closed bug and filter the query to bugs closed in the last 30 days within the product area we care about. I would report the median and the spread, not just the average, so a few very old bugs do not hide the typical case. The main limit is that the measure depends on how consistently people move items between states. If some people leave bugs active after fixing them, the number looks worse than the real fix time, so I would note that in the report before the team draws conclusions from it.
rubricPoints: Defines a specific start event and end event from stored history
Describes the query filter that limits the scope and time window
Explains why a median or spread is safer than a plain average
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as inconsistent state changes

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises choosing metrics and queries, so the core skill is naming the right measure and explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Testing metrics are numbers that tell a team how well its automated checks are doing: how many tests pass, how long they take, how much of the code they exercise, and how often the same test flips between passing and failing for no clear reason. A query is a question you ask the stored records, such as 'show me every failed test run from the last two weeks on the main branch.' Designing these means deciding which numbers matter, where the raw test results are kept, and how to ask for them so the answer is trustworthy enough to act on, not just pretty to look at.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's pipeline shows 98% of tests passing, yet customers keep reporting the same bug in the checkout flow. Name one test metric that would have revealed the gap, and say why the pass rate alone hides it.
lessons.teach:
A test run is one execution of a set of automated tests, usually triggered by a pipeline. The pass rate is the number of passing tests divided by the total in the run, shown as a percentage. Code coverage is the share of code lines or branches that the tests actually execute. A flaky test is a test that gives different results on the same code with no change, often because it depends on timing, shared data, or the order tests run in. A query is a stored question you ask the system that keeps test results, filtering and counting them. Azure DevOps keeps test results where its Analytics service can query them, and GitHub Actions keeps workflow run history you can filter the same way.

Why it works: a pass rate only counts tests that exist, so it cannot show what is missing. Coverage shows which code runs during tests, not whether the tests check anything useful. Flakiness shows up only when you compare results over time for the same code, which is why a query over history matters more than a single run.

Worked example: a main-branch pipeline runs 500 tests and 490 pass, so the pass rate is 98%. Step 1: filter the stored results to the main branch over the last 14 days. Step 2: group the failed results by test name. Step 3: for each test that failed, check whether the same commit also has a passing result from a rerun. Step 4: a test with both outcomes on one commit is a flaky candidate. Here, 4 of the 10 failures are flaky, so the real red count is 6.

Common mistake: treating a rerun pass as a clean pass. Reruns hide flakiness from the pass rate, so the number looks healthy while the team quietly learns to rerun until the build turns green.

Consequence: when a red build is routinely dismissed as flaky, a genuine regression can ship under the same red signal nobody reads. Good testing metrics make flakiness a visible number, so the team can fix or quarantine those tests on purpose.

questions.prompt: Northwind Parcels runs tests for its label service on a release branch called release/2.4, using GitHub Actions to run them. Over the last 7 days the stored results show 300 tests run and 288 pass, so the pass rate is 96 percent. Step 1: filter the stored results to release/2.4 over the last 7 days. Step 2: group the 12 failed results by test name. ship_label_retry failed 4 times, addr_validate failed 3 times, and the other 5 failures are spread across three tests with no repeating pattern. Step 3: every failing result for ship_label_retry has a passing rerun on the same commit, so it is a flaky candidate. The other failing tests never have a passing result on the same commit. Step 4 is left for you: state the number of genuine failures the team should count as real red.
questions.why: The 4 flaky candidate failures are set aside, which leaves 12 minus 4, or 8, genuine failures.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a flaky test?
choices: A test that executes no lines of the code under test
A test whose pass rate falls below 50 percent across all runs
A test that gives different results on the same code with no change to that code
A test that fails on every commit because its code is broken
questions.why: The teaching text defines flakiness as different results on the same code with no change, often caused by timing, shared data, or test order.

questions.prompt: A pipeline run includes 1,050 tests, and 1,029 of them pass. What is the pass rate for this run?
choices: 2.0 percent
98.0 percent
97.0 percent
99.0 percent
questions.why: The pass rate is passing tests divided by total tests, so 1,029 divided by 1,050 is 0.98, which is 98.0 percent.

questions.prompt: A team reruns failing tests until they pass, then reports the pass rate from the final run only. What is the main problem with this practice?
choices: The pass rate ignores tests that exist in the suite, so it can never show missing tests
A pass rate cannot be calculated at all once reruns are used
Coverage is being measured on the wrong branch, so the pass rate is inflated
Reruns that pass are treated as clean passes, which hides flaky tests from the pass rate
questions.why: A rerun pass counted as a clean pass hides flakiness, so the number looks healthy while the team learns to rerun until the build turns green.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a team should track a flaky-test count alongside the pass rate, and name one limit of the flaky-test measure.
lessons.modelAnswer: Pass rate tells you how many tests succeeded in one run, but it hides two things: tests that were never written, and tests that fail sometimes for no code reason. A flaky-test count, found by comparing pass and fail results for the same commit over time, makes the second problem visible. If we only watch pass rate, a team can rerun a red build until it goes green and never notice the signal is unreliable. One limit: the flaky measure only finds tests that flipped during the window we query. A test that always fails, or a bug no test covers, will not appear as flaky at all, so we still need coverage data and a review of which behaviours are actually tested. The measure is also only as good as the stored history, so if reruns are not recorded, flakiness stays invisible.
rubricPoints: Pass rate alone cannot show missing tests or unreliable tests.
Flakiness is found by comparing outcomes for the same code across time.
Reruns that pass should be recorded, not treated as clean passes.
A named limit: the flaky measure misses always-failing tests and untested behaviour.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes you diagnose a flaky test in CI, which is the exact pattern these metrics are meant to surface.

lessons.plain: Security metrics and queries are the way a team counts and filters its security problems so it can tell whether things are getting better or worse. Instead of saying 'we have some vulnerabilities', you can ask how many open high-severity findings each project has, how old the oldest one is, and how many were fixed this month. A query is a saved question that a tool runs against the team's records each time it is asked. A metric is a number produced from those records, such as a count or an average age. Choosing the right question matters: a total that only grows tells you little, while a count of overdue items tells you what to do next.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team reports 'we found 300 security alerts this year'. Before learning anything else, what one extra number or filter would you want before deciding whether the team's security is improving?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number that summarises a group of records, such as the count of open items or the median age of open items. A query is the filter that selects which records a metric counts, written in the tool's own language. In Azure Boards, work items are selected with a query language called WIQL, and an Analytics view can chart them over time. GitHub's security features (code scanning, secret scanning and Dependabot) create alerts that you can filter by state, severity and repository, and read through the Security tab or the REST API. The underlying idea is generic: a security finding is an alert with a state (open, fixed, dismissed), a severity, and a date, and useful metrics combine those three fields.

Worked example. A team has 40 open alerts: 4 critical, 12 high and 24 medium. Step 1: filter to state equals open. Step 2: filter severity to critical or high, which leaves 16. Step 3: group those 16 by repository, say 10 in the payments repo and 6 in the portal repo. Step 4: compare with last week's count of 19. Now the team knows the high-risk backlog fell by three and where it sits.

Common mistake: counting every alert ever raised, including fixed and dismissed ones. The total looks alarming and never falls, so nobody trusts it. Count open items, and separately track how long items stay open.

Consequence: a dashboard that shows only new alerts can look green while a critical finding has been open for 90 days. A secret exposed in a repository stays usable for as long as it stays open, so age is part of the measure, not decoration.

A security metric is only useful when its query states exactly which records it counts and how old they are.

questions.prompt: A logistics company tracks security alerts across three GitHub repositories. Its metric is 'critical alerts that have been open for more than 30 days.' The query is built in four steps. Step 1: filter state equals open. Step 2: filter severity equals critical. Step 3 is missing from the query notes. Step 4: count the records that remain, which gives 3. Which step fills the gap at Step 3?
choices: Keep only alerts whose created date is more than 30 days before today, so that age is part of the measure.
Sort the alerts by severity from highest to lowest before counting.
Add fixed and dismissed critical alerts back in, so the total reflects every critical alert ever raised.
Group the remaining alerts by repository so the count can be split across the three repos.
questions.why: The metric is defined by open critical alerts older than 30 days, so the missing step must apply the age filter based on the created date, which the teaching text says is part of a useful security metric.

questions.prompt: Which query best matches a security metric that tracks the current exposure of a company's repositories?
choices: Count only alerts whose state is dismissed, because those were judged safe by a person.
Count alerts whose state is open, and record how many days each has been open.
Count every alert ever raised across all repositories since the tool was enabled, including fixed and dismissed ones.
Count the number of repositories that have any alert at all, regardless of its state or date.
questions.why: A useful security metric counts open items and includes their age, while counting all alerts ever raised or only dismissed ones does not show what is currently exposed.

questions.prompt: A dashboard for a retail company's security shows only alerts raised in the last seven days, and it looks green. Why can this dashboard still hide a serious risk?
choices: The dashboard cannot read severity, so it treats every alert as low risk.
Seven days is too short a window, so the dashboard must use a window of at least one year.
The dashboard counts dismissed alerts, which always inflate the number shown.
The dashboard ignores alerts that were raised earlier and are still open, so a critical finding can stay open for months without appearing.
questions.why: A metric that only counts new alerts drops older open items out of view, so a long-open critical finding is invisible even though it is still a live exposure.

questions.prompt: A payments team wants a metric showing how many high-severity secret-scanning alerts remain unresolved across its GitHub repositories. Which query is correct?
choices: Filter state equals fixed, filter severity equals high, and count the records.
Filter alert type equals code scanning only, since secret alerts are not security findings.
Filter severity equals high only, and count the records, since severity alone shows the risk.
Filter state equals open, filter severity equals high, and record the date each alert was raised so age can be measured.
questions.why: The metric needs the open state, the severity, and the raised date, which are the three fields the teaching text says a useful security metric combines.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which two or three security metrics you would put on a team dashboard for open vulnerabilities, and name one limit or tradeoff of the metric you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer:
I would show three things. First, the count of open critical and high alerts per repository, filtered by state, so the team sees the backlog that matters most. Second, the age of the oldest open critical alert, because a count alone hides a finding that has been ignored for months. Third, the number of alerts fixed in the last 30 days, so we can see whether the team is making progress rather than just being shown a big number.

The limit of the open-count metric is that severity labels come from the scanner and can be wrong, so a low-severity label might hide a real risk. Also, a team can make the count fall by dismissing alerts, which is why I would check dismissals separately. The metric shows a trend and a backlog, not whether the software is actually safe.
rubricPoints: Names a concrete filter such as state equals open combined with severity.
Includes age of open items, not only a raw count.
Separates fixed or dismissed items from open items.
States a limit, such as scanner severity labels being imperfect or dismissals hiding the count.

suggested.rationale: Choosing and defending which security metrics to show is a reasoning skill best practised by explaining the tradeoffs back, and no listed mission covers security metrics directly.

lessons.plain: Delivery metrics are a small set of numbers that show how well a team gets working changes into users' hands: how often they ship, how long a change takes from first commit to production, how often a release breaks something, and how long recovery takes. A metric query is the question you ask a tracking system to produce one of those numbers, such as 'list every bug closed this week that was fixed by a release'. Good metrics answer a decision someone needs to make. Weak ones get tracked only because they are easy to count. This lesson shows how to pick the numbers and write the questions that produce them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team wants to know whether it is getting faster at shipping. Name two numbers you would pull from the tracking system, and say what each one tells you that the other does not.
lessons.teach:
A delivery metric is a number that summarises how your change process behaves over time. A query is a request to a work-tracking system that filters items and counts or lists them, such as work items, builds or deployments. In Azure Boards, queries are written in WIQL, the Work Item Query Language, a SQL-like syntax for filtering work items by field values. Analytics views give a faster, reporting-oriented way to group the same data.

Four measures cover most delivery questions. Deployment frequency counts how often changes reach production. Lead time for changes is the elapsed time from a commit being made to that commit running in production. Change failure rate is the share of deployments that cause a problem needing a fix or rollback. Time to restore is how long it takes to recover from such a failure. Together these are often called the DORA metrics, after the research program that popularised them.

Why it works: each measure needs timestamps or counts that a tool records automatically. A metric that depends on people typing values into fields by hand drifts out of date.

Worked example. Step 1: a commit is made on Monday at 10:00. Step 2: it is merged and deployed to production on Wednesday at 14:00. Step 3: lead time for that change is 52 hours. Step 4: the team reports the median across all changes shipped in the sprint, so one unusually slow change does not dominate the figure.

Common mistake: averaging a team-level metric and treating it as an individual performance score, or counting deployments in a way that rewards many trivial releases.

Consequence: if deployment events are not recorded, frequency and lead time quietly fall to zero or go stale. The dashboard then looks healthy while nothing is actually shipping.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company tracks lead time for changes, which is the elapsed time from a commit being made to that commit running in production. Change X was committed on Tuesday at 09:00 and was running in production on Thursday at 11:00. Step 1: record the commit time, Tuesday 09:00. Step 2: record the production time, Thursday 11:00. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the team reports the median lead time across the five changes shipped this sprint, which were 4, 6, 50, 7 and 5 hours, so the reported median is 6 hours. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Subtract the commit time from the production time to get 50 hours.
Use the time the code review was approved as the start point instead of the commit.
Count how many deployments happened during the sprint, which is five.
Add the two timestamps together and divide by two to find the midpoint.
questions.why: Lead time is the elapsed time between the commit and the change running in production, so Step 3 must subtract the commit timestamp from the production timestamp, giving 50 hours.

questions.prompt: Which delivery measure is the share of deployments that cause a problem needing a fix or a rollback?
choices: Deployment frequency
Change failure rate
Lead time for changes
Time to restore
questions.why: Change failure rate is defined as the share of deployments that lead to a problem needing a fix or rollback, while the other three measure different things.

questions.prompt: A team made 40 production deployments in a month. Six of those deployments later needed a rollback. What is the change failure rate for that month?
choices: 40 deployments per month
15 percent, since 6 of 40 deployments failed
About 67 percent, from dividing 40 by 6
6 failures per month
questions.why: Change failure rate is the share of deployments that caused a problem, so 6 divided by 40 gives 15 percent; the other choices report a count or invert the division.

questions.prompt: A team's deployment frequency dashboard is fed by an automatic record of each production deployment. Last month someone turned off that recording step, and no new deployments were logged afterwards, yet the dashboard keeps showing values from before the change. What is the most accurate description of the situation?
choices: The figures have gone stale, and the dashboard hides that nothing is being recorded or shipped.
The figures are correct because the dashboard shows the most recent full month of work.
The figures will rise over time as the team catches up on unlogged deployments automatically.
The figures show that the team is shipping more often, because the same numbers are being repeated.
questions.why: Because deployment events are no longer recorded, the metric does not update and goes stale, so the dashboard can look healthy while nothing is actually reaching production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why you would track median lead time and change failure rate together rather than either one alone. Name one limit or tradeoff of using the pair.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lead time alone shows how quickly changes travel, but a team can shrink it by shipping risky changes faster, so it can look good while quality collapses. Change failure rate alone shows how often releases break, but a team can drive it to zero by releasing rarely in large batches. Read together, they show speed and safety moving in the same direction. I would use the median rather than the mean for lead time so one stuck change does not distort it, and I would define a failure precisely in advance, such as a deployment followed by a rollback or hotfix within a set window, so the number means the same thing each sprint. The tradeoff is that both depend on how reliably deployments and fixes are recorded, so the numbers are only as honest as the tracking data behind them.
rubricPoints: Lead time and change failure rate guard against each other: speed without safety, or safety bought with rare releases.
The median is preferred for lead time because a few outliers distort the mean.
A failure needs a precise, agreed definition, such as a rollback or hotfix within a set window.
Both metrics depend on accurate recording of deployments and fixes, so data quality limits them.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which delivery metric answers which question is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, which a multi-step exam-style situation adds the most to.

lessons.plain: An operations metric is a number you measure repeatedly to see how a running service is doing, such as how many requests failed in the last hour or how long it took to restore service after an outage. A query is a question you ask of stored records or measurements: it picks out only the rows that match your conditions, then counts, sums or averages them. Together they answer questions like is the service getting worse, and did our last change help? Good metrics are chosen before a problem happens, so you can tell real trouble apart from normal noise.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team wants to know whether the service has become less reliable since last month. Before reading anything, name two numbers you would measure and say what each one would tell you.
lessons.teach: A metric is a named number recorded over time, such as failed requests per minute or minutes from incident opened to service restored. A query is a filter plus a calculation applied to stored records: it selects the rows that match conditions, such as incidents with severity 1 opened this month, and then counts, sums or averages them. Work-tracking tools such as Azure Boards use a query language called WIQL (Work Item Query Language) to filter tickets, and log platforms such as Azure Monitor Log Analytics use KQL (Kusto Query Language) to filter and aggregate telemetry. The ideas transfer across tools: choose the records, choose the time window, choose the calculation. A single number means little on its own, but the same number measured over fixed windows shows direction. A ratio such as failed divided by total stays meaningful when traffic doubles, while a raw count does not. Worked example: in one five-minute window the service handled 1,000 requests and 25 returned errors. Step 1, select the requests in that window. Step 2, count the errors: 25. Step 3, divide: 25 divided by 1,000 gives 0.025. Step 4, report a 2.5 percent error rate. Repeat for each window and you have a trend line. Common mistake: averaging per-window percentages instead of recomputing from the totals. Five windows at 0 percent and one at 10 percent average to about 1.7 percent, but total errors over total requests can differ sharply when windows carry different traffic. Another mistake is including still-open incidents in a recovery-time figure, which skews the result. Consequence: an alert built on a raw error count fires every busy afternoon, so on-call engineers learn to ignore it, while a ratio over a sensible window makes the alert trustworthy. A metric is only as useful as the definition behind it, so write that definition down before you build the dashboard.

questions.prompt: A parcel-sorting team counts failed barcode scans in two shifts. Each shift is a fixed window. Step 1: select the scans in each shift. Shift A had 4,800 scans. Shift B had 2,200 scans. Step 2: count the failed scans in each shift. Shift A had 96 failures and Shift B had 66. Step 3: divide failures by scans for each shift. Shift A gives 2.0 percent and Shift B gives 3.0 percent. Step 4 is missing. Step 4 is to combine the two shifts into one rate for the whole day. What should Step 4 be?
choices: Keep the larger shift rate as the daily figure, which is 3.0 percent.
Add the two percentages together, which gives 5.0 percent for the day.
Average the two shift percentages: (2.0 + 3.0) / 2 = 2.5 percent for the day.
Add the failures and the scans across both shifts first: 162 failures over 7,000 scans, about 2.3 percent for the day.
questions.why: A combined ratio must be recomputed from the summed totals, because the shifts carry different volumes and averaging their percentages gives the wrong answer.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, why is a ratio such as failed divided by total usually a better alert signal than a raw count of failures?
choices: Because a ratio stays comparable when traffic changes, while a raw count rises simply with busier periods.
Because a ratio is always smaller than a count, so alerts fire less often.
Because a ratio removes the need to choose a time window.
Because raw counts cannot be stored in a log platform.
questions.why: A ratio normalises the failures against the traffic, so it still means the same thing when volume doubles, whereas a raw count mostly tracks how busy the system is.

questions.prompt: A team measures mean time to restore for incidents in a given month. Incident 1 was opened at 09:00 and restored at 09:40. Incident 2 was opened at 14:10 and restored at 14:55. Incident 3 was opened at 16:30 and is still open. Which set should go into the recovery-time figure, and why?
choices: All three incidents, because every opened incident is a recovery event.
Incidents 1 and 2 only, because incident 3 has no restore time yet and including it would distort the figure.
Only Incident 3, because it is the most recent problem.
Incidents 1 and 2 plus incident 3 measured up to the current time, to keep the number fresh.
questions.why: Recovery time needs a restore moment, so an incident that is still open has no value to compute and must be left out of the figure.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows a daily error rate for each of five days, and the first four days each had 0 percent, while the fifth day had 10 percent. Someone reports the week's rate by averaging the five daily percentages. What is the problem with that approach?
choices: The average can differ sharply from the true rate because the days may carry different traffic, so the weekly rate should be total errors over total requests.
Percentages cannot be averaged at all, so the team should discard the weekly figure.
The average of percentages ignores the rule that rates must be shown to one decimal place.
Averaging percentages is always correct when the days are the same length.
questions.why: Each day's percentage is weighted equally in an average, but the true weekly rate weights each day by its traffic, so the correct method recomputes from the summed totals.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would define a metric and a query that show whether operations are getting healthier after a release. Name one limit or tradeoff of the measure you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a question, not a tool: did the release make the service more reliable? I would pick an error rate, failed requests divided by total requests, measured in fixed windows of five minutes, and filter the query to the service and environment that changed. I would compare the windows before and after the release using the same definition, so the comparison is fair. The limit is that a ratio hides volume: a 1 percent error rate at three requests an hour looks the same as at three million, so I would show the request count beside it. I would also keep the definition written down so nobody later changes what counts as a failure and quietly shifts the trend.
rubricPoints: States a clear question the metric should answer before choosing a measure
Defines the metric precisely, including the numerator, denominator and time window
Explains that a ratio is preferred over a raw count when traffic changes
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen measure

suggested.rationale: The planned metric alarm builder would have the learner set thresholds and windows on operational metrics, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: A project wiki is a set of linked pages that explains how a team works: what the system does, who owns what, and how work moves from idea to production. Markdown is a plain-text way to write those pages, using simple symbols for headings, bullet lists and links, so the text stays readable even before it is rendered. Mermaid is a text language for drawing diagrams such as flowcharts and sequence diagrams. You describe the boxes and arrows in words, and the wiki draws them. Because both are plain text, the documentation can be stored in version control and reviewed like code.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted a team to see the steps of a release at a glance and keep that picture current, would you rather store a screenshot from a drawing tool or a short text description that the wiki turns into a picture? Explain which one stays accurate longer when someone changes the process.
lessons.teach: A wiki is a collection of linked pages edited in a browser, and a project wiki is one attached to a team project or repository. Markdown is a lightweight markup language: a line starting with hash signs is a heading, a line starting with a dash is a bullet, and text in square brackets followed by a URL in parentheses is a link.
