Mermaid is a diagram language in which you write nodes (the boxes, named in square brackets or braces) and edges (the arrows, written with two dashes and a greater-than sign). You place the Mermaid text inside a fenced block labelled mermaid, and the wiki renderer draws the diagram whenever the page is viewed. This works because the text is the source of truth: the picture is regenerated from the description each time, so it cannot drift away from the process the way a screenshot does. Worked example: the text 'flowchart LR; Commit[Commit] --> Build[Build]; Build --> Test{Tests pass?}; Test -->|yes| Deploy[Deploy]; Test -->|no| Fix[Fix code]' has one flowchart keyword that sets a left-to-right layout, then three plain edges running from Commit to Build to Test, then two labelled edges leaving the decision node Test. Read step by step, a commit starts a build, the build feeds the test decision, and the decision branches to deploy on yes or to a fix on no. Common mistake: putting a special character such as a parenthesis, colon or quote inside an unquoted label, which breaks parsing; the page then shows an error message where the picture should be, and readers see a broken document. Also, in an Azure DevOps project wiki each page is stored as a Markdown file in a Git repository, so two people editing the same page can create a merge conflict, just as they would with code. Keep each diagram small enough to read on a laptop screen, and split large processes into several linked diagrams.

questions.prompt: A team documents its alert handling in a project wiki using Mermaid, a diagram language where you write boxes called nodes and arrows called edges. The Mermaid text is: flowchart LR; Alert[Alert fired] --> Triage{Severity high?}; Triage -->|yes| Page[Page on-call]; Triage -->|no| Backlog[Add to backlog]. Step 1: an alert fires and the trace starts at the Alert node. Step 2: the Triage node is a decision node that asks whether severity is high, and it splits into two labelled arrows. Step 3 is missing: a reader asks what happens to a low-severity alert, the arrow labelled no. Which completion of step 3 is correct?
choices: The Triage node is read again, looping until the severity label changes on its own.
The no arrow carries the alert to the Backlog node, where it is recorded as an item to handle later.
The layout flips from left to right into top to bottom, so the alert moves to a new node.
The Page node runs, because every alert pages someone regardless of severity.
questions.why: The arrow labelled no leads to the Backlog node, so a low-severity alert is recorded for later handling rather than paged.

questions.prompt: A team's process diagram is kept in a wiki as Mermaid text rather than as a screenshot. Why does the diagram stay accurate when the process changes?
choices: Mermaid draws the picture from the text each time the page is viewed, so editing the text changes the picture.
Mermaid text is compressed into the page, so the picture is saved permanently and cannot change.
The wiki stores a photo of the diagram and refreshes it nightly from the build server.
The renderer checks the diagram against the live pipeline and only then draws it, which makes it slower.
questions.why: Because the text is the source and the picture is regenerated from it on every view, updating the text updates the diagram.

questions.prompt: Two engineers edit the same page in an Azure DevOps project wiki at the same time, and the second save reports a conflict. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Each wiki page is a Markdown file in a Git repository, so overlapping edits to the same lines must be resolved, as with code.
The wiki is locked to one editor at a time, so the second edit is refused outright.
Wiki pages cannot contain Markdown headings, so the parser discards the second engineer's edit.
The browser cached the older page, so the second editor saw stale text and the renderer rejected it.
questions.why: Project wiki pages are stored as files in Git, so two people changing the same lines create a merge conflict that someone must resolve.

questions.prompt: A team has a process diagram with 25 nodes that wraps badly on a laptop screen and is hard to read. Which change best fits the guidance for wiki diagrams?
choices: Wrap the whole Mermaid text in a quoted block so the renderer scales it to fit.
Split the process into several smaller diagrams and link them to each other from the wiki.
Shrink the font of the Mermaid text so all 25 nodes fit on one screen.
Replace the diagram with one long bulleted list so that nothing needs to be drawn.
questions.why: Keeping each diagram small enough to read on a laptop and splitting large processes into linked diagrams is the recommended fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: A new teammate asks why we keep our process diagrams as Mermaid text in the repository instead of exporting them as images. Explain it to them in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of the text approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main reason is that the Mermaid text is the source, so the diagram is redrawn from the description every time the page is viewed. If the release process changes, someone edits a few lines in a pull request, the change is reviewed like any other code change, and the picture updates with it. An exported image has no link to the process it describes, so it quietly goes stale and nobody knows which copy is correct. The tradeoff is that complex diagrams are harder to lay out precisely in text, and a single unquoted special character can break rendering, so the page shows an error until someone fixes the syntax. For very detailed artwork, a drawing tool may still be the better choice, but for a process that changes often, text wins.
rubricPoints: Explains that the text is the source of truth, so the diagram stays in sync with the process
Connects keeping the text in version control to review, history and merge conflicts
Names a real limit, such as hard-to-control layout or a syntax error breaking the render
Notes that exported images go stale and do not show which copy is current

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly syntax, product features and page setup, which a reference read covers better than any listed mission.

lessons.plain: Release documentation is the written record that goes with a software release: what changed, what people need to know before using it, and how other programs call the new version. Release notes are the human-readable summary of changes, written for users and support staff. API documentation describes the doors other software uses to talk to your system: which requests are allowed, what they must contain, and what comes back. The core idea is that these documents should be produced from the work already recorded in your tools, so they stay accurate instead of being rebuilt from memory the night before a launch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team ships twelve pull requests in one release, and customers ask what changed. Where should the list come from, and what could go wrong if someone writes it by hand a week after shipping?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A release note is a short list, written for people who use the product, of what changed in a version. A changelog is a longer, developer-facing history of changes. An API (application programming interface) is the set of requests a program accepts from other programs, and API documentation describes those requests. OpenAPI is a common plain-text format for describing an API, so tools can read it and generate a reference page. A pull request is a proposed code change that someone reviews before it is merged. A label is a tag attached to a pull request or issue, such as 'bug' or 'breaking-change'.

Why it works: every change should already carry a link to its work item and a category. If the release process collects those links when a release is cut, the release notes become a query over recorded facts rather than a memory exercise. GitHub can draft release notes from merged pull requests and group them by label, configured in a file in the repository. Azure DevOps can link work items to builds and releases, so you can see which items shipped in a given version.

Worked example: release v2.4.0 contains three merged pull requests. PR 101 is labelled 'feature' and links work item 882. PR 104 is labelled 'bug' and links 877. PR 107 is labelled 'breaking-change' and links 890. Step 1: the release is cut from the main branch. Step 2: the tooling collects merged pull requests since v2.3.0. Step 3: it groups them by label into Features, Fixes and Breaking changes. Step 4: the breaking-change entry is placed first, noting that a request field has been renamed. Step 5: a person reviews the draft before it is published.

Common mistake: writing the notes by hand from memory after shipping, which omits changes and misstates behaviour. Consequence: support staff who trust an incomplete note may tell a customer that a breaking change is absent, and their integrations fail after the upgrade.

Release documentation is only as accurate as the links and labels behind it, so tagging changes consistently is part of the documentation work.

questions.prompt: A hotel-booking API team cuts release v2.0.0 from its main branch. Their tooling collects the merged pull requests since v1.9.0. PR 12 is labelled 'breaking-change' and links work item 455. PR 15 is labelled 'feature' but links no work item. PR 19 is labelled 'bug' and links work item 460. The tooling groups the changes by label and places the breaking-change entry first. Step 4 is missing from this trace: before the draft is published, ___. Then the notes are published to the release page.
choices: the release is tagged a second time from a feature branch so the version number changes
a person reviews the draft, and the missing work item link on PR 15 is flagged for fixing before the notes are trusted
the team rewrites each entry from memory so the wording reads more smoothly
the draft is sent to support staff, who decide which changes belong in the notes
questions.why: The draft is only as accurate as the links and labels behind it, so a human reviews it before publishing, and the unlinked PR 15 is exactly the kind of gap that review should catch.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates a release note from a changelog?
choices: A release note is a short user-facing list of what changed in a version; a changelog is a longer, developer-facing history of changes.
A release note and a changelog are the same document, with the only difference being the file name they are stored under.
A release note is the full commit history of a branch, and a changelog is a summary written for customers after launch.
A release note is a machine-readable API description, and a changelog is a list of pull request labels.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a release note as a short list for product users and a changelog as a longer developer-facing history, so the correct choice states that split.

questions.prompt: A team writes its release notes by hand a week after shipping, working from memory. Which outcome is the main risk the teaching text warns about?
choices: Pull requests get merged without a reviewer, because the notes were not written at merge time.
Changes are omitted or misstated, so support may wrongly tell a customer that a breaking change is absent and integrations then fail.
The notes are published more slowly, but the content stays complete and accurate.
The API documentation is regenerated automatically and the reference page becomes unreadable.
questions.why: The common mistake named in the teaching text is writing notes from memory, which omits changes and misstates behaviour, and the consequence is failed customer integrations after an upgrade.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know which work items were included in version 4.0.0 of a service that it deploys through Azure DevOps. Which approach fits the way the teaching text describes linking work to releases?
choices: Use the work items linked to the builds and releases for version 4.0.0, since Azure DevOps records which items shipped in that version.
Search all work items created during the last sprint and assume those are the ones in version 4.0.0.
Read the commit messages on the main branch from the last month and copy any ticket numbers mentioned.
Ask each developer to list, from memory, the tasks they closed while version 4.0.0 was in progress.
questions.why: Azure DevOps can link work items to builds and releases, so the recorded links answer which items shipped, while the other options rely on guesswork or memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should write release notes by hand at the end of each sprint and skip any tooling. Explain how you would produce release notes and API documentation for a release, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would make the release notes come from the work we already record. Every pull request gets a label such as feature, bug or breaking-change, and links to its work item. When we cut the release, the pipeline or the platform's release-notes feature collects the merged pull requests since the last tag and groups them by label. A person then reviews the draft, adds plain-language context for anything users must act on, and publishes it. For API documentation, I would keep an OpenAPI description in the repository, updated in the same pull request as the code change, and generate the reference page from it at release time. The main tradeoff is that this only works if people label changes consistently. A missing or wrong label puts an entry in the wrong section, so the review step is not optional. Tooling also cannot explain why a change matters, so a human still writes the summary of breaking changes.
rubricPoints: Release notes are generated from recorded links and labels, not from memory.
A person reviews the draft before publishing, especially for breaking changes.
API documentation is kept in the repository and updated with the code change.
A named limit: output is only as accurate as the labelling discipline and still needs human explanation.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises writing release notes or API docs, and explaining the labelling-to-notes chain back is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Every time a team ships a new version, someone has to write down what changed. Git keeps a history of every change, with a short message attached to each one. Automating documentation from Git history means letting a script or pipeline read that history and produce the change list for you, such as release notes or a changelog file. The result is more accurate than memory and comes out the same way every time. The output is only as good as the messages and links people leave when they commit, so those habits matter as much as the tool.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a team wants release notes for version 2.0 without anyone typing them by hand, what information would a program need to read, and where would it find that information?
lessons.teach:
Git is a version control system: it stores a history of snapshots of a project, and each snapshot, called a commit, carries an author, a timestamp, and a message. A tag is a fixed name pointing at one commit, such as v1.3.0, often used to mark a release. A range is the set of commits between two points, for example from the previous tag up to the current branch tip. Automated documentation reads a range and turns each commit into a line of text.

Why it works: the history already records what changed, and a message written at commit time is fresher than anything written later from memory. A tool only needs a rule for sorting lines into sections. A common rule is a message prefix such as feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, or docs for documentation. Another is a link: a commit can reference an Azure Boards work item with a token like AB# followed by the item ID, so the change list points back to the request that caused it. Pull request labels can do the same job when squash merging hides individual commit messages.

Worked example. The last tag is v1.3.0. A pipeline reads the range v1.3.0..HEAD and gets three commits: 'feat(api): add positions endpoint AB#812', 'fix(auth): refresh expired token AB#830', and 'docs: correct install steps'. Step 1: the script reads each line. Step 2: it matches the prefix to a section, so the first goes under Features, the second under Fixes, the third under Documentation. Step 3: it extracts AB#812 and AB#830 and writes them as links. Step 4: it saves the result as a file and attaches it to the release.

Common mistake: squash-merging a pull request with a vague title such as 'updates' produces a commit the rules cannot classify, so a security fix can silently disappear from the notes. The fix is to enforce a title convention on pull requests before merge.

Consequence: a published release with missing notes leaves operators unaware that a fix is present, and a wrong link sends people to the wrong work item.

questions.prompt: A team at a different company marks its last release with the tag v2.0.0. Their pipeline reads the range v2.0.0..HEAD and gets two commits: 'fix(billing): round tax per line AB#455' and 'feat(reports): export to CSV AB#461'. Step 1: the script reads each line. Step 2: it matches the prefix fix to the Fixes section and the prefix feat to the Features section. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: it saves the result as a file and attaches it to the release. Which action belongs in the missing step 3?
choices: It squash-merges the two commits into one so that the work item links are no longer needed.
It extracts AB#455 and AB#461 and writes them as links back to those work items.
It reads the range again starting from the very first commit in the repository's history.
It creates a new tag v2.0.0 on the HEAD commit before writing the file.
questions.why: Step 3 is the link step: the script pulls out each AB# ID and writes it as a link, so every note points back to the work item that caused the change, as the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A team's most recent release is marked with the tag v0.9.4. Which commit does that tag refer to?
choices: The newest commit on the main branch at the moment the notes script happens to run.
The commit of whichever author last changed the release notes file.
Every commit made since the previous release, because a tag marks the whole span of work.
Exactly one fixed commit, the one the tag was placed on, which does not move when new commits arrive.
questions.why: A tag is a fixed name pointing at a single commit, so it identifies one snapshot rather than a moving branch tip or a set of commits.

questions.prompt: A pipeline reads the range v3.1.0..HEAD. A developer squash-merged a pull request titled 'misc' that contained an important security fix. What is the most likely result in the generated release notes?
choices: The pipeline stops with an error because a squash-merged commit makes the range v3.1.0..HEAD invalid and cannot be read.
The security fix appears under Documentation, because any commit without a recognised prefix is filed there by default in every tool.
The fix may be missing from the notes entirely, because the title 'misc' gives the classification rules no prefix to sort it by.
The release notes list the security fix under a Security section automatically, because squash merges keep every individual commit message intact.
questions.why: A vague squash-merge title produces a commit the rules cannot classify, so the change can silently drop out of the notes, which is why the teaching text recommends enforcing a title convention before merge.

questions.prompt: A team squash-merges every pull request, so only one commit per pull request remains in history. They want the generated notes to still sort each change by type and link it to its Azure Boards work item. Which approach fits this situation?
choices: Rely on the individual commit messages written inside each pull request, since they will still be readable after the merge.
Remove the Documentation section from the notes so that fewer commit messages need to be sorted by the rules.
Tag every commit with a version number so that the range read by the script becomes smaller and easier to classify.
Put the AB# work item token and a type label on the pull request itself, so the notes can read them from the merged change.
questions.why: Pull request labels and titles are kept when a squash merge hides the individual commits, so they can carry the type and the AB# link that the notes script needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how we would generate release notes from Git history instead of writing them by hand, and name one limit of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We would take the range from the previous release tag to the current head, read each commit or merged pull request title in that range, and group them by a prefix or label such as feature, fix, or docs. Work item references like AB# followed by an ID would become links back to Azure Boards so people can trace each change to its request. The output gets saved as a changelog file and attached to the release. The main limit is that the notes are only as good as the input: vague commit messages or squash merges that lose the original titles produce notes that miss changes or group them wrongly. So we would enforce a title convention on pull requests and review the generated file before publishing rather than trusting it blindly.
rubricPoints: Notes are generated from a range of commits between two points, usually the previous release tag and the current head.
Grouping depends on a consistent convention such as message prefixes or pull request labels.
Work item references let each entry trace back to the request it came from.
Names a real limit: poor messages or squash merges can misclassify or drop changes.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which Git history source and convention feeds the notes is a situation to reason through, and no listed mission covers it.

lessons.plain: A webhook is a way for one online service to tell another service that something happened, by sending a short message to a web address you choose. Instead of your tool asking 'anything new yet?' over and over, the source pushes a notification the moment a change occurs. Think of a shop bell on the door: the shop does not need you to keep checking, it rings when someone walks in. In DevOps, a work item being moved to Done or a code push to a repository can trigger a message that posts to a chat channel, updates a dashboard, or starts another process. The receiving end must be ready to accept these messages, check that they really came from the sender, and cope when the same message arrives twice.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bug work item is marked Resolved in your tracking tool, and your team wants a chat message within seconds. Would you rather have a script ask the tool every minute whether anything changed, or have the tool call your receiving address when the change happens? Explain your choice in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A webhook is an HTTP callback. HTTP is the request and response protocol the web runs on. When a chosen event happens in a source system, that system sends an HTTP POST request to a URL you registered, and the request body is JSON, a plain text format for structured data, describing what happened. The setting that links one event type, such as a work item being updated or a pull request being completed, to one target URL is called a subscription. Azure DevOps calls these service hooks. A subscription can be filtered, for example by project, branch, or field value.

Why it works: polling means your tool repeatedly asks for changes, which wastes requests and adds delay. A webhook reverses the direction. The source calls you only when there is something to report, so the delay is usually a few seconds. The receiver must answer quickly with a success status such as 200. If it does not, the sender treats the delivery as failed and may retry it.

Worked example. A team wants a chat post whenever a Bug work item moves to Resolved. Step 1: create a subscription for the work item updated event, filtered to type Bug and state Resolved. Step 2: point it at the receiving URL of a small service. Step 3: a developer resolves bug 412, and the service sends a POST with a JSON body naming the event, the work item id, and the new state. Step 4: the receiver checks the shared secret or signature, reads the id, posts to the chat channel, and returns 200.

Common mistake: assuming each event arrives exactly once and in order. Retries can deliver duplicates, and deliveries can arrive out of order, so the receiver should use the event or resource id and version to ignore repeats.

Consequence in a running system: if the receiver is down or times out, deliveries fail, and retries are often limited. Events can then be lost unless you check the delivery history and replay them. A webhook is a notification, not a record of truth, so the source system stays the authority.

questions.prompt: Lumen Health's clinic team wants an on-call ticket created whenever an Incident work item in project Clinic-Ops moves to Active. Here is the flow. Step 1: create a subscription for the work item updated event, filtered to type Incident, state Active, and project Clinic-Ops. Step 2: point the subscription at the receiving URL of the ticketing service. Step 3: [MISSING]. Step 4: the receiver reads the work item id, creates the ticket, and returns 200. Which choice fills in the missing Step 3?
choices: The incident is closed, which stops the subscription from firing for that item.
The ticketing service polls Azure DevOps every five minutes for Incidents that have changed.
The subscription is edited to match all projects so that no Incident change is missed.
An engineer changes an Incident in Clinic-Ops to Active, and Azure DevOps sends a POST with a JSON body naming the event, the work item id, and the new state to the receiving URL.
questions.why: Step 3 is the moment the source system sends the HTTP POST with the JSON body, which is what Step 4's receiver then acts on, and only choice B describes that send.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a webhook and polling?
choices: With polling the source copies every record nightly, while a webhook keeps the receiver's copy permanently in sync.
Polling requires a subscription, while a webhook works without any registered URL.
With polling the receiver checks the source on a fixed timer, while a webhook has the source call the receiver's registered URL only when a chosen event occurs.
With polling the receiver deletes its own data, while a webhook asks the source to delete its data.
questions.why: A webhook is a push from the source to a registered URL when an event happens, whereas polling is the receiver repeatedly asking for changes.

questions.prompt: A payments receiver takes about 40 seconds to answer each webhook delivery, and the sender gives up after 30 seconds. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The sender counts the delivery as successful as soon as the request leaves, so no retry happens.
The sender deletes the subscription after one timeout so that the broken endpoint stops receiving events.
The event is saved in the source's own record as a backup, so the receiver never needs to handle it again.
The sender treats the delivery as failed and may retry it, so the receiver must be ready to handle a repeat of the same event.
questions.why: A slow or missing success response is treated as a failed delivery, which can trigger a retry, so repeats must be expected and handled by the receiver.

questions.prompt: A receiver gets two deliveries for work item 88 in Harbor Labs: revision 9 showing state Done, then revision 8 showing state Active, arriving after revision 9. Which action is correct?
choices: Apply both updates in arrival order, because each delivery is a complete copy of the item.
Ask the sender to resend every event in order before changing anything in the receiver.
Keep the update with the higher revision (9) and ignore the older revision 8 delivery.
Apply revision 8 last because it arrived later, so its state is the newest one.
questions.why: Deliveries can arrive out of order, so the receiver should use the resource id and version to decide which update is newer and ignore older ones.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a webhook differs from polling for a notification from Azure Boards to a chat channel, and name one limit or tradeoff you would design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: With polling, our receiver asks Azure Boards on a timer whether any bug changed, so it wastes calls and posts late. With a webhook, we create a service hook subscription for the work item updated event, filtered to bugs in the Resolved state, and Boards sends a JSON POST to our receiving URL when it happens. The main tradeoff is reliability. Our receiver must answer fast with a 2xx status, or deliveries fail and retries are limited, so events can be missed. It may also get the same event twice or out of order. So I would make the handler idempotent, using the work item id and revision to skip repeats, verify the shared secret, and check the delivery history in the service hook console to replay anything that failed.
rubricPoints: Webhook is an HTTP POST pushed by the source when an event occurs, instead of the receiver polling
A subscription links an event type and filters to a target URL
The receiver must respond quickly with success, or deliveries fail and may be retried
Duplicates and out-of-order delivery mean the receiver should be idempotent, and it should verify the sender
Delivery failures can lose events, so check delivery history and replay when needed

suggested.rationale: A planned messaging and events engine would let learners build the sender, receiver, retries and duplicate handling that this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Azure Boards is Microsoft's work-tracking tool, a place where a team keeps its tasks, bugs and user stories. Your code lives in GitHub, which is a separate place. Linking the two means that when someone writes code for a task, the task and the code point at each other. Anyone looking at the task can see which change was made for it, and anyone looking at the change can see which task it answers. This is a small setup step, but it lets a team answer questions like 'what shipped for this feature?' without digging through chat messages or memory.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a developer merges a change on GitHub that fixes bug number 412 on your team's board, how could someone reading that bug later find out which change fixed it, without asking anyone?
lessons.teach:
A work item is a single tracked thing on the board, such as a bug, task or user story, and each one has a numeric ID. A GitHub repository is the code store. It holds commits, which are saved changes each with a message, and pull requests, which are proposed changes reviewed before they merge into the main branch. The integration is a trust link between the two tools, set up through a GitHub app that Azure DevOps uses to read repository activity.

Why it works: the link is built from text. After the GitHub connection is set up for an Azure DevOps project and the chosen repositories are granted to it, Azure Boards watches for the token AB# followed by a work item number. When that token appears in a commit message, a pull request title, or a pull request description, Azure Boards records a link and shows it in the work item's Development section. The pull request or commit shows the linked work item in the other direction.

Worked example, step by step. First, a project admin opens the project settings, adds a GitHub connection, authorizes the Azure Boards app on the GitHub account, and grants it the repository shop-api. Second, a developer commits a fix with the message 'Fix null cart total AB#412'. Third, the developer opens a pull request titled 'Fix null cart total (AB#412)'. Fourth, Azure Boards records the link, so work item 412 lists the commit and the pull request, and the pull request points back to 412.

Common mistake: the repository was never granted to the connection, or the token is typed as AB 412 or #412 without the AB prefix. Nothing errors. The link is simply missing, so later traceability and release notes have quiet gaps. Check that the link appears on the work item rather than assuming it does.

In a running team, a missing link means a release can ship a fix whose ticket nobody can find when an incident is reviewed. A missing link does not fail loudly, so you verify it exists.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics has an Azure DevOps project whose GitHub connection already grants the repository dispatch-web. Step 1: a developer commits the message 'Retry failed route sync AB 3078' and pushes it. Step 2: the developer opens a pull request titled 'Retry failed route sync' with the description 'Fixes AB#3078'. Step 3: the team opens work item 3078 and sees the pull request in its Development section, but the commit is not listed. Step 4 is missing from this account: what must the team do so that the commit is also linked to work item 3078?
choices: Wait for Azure Boards to scan older commits overnight, since commit links are added in a batch.
Add the label 3078 to the commit in GitHub, since Azure Boards reads labels to build links.
Change the commit message so it contains AB#3078 (for example in a new commit that is pushed), because AB 3078 without the # is not the token Azure Boards watches for.
Ask a project admin to grant dispatch-web to the GitHub connection again, because the commit link must be re-authorised.
questions.why: Azure Boards only records a link when the exact token AB# followed by the number appears in a commit message, pull request title, or pull request description, and the commit's text 'AB 3078' lacks the #, while the repository is already granted (shown by the pull request link).

questions.prompt: In Azure Boards with a GitHub connection, what is the AB# token?
choices: A badge that GitHub displays next to a pull request once its checks pass.
A setting in the GitHub repository that marks which branch is protected from direct pushes.
A text pattern, the letters AB followed immediately by # and a work item number, that Azure Boards scans for in commit messages and pull request text to record a link.
A unique key that GitHub generates for each commit to prove the author's identity.
questions.why: The token is a text pattern that Azure Boards watches for in commit messages and pull request text, and it is the only thing that creates the link to the work item number.

questions.prompt: A bank's team stores its code in the GitHub repository ledger-core. The connection to Azure DevOps was set up, but the repository was never granted to it. A developer opens a pull request titled 'Tighten daily limits AB#88' that refers to bug work item 88. What happens?
choices: Azure Boards records the link on work item 88 immediately, because the token is correct.
No link is recorded and no error is shown, so work item 88 shows no pull request, and the gap goes unnoticed until someone checks.
The pull request fails its checks until the repository is granted, so the developer sees an error.
Azure Boards adds the pull request to work item 88 only after the next release is deployed.
questions.why: Azure Boards only reads activity from repositories granted to the connection, so an ungranted repository produces no link and no error, even when the token is typed correctly.

questions.prompt: A release manager for a mobile app team wants to confirm that a pull request in the repository mobile-app is linked to work item 2210. The pull request description reads 'Relates to #2210'. What should the release manager conclude?
choices: The link exists, because GitHub's own #2210 reference is shown in the Azure Boards Development section.
The link exists only if the work item is in the same sprint as the pull request.
The link will appear automatically after the pull request is merged into the main branch.
The link does not exist, because the text lacks the AB# token that Azure Boards watches for, so the manager should ask for the description to be changed and then check work item 2210 again.
questions.why: Azure Boards records links only from the AB# token, and a plain #2210 reference does not create a link, so the correct step is to fix the text and then verify the link on the work item.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a commit or pull request gets linked to an Azure Boards work item, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on that link.
lessons.modelAnswer: The link is created by text, not by a button on each commit. After the GitHub connection is set up for the Azure DevOps project and the repository is granted to it, any commit message, pull request title or pull request description that contains AB# followed by the work item number gets recorded against that work item. You can then see the commits and pull requests under the work item's Development section, and the pull request points back to the item. The tradeoff is that this depends on people typing the token correctly and on the repository being granted to the connection. A typo such as AB 412 creates no link and gives no error, so the traceability you assume is missing. Also, a link only shows that a change mentions the item. It does not prove the change was tested or deployed. So a team should check links during review and treat them as one part of traceability, not the whole.
rubricPoints: Names the connection: the GitHub connection set up for the Azure DevOps project, with the repository granted to it.
Names the mechanism: the AB# token followed by the work item number in commit messages or pull request text.
Explains where the link shows: the work item's Development section, with the pull request pointing back.
States a limit: text-based linking fails silently on typos or missing repository grants, and a link does not prove testing or deployment.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console setup steps and product facts, which reading covers better than any existing mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Microsoft Teams is a chat and meeting tool where teams talk. Connecting it to your code host or work tracker means that when something happens there, such as a build failing, a pull request opening, or a work item changing state, a short message appears in a chat channel. Think of it as a doorbell wired to a room: the event rings where people already are, so nobody has to keep refreshing a web page to find out what changed. Setup is a one-time permission grant plus a choice of which events go to which channel.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your team wants a chat message every time a build fails, what do you think has to be true before the chat tool can know about that failure at all?
lessons.teach:
A Teams integration is a trust link between a source system, either GitHub or Azure DevOps, and a Microsoft Teams channel. Four terms matter. An app is the packaged piece Teams installs, which knows how to talk to your source system. A channel is the place in Teams where messages land. An event is something that happens in the source, such as a pipeline run finishing, a pull request being opened, or a work item changing state. A subscription is a rule that says which events should be posted to which channel, often narrowed by repository, pipeline, or project area.

Why it works: the source system does the watching. Once a subscription exists, the source emits an event when a matching thing happens, and the Teams app posts a card into the channel. Nothing in Teams polls the source. This is also why a subscription that names the wrong repository stays silent without raising any error.

Worked example. A team wants failed runs of its payments pipeline posted to a payments channel. Step 1: install the Azure Pipelines app in Teams and sign in with an account that has access to the project. Step 2: in the channel, add a subscription for the pipeline-failed event, naming the project and the pipeline. Step 3: trigger a run that you know will fail. Step 4: confirm a card appears. If it does not, check the subscription's filter before anything else.

Common mistake: subscribing a busy channel to every event in a repository. The channel fills with noise, people mute it, and the one failure that matters gets lost. Subscribe only to events that someone is expected to act on.

Consequence: a missed failure notification can leave a broken main branch unnoticed for hours. The alert is only as useful as the subscription behind it, and the channel hears only what its subscriptions describe.

questions.prompt: A logistics team wants its GitHub repository inventory-api to post pull request openings into a Teams channel called logistics-review, but only for that one repository. Step 1: install the GitHub app in Teams and sign in with an account that can see inventory-api. Step 2: in logistics-review, add a subscription for the pull-request-opened event, narrowed to inventory-api. Step 3: ___ (missing). Step 4: confirm that a card for the pull request appears in logistics-review.
choices: Open a test pull request against inventory-api and check that a card appears in logistics-review
Ask the channel members to pin the GitHub app to the top of the channel
Delete the subscription and recreate it with no repository filter so every repository posts
Rename logistics-review to match the repository name before testing
questions.why: Step 3 is the trigger: you create a real pull request that matches the subscription so you can confirm the card arrives, and the other options either remove the narrowing or do not produce a matching event.

questions.prompt: In a Teams integration, which term refers to the rule that says which events should be posted to which channel, often narrowed by repository, pipeline, or project area?
choices: Channel
Event
Subscription
App
questions.why: A subscription is the rule that links events to a channel and can be narrowed by repository, pipeline, or project area, while the other terms name the installed package, the destination, and the happening itself.

questions.prompt: A subscription in a Teams integration names a repository that has been renamed, so it no longer matches anything. What is the most likely result?
choices: Every event from every repository is posted to the channel as a fallback
The channel stays silent and no error is raised
Teams shows an error banner in the channel naming the broken subscription
The Teams app uninstalls itself from the channel
questions.why: Because the source system does the watching and only emits events that match a subscription, a subscription that names the wrong repository produces no events and no error, so the channel simply hears nothing.

questions.prompt: A platform team's project 'ledger' runs about 60 pipelines a day. The team wants its channel to hear only when the pipeline named ledger-release fails. Which setup fits this requirement?
choices: Create a new channel for every pipeline run and subscribe each one to all events
Subscribe the channel to every event in the ledger project so nothing is missed
Add a subscription for the pipeline-failed event, narrowed to the ledger-release pipeline
Install the Azure Pipelines app a second time so that each install posts one failure
questions.why: A subscription can be narrowed to one event type and one pipeline, which keeps the channel limited to the failure that someone must act on, whereas subscribing to everything creates the noise the teaching text warns against.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an event in GitHub or Azure DevOps ends up as a message in a Teams channel, and name one limit or tradeoff of sending too many events to that channel.
lessons.modelAnswer: The source system is the one that notices an event, such as a failed pipeline run or a new pull request. A Teams app that has been installed and granted access holds subscriptions, which are rules listing the event types and filters, such as a specific repository or pipeline, and the channel each should post to. When an event matches a rule, the source hands it to the app, and the app posts a card into the channel. Nothing polls, so a wrong filter means silence rather than an error. The main tradeoff is volume: a channel that receives every event becomes noise, people mute it, and the one important failure is missed. So subscribe only to events someone is expected to act on, and keep the rest in the source tool's own history.
rubricPoints: Explains that the source system emits events and the installed Teams app posts them, rather than Teams polling
Defines a subscription as a rule of event types, filters, and target channel
Names a wrong filter causing silent failure as a practical trap
States the tradeoff of noise versus missed signals when too many events are routed

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product setup steps and terminology that a reading lesson covers better than any current OpsForge mission.

lessons.plain: A branch strategy is a team's agreed rule for how people create, name, and combine separate copies of the code while they work. Picture several people editing one shared document: you need rules for who works on which copy, when copies get combined back into the main version, and which version customers receive. Three common styles are trunk-based development, where everyone merges small changes into one main line often; feature branches, where each piece of work gets its own copy until it is finished; and release branches, where a snapshot is kept for a version already in customers' hands so fixes can be made without pulling in new work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of six ships a web app to customers every two weeks. Two members say a feature takes three days to write and then a week to merge back. Without reading anything, what do you think is the main cause of the slow merges, and what single habit would you change first?
lessons.teach:
A branch is a named line of commits in a Git repository, a separate path of history that can diverge from the main line. A merge combines the changes from one branch into another. A branch strategy decides how many long-lived lines exist, what each one is for, and how often work flows back into the shared main line.

Trunk-based development keeps one main line, usually called trunk, and asks people to integrate small changes into it at least daily. Automated tests check each change, and unfinished features are often hidden behind feature flags, which are switches that keep new code switched off in production. Integration problems stay small and frequent. The requirement is fast automated checks and discipline.

Feature branches give each piece of work its own branch cut from main, merged back through a reviewed pull request when done. They are easy to understand, but a branch that lives for days drifts away from main, and its final merge can conflict badly.

Release branches are cut from main when a version is prepared for shipping. Customers run that version while main moves on, so urgent fixes go to the release branch and must also be carried back to main. A release branch is a maintenance line, not a place for new features.

Worked example: a five-day feature. On a feature branch, main receives four other merges during those five days, so the final merge touches files that changed underneath it. Under trunk-based flow, the same work is split into five one-day slices, each merged to main behind a flag that stays off until the feature is complete.

Common mistake: calling a team trunk-based while letting branches live for two weeks. The consequence in a running system: if a fix lands on a release branch but never returns to main, the next version ships the same bug again.

The right strategy matches how often you ship and how many versions you must support at the same time.

questions.prompt: A payments team ships a new version every six weeks and keeps version 3.1 in the field for customers who have not upgraded. At the freeze, the team cuts a release branch from main, named release/3.1. Step 1: On Monday, release/3.1 is cut from main. Step 2: On Wednesday, a fix for a card-decline bug is committed to release/3.1 and tested there. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: Version 3.1 is tagged and shipped to customers. Which step completes the sequence so the bug does not come back in the next version?
choices: Delete release/3.1 once it is tagged, so only main remains
Rebase main onto release/3.1 so the two histories match
Start a feature branch from release/3.1 for the next six-week cycle
Merge the fix from release/3.1 back into main
questions.why: The next version is built from main, so the fix must be merged back into main or that version will reintroduce the bug.

questions.prompt: A team of 12 engineers merges changes into one shared main line several times a day. Each change runs automated tests, and unfinished features stay switched off in production behind flags. Which branch strategy is this?
choices: A release branch cut for every individual merge
One long-lived environment branch per deployment stage
Feature branches, each merged through a pull request after about two weeks
Trunk-based development
questions.why: Trunk-based development keeps a single main line that people integrate into at least daily, with automated checks and feature flags hiding unfinished work.

questions.prompt: A library team maintains version 5 for existing customers while version 6 is developed on main. A security bug is fixed on the version 5 maintenance branch and released. Six months later version 6 ships and still contains the same bug. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The version 5 fix was never carried back to the main line that version 6 was built from
Main was not tagged before version 6 was shipped
The version 5 branch was cut from main too early in the cycle
Feature flags were left switched on in version 6
questions.why: A fix made on a maintenance line only reaches later versions if it is merged back into main, so omitting that step lets the bug return.

questions.prompt: A hardware team ships once a quarter and must support the two most recent versions in the field at the same time. Which branch layout fits this requirement best?
choices: One long-lived branch per customer account
Main plus one release branch for each of the two supported versions, with fixes carried back to main
Only feature branches, one per ticket, merged to main when each ticket closes
A single trunk with no other branches, because customers can all upgrade at once
questions.why: Supporting several versions at once needs a maintenance line for each one, and fixes made there must return to main so later versions keep them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever used one long-lived branch when your team should choose trunk-based development instead of feature branches. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would explain it this way. Trunk-based development means everyone merges small changes into main at least daily, so conflicts stay small and main stays close to shippable. It only works well with fast automated tests and feature flags to hide unfinished work. Feature branches give each piece of work its own copy, which is easier to reason about and suits a team that reviews every change through a pull request. The catch is that a branch living a week drifts from main, and its merge gets harder. The tradeoff I would name for trunk-based is that without strong tests, a broken change lands on main for everyone. For our team with thin test coverage, short-lived feature branches are the safer first step, and we move toward trunk as the tests improve.
rubricPoints: Describes trunk-based development as frequent small merges into one shared main line.
Describes feature branches as separate copies per piece of work, merged after review, and notes that long-lived branches drift and conflict.
Describes release branches as a snapshot for a shipped version, with fixes carried back to main.
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as trunk needing fast tests and feature flags, or merge pain from long-lived branches.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which strategy fits a team's release cadence and support needs tests the choice better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A pull request workflow is the agreed route a change takes from a developer's own copy of the code into the shared main line. Instead of pushing straight to the shared branch, the developer proposes the change, teammates review it, automated checks run on it, and only then is it allowed in. Branch policies and branch protection rules are the locks that make this route mandatory. They are settings on the shared branch that refuse a merge until the conditions you chose are met, such as a second person approving it or the build passing. Think of a building where the front door only opens after a guard checks your badge and a colleague has signed the visitor log. The hosting platform enforces these rules, so good intentions alone are not relied on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer says, I already tested this on my laptop, so I can push it straight to the main branch and skip the review. What single setting would stop that push and what would you have to add to make a second person's approval necessary before any merge?
lessons.teach: A pull request is a request to merge one branch of commits into another. It gives the team a place to comment on the change and a place where automated checks report results. A branch is a named line of commits, and the main branch is the shared line that releases are normally built from. A protected branch is a branch where the hosting platform enforces rules before any change can land on it. Azure DevOps calls these rules branch policies, and GitHub calls them branch protection rules. The same idea sits under both names. Typical rules include requiring a pull request instead of a direct push, requiring a minimum number of approvals from people other than the author, requiring named status checks (results reported by a build or scan) to pass, and requiring discussion threads to be resolved. The platform checks these rules at the moment of merge, so a rule cannot be skipped by forgetting it. Worked example: the main branch requires one approval and a passing build check. Ana opens a pull request from her feature branch. The pipeline runs against the proposed result and reports success. Ben comments, and Ana pushes a fix as a new commit. If the policy resets approvals when new commits arrive, Ben's earlier approval no longer counts. Ben re-approves the latest version, the check passes on that version, and the merge button unlocks. Common mistake: setting the rules but leaving a path around them, such as letting administrators bypass the rules or allowing direct pushes from a tool account. Consequence: an unreviewed change reaches the main branch, and any release pipeline that builds from main ships it to users. A pull request workflow is only as strong as the rules that every route to the shared branch must pass through.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Tools protects a branch named release/3.0 with two rules: two approvals from people other than the author, and a passing check named contract-tests. Here is the trace. Step 1: Lin opens a pull request from fix/rate-limit into release/3.0. Step 2: contract-tests runs on the proposed merge and passes. Step 3: Ravi and Dee each approve. Step 4: Lin pushes a follow-up commit that answers a review comment. Step 5: Because new commits arrived, the approvals reset and contract-tests reruns on the new commit. Step 6: [missing]. What must happen before the merge button unlocks?
choices: A repository administrator switches off the approval rule so the merge can proceed.
Lin deletes release/3.0 and recreates it so the old results are cleared.
Ravi and Dee each approve the latest commit again, and contract-tests passes on that commit.
Lin merges at once, since contract-tests already passed on an earlier commit.
questions.why: The approvals were reset by the new commit and the check must pass on the version being merged, so both reviewers must approve the latest commit and the check must pass on it.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a branch to be protected on a Git hosting platform?
choices: It is deleted automatically once a pull request closes.
The platform checks its configured rules at the moment a change tries to land on it.
Its commits are signed so that no one can alter them.
A copy of it is kept in a backup repository each night.
questions.why: A protected branch is one where the hosting platform enforces configured rules before any change can land, which is the defining feature of protection.

questions.prompt: Under a branch rule that requires two approvals from people other than the author, Priya opens a pull request in the claims-api repository and approves it herself. No colleague has reviewed it. What happens when she tries to complete the merge?
choices: The merge is blocked, because her own approval does not count toward the required approvals from others.
The merge goes through, but the pull request is flagged for later review.
The merge is blocked only if the build check has failed.
The merge goes through, because any reviewer including the author counts toward the approvals.
questions.why: Approvals from the author do not count toward the minimum, so the platform checks the rule at merge time and blocks the merge until another person approves.

questions.prompt: A team protects its main branch with one approval and a passing lint check, but leaves an administrator bypass switched on. An administrator pushes a fix straight to main at night without a pull request, and the nightly release pipeline builds from main and ships it. What is the root gap?
choices: The rules were not enforced on every route to main, because the bypass left a path around them.
Lint checks cannot detect unreviewed changes, so approvals were needed instead.
Branch protection only applies to pull requests opened by the author, not to direct pushes.
The release pipeline should have been pointed at a feature branch instead of main.
questions.why: A pull request workflow is only as strong as the rules every route to the shared branch must pass through, and the bypass gave a route that skipped them, so the unreviewed change reached main and then shipped.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a pull request workflow using branch policies or branch protection rules keeps unreviewed code out of the main branch, and name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main branch is protected, so the platform refuses a merge unless the pull request meets the conditions we set, such as at least one approval from someone other than the author and a passing build check on the latest commit. Because the check happens at merge time, nobody can skip the review by accident. The limit is that the rules only see what the platform can measure. An approval is a human judgment and can be given carelessly, and a passing check only proves what the pipeline tests. Also, the rules only protect the branches they are applied to, and administrators or tool accounts may bypass them unless we deliberately include them. So the workflow reduces risk but does not replace careful review or a clear rule about who can override the policy.
rubricPoints: Explains that branch policies or branch protection rules are enforced by the platform at merge time, so the merge is blocked until conditions are met.
Names at least two typical conditions, such as a required approval and a required passing status check.
Explains that new commits can reset approvals, so the final version must be the one reviewed.
States a real limit, such as approvals being human judgment, checks only testing what they cover, or bypass routes for administrators.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which combination of required approvals, status checks and bypass settings stops a specific bad merge is an exam-style reasoning task that adds the most here.

lessons.plain: A branch merge restriction is a rule that stops code from landing on an important line of work, such as the main branch, unless it passes checks first. Think of a shared document where edits go into a draft and a reviewer must approve before the final copy changes. The rules can require another person to review the change, require the automated build and tests to pass, and block anyone from pushing straight to the protected branch. In Azure DevOps these are called branch policies, and in GitHub they are called branch protection rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a developer tries to merge a change whose automated tests failed into the branch that gets deployed, what would you want to happen, and what mechanism would make that happen without relying on the developer's memory?
lessons.teach:
A branch merge restriction is a setting on a repository that decides which changes are allowed to enter a protected branch. A branch is a named line of commits in Git, the version control tool that records every change to a project. The protected branch is usually the one that gets released, often called main. Azure DevOps calls these settings branch policies; GitHub calls them branch protection rules. Both are enforced by the server, so they apply no matter which laptop or tool a person uses.

Common restrictions include: changes must arrive through a pull request (a proposed merge that others can read and comment on); a minimum number of reviewers must approve; a build validation or required status check must pass, meaning an automated pipeline ran against the proposed merged result and reported success; and direct pushes to the protected branch are refused.

Why it works: the server checks the rule at the moment of merge, so safety does not depend on people remembering a convention.

Worked example. The branch main is protected with one required reviewer and a required check named ci-tests. First, Priya pushes a feature branch called fix-timeout and opens a pull request into main. Second, the pipeline builds the merged result and one test fails. Third, the check reports failure, so the merge is blocked. Fourth, Priya fixes the test and pushes again; the check passes. Fifth, a reviewer approves, and only then can the merge complete.

Common mistake: assuming a rule on one branch protects another. A rule written for main does nothing for a release branch such as release/2.0 unless the rule's branch name pattern matches that branch too. Always check which branches a rule actually applies to.

Consequence: if a failing change lands on main, the release pipeline may deploy it to customers, so a missing check turns a test failure into a production incident.

questions.prompt: Team Harbor protects its main branch with a branch policy that requires two reviewers and a required check named api-contract. Step 1: Mei opens a pull request from report-cache into main. Step 2: The pipeline runs api-contract against the merged result and it passes. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: Mei completes the merge, and it succeeds. Which missing step makes the sequence correct?
choices: Mei pushes her change directly to main to skip the remaining review.
The pipeline runs api-contract again on the report-cache branch alone, without the merged result.
A second reviewer approves, because the policy needs two approvals before the merge can complete.
An administrator deletes the branch policy so the merge is no longer restricted.
questions.why: The policy requires two approvals, and the merge stays blocked until a second reviewer approves, so that approval is the missing step between the passing check and the completed merge.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Bank has a branch policy on main that requires the check ledger-tests to pass. Its branch name pattern is set to main only. A developer pushes a fix straight to release/4.2 with no pull request. Which statement is true?
choices: The policy on main copies itself to every branch whose name starts with release, so the push is refused.
The push is accepted, but the server queues it until ledger-tests has been run on main.
The main policy does not apply to release/4.2, so nothing requires ledger-tests to pass before that change is accepted there.
The release/4.2 branch is blocked because it is a release branch, and the check runs automatically.
questions.why: A rule only covers the branches its name pattern matches, so a rule written for main does nothing for release/4.2 unless that branch is also matched.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, why do branch merge restrictions get enforced by the server rather than by a written team convention?
choices: Because a convention can only be written in the pipeline file, and the server reads that file on every push.
Because servers can approve pull requests on behalf of reviewers when the team is too busy.
Because the server stores a copy of every developer's laptop, so it can check local habits.
Because the server checks the rule at the moment of merge, so the safety does not depend on each person remembering the rule or on which tool they use.
questions.why: Server-side enforcement checks the rule at merge time for any tool or laptop, so it does not rely on people following an unwritten convention.

questions.prompt: A team on main has a required check named smoke-tests that fails on a proposed merge. The pull request has two approvals. A reviewer asks whether the merge can complete now. What is the correct answer?
choices: No, the merge stays blocked, because a required check that reports failure stops the merge regardless of approvals.
Yes, approvals override a failing check when the reviewers are senior.
No, the merge is blocked only if the failing check is also a required reviewer.
Yes, but only after the failing check is marked as a warning instead of an error.
questions.why: A required check that reports failure blocks the merge, and approvals alone do not override it, so the correct answer here is that the merge cannot complete while the check fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says branch policies and branch protection rules make main safe, so reviewers can stop checking code. Explain to them, in your own words, what these rules enforce, what they cannot guarantee, and one tradeoff of making them strict.
lessons.modelAnswer: They enforce a few things at merge time on the server: changes come through a pull request, a set number of reviewers approve, required automated checks pass, and direct pushes are refused. That stops a broken or unreviewed change from reaching main without anyone having to remember the process. But they cannot make the code correct. A passing check only proves what the tests cover, and a reviewer can still approve a poor change. Admins or users with bypass permission may also be able to override the rule, so who holds that permission matters. The tradeoff is speed: strict rules add waiting for reviews and slower pipelines, so a team may be tempted to loosen them. I would keep the checks on the release branch strict and be more relaxed on short-lived feature branches.
rubricPoints: Branch policies or protection rules are enforced by the server at merge time, not by convention.
Typical rules include pull requests, required reviewers, and required automated checks.
The rules cannot guarantee correct code; tests only cover what they test and reviewers can err.
Bypass permissions or admin overrides can weaken the rules, so access to them matters.
Strict rules slow delivery, so teams trade speed against protection.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which rule blocks a specific bad merge teaches the reasoning better than reading settings alone.

lessons.plain: Some files are huge: design files, videos, compiled game assets, datasets. Git was built for small text files, so putting huge binaries straight into a repository makes every clone slow and bloats the history forever. Large file management is the strategy for keeping those files out of the normal repository path. The usual answer is to store a tiny stand-in file in the repository and keep the real content on a separate server that Git fetches on demand. You will learn the two main tools, Git Large File Storage and git-fat, and when to choose each one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate commits a 400 MB video into a repository and pushes it. Two months later, every new clone takes ages. Why do you think that happens, and what would you change so the next video does not do the same?
lessons.teach:
Large file storage is a set of Git extensions that replace big files with small pointer files. A pointer is a short text file that records the file's SHA-256 checksum (a fingerprint of its contents) and its size. The real bytes go to a separate store, and Git only downloads them when someone checks out the file.

Git LFS (Large File Storage) is the most widely supported option. You install its hooks once per machine with git lfs install, then declare which file patterns to manage with git lfs track '*.psd'. That command writes a line into a file called .gitattributes; the line tells Git to run the LFS filter on matching files. Commit .gitattributes before adding the big files, so the filter applies from the first commit.

git-fat is an older, simpler third-party tool that uses the same idea of placeholders backed by a separate store. It has a smaller following today, so check that your hosting and team tooling support it before choosing it.

Worked example. To track design files, run git lfs track '*.psd', commit .gitattributes, then add and commit design.psd. Git stores a pointer text file with a version line, an oid sha256 line and a size line, while the 300 MB content goes to the LFS store. A fresh clone downloads the pointers quickly, and the real files are fetched when checked out.

Common mistake: adding the pattern after the big file is already committed. The original blob stays in history, so the repository stays large. Moving existing history is a rewrite, which is a different topic.

Consequence: a build agent without Git LFS installed, or without a fetch step, gets the small pointer text instead of the real binary, and the build fails in confusing ways.

questions.prompt: A mapping company wants its satellite imagery tiles, which are large .tif files, kept out of normal Git history. A developer runs these steps on a laptop that already has Git LFS hooks installed: 1) git lfs track '*.tif' 2) git add .gitattributes and git commit -m 'track tiles' 3) ... 4) git push. Which step is missing between step 2 and the push?
choices: Add the .tif files and commit them, so the pointer files are created and stored.
Rewrite the history with a filter command to shrink any earlier commits.
Run git lfs untrack '*.tif' so the filter is removed before pushing.
Run git-fat init so that a second placeholder tool handles the tiles.
questions.why: After .gitattributes is committed, the tile files still have to be added and committed so that Git LFS replaces each one with a pointer file and sends the bytes to the LFS store.

questions.prompt: In Git LFS, what does a pointer file contain?
choices: The full binary contents of the large file, compressed.
A list of every developer who has edited the large file.
A link to the build agent that last compiled the file.
A version line, a SHA-256 checksum of the contents, and the file size.
questions.why: A pointer is a short text file that records the SHA-256 fingerprint and size of the real file, while the bytes live in a separate store.

questions.prompt: A team committed a 4 GB disk image named release.iso last week. Today they add '*.iso' to .gitattributes and commit it. A new clone of the repository is still large. What best explains this?
choices: The clone is large because git-fat was never installed on the hosting server.
The pattern was written with the wrong quote characters, so the filter did nothing for any file.
The original 4 GB blob remains in the existing commit history, and the new pattern does not rewrite that history.
Git LFS only tracks files created after the pattern is added, so the new clone needs a fresh init.
questions.why: Adding a tracking pattern only affects files added after the rule is in place; the old large blob stays in history, and removing it would require a separate history rewrite.

questions.prompt: A team's Git hosting service does not support git-fat, but their build agents already have Git LFS installed. Which choice fits best for storing large design binaries?
choices: Store the binaries directly in Git without any placeholder, to avoid choosing a tool.
Use Git LFS, because it is the most widely supported option and the hosting tooling needs to match the chosen tool.
Use git-fat anyway, since it is simpler and the hosting service will adapt.
Use git lfs track on the agents only, without committing anything to the repository.
questions.why: git-fat has a smaller following and must be checked against hosting and team tooling, so Git LFS is the practical choice when the platform supports it and the agents already have it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Git LFS keeps large files out of normal repository history, and name one limit or tradeoff the team must plan for before adopting it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Git LFS swaps each large file for a small pointer file in the repository. The pointer holds a SHA-256 checksum and the file size, and the real content lives in a separate LFS store. Clones stay fast because they download pointers first and fetch content only at checkout. The tradeoff is that the team must install LFS on every machine and every build agent, and the pipeline needs an LFS fetch step, or it will build against pointer text. Another limit: the pattern only applies to files committed after it is tracked, so existing large files in history need a deliberate history migration, which is a rewrite with its own coordination cost. Storage and bandwidth quotas on the LFS server also need to be planned.
rubricPoints: Explains that large files are replaced by small pointer files with a checksum and size
Says the real content is stored separately and fetched on checkout
Names a tradeoff such as tooling needed on every machine or agent
Notes that existing history is not fixed by tracking a pattern later

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying a large-file strategy depends on explaining the tradeoffs back, and no listed mission or engine practises this directly.

lessons.plain: A Git repository is the folder that stores a project's full history of changes. When a repository grows very large, with years of history, huge files, or hundreds of people working in it, ordinary Git can become slow to copy, check out, and search. Scaling and optimizing a repository means choosing ways to download less, store less, and keep the tool fast without changing how the team works. This lesson covers the main levers: fetching only the history and files you need, letting Git do its housekeeping in the background, and deciding how code is shared between separate repositories rather than copied around by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's repository has ten years of history and a 40 GB working folder, so every new developer waits an hour to make a first copy of it. Without knowing any Git internals, name two different ways you could make that first copy faster, and say what each one might cost the developer.
lessons.teach:
A clone is the first full copy of a repository onto your machine. A shallow clone downloads only recent commits instead of the whole history. A partial clone downloads the history and folder listings now but fetches the contents of individual files only when Git actually needs them. A sparse checkout limits your working folder to the parts of the tree you name, so the other folders exist in history but not on disk. Background maintenance is a set of housekeeping jobs, such as packing stored objects and refreshing the index of commit relationships, that Git runs on a schedule so the repository stays fast. Scalar is a command-line tool, shipped with Git for Windows and available for other platforms, that switches on a recommended bundle of these settings for a repository and enables background maintenance.

Worked example: the 40 GB repository holds a mobile app folder and a web folder. Step 1: a partial clone downloads commits and folder listings, which is quick. Step 2: a sparse checkout restricts the working folder to the mobile folder, so Git fetches file contents only for that folder. Step 3: when a developer later opens the web folder, Git fetches those files on demand. The first copy is now a small download, and the bulk arrives only as needed.

Common mistake: treating a shallow clone as a complete repository. Tools that compute version numbers from history, or commands that need older commits, will fail or give wrong answers. On a build agent this shows up as a version number of zero or a failed changelog step.

For sharing code across repositories, the common options are submodules, which pin a repository to a specific commit of another repository; subtrees, which merge another repository's code into a folder; and versioned packages, which publish a built artifact that others consume by version. Each one trades simplicity against how tightly the repositories stay coupled.

questions.prompt: A finance firm keeps a 12 GB repository, and its build agent stamps version numbers using the repository's history and tags. Step 1: the agent makes a shallow clone, which downloads only the latest commits and so finishes quickly. Step 2: ____ Step 3: the version step runs and produces the correct number.
choices: Turn on background maintenance so the commit index refreshes on a schedule
Convert the clone into a submodule of the release repository
Switch the clone to a sparse checkout limited to the build scripts folder
Fetch the full history and tags so the version step can see older commits
questions.why: A shallow clone lacks older commits and possibly tags, which a version calculation from history needs, so the agent must fetch the full history and tags before that step runs.

questions.prompt: A developer's clone of a 60 GB monorepo must be quick to create, and they only work in the payments folder. Which feature limits the working folder to chosen parts of the tree while the other folders still exist in history?
choices: Shallow clone
Background maintenance
Subtree merge
Sparse checkout
questions.why: A sparse checkout restricts the files on disk to the folders you name, while the rest of the tree remains in the repository's history.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants a shared logging module from another repository, pinned to one exact commit so their repository always builds against that snapshot. Which sharing option fits best?
choices: Submodule
Versioned package
Subtree
Partial clone
questions.why: A submodule pins a repository to a specific commit of another repository, which matches the requirement of a fixed snapshot.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Scalar is accurate?
choices: Scalar only runs on Linux and cannot be installed alongside Git
Scalar switches on a recommended bundle of settings and enables background maintenance
Scalar deletes commits older than thirty days to keep the repository small
