Scalar is a hosted service that stores a cloud copy of your repository
questions.why: Scalar is a command-line tool that turns on a recommended set of repository settings and background maintenance jobs, without deleting history or running as a hosted service.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would recommend Scalar for a repository and what a partial clone gives up. Then name one situation where splitting code into separate repositories is better than keeping one large repository, and name the tradeoff that comes with it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would recommend Scalar when a repository is large enough that clones and status checks are slow, because it turns on partial clone, sparse checkout, and background maintenance in one step. The cost of a partial clone is that some operations need the network: if you go offline, or run a command that reads old file contents, Git has to fetch them, and that can be slow or fail. Sparse checkout also means you only see the folders you chose, so cross-team searches may miss code. For splitting repositories, a good case is a shared library used by several products that need different release schedules. The tradeoff is coordination: each consumer must pin or update a version, and a change to the library needs a release and an update step rather than a single commit.
rubricPoints: Scalar bundles partial clone, sparse checkout, and background maintenance for large repositories
A partial clone defers file downloads, so some operations need the network or fail offline
Sparse checkout limits the working folder, which can hide code from searches
Splitting into repositories suits independent release schedules but adds version coordination

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers Git repository scaling, so an exam-style scenario asking which strategy fits a given requirement is the most useful practice here.

lessons.plain: A source control repository holds a project's code and its full change history. Permissions decide who may do what to it: read the code, add changes, create a new line of work, rewrite history, or change the rules themselves. Think of a shared filing cabinet where some people may read files, some may add new folders, and only a few may shred old pages. Setting these rights carefully lets people work quickly without letting one mistake or one compromised account damage the shared record. Rights can be set for the whole repository and then narrowed for important branches, such as the main line that production is built from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new teammate needs to fix a typo in the README on the main branch. Should they be given the right to force-push over main to do it? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A permission is a rule that says whether a named person or group may take a specific action. In source control the actions include reading code, adding commits, creating a branch, creating a tag, force-pushing (overwriting shared history with a rewritten version), and bypassing review rules. Most hosted platforms store these rules as an access control list, or ACL: a list of entries, each naming a principal (a user, a team or a group) and marking each action as allowed, denied, or not set. Settings can apply to a whole repository and be inherited by its branches, and a more specific setting on one branch can override the broad one.

Why it works: each entry is checked against the user's own groups, and an explicit deny beats any allow, wherever that allow came from. That lets you grant a broad group a wide right, then carve out one protected branch where the same group is blocked. The guiding principle is least privilege: give each group only the rights its job needs, and nothing more.

Worked example. A team has a group called Developers and a repository whose main branch is the source for production builds. Step 1: at repository level, Developers are allowed to contribute, so they can push feature branches. Step 2: on the main branch, you set force-push to Deny for Developers. Step 3: Alice, a developer, tries to force-push a rewritten main. The platform checks her groups, finds the explicit deny on main, and refuses, even though the repository-level allow permits pushing elsewhere. Step 4: a release group, set up separately, keeps the right, so an approved rebuild is still possible.

Common mistake: granting the whole team administrator rights just to unblock one action. That quietly lets anyone change the rules themselves, which defeats the point of the setup.

Consequence: if a force-push reaches main, history is rewritten underneath everyone else's clones, commits that a deployment was built from can disappear, and tracing a production fault back to its exact code becomes unreliable.

questions.prompt: Lumen Labs keeps a repository called billing-api. At repository level, the group Contractors is allowed to contribute, so they can push feature branches. The team then sets force-push to Deny for Contractors on the branch release-2.4. Step 3: a contractor named Ravi runs a force-push that rewrites release-2.4. The step that is missing from this trace is what the platform does when it checks Ravi's groups against the rules. Which outcome completes the trace?
choices: The push is refused only if Ravi is listed directly on the branch, not when he gets the right through the Contractors group.
The push succeeds and the platform records it for a later review, since force-pushes are never blocked outright.
The push is refused, because the explicit deny on release-2.4 beats the allow inherited from repository level.
The push succeeds, because the repository-level allow was set first and takes priority over later branch rules.
questions.why: An explicit deny on a specific branch overrides an inherited allow from the repository, wherever that allow comes from, so Ravi's force-push is refused.

questions.prompt: In an access control list used for source control, what does a single entry contain?
choices: A repository name, a branch name, and a date after which the rule expires.
A list of commit hashes that the named user is permitted to change.
A principal such as a user, team or group, plus an allowed, denied, or not-set mark for each action.
A password hash and a list of the pipelines the user may trigger.
questions.why: Each ACL entry names a principal (user, team or group) and marks each action as allowed, denied, or not set.

questions.prompt: A team lead wants a QA group to delete a stale tag. To unblock this one action, the lead gives the whole QA group administrator rights on the repository. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: The QA group can no longer read the code, because administrators are blocked from reading.
Administrators can change the permission rules themselves, so the access setup no longer protects anything.
The tag deletion is rolled back on the next build, so the change has no lasting effect.
Existing branch protections are removed automatically when any group receives administrator rights.
questions.why: Administrator rights let a group change the rules, which defeats the purpose of configuring permissions; the right fix is to grant only the single tag right needed.

questions.prompt: A company has an Auditors group that must be able to look at the code in a repository but must never add commits, create branches, or force-push. Which permission setup follows the least-privilege principle?
choices: Grant Auditors administrator rights so they can review the permission settings directly.
Allow every action at repository level, then deny contribute on each branch one by one.
Allow read at repository level, and leave all other actions not set for Auditors.
Allow read, contribute, and create branch at repository level, then deny force-push on the main branch only.
questions.why: Least privilege means granting only what the job needs, so Auditors get read and nothing else; the other options hand out rights the auditors do not need.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set repository permissions for a team of developers and one release manager so that nobody can rewrite the main branch. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would grant the developers group the rights it needs to do daily work, such as contributing to feature branches, but leave force-push and branch deletion off at repository level. Then, on the main branch specifically, I would explicitly deny force-push to the developers group. Because an explicit deny overrides any allow, that holds even if someone is also in another group that has broader rights. The release manager sits in a separate group that keeps the right to rewrite history, so a sanctioned rebuild or repair is still possible, and I would keep that group small. The tradeoff is that explicit denies are easy to forget and hard to see in a long list, so a developer who suddenly cannot do something may not know why. I would document each deny and review the list when people change teams. Also, the release group becomes a high-value target, so its membership needs the same care as production access.
rubricPoints: Grant broad team rights at repository level but only the rights each group needs.
Protect the main branch with an explicit deny for force-push or history rewriting.
Explain that an explicit deny overrides allows, including allows from other groups.
Name a limit, such as hidden or forgotten denies or a small high-risk admin group.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine has the learner set repository or branch permissions, so this is best learned by reading the permission model and reasoning about it.

lessons.plain: A tag is a short, human-readable name stuck on one specific saved point in a project's history, such as the exact version that shipped to customers as version 2.3. Unlike a branch, which is a label that moves forward every time someone adds work, a tag stays where it was put. Teams use tags to organize a repository so anyone can later find the exact snapshot behind a release, a milestone, or a known-good build. Think of it as a bookmark placed on one page of a logbook, where the bookmark never gets moved.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team released version 2.3.0 from commit a1f3, then kept committing to the main branch for months. Without looking anything up, how would you let a colleague later get exactly the code that became 2.3.0, and why would a branch named 2.3.0 be a weaker choice than a fixed label?
lessons.teach:
A commit is a recorded set of changes to a project, identified by a unique ID, and a Git repository is the stored history of those commits. A branch is a name that moves forward whenever new commits land on it. A Git tag is a name that points at one commit and does not move on its own. There are two kinds. A lightweight tag is just a name pointing at a commit. An annotated tag is a full object that also records who created it, when, and a message, and it can be cryptographically signed. Teams that ship versions usually use annotated tags for releases because they carry that record.

Why it works: Git stores tags as fixed references, so creating one is cheap and never rewrites history. Because the name is fixed, anyone who checks out v2.3.0 gets the same files every time, which is what makes a release reproducible.

Worked example. Main is at commit a1f3 and the team is ready to release. Step 1: create an annotated tag named v2.3.0 with a release message. Step 2: the tag now points at a1f3. Step 3: developers keep committing, so main moves on to c9d2, but v2.3.0 still points at a1f3. Step 4: push the tag to the remote, meaning the shared copy on a server, using an explicit push, because pushing commits does not send tags by default. Now anyone asking for v2.3.0 gets exactly a1f3.

Common mistake: moving a tag after it has been pushed. Someone deletes v2.3.0 and recreates it on a newer commit to fix a release. Anyone who already fetched the old tag now holds a different commit under the same name, so a rebuild can no longer be trusted.

Consequence: in a running system, the release pipeline often keys on the tag. If the tag moves, the artifact you deployed and the code the tag names can disagree, so an incident review cannot tell which code was really live.

questions.prompt: A payments team names release 4.0.1 and creates it with git tag -a v4.0.1 -m 'Release 4.0.1' 7e21 while 7e21 is the commit at the tip of their develop branch. The branch then moves forward to 0f8b after more merges. Steps 1 and 2 are done: the annotated tag v4.0.1 exists on their laptop and points at 7e21. Step 3 is blank: a colleague fetches from the shared server and cannot see v4.0.1 there. Which command completes step 3 so the tag is available to everyone?
choices: git tag -f v4.0.1 0f8b, to move the tag to the newest commit before anyone fetches it
git push origin v4.0.1, to send that one tag explicitly to the shared remote
git branch v4.0.1 7e21, to turn the tag into a branch so the server accepts it
git commit --amend -m 'Release 4.0.1', to attach the release message to the latest commit
questions.why: Pushing commits does not send tags by default, so the tag must be pushed explicitly by name to appear on the shared remote.

questions.prompt: Which kind of Git tag records who created it, when it was created, and a message, and can be cryptographically signed?
choices: A branch named after the version
An annotated tag
A commit message that contains the version number
A lightweight tag
questions.why: An annotated tag is a full object that stores creator, date, and message and can be signed, while a lightweight tag is only a name pointing at a commit.

questions.prompt: A mobile app team tags v7.2.0 on commit 3c8e. Two weeks later a hotfix lands on main at commit 9ab1. Assuming nobody has moved the tag, what does v7.2.0 point at now?
choices: 9ab1, because tags follow the newest commit on the branch
3c8e, because a tag stays fixed on its commit unless someone moves it
Nothing, because Git removes a tag when its branch advances
The newest commit tagged by the CI server that day
questions.why: A Git tag is a fixed reference that does not move when the branch advances, so v7.2.0 still points at 3c8e.

questions.prompt: A team pushed tag v3.1.0 to the shared server, then deleted it locally and on the server, and recreated it on a newer commit to fix a bug. A teammate who fetched the original v3.1.0 weeks ago now rebuilds from that name. What is the main risk?
choices: The server keeps both versions of the tag and asks the teammate to choose one at each fetch
Git rejects the teammate's rebuild because the tag was recreated
The teammate's local copy of the tag silently updates to match the server, so nothing is wrong
The teammate's local v3.1.0 still points at the original commit, so the same name now refers to two different builds
questions.why: Moving a pushed tag leaves earlier fetchers holding the old commit under the same name, so the name no longer identifies one set of files and rebuilds cannot be trusted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Git tag is, how it differs from a branch, and one limit or tradeoff you would watch for when using tags in a release process.
lessons.modelAnswer: A tag is a fixed name on one commit, so when we release 2.3.0 we tag that exact commit and anyone can check out the same files later. A branch is a name that moves forward as new commits are added, so it is wrong for pinning a release, because main will have changed within a week. The main tradeoff is that a tag is only a label. If someone deletes and recreates a pushed tag on a different commit, the name stops meaning what it meant for everyone who already fetched it. That is why we use annotated tags for releases, since they record who made them and when, and why we agree not to move them once pushed. Also, git push does not send tags automatically, so the tag must be pushed explicitly or the release pipeline will never see it.
rubricPoints: A tag is a fixed name pointing at one specific commit, unlike a branch that moves forward.
Annotated tags record the creator, date and message, while lightweight tags are only a name.
Tags let a release be reproduced later by checking out the same snapshot.
Tags must be pushed explicitly, and a pushed tag should not be moved or recreated.

suggested.rationale: Tag types, push behaviour and naming conventions are reference facts best learned from reading, and no listed mission practises tagging.

lessons.plain: Git keeps a history of the changes that were committed, so work that looks lost is often still stored. Recovering data means finding the saved version you want and bringing it back into your files or a branch. Think of an old drafts folder: the paragraph you accidentally deleted may still be there, as long as you know which saved copy to open. The skill is knowing where Git keeps those saved copies and which command brings one back without disturbing anything else.
lessons.guessPrompt: Last week a colleague committed a change that deleted a configuration file, and the deletion was pushed to the shared branch. Before reading on, what would you guess Git still remembers about that file, and how would you try to get it back?
lessons.teach: A commit is a saved snapshot of your project, identified by a long hash called a SHA. A branch is a movable label that points at one commit. HEAD is Git's pointer to where you are right now, usually a branch. The reflog is a local log that records where HEAD and branches pointed recently, including commits you can no longer reach from any branch. Because of the reflog, a commit that looks deleted is usually still stored until Git cleans up unreachable objects, which normally takes weeks. Worked example: a teammate ran a hard reset on main and two commits vanished from the history. Step 1: run git reflog and find the entry just before the reset, say def5678 with the note that HEAD moved from it. Step 2: create a new branch at that SHA with git branch recovered-main def5678. Step 3: check the result with git log recovered-main. Step 4: once it looks right, point main at it or merge it back. For one deleted file, find the last commit that still had it, then restore it with git restore --source followed by that SHA and the file path. Common mistake: a hard reset discards uncommitted edits, and Git cannot recover those, so commit or stash work before experimenting. In a shared repository, recovering history on main and then force pushing it means teammates' local copies must be coordinated before anyone pulls. Recovery is possible only while the saved commit still exists locally, so act before cleanup runs.

questions.prompt: A logistics team keeps its routing code in a repository called route-planner. A developer on the branch dispatch-fix ran git reset --hard HEAD~2 by mistake and lost two commits. HEAD is Git's pointer to where you are right now. The recovery goes like this. Step 1: run git reflog, the local log of where HEAD and branches recently pointed, and find the entry a31f0c8, which is where HEAD sat just before the reset. Step 2: create a new branch at that SHA (the long hash that names a commit) with git branch rescue-dispatch a31f0c8. Step 3: ____. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: Run git log rescue-dispatch to confirm the two lost commits are present before you move anything else
Run git reflog expire --expire=now --all to clear the old entries and free space
Run git push --force so the rescued commits reach the shared remote straight away
Run git gc so Git keeps the unreachable commits for good
questions.why: Checking the rescued branch with git log confirms the commits are back before you merge or point a branch at them, and the other three options either risk the shared history or discard the recovery trail.

questions.prompt: A developer deleted a feature branch with a git branch delete command and thinks the commits on it are gone for good. Which explanation best fits the teaching text?
choices: The commits are removed from the repository the moment the branch name is deleted, so only a remote copy can bring them back
The commits are moved into the stash automatically, so running git stash pop restores them
The commits are stored on the server only, so they can be recovered only from the hosting site's web interface
The commits remain stored locally, and the reflog still records where the deleted branch pointed, so the SHA can be found and a new branch created there, until Git cleans up unreachable objects
questions.why: The teaching text explains that the reflog records where branches pointed, and a commit no longer reachable from a branch is usually still stored until cleanup runs.

questions.prompt: A developer runs git reset --hard on a branch to undo two bad commits. Afterwards they realise they had also edited three files and never committed or stashed those edits. What is the most accurate statement about recovering those edits?
choices: They can be recovered with git restore --source using the SHA of the last commit
They reappear after the next git gc, which stores all uncommitted changes
They are not recoverable through Git's commit history, because the reflog tracks commits and branch pointers rather than uncommitted work
They can be recovered by finding the matching SHA in git reflog and creating a branch there
questions.why: The reflog only tracks where HEAD and branches pointed, and uncommitted edits were never saved as commits, so a hard reset discards them beyond Git's ability to recover.

questions.prompt: After recovering commits on main in a shared repository, a team lead plans to force push the recovered history to the remote. What must happen before teammates pull?
choices: Nothing, because a force push updates every teammate's local copy automatically
Teammates' local copies of the branch must be coordinated first, since their history no longer matches the rewritten remote and pulling could mix the two versions
Each teammate must run git reflog and create a new branch at the old SHA before anyone else pushes
The remote must delete its reflog so that the old commits stop interfering with the new ones
questions.why: A force push rewrites the shared history, so teammates whose local copies differ must be coordinated before they pull, or their work can clash with the rewritten branch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would recover a branch that someone accidentally reset, and name one limit of that recovery.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with git reflog, because it records where the branch and HEAD pointed before the reset. I would find the entry just before the reset and note its SHA, then create a new branch at that commit so the old work is reachable again. I would check the commits with git log before changing main. The limit is that the reflog is local to the machine that ran the reset, so if the reset happened on someone else's clone, I cannot recover from my copy. Also, uncommitted changes were never saved as commits, so a hard reset may have erased them for good. If I need to restore the shared branch on the remote, a force push would overwrite other people's history, so I would coordinate with the team first.
rubricPoints: Names the reflog as the place to find the pre-reset commit SHA
Explains creating a new branch at that SHA to make the work reachable again
States that reflog data is local to the machine where the change happened
Notes that uncommitted changes are not recoverable from commits
Warns that force pushing a recovered shared branch needs coordination

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which recovery command fits a given loss situation adds the most practice beyond reading the commands.

lessons.plain: Sometimes a file or value gets saved into a project's version history by mistake: a password, a private key, or a huge video. Even after you delete it in a newer save, the older saves still hold it, and anyone who copies the project can read those older saves. Removing specific data means rewriting that history so the unwanted content disappears from every past snapshot, then dealing with the fact that copies of the old history may already exist. It is a rare, careful operation, and it is only part of the fix, because an exposed secret must still be replaced.
lessons.guessPrompt: You commit a file containing a database password, then delete that file in the next commit and push. Is the password now gone from the project's history? Why or why not?
lessons.teach: A commit is a saved snapshot of the project, and the history is the chain of commits leading back to the first one. Each commit points to the commit before it, so content stays reachable as long as any commit in the chain still contains it. Deleting a file in a new commit only changes the latest snapshot; the earlier snapshots still hold the old bytes. To truly remove specific data, you rewrite history: a tool such as git filter-repo walks every commit, strips the unwanted path or pattern, and produces new commits with new identifiers. Because the identifiers change, the cleaned branches must be force-pushed, meaning the shared branch on the server is replaced outright, which is a deliberate and disruptive act. Worked example: history is A, B, C, where B adds config/secrets.env containing a password and C deletes it. Step 1: run the rewrite tool to remove config/secrets.env from every commit. Step 2: the chain becomes A, B', C', where B' no longer touches that file. Step 3: force-push the cleaned branch. Step 4: every teammate re-clones or carefully rebases, because their old local copies still contain B. Common mistake: believing the rewrite is enough. The password was exposed the moment it was pushed, so it must be rotated, meaning revoked and replaced at its source, and copies in forks (personal copies of the repository), CI caches and clones must be treated as possibly exposed. Consequence: open pull requests and local branches built on old commits break, and the server may keep unreferenced data until cleanup runs. Removing data from history reduces future exposure but cannot undo past exposure.

questions.prompt: A logistics team at Harbor Freight Lanes commits a database connection string into ops/db.yaml in commit 3 of a five-commit history, then deletes the file in commit 4. They want the string gone from the repository. Step 1: they run git filter-repo to strip ops/db.yaml from every commit, which produces new commit IDs. Step 2: they force-push the cleaned main branch so the server's history is replaced. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: every developer re-clones, because their local copies still hold the old commits.
choices: Delete the repository and recreate it under a new name
Run git revert on commit 3 and push normally
Ask the team to delete their local branches and nothing else
Rotate the database password at its source so the old one stops working
questions.why: The string was exposed the moment it was first pushed, so the real fix is to revoke and replace the credential at its source, because rewriting history cannot undo past exposure.

questions.prompt: A developer at a small bakery-software firm deletes a 40 MB rendered image from the repository in a new commit and pushes. A month later a teammate finds the image still retrievable from the repository's history. Why?
choices: The server backs up each push, and the backup contains the image
The deletion commit was never applied to the server
Earlier snapshots still hold the image, since a new commit only changes the latest one
Git keeps every deleted file in a hidden trash folder
questions.why: Each commit points to its predecessor, so earlier snapshots keep the old bytes even after a later commit removes the file from the latest snapshot.

questions.prompt: A team rewrote its history to remove an API key and force-pushed the result. A contractor says the key can no longer be exposed because the server's branch is clean. What is the gap in that reasoning?
choices: The rewrite tool only removes secrets from the most recent commit
The contractor's personal fork and local clones may still hold the key, and the key itself still needs rotating
Force-pushing is only permitted on private repositories, so the key was never public
A force-push leaves a public backup of the old branch by default
questions.why: Copies in forks, clones and caches may still contain the secret, and only revoking and replacing the credential at its source closes the exposure.

questions.prompt: After a history rewrite and force-push, an open pull request built on an old commit now shows errors. What is the right response?
choices: Rebase the work onto the new commits or recreate the pull request, since its old base no longer exists
Close the repository and ask the author to resubmit everything from scratch
Force-push the old commits back to the server to restore the pull request
Merge the pull request into the rewritten branch as it stands
questions.why: Rewriting changes commit identifiers, so work built on the old commits must be rebased or reopened against the new history.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that deleting the secret file in a new commit is enough, and that rewriting history is risky overkill. Explain to them, in your own words, what really happens, what removing data from history involves, and one tradeoff or limit of doing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deleting the file in a new commit only changes the newest snapshot. The older commits still contain the secret, and anyone who clones the repository can read them with ordinary history commands. To remove it from history we rewrite the commits with a tool like git filter-repo, which drops that path from every commit and gives them new identifiers. The tradeoff is real: everyone's local copies and open pull requests point at old commits, so the cleaned history must be force-pushed and the team has to re-clone. Forks and caches may still hold the old data, and the server can keep unreferenced objects until cleanup. That is why rewriting is never the whole fix. The credential must be rotated, because once it was pushed we have to assume someone already saw it.
rubricPoints: Deleting a file in a new commit leaves the data in earlier commits.
Removing data from history means rewriting commits, which changes their identifiers.
Rewriting requires a force-push and coordinated re-cloning, disrupting open work.
Forks, caches and clones may still hold the removed data.
A leaked secret must be rotated, since history rewriting cannot undo exposure.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a leaked-credential scenario, deciding what to rewrite, rotate and communicate, is the exam-style skill, and no listed mission teaches history rewriting directly.

lessons.plain: A package is a bundled, versioned chunk of reusable code, such as a library or a tool, that other projects can download instead of copying its files. A package manager is the system that stores those bundles, keeps track of their version numbers, and hands them to whoever asks. Think of a shared locker where a team keeps approved parts: it has labelled shelves, a sign-in list for who may take or leave items, and a way to borrow parts from a central warehouse when the locker lacks them. Choosing a package tool means deciding where your team's parts live, who may read or publish them, and whether outside parts also pass through your locker.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's build downloads a public library from the internet, and the build sometimes fails when that website is slow. What would you change first, and why do you think it helps?
lessons.teach:
A package registry, also called a feed, is a server that stores published packages and serves them to tools that request them. Each package has a name and a version, and each belongs to an ecosystem such as npm for JavaScript, NuGet for .NET, Maven for Java, or pip for Python. A publisher pushes a version to a feed. A consumer's build restores that package by name and version. Two products cover most Microsoft-centred teams. GitHub Packages stores packages alongside a repository or organisation and follows the same permission model, so access generally follows repository rights. Azure Artifacts provides feeds inside an Azure DevOps organisation. It can also act as an upstream cache: when a consumer asks for a public package the feed does not hold, the feed fetches a copy from the public source, stores it, and serves it from then on.

Why this works: a feed gives one controlled place to publish, one place to authenticate, and one cache of public packages, so builds are faster and do not depend on a public site being reachable at that moment.

Worked example: a team publishes a private npm library called geo-utils at version 1.4.0 from a pipeline. First, the pipeline signs in with its own build identity and pushes the package to the feed. Second, the web app's pipeline restores its dependencies, asking the feed for geo-utils 1.4.0 and also for express, which the feed does not hold. Third, the feed serves geo-utils from its own storage, fetches express from the public registry, keeps a copy, and returns it to the build.

Common mistake: republishing different code under a version number that already exists. Many feeds refuse to overwrite a published version. Where overwriting is allowed, caches may keep serving the old bytes, so different environments quietly run different code.

Consequence: if the library is published to GitHub Packages but the consuming pipelines run in Azure DevOps, those pipelines still need explicit read access, or the restore step fails only when the deployment runs.

questions.prompt: Northmere Labs publishes a NuGet library called Northmere.Calc at version 4.0.1 from a pipeline in its GitHub repository, using GitHub Packages. Its separate Azure DevOps pipeline must restore that version. The steps are: (1) the publishing pipeline pushes Northmere.Calc 4.0.1 to the GitHub Packages feed for that repository. (2) Step missing here. (3) The Azure DevOps restore asks for Northmere.Calc 4.0.1 and receives it from the feed.
choices: The publisher re-uploads 4.0.1 with a changed build, replacing the old bytes under the same version.
The feed copies Northmere.Calc from the public nuget.org site into its storage and serves it.
The consumer renames the package to Northmere.Calc.Azure so that the feed will accept the restore request.
The consuming Azure DevOps pipeline is given read access to the package, because GitHub Packages access follows repository rights.
questions.why: GitHub Packages follows the permission model of the repository, so a pipeline running in another product still needs explicit read access before its restore can succeed.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a package feed?
choices: A branch naming rule that tells developers which source-control branch to merge into.
A deployment slot that swaps live traffic between two copies of an application.
A compiler that turns source files into runnable binaries before they are deployed.
A server that stores published packages by name and version and serves them to tools that request them.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a feed as a server that stores published packages and serves them to requesting tools, with each package identified by name and version.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Health uses an Azure Artifacts Maven feed. Its build needs org.example:cache-kit 2.3.0, which the team published, and commons-io 2.11.0, which the feed does not hold. The feed is configured as an upstream cache for public packages. What happens when the build asks for commons-io?
choices: The feed returns an empty package, and the build continues with a warning and no library code.
The feed fetches commons-io from the public source, stores a copy, and serves it to the build from then on.
The build fetches commons-io from the public site itself, and the feed is bypassed for that request.
The build fails every time, because a feed can only serve packages that were pushed to it directly.
questions.why: With an upstream cache, the feed retrieves a public package it lacks, keeps a copy, and serves it on later requests, so the build does not depend on the public site after the first fetch.

questions.prompt: A team published widgetsvc version 1.0.6 to its feed. After a bug fix, the pipeline runs again and tries to publish the new code under the same 1.0.6 number, and the feed refuses. Which response is correct?
choices: Publish the fixed code as 1.0.7, so that each version number always maps to the same contents.
Push the fixed code under 1.0.6 again and rely on caches to pick up the new bytes automatically.
Delete 1.0.6 from the feed and publish the fixed code under 1.0.6 so the feed accepts it.
Leave the feed as it is and ask consumers to copy the fixed files into their own projects by hand.
questions.why: A published version should keep the same contents, so a fix needs a new version number; overwriting it lets caches and environments quietly run different code under one name.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between GitHub Packages and Azure Artifacts for a team's private library. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with where the consumers live and who needs access. If the code and its pull requests are in GitHub and the consumers are GitHub Actions workflows in the same organisation, GitHub Packages keeps permissions in one place, so I would lean that way. If the pipelines, work items and other packages already run in Azure DevOps, Azure Artifacts fits better, and it can cache public packages through an upstream source so builds keep working when a public registry is slow. The tradeoff I would name for GitHub Packages is that consumers outside the repository's permission model need extra tokens or access grants. For Azure Artifacts, the tradeoff is that it adds a second system to manage when the code itself lives in GitHub. Whichever I choose, I would forbid overwriting published versions.
rubricPoints: States that the choice depends on where consumers and permissions already live
Explains the difference between hosting packages next to a repository and hosting them in an Azure DevOps feed
Names one concrete limit or tradeoff of the option not chosen
Mentions upstream caching of public packages as a reason to use a feed
Notes that published versions should not be overwritten

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers package hosting, so a scenario-based reasoning exercise is the closest fit for choosing between these tools.

lessons.plain: A package feed is a shared shelf where a team stores the reusable bundles of code it builds, such as libraries and tools. Some packages your own team writes and publishes there. Others come from public catalogues that anyone can download from. A view is a named window onto that shelf that shows only the packages that have reached a certain stage, such as passing its checks, so a build reading through that window cannot grab something untested. An upstream source is a link that lets your feed fetch and keep a copy of a public package the first time someone asks for it. Together these let a team control exactly what its builds are allowed to install.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's production build installs a library by name from a shared shelf. Someone publishes an untested beta version of that library there. What would stop production builds from ever installing that beta, and why might pointing every build at the shelf's full, unfiltered address be risky?
lessons.teach: A package feed is a named store that holds versioned packages, such as libraries for npm, NuGet, Maven or Python. Local packages are ones your own team publishes to the feed. Upstream sources are other registries, usually public ones, that the feed is connected to. When a consumer asks for a package the feed does not hold yet, the feed fetches it from the upstream, keeps a copy, and serves that copy from then on. A view is a named subset of a feed that consumers read from. Teams usually keep one view for everything published, and a release view that contains only packages that passed checks. Promoting a package means adding that same package to a later view; it is not copied or rebuilt. Why it works: consumers point at one view address and receive only what that view admits, so the rule about what is safe is enforced in one place instead of in every build script. Worked example: a team publishes Acme.Geo version 2.0.0-beta to the feed. It appears in the local view. The pipeline's tests pass, so the pipeline promotes that exact package to the release view. Production builds read the release view and can see it. A version still only in the local view stays invisible to them. Common mistake: pointing production builds at the feed's full unfiltered address, so any published pre-release gets installed. A second mistake is naming an internal package the same as a public one, so a build resolves the public copy instead. Consequence: a build that pulls an untested version can ship a break to production within minutes of publishing. If an upstream package disappears and no cached copy exists, every build that depends on it fails. A feed view is a control on what builds may consume, and it only works when consumers are pointed at it.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics keeps a package feed called ops-packages for Python wheels. A feed is a named store that holds versioned packages, and a view is a named subset of that feed that consumers read from. The team's all-published view lists everything published. Here is the sequence. Step 1: the team publishes tracklib 1.4.0 to the feed, so it appears in all-published. Step 2: the nightly test stage passes for that exact file. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the deployment agents read the release view address and install tracklib 1.4.0 from it. Which action belongs in step 3?
choices: Rebuild the wheel from the same commit and add the new build to the release view
Copy the package into a second feed named release-prod
Add that same package version to the release view
Delete the package from the all-published view so only the release view holds it
questions.why: Promotion means adding the same package version to a later view without copying or rebuilding it, so the tested file is the one production installs.

questions.prompt: In a package feed, what is an upstream source?
choices: Another registry, often public, that the feed is connected to and fetches missing packages from
The first version number a team ever publishes for a library
A saved list of package names that consumers are allowed to install
A build agent that runs before the main pipeline stage
questions.why: An upstream source is another registry the feed is linked to, and the feed fetches a copy from it when a consumer asks for a package the feed does not yet hold.

questions.prompt: Northwind's team names its internal library Auth.Core, which is also the name of a public package on an upstream registry. A consumer's build asks for Auth.Core through the feed. What is the main risk?
choices: The build will refuse to start until one of the two copies is deleted
The internal package is copied into every view, so it gets installed twice
The build can resolve the public copy instead of the internal one, because the names collide
The internal package gets renamed automatically when it is promoted to a release view
questions.why: When an internal and a public package share a name, resolution can pick the public copy, so the team's own package is silently bypassed.

questions.prompt: A team's deploy script installs hotfix 3.2.1 from the feed's full address, which also holds unpromoted pre-releases. What change best limits what the script can install?
choices: Add a comment to the script saying only stable versions are allowed
Delete all pre-release packages from the feed each night
Point the script at the release view address instead of the full feed address
Rename the hotfix to 3.2.1-final so the script skips it
questions.why: A view is the single place where the rule about what is safe is enforced, so pointing the script at the release view stops it from seeing unpromoted packages, while a comment or renaming enforces nothing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a feed view does and why a team would keep both a local view and a release view. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on upstream sources.
lessons.modelAnswer: A feed is where packages live, and a view is a filtered window onto that feed that consumers read from. The local view holds everything the team publishes, including betas and experiments, so builds inside the team can try new work. The release view admits only packages that passed the pipeline's checks, and production builds point at that view, so they cannot pick up something untested. Moving a package from local to release is a promotion of the same package, not a rebuild, which keeps the tested bytes identical. The tradeoff with upstream sources is that the feed caches public packages on first request. That protects builds if the public copy later vanishes, but it also means a public package with a clashing name can be picked up unless names are kept distinct and the order of sources is set carefully.
rubricPoints: A feed stores packages, and a view is a filtered subset that consumers read from.
Promotion moves a tested package between views without rebuilding it.
Production consumers should read the release view, not the full feed, so untested versions stay hidden.
An upstream source caches public packages, which protects against upstream removal but risks name clashes with internal packages.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers feeds, so an exam-style scenario asking which view a production build should read is the closest practice available.

lessons.plain: Every piece of software you build leans on other pieces: libraries, packages, and shared modules written by others or by your own team. A version number tells you which exact release of one of those pieces you are using. A versioning strategy is the agreed rule for how those numbers change when the code changes. Semantic Versioning (SemVer) uses three numbers that signal how risky a change is. Calendar Versioning (CalVer) uses dates instead, which tells you when something shipped but not whether it breaks anything. Choosing between them is a decision about what your team and your users need to read from a number at a glance.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service works with a logging library at version 2.3.1. The maintainer then publishes 2.4.0, and later 3.0.0. Without reading any documentation, what would you guess a jump from 2.3.1 to 2.4.0 tells you about the change, and what would a jump to 3.0.0 tell you?
lessons.teach:
A dependency is another component your code relies on, such as a library pulled in from a package feed. A package is a bundled, versioned release of that component. A version label is the name that identifies one release. A versioning strategy is the rule your team uses to choose those labels.

Semantic Versioning (SemVer) writes versions as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR when you make a breaking change that existing callers must adapt to. Bump MINOR when you add functionality that old callers can simply ignore. Bump PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes. A pre-release label such as 2.0.0-rc.1 marks a candidate that is not yet final, and it sorts before 2.0.0.

Calendar Versioning (CalVer) puts dates in the number, for example 2024.06 or 24.6.1. It tells you when a release was cut, which helps products with time-based support windows, but it says nothing about whether the change breaks callers.

A version range lets a consumer say which releases it accepts, such as any 2.x release at or above 2.3.1. A lock file records the exact version a build resolved to, so a rebuild next month uses the same code.

Worked example: your service depends on logger 2.3.1 with a range that accepts any 2.x at or above 2.3.1. Step 1: the maintainer ships 2.4.0 with a new option. It is a minor bump, so the range accepts it and the next install may pick it up. Step 2: the maintainer ships 3.0.0, which removes an old function. The range excludes it, so your build stays on 2.x until someone deliberately upgrades and fixes the affected call sites.

Common mistake: trusting a version label without checking it. Teams assume a minor or patch bump is safe and skip tests, yet maintainers sometimes change behaviour inside minor releases. Treat the label as a promise to verify, not a guarantee.

Consequence in a running system: without a committed lock file, two builds of the same commit can run different dependency code, and a silent minor update can break production overnight.

questions.prompt: A payments team's service depends on the SDK acme-pay with the range 'any 4.x at or above 4.1.0'. Step 1: the SDK maintainer ships 4.1.4, which fixes a rounding bug without changing any public function. This is a PATCH bump, so the range accepts it. Step 2: the maintainer ships 4.2.0, which adds an optional refund method that old callers can ignore. This is a MINOR bump, so the range accepts it. Step 3 (missing, to fill in): the maintainer then ships 5.0.0, which renames the charge function. State whether the range accepts 5.0.0 and what the team should do.
choices: The range accepts 5.0.0 because a rename is only a minor change, so running the tests and keeping the range as it is should be enough.
The range excludes 5.0.0 only when no lock file exists, so a committed lock file would still resolve the build to 5.0.0.
The range excludes 5.0.0 since it is outside 4.x; the build stays on 4.x until someone deliberately upgrades and fixes the renamed call sites.
The range accepts 5.0.0 since it is the newest release, so the team should expect the next install to pick it up without any changes to its own code.
questions.why: The range stops at the 4.x line, and a MAJOR bump signals a breaking change, so the build stays on 4.x until a deliberate upgrade fixes the call sites.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Calendar Versioning (CalVer) is correct?
choices: A release labelled 2025.04 is a breaking change because the year number changed from the previous release's label.
A release labelled 2025.04 signals that it is backward compatible, so callers can upgrade without reading the release notes at all.
A release labelled 2025.04 tells you when it was cut but does not tell you whether it breaks existing callers.
A CalVer label must always be followed by a patch number, otherwise the release sorts before its predecessor in every feed.
questions.why: CalVer puts the release date in the number, so it shows when a release was cut but says nothing about compatibility.

questions.prompt: A maintainer changes the return type of a public function. The package is currently at 3.4.2. Under Semantic Versioning (SemVer), which label should this change carry?
choices: 2025.01, because a date-based label shows when the change was cut and so fits this release.
3.4.3, because it is a bug fix and only the patch number needs to move.
3.5.0, since the function still exists and only its behaviour has become richer than before.
4.0.0, because existing callers must adapt to the new return type.
questions.why: A change existing callers must adapt to is a breaking change, which under SemVer requires a MAJOR bump, here 3.4.2 to 4.0.0.

questions.prompt: A team's package feed lists both 4.0.0-rc.2 and 4.0.0 for the same library. Which statement is true?
choices: 4.0.0 sorts before 4.0.0-rc.2 because the plain number is shorter and so it is treated as earlier.
4.0.0-rc.2 is newer than 4.0.0 because release candidates always come after the final tag in the sequence.
The two labels are equal, since the suffix only describes packaging and does not affect ordering at all.
4.0.0-rc.2 sorts before 4.0.0, marking it as a candidate that is not yet the final release.
questions.why: A pre-release label such as rc.2 marks a candidate that is not final, and it sorts before the plain version it leads up to.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between SemVer and CalVer for an internal shared library that three services depend on, and name one limit or tradeoff of the scheme you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use SemVer for the shared library, because three services consume it and each needs to know whether an upgrade can break them. The major number changes only on breaking changes, so consumers can accept any 2.x release to pick up new features and fixes, while a 3.0 waits until someone has tested it. CalVer would tell us when the library shipped, but a 2025.04 release could still remove a function and nobody would know from the number. The tradeoff with SemVer is that its meaning depends on discipline: if someone labels a breaking change as a minor bump, consumers get surprised. So I would back the labels with automated compatibility tests and a changelog, and commit lock files in each service so builds stay reproducible.
rubricPoints: Names the three parts of SemVer and what each signals to a consumer.
Explains that CalVer shows the release date but not whether the change breaks callers.
Picks a scheme and justifies it using the needs of the people who consume the library.
States a real limit, such as SemVer relying on honest labelling, and a mitigation like tests or lock files.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is choosing a scheme and explaining its tradeoffs in your own words, and no listed mission or planned engine covers versioning directly.

lessons.plain: When a pipeline builds something you will ship, such as a package, a container image or a compiled program, that thing needs a name that says which build made it. A versioning strategy is the rule for those names. Good rules make it obvious which code is inside, let you find it again later, and make sure the thing you tested is exactly the thing that reaches users. Bad rules, like reusing the same name for every build, turn a rollback into guesswork.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's pipeline publishes a new container image on every merge to main, and every image is tagged 'latest'. Production breaks, and someone asks which build is running there. Why is that question hard to answer with this scheme, and what would you change?
lessons.teach: An artifact is anything a pipeline produces that gets deployed or reused: a package, a container image, a compiled binary, a zip file. A version is the label that identifies one specific artifact. A versioning strategy is the rule that decides how those labels are built. The core idea is that a label should point to exactly one set of bits, permanently. Once a version is published it is immutable, meaning it is never overwritten with different contents. Two terms matter here. A build number is a counter the CI system (the service that runs your pipelines) assigns to each run, so it is unique within that pipeline. A commit identifier, often a short hash, names the exact source code the build used. Why it works: if each artifact carries a unique version, a running system can always answer which code it runs, a rollback can name its target, and the same file can move through test and production without being rebuilt. Worked example. The project file says the base version is 1.4.2. Build run 1042 starts on commit a3f9c1. The pipeline composes the version 1.4.2-build.1042 and records commit a3f9c1 in the artifact metadata. It publishes to the feed, and the feed refuses any later attempt to publish 1.4.2-build.1042 with different contents. Staging deploys that file and its tests pass. Production deploys the same file rather than a fresh build. If production breaks, the team rolls back by naming 1.4.2-build.1041. Common mistake: tagging every image 'latest' and rebuilding separately for each environment. Then the tested artifact and the shipped artifact can differ, and 'latest' quietly moves to a newer build. Consequence in a running system: during an incident, a rollback to 'latest' can pull an untested image, turning a fast fix into a second outage. A version is only useful if it can never change, so treat every published version as a permanent record.

questions.prompt: A mobile backend team uses a container registry, a service that stores built container images under name-and-tag labels. Their project file sets the base version to 4.1.0. Build run 317 starts on commit 9d2e55. The pipeline tags the image 4.1.0-build.317, records commit 9d2e55 in the image metadata, and pushes it to the registry. The registry is set so that a published tag cannot be overwritten with different contents. Staging pulls 4.1.0-build.317, and its integration tests pass. The release lead then asks how production should receive this release. The missing step is what production deploys. Production should deploy:
choices: The exact image 4.1.0-build.317 that staging tested, pulled by that tag, so the tested artifact is the shipped artifact
A copy of the staging container, including its running state and data, so production starts where staging stopped
A fresh image rebuilt from commit 9d2e55 on the production build agent, since rebuilding from the same commit gives the same result
The image tagged latest, since it always points to the newest build and is the simplest label to deploy
questions.why: The core rule is that one label points to one set of bits, so production should deploy the same published image that staging tested rather than a rebuild or a moving tag.

questions.prompt: In a CI system, what is a build number?
choices: The short hash of the source commit that the build used
A counter the CI system assigns to each pipeline run, unique within that pipeline
The timestamp at which the artifact was published to a feed
The base version written in the project file, shared by every build of that project
questions.why: A build number is a per-run counter assigned by the CI system and is unique only within its own pipeline, while a commit hash names source code and a base version is shared across builds.

questions.prompt: A service in production reports its version as 5.8.1-build.2290. Which piece of information lets an engineer find the exact source code that produced that artifact?
choices: The build number 2290, because it is unique across all pipelines in the organisation
The deployment date, because the pipeline records when each release went live
The base version 5.8.1, because every build of that project shares it
The commit identifier recorded in the artifact metadata for build 2290
questions.why: The commit identifier in the artifact metadata names the exact source the build used, whereas the build number is only unique within one pipeline and the base version is shared across many builds.

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs again for version 3.2.0 after a dependency update and tries to publish 3.2.0 to a feed with different file contents than the first publish. Under an immutable versioning rule, what should happen?
choices: The feed stores both versions under the same label and serves whichever was uploaded last
The publish is refused, and the rebuilt contents must get a new unique version label
The pipeline deletes the feed entry for 3.2.0, republishes it, and keeps the old label in use
The feed overwrites the old 3.2.0 so that consumers always get the newest contents
questions.why: An immutable version can never be overwritten with different contents, so the changed bits need a new unique label such as a new build-number suffix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why each published artifact should get a unique version that is never reused, and name one limit or tradeoff of the scheme you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each time the pipeline publishes, the artifact gets a version built from a base version plus the run's build number, and ideally the commit identifier too. The point is that the version names exactly one set of bits. If the feed refuses to overwrite it, then when someone says rolled back to 1.4.2-build.1041, we know what is running and can reinstall exactly that file. The same file should be promoted from test to production rather than rebuilt, because a rebuild can pull newer dependencies and produce different bits under the same label. The tradeoff is that build-number versions say little to consumers: 1.4.2-build.1042 does not tell a user whether it contains a breaking change. So the base version still has to follow whatever compatibility rules the team uses, and the build number only handles uniqueness and traceability.
rubricPoints: Each published artifact gets a unique version that is never overwritten.
The version traces back to the build run and the source commit.
The same artifact is promoted across environments instead of being rebuilt.
Build-number-based versions give traceability but say little about compatibility.

suggested.rationale: Rolling back to a known earlier build depends on the unique artifact versions this lesson covers, and that mission practises it.

lessons.plain: Quality and release gates are checkpoints that a change must pass before it moves closer to users. Think of a lock on a lift door: it opens only when the conditions are right. Those conditions might be that tests passed, a security scan found no serious problems, a named person signed off, or the live system looks healthy. Governance is the set of rules that decides who may approve what, and which steps can never be skipped. Designing gates well means choosing which conditions matter, where each one sits on the path to production, and what happens when one fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a rule that stops a release from reaching customers if a security scan finds a known critical vulnerability. Where in the delivery path would you put that rule, and what should happen to the release when the rule is not met?
lessons.teach: A quality gate is an automated check that must pass before work is allowed to continue. A release gate is a check placed in front of a deployment, usually to a named target such as staging or production. That named target is called an environment, and it can carry its own rules. A check is a condition attached to an environment or resource. An approval is a check that waits for a person to say yes. Governance means the rules about who may approve, which steps are mandatory, and how decisions are recorded. Why it works: a gate turns a judgement into a condition the system enforces on every run, so nobody has to remember it under pressure. Gates evaluate facts that exist at that moment, such as test results, scan results, the status of open work items, or the live health of a service. Worked example: a pipeline deploys to a production environment, and that environment has three rules. Step 1, a human approval from the release group is required. Step 2, a query confirms that no open work item tagged as a blocking defect exists. Step 3, a check asks the monitoring system whether any critical alert is firing. The pipeline reaches the production stage and pauses. The defect query returns one open item, so the gate does not pass. The pipeline re-evaluates on a schedule and fails at its timeout if the item is still open. Nothing reaches users, and the failure is recorded. Common mistake: treating a security scan as advisory, so it prints a warning nobody reads and never actually blocks. A gate that cannot fail is decoration. Another mistake is a gate with no timeout, which leaves a run waiting forever. Consequence: a missing gate lets a vulnerable or untested build reach customers, while an over-strict gate with no owner pushes teams toward manual overrides that go unrecorded. A release gate is only as useful as the facts it checks and the consequence it enforces.

questions.prompt: A team protects an environment called pre-prod-eu, which runs an invoice service, with three rules. Step 1: a human approval from the platform group is required. Step 2: a scan check passes only if the latest dependency scan reports zero high-severity findings. Step 3 is missing from the team's notes, and it is the rule you must supply. Today the approval has been given and the scan reports 2 high-severity findings, so the gate cannot pass. Which completion of Step 3 keeps the run from waiting forever?
choices: Step 3: the approval is recorded only in the team's chat channel
Step 3: the scan is changed to print a warning instead of blocking the run
Step 3: the scan reruns every hour with no limit on how many times it tries
Step 3: the run is cancelled and marked failed if the gate has not passed within 48 hours
questions.why: A timeout ends a run that would otherwise wait indefinitely, and it records the failure, which is the missing consequence here.

questions.prompt: In a release gate, what distinguishes an approval from a check?
choices: A check always needs a named person, while an approval is fully automatic
They are the same thing, and the two names are used interchangeably
An approval runs after deployment, while a check runs before the build starts
An approval is a check that waits for a person to say yes, while a check is any condition attached to an environment or resource
questions.why: An approval is defined as a check that waits for a person, while a check is the broader term for any condition attached to an environment or resource.

questions.prompt: A booking app's live environment has a gate that queries for open work items tagged sev-1, and the gate passes only when the count is zero. The query returns 3 open items. What happens to the run?
choices: The items are closed automatically and the run proceeds to the live stage
The gate does not pass, so the run waits and fails at its timeout if the items stay open
The gate prints a warning to the log and the run continues
The gate passes because the items are not yet closed
questions.why: The gate evaluates the current facts, and a nonzero count means it does not pass, so the run waits and fails at the timeout if the items remain open.

questions.prompt: A team's container scan finds a critical vulnerability, but the scan is configured only to log the result and never to stop the pipeline. What is the main problem?
choices: Because logs are stored for only a short time, the scan cannot be audited later
Because the scan writes a log, the vulnerability is automatically fixed
Because the scan can never stop a run, it is advisory, so the vulnerable build can still reach customers
Because the scan runs before the build, it cannot find vulnerabilities in the container
questions.why: A check that cannot fail is decoration, so a critical finding that only gets logged lets a vulnerable build pass through to customers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a quality gate and an approval on a production environment, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on gates for security.
lessons.modelAnswer: A quality gate checks facts automatically: tests pass, a scan has no blocking findings, a monitoring signal is healthy. An approval waits for a named person to decide. Both sit in front of a step, but the gate is repeatable and evaluated on every run, while an approval depends on someone being available and on their judgement. On a production environment I would usually combine them: automated checks confirm the build meets the bar, and an approval records who accepted any remaining risk. The main limit is that a gate only checks what it was written to check. If the scan rules are outdated or the tests miss a code path, the gate passes a bad release with a green result, so gates reduce risk rather than prove safety. The tradeoff is time: every extra gate adds waiting, so I would keep gates that catch real failures, and give each one an owner and a timeout.
rubricPoints: A quality gate is an automated condition, while an approval is a human decision recorded against an environment
Gates should be evaluated on every run, so they are repeatable
A gate only checks what it was written to check, so it reduces risk without proving safety
Each gate adds waiting time, so gates need owners, timeouts, and a reason to exist

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style release scenario about which gate fits which risk adds the most here, since no listed mission practises gates directly.

lessons.plain: A testing strategy is a plan that decides which kinds of checks run, where they run, and how often, so that bugs are caught at the cheapest point. Think of building a bridge: you test individual bolts in a workshop, test how sections fit together on site, and load-test the finished span with heavy trucks before opening it. In software, local tests run on your own computer, unit tests check one small piece of code alone, integration tests check that pieces work together with real dependencies such as a database, and load tests check how the system behaves under many simultaneous users. The skill is choosing the right mix and placing each layer in the delivery pipeline.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a team has a suite of quick tests that all pass, what is still unknown about whether the service will work for customers at peak traffic, and why?
lessons.teach:
A unit test checks one small piece of code, such as a single function, with its outside dependencies replaced by stand-ins. It runs in milliseconds and fails for one clear reason. An integration test checks that several real parts work together, for example that the order service really writes to a database and reads the record back. A load test sends a controlled, realistic volume of requests and measures response times and error rates, so you can find the point where the system slows down or fails. A local test is simply a unit or integration check run on a developer's own machine before the code is pushed, which gives the fastest feedback.

Why layer them? Fast tests are cheap and can run often; slow tests are expensive and should run less often. A common shape is many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a few load tests, placed at different pipeline stages: unit tests on every commit, integration tests when code merges, load tests before a release reaches production.

Worked example: a payment function has a unit test that calls the fee calculation with 100 and expects 2.90, with the card processor replaced by a stand-in. Next, an integration test starts a real test database in a container, saves a payment, and reads it back. Last, a load test sends 200 requests per second for ten minutes and records that the 95th-percentile response time stays under 300 ms. Each layer answers a different question.

Common mistake: treating a passing unit suite as proof that the system works with real databases or under load, or running only the slow layers so that feedback arrives too late to act on.

Consequence: if the load test is skipped, a release that passes every quick check can still time out at peak traffic, and the first sign of the problem is a customer-facing outage.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team is building a service that copies stock counts from its warehouse system to the online store. Step 1 is done: a developer runs the copy logic on their own laptop against a fake warehouse feed, which is a local test. Step 2 is done: when code merges, the pipeline starts a real message broker (the queue that carries messages between services) in a container, sends one stock update, and checks that the store's table changed, which is an integration test. Step 3 is defined but not yet placed: the team wants to confirm the service keeps up when 400 stock updates arrive per second, so they will send that volume for ten minutes to a staging broker and check that the message backlog never passes 2,000. Missing step: decide where in the pipeline this load check runs and why.
choices: Replace it with a unit test that replaces the broker with a stand-in, because stand-ins are faster.
Before a release reaches production, because it is slow and measures behaviour at sustained volume.
On every commit, because it gives the fastest feedback of any check.
Run it only on the developer's laptop, because a laptop is the closest place to the real traffic.
questions.why: Load tests are slow and expensive and measure behaviour under sustained volume, so they belong late in the pipeline before a release reaches production, not on every commit.

questions.prompt: In testing terms, what does a unit test do that an integration test does not?
choices: It sends a controlled volume of requests to measure response times.
It checks that several real parts work together.
It checks one small piece of code with its outside dependencies replaced by stand-ins.
It runs the whole system with real databases and queues.
questions.why: A unit test isolates one small piece of code by replacing its outside dependencies with stand-ins, whereas an integration test uses the real parts together.

questions.prompt: A team's unit tests all pass and the release ships, but the next deployment fails because a database schema change does not match what the application writes. Which test layer would most likely have caught this before release?
choices: A local test run on one developer's machine with a mocked database.
An integration test that writes to and reads back from a real test database.
A unit test that checks the fee calculation with a stand-in for the database.
A load test that sends 200 requests per second for ten minutes.
questions.why: Only a check that uses a real database can reveal a mismatch between the schema and the application's writes, so a local integration test on a real database would be the layer that catches it, which is the first option.

questions.prompt: A load test shows that the 95th-percentile response time (the value below which 95 percent of requests finish) stays under 250 ms at 200 requests per second, but jumps to 1,400 ms at 300 requests per second. What is the most useful conclusion?
choices: The release is safe, because the average response time at 300 requests per second is still under one second.
The unit tests must be rewritten, because the slowdown is in the code logic.
The system has a capacity limit between 200 and 300 requests per second that should be investigated before release.
The load test is faulty and should be discarded, because the results are inconsistent.
questions.why: A sharp jump in response time between two load levels reveals a capacity limit that the load test was designed to find, so it should be investigated before the release reaches production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only written unit tests why we also need integration and load tests, and name one limit or tradeoff of running the slow layers on every commit.
lessons.modelAnswer: Unit tests are great at catching logic mistakes in one function, but they replace the database and other services with stand-ins, so they cannot show that our code really talks to those services correctly. Integration tests use real parts, like a test database, to catch wiring and data problems that unit tests miss. Load tests answer a different question entirely: does the system still respond quickly and reliably when many users arrive at once? Each layer covers a blind spot of the others. The tradeoff is cost and time. Integration and load tests are slower and need more infrastructure, so running them on every commit can make feedback take many minutes and cost real money. A sensible approach is to run unit tests on every commit, integration tests when code merges, and load tests before a release, so the expensive checks still happen before anything reaches customers.
rubricPoints: Unit tests isolate one piece of code and miss problems with real dependencies.
Integration tests check that real components work together, such as a database.
Load tests check response times and error rates under realistic volume.
Slower layers cost time and money, so they are placed at suitable pipeline stages.

suggested.rationale: That mission exposes the gap between tests that pass on a laptop and tests run in CI, which is the core reason a layered testing strategy needs deliberate placement.

lessons.plain: Running tests inside an automated pipeline means the machine that builds your software also runs its checks every time someone changes the code, so a broken change is caught before it reaches users. The pipeline step that starts the checks is a test task, the machine that does the work is an agent, and the report of which checks passed or failed is shown back on the pipeline run. Think of a factory line with a quality inspector at one station: the inspector marks each part pass or fail, and the line stops on a fail. This objective is about setting up that station so the tests are both run and their results are readable.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer's change makes one of 400 unit tests fail on their laptop, but the pipeline reports only a red job with no detail. Before any teaching, what should the pipeline do with that change, and what should the team be able to see about which test failed and why?
lessons.teach:
A test is a small automated check that runs code and compares the result with an expected answer. In a pipeline, a test task is the step that starts a test runner, the program that finds and executes the tests and reports the outcome. An agent is the machine or container that runs the job; it must have the language tools and the test runner installed, because a test task cannot run tests it cannot start. Most runners can write a results file in a standard layout such as JUnit XML or TRX. A publish step uploads that file so the pipeline run shows each passed, failed and skipped test, instead of only a green or red job.

The mechanism is simple. The runner exits with a code: zero means every test passed, and any other value means something failed. The pipeline reads that code and marks the job failed. Publishing the results file adds detail, so someone can open the run and see the failing test's name and message.

Worked example. Step one: the agent fetches the code. Step two: the test task runs the suite and writes results to a file. Step three: one test fails, so the runner exits with a non-zero code. Step four: the publish step is set to run even after a failure, so the failed test name appears on the run. Step five: the job is marked failed and later stages, such as deployment, are skipped.

Common mistake: setting the test step to continue on error so the build stays green. The failure is hidden, and a broken change can move on to deployment.

Consequence: if the results file is never published, or its path is wrong, the team sees a red job with no reason, and diagnosis becomes slow. Test results should be published even when tests fail, because that is when the evidence matters most.

questions.prompt: A small team at a bakery-ordering company runs a JavaScript test suite with Jest on a hosted agent. The steps are: 1) the agent fetches the code and installs its packages; 2) the test task runs Jest and writes a JUnit XML results file to reports/junit.xml; 3) Jest reports two failing tests in the checkout-totals module, and the runner exits with code 1; 4) a publish step, set to run even after a failure, uploads reports/junit.xml so the two failed test names appear on the run. Step 5 is not yet filled in: the pipeline reads the non-zero exit code from step 3 and marks the job. What is the correct outcome for the job, and for the deployment stage that comes after it?
