choices: The job is retried automatically until Jest exits with code 0, and then deployment runs.
The job is marked succeeded with warnings, and the deployment stage runs but the two failed tests are removed from the report.
The job is marked failed, and the deployment stage is skipped.
The job is marked succeeded because the failing results were published, so the deployment stage runs as normal.
questions.why: A non-zero exit code from the runner makes the pipeline mark the job failed, and the later deployment stage does not run, while publishing the results only adds the failure detail.

questions.prompt: In a pipeline, what does a test runner's exit code tell the pipeline?
choices: How many tests were written in total, so the team can track coverage over time.
Which individual test names failed, so the failed test appears by name on the run page.
Whether the tests passed: zero means every test passed, and any other value means something failed.
How long the test suite took, so slow suites can be flagged for splitting.
questions.why: The runner exits with zero when every test passes and a non-zero value otherwise, and the pipeline uses that code to decide whether the job fails; the names of failing tests come from the published results file, not the exit code.

questions.prompt: A team's pipeline agent is a Linux machine with Python installed, but the Go toolchain and the go test runner are not installed on it. The team adds a test task that runs go test ./... on that agent. What is the most likely result?
choices: The publish step creates a results file that replaces the missing toolchain.
The tests run in a sandbox the agent creates automatically, so they pass.
The job is skipped with no error, since no tests were found to run.
The test task fails before any Go test runs, because the agent cannot start the runner it needs.
questions.why: An agent must have the language tools and test runner installed, because a test task cannot run tests it cannot start, so the failure happens at startup rather than inside the tests.

questions.prompt: A team's test step writes its results to test-output/results.xml, but the publish step is configured to look for results/junit.xml. The tests all pass. What will the learner most likely see on the pipeline run?
choices: A green run with a warning that the results were published with zero tests.
A failed run that names the exact path mismatch, because the publish step reports its own error.
A green run with every test listed by name, because passing tests are always shown.
A red run with no reason attached, because the results file was never found at the configured path.
questions.why: When the publish path is wrong, the file is never uploaded, so the run shows no test detail; the learner should see the run without per-test results, and the description in the choice is the misconception being tested, which is why the correct option here is the one stating the run carries no detail, not a named error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a failing test in a pipeline stops a change from being released, and name one limit or tradeoff of running the full test suite on every commit.
lessons.modelAnswer: A test task runs the test runner on an agent, and the runner's exit code tells the pipeline whether everything passed. A non-zero code fails the job, so later stages such as deployment do not run and a broken change cannot move on automatically. I would also publish the results file, so the failing test name and its message show on the run without digging through raw logs. The tradeoff is time: running a full suite on every commit makes feedback slower and uses agent minutes, so teams often run fast unit tests on every commit and heavier integration or load tests less often. Another limit is flaky tests, which fail intermittently and erode trust in the signal. Those need tracking and fixing, not blanket retries that hide the problem.
rubricPoints: The test runner's exit code determines whether the pipeline job passes or fails.
A failed job stops later stages such as deployment from running.
Publishing the results file shows which individual tests failed and why.
A tradeoff such as run time, agent cost, or flaky tests is named and reasoned about.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a red CI pipeline makes the learner read failing test output and fix the step that reports it, which is the core of wiring test results into a run.

lessons.plain: Code coverage analysis measures how much of your program the automated tests actually run. Think of checking a building by counting which rooms an inspector walked through. If the inspector never entered the kitchen, you know the kitchen is unchecked, even if the rest passed. A build pipeline can run the tests, record which lines and decisions were exercised, and publish that number so the team sees it on every change. It tells you where testing is missing. It does not tell you whether the tests check anything useful.
lessons.guessPrompt: A test suite passes and reports 90 percent coverage. Before reading on, name one thing that 90 percent could still hide about the quality of the code.
lessons.teach:
Code coverage is the share of your code that ran while the tests were executing. Two measures matter most. Line coverage counts the executable lines that ran at least once. Branch coverage counts the decision outcomes, such as the true and false sides of an if statement, that ran at least once. Branch coverage is usually the stricter and more useful number, because a line can run even when one of its possible paths never does.

A coverage tool instruments the code during the test run and records what executed. The result is written to a report in a standard format, commonly Cobertura or JaCoCo XML. A pipeline then publishes that report, so each run shows a percentage, and a gate can fail the build when the percentage falls below a threshold. Good pipelines usually apply the threshold to new or changed code, so old untested code does not block every change at once.

Worked example. A function applies a discount: if the customer is a member, it subtracts 10 percent; otherwise it leaves the price alone. The only test passes a member. Step 1: the if line runs, and so does the discount line, so line coverage looks fine at 2 of 3 executable lines, about 67 percent. Step 2: the else path never runs, so branch coverage is 1 of 2 outcomes, 50 percent. Step 3: the report exposes the gap, and a developer adds a non-member test.

Common mistake: treating a high percentage as proof of good tests. A test that calls the code and asserts nothing raises coverage while catching no bugs. Coverage shows what ran; assertions decide what was checked.

Consequence: in a running pipeline, a gate set too high pushes people toward empty tests, and one set too loosely lets untested changes ship. The threshold is a policy choice, not a measure of quality.

questions.prompt: A small function retries a failed request. If the attempt count is below 3, it tries again. Otherwise it raises an error. The test suite has one test, where the attempt count is 1, so the retry runs. There are three executable lines: the if line, the retry line, and the raise line. Step 1: the if line and the retry line ran, so line coverage is 2 of 3, about 67 percent. Step 2: only the true side of the if ran, so branch coverage is 1 of 2 outcomes, 50 percent. Step 3: a second test is added where the attempt count is 3, so the error path runs. What is the branch coverage now?
choices: 50 percent
75 percent
67 percent
100 percent
questions.why: Branch coverage counts the true and false outcomes of the if, and the new test makes both run, so 2 of 2 outcomes is 100 percent.

questions.prompt: A team's report shows 90 percent line coverage but only 40 percent branch coverage. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The tests failed to compile, so the numbers are stale
Many decisions have one side, true or false, that no test has run
The coverage gate has been set to the wrong file type
The code contains too many duplicate lines for the tool to count
questions.why: A line can run while one path through a decision never runs, so a high line figure with a low branch figure points to untaken decision outcomes.

questions.prompt: A repository gate requires 80 percent coverage on new or changed code only. Old code has 200 untested lines that are not part of this change. A pull request adds 20 new lines, and 15 of them run during tests. What happens?
choices: The build passes because the 200 untested lines are included in the overall figure
The build fails because new code coverage is 75 percent, below the 80 percent threshold
The build passes because 15 is more than half of 20
The build is skipped because the gate only applies to old code
questions.why: Only the 20 changed lines count toward the gate, and 15 of 20 is 75 percent, which is under the 80 percent threshold.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a test that calls a discount function but contains no assertions. The team's coverage rises from 60 percent to 85 percent. Why does this not prove the tests now catch more bugs?
choices: Coverage can only rise when the test uses a mocking library
Branch coverage falls when a test has no assertions, so the rise is offset
Coverage tools ignore any test that has no assertions, so the figure is wrong
Coverage only records which code ran, and without assertions nothing checks whether the results are correct
questions.why: Coverage measures execution, while assertions are what check results, so a test with no assertions can raise coverage without catching anything.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what code coverage tells you, what it cannot tell you, and one tradeoff in setting a coverage gate in the pipeline.
lessons.modelAnswer: Coverage tells us which lines and branches ran while the tests executed, so it shows where testing never reaches. It cannot tell us whether the tests check the right results, because a test with no assertions still raises the number. So a high percentage is a sign of reach, not of correctness. The tradeoff with a gate is the threshold. Set it high and people write hollow tests just to pass; set it low and untested changes slip through. Many teams enforce the bar on new code only, so legacy code does not block every change, and they review assertions in code review alongside the number.
rubricPoints: Coverage measures which code ran during tests, not whether the results are correct.
Line coverage and branch coverage differ; branch coverage reveals untested decision paths.
Assertions are what make a test check behaviour; coverage alone does not.
A gate threshold trades off between blocking progress and encouraging hollow tests.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers coverage reporting, and explaining what the number does and does not prove is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Deployment automation is software that takes a finished build of your application and puts it where people or other systems use it, the same way every time, without someone clicking through steps by hand. Choosing a tool means deciding where the instructions live, which machines carry them out, and how approvals and access are controlled. Two common choices are GitHub Actions, which runs workflows next to code hosted on GitHub, and Azure Pipelines, Microsoft's service for building and releasing code from many hosts, with close integration into Azure. Both read a file of steps stored alongside the code. The right pick depends on where your code lives, where your environments run, and how your team wants approvals and access handled.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your code is hosted on GitHub and your production servers run in Azure. Before you read further, what single factor would most affect whether you pick GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines, and why?
lessons.teach:
Deployment automation is the set of steps that moves a built version of software into an environment such as a test or production system. A pipeline is the defined sequence of those steps, usually written as a file stored with the code. A runner or agent is the machine that actually executes the steps. A trigger is the event that starts a run, such as a push to a branch. An environment is a named target, such as production, that can carry its own secrets and approval rules. An approval gate is a pause that waits for a named person to accept before the run continues.

The choice between GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines turns on four questions: where the code is hosted, where the runners execute, how identity and secrets are granted to the deploy step, and how approvals are modelled. Tools that sit next to the code tend to be simpler for code on that host. Tools with deep integration into a cloud provider tend to be simpler for deploying to that cloud.

Worked example: code lives on GitHub, production runs on Azure, and production needs a human approval. A push to the main branch triggers the workflow file. A build job runs on a hosted runner and produces an artifact. A deploy job names the production environment. That environment requires a reviewer, so the job pauses. After approval, the job runs with credentials scoped only to production, and nothing else can read them.

Common mistake: choosing a tool by familiarity alone, or storing production credentials where every branch can read them. Consequence: if approvals live only in a chat message rather than in the environment rule, a deploy can happen without the review anyone assumed was there.

The deployment tool is a separate decision from the deployment strategy, which decides how traffic moves to a new version.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps its code in Azure DevOps Repos and deploys a tracking service to a staging environment. The setup has four steps. Step 1: the pipeline file on the main branch runs a build stage that publishes a package. Step 2: the staging environment is created with a checks rule that requires the operations lead to approve. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the deploy stage runs using the staging connection, and no other stage can read it. Which statement fills step 3?
choices: The deploy stage names the staging environment, so the approval rule applies before it starts.
The team copies the staging credentials into a repository variable so the build stage can read them.
The build stage is moved onto a hosted runner so it can see the approval status.
The team sends the approval request by email and records the reply in the ticket.
questions.why: The approval rule belongs to the named environment, so the deploy stage must reference that environment for the pause to take effect.

questions.prompt: Which term describes the machine that actually executes the steps of a pipeline run?
choices: An environment
An approval gate
A trigger
A runner or agent
questions.why: The teaching text defines a runner or agent as the machine that executes the steps, while a trigger starts a run, an environment is a named target, and an approval gate is a pause.

questions.prompt: A release manager assumed a production deploy could not run until a senior engineer approved it in a chat thread, but the production environment had no approval rule attached. What is the consequence?
choices: The pipeline refuses to start because the approval is missing.
The deploy can run without any formal review, because the review existed only in chat.
The build is re-run automatically to collect the approval.
The deploy job pauses until the senior engineer replies in the chat thread.
questions.why: Approvals enforced only in a chat message are not part of the environment rule, so the pipeline has nothing to pause on and the deploy can proceed unreviewed.

questions.prompt: A team's code is hosted on GitHub, but the deploy step must reach a server inside a private network that a cloud-hosted runner cannot see. Which of the four decision questions does this scenario mainly answer?
choices: How approvals are modelled
Where the code is hosted
Where the runners execute
How the deployment strategy moves traffic
questions.why: The problem is about which machine can reach the target, which is the question of where the runners execute, not where the code lives or how approvals work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines for a team whose code is on GitHub and whose production runs on Azure. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with where the code and the runners live, because that drives most of the setup cost. Code on GitHub with workflows beside it makes GitHub Actions the simpler default, since triggers and reviews are already there. Because production is on Azure, I would still check how the deploy job authenticates, ideally with a federated identity scoped to one environment rather than a long-lived password. The tradeoff is that if we later need many pipelines across repositories on other hosts, or classic release-style approvals across stages, Azure Pipelines may fit better. I would also check that runner maintenance is owned by someone, because self-hosted machines need patching whichever tool we pick.
rubricPoints: Names where the code is hosted and where the runners execute as the first decision factors
Explains that deploy credentials should be scoped to an environment and not shared broadly
Gives a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen tool
Notes that approvals must be enforced by the tool, not by convention

suggested.rationale: Choosing a deployment tool from a scenario with competing constraints is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation rather than reading a feature list.

lessons.plain: When a pipeline runs, something has to do the work: fetch the code, run the build, run the tests. That worker is called a runner (GitHub's name) or an agent (Azure DevOps' name). You can use workers the vendor keeps running for you, or run your own machines and register them with the service. Designing this layer means choosing where the workers live, how many you need, what they cost, what they are allowed to reach on the network, and how you keep them updated and healthy over time. Getting it wrong shows up as slow queues, surprise bills, or builds that cannot reach the systems they must deploy to.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's build takes four minutes on a shared cloud worker, but one deployment step must reach a database that sits inside your company's private network. Which kind of worker would you expect that deployment step to need, and why?
lessons.teach:
A runner or agent is a program on a machine that asks the CI/CD service for queued jobs, downloads each job's steps, runs them, and reports the results back. There are two families. A hosted worker is provisioned and patched by the vendor, starts from a clean image for each job, and is billed by minutes used or by a count of parallel jobs. A self-hosted worker is a machine you own or rent, such as a virtual machine or a container host, where you install the runner software and register it into a group (called a pool or runner group) that jobs can target by label.

Why it works: the service only hands jobs to whichever registered workers are free and match the label. So four questions decide the design. Cost: hosted workers charge per minute and per concurrent job, while self-hosted workers cost the machine plus the time to maintain it. Licences: the number of jobs that can run at once is usually capped by a purchased or included parallel-job allowance, so adding workers does not help if that cap is the bottleneck. Connectivity: a self-hosted worker usually only needs outbound access to the service, but it must reach any private targets such as a database or internal registry. Maintainability: someone must patch the operating system, update the runner software, and remove stale files.

Worked example: a deployment job is labelled for the private network. First, the job is queued. Second, a registered self-hosted worker with that label and a free slot picks it up. Third, it connects to the internal database. Fourth, it reports success. If no worker carries that label, the job waits in the queue indefinitely.

Common mistake: keeping one long-lived self-hosted worker and reusing it for every job, so files and credentials from one job leak into the next. Prefer ephemeral workers that are discarded after each job, or at least clean up between jobs.

Consequence: when the only worker with the right label goes offline, every deployment queues silently until someone notices.

Designing this layer means matching the worker type to cost, licence limits, network reach and upkeep, rather than defaulting to one choice.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its deployments on four self-hosted agents, all registered to one pool and all idle, yet twelve release jobs are waiting in the queue. The team traces the problem step by step. Step 1: the queue shows twelve jobs waiting with the label 'release-west'. Step 2: the four agents show as idle and carry that label, so they are free and matching. Step 3: the account's purchased parallel-job allowance is two, so the service will start only two jobs at once no matter how many agents are free. Step 4: the team needs to decide the fix. The correct next move is to ____
choices: buy additional parallel-job allowance, because the licence cap, not the number of free agents, is what limits running jobs
raise the timeout on each release job, because jobs are waiting for their time limit to run
move all release jobs onto hosted workers with a larger image, because hosted workers ignore the parallel-job cap
add eight more self-hosted agents to the pool, because more machines always means more running jobs
questions.why: When the licence's parallel-job cap is the bottleneck, adding more free workers cannot start more jobs, so the cap itself must be raised.

questions.prompt: A pipeline job is labelled 'gpu-build'. What does that label do?
choices: It names the job in the logs so people can read it more easily.
It sets how much graphics memory the job is allowed to use.
It tells the service which registered workers are allowed to pick up the job.
It encrypts the job's secrets so only that job can read them.
questions.why: Labels are how the service matches a queued job to a registered worker, so only workers carrying the matching label can take it.

questions.prompt: A company runs about 300 short test jobs a day on hosted workers. Each job needs to query a database that sits on a private network with no public address. Which option fits best?
choices: Have each developer run the tests on their own laptop.
Register a self-hosted worker inside the private network, with outbound access to the service, and label it for these test jobs.
Buy more hosted parallel jobs so the tests finish sooner.
Open the database to the public internet so hosted workers can reach it.
questions.why: A self-hosted worker placed inside the network can reach the private database while needing only outbound access to the service, whereas a hosted worker cannot reach it without exposing the database.

questions.prompt: A team has used one long-lived self-hosted worker for six months. A new job's log now shows a credential that a previous job wrote to a temporary folder. What is the root cause and the right fix?
choices: The worker keeps files and credentials between jobs; use ephemeral workers that are discarded after each job, or clean up between jobs.
The hosted parallel-job allowance was exceeded; buy more hosted allowance.
The worker's disk is too small; attach a larger disk to the virtual machine.
The label on the worker is too short, so the wrong job picked it up; lengthen the label.
questions.why: Reusing one long-lived worker carries leftover files and credentials from one job into the next, so the fix is to discard workers after each job or clean them thoroughly between jobs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose self-hosted workers over hosted ones, and name one limit or tradeoff you would have to manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would choose self-hosted workers when a job needs something the hosted workers cannot reach, such as a private database, an internal package registry, or hardware with special requirements. Hosted workers are simpler because the vendor patches them and gives each job a fresh machine, but they cannot see inside our network. The main tradeoff is upkeep: we would own the operating system patching, the runner software updates, and the cleanup between jobs. The second tradeoff is licensing. Parallel jobs are limited by our allowance, so adding machines does not speed up the queue if that allowance is the real bottleneck. To manage both, I would keep self-hosted workers ephemeral where possible, label them clearly so jobs only land on the right ones, and monitor for offline workers so a silent queue never goes unnoticed.
rubricPoints: Explains that hosted workers are vendor-managed while self-hosted workers run on machines the team owns
Connects self-hosted workers to private network reach or special hardware needs
Names upkeep as a real cost: patching, updates, and cleaning up between jobs
Notes that parallel-job licence limits can bottleneck the queue regardless of worker count

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through cost, licence, connectivity and upkeep tradeoffs and explaining the choice back, which fits explain better than a single mission.

lessons.plain: When a team keeps its code in a shared place (a repository, which is a version-controlled folder of files and their full change history), they often want a separate automated service to build and test that code each time someone changes it. Connecting the two means setting up a trust relationship so the pipeline service can read the code and report results back, plus a trigger so that a new change starts a run. It works a bit like a kitchen that is told when a new order arrives and sends the finished dish back to the counter.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer pushes a commit to a feature branch and opens a pull request into main. Without any further setup, what do you think the pipeline service would need in order to run tests on that commit and show the result on the pull request?
lessons.teach:
A repository (repo) is the version-controlled store for code, and a branch is a named line of changes within it. A commit is one saved set of changes. A pipeline is an automated sequence of build and test steps. In this setup, the pipeline definition is usually a YAML file kept inside the repository itself, so the steps change along with the code. A trigger is a rule that starts a pipeline run, such as a push to a branch or the opening of a pull request. Authorization is the grant that lets the pipeline service read the repository and write results back; the connection between the two services stores that grant, often through an app installed on the repository or an OAuth grant tied to a user. A status check is a pass or fail report attached to a specific commit, and a branch protection rule can require particular status checks to pass before a pull request may merge.

Why it works: the code host sends an event to the pipeline service, the service fetches that exact commit, runs the YAML steps, and posts a status back to the commit. Worked example: a developer opens a pull request from feature-x into main. The host sends a pull request event. The pipeline service checks out the commit, runs the unit tests, and posts the status build passed. Branch protection on main sees the required check is green and allows the merge. If the tests fail, the status is red and the merge button stays blocked.

Common mistake: the connection is authorized with one person's account, and when that person leaves or loses repository access, every pipeline stops. Another frequent error is leaving the status check off the required list, so a red build can still merge into main and reach the release pipeline.

In a running system, the required check is the safety net between a developer's change and production. Without it, the trigger still runs but nothing stops broken code from advancing.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps its parcel-api repository on GitHub, with its pipeline defined in a YAML file inside that repository. A developer opens a pull request from hotfix-17 into release. Step 1: the code host sends a pull request event to the pipeline service. Step 2: the service checks out that exact commit and runs the test steps, and all of them pass. Step 3 is missing. Branch protection on release requires a status check named build-and-test before a merge is allowed. What completes the chain?
choices: The host deletes the pull request as soon as the event is sent, so no merge is needed.
The branch protection rule runs the tests a second time on the release branch before it reads any status.
The service posts a passing status named build-and-test to that commit, so the protection rule sees a green check and allows the merge.
The service copies the hotfix-17 commit into release directly, which skips the need for any status.
questions.why: The pipeline service reports its result as a status attached to the specific commit, and branch protection reads that status to decide whether the merge may proceed.

questions.prompt: A team stores its pipeline steps in a YAML file. A developer on a feature branch edits that file to add a lint step, then opens a pull request. Which version of the steps runs for that pull request?
choices: No steps run until the YAML file is copied into a separate pipeline settings page.
The steps from whichever branch was most recently merged into main.
The steps from the feature branch commit being built, because the YAML lives in the repository and changes with the code.
The steps from the main branch, because the pipeline always reads its definition from the default branch.
questions.why: Because the pipeline definition is stored in the repository, the pipeline service fetches the YAML from the exact commit it is building, so the feature branch's version of the steps is the one that runs.

questions.prompt: A pipeline connection to a company's GitHub repository was authorized through an OAuth grant tied to a contractor's personal account. The contractor's access to the repository is removed on Friday. What is the most likely result on Monday?
choices: The pipelines stop, because the grant the connection relies on is tied to an account that no longer has repository access.
The pipelines switch automatically to the repository owner's account without any action from the team.
The pipelines keep running because the grant is copied to the service and no longer depends on the account.
Only pull request triggers stop, while push triggers continue to work normally.
questions.why: A grant tied to one person's account is only valid while that account can read the repository, so losing that access stops every pipeline that depends on the connection.

questions.prompt: A repository's branch protection on main requires a status check named unit-tests to pass. The team renames the job in the YAML to unit-test, singular. A developer opens a pull request, and the pipeline posts a passing status named unit-test. What happens when the developer clicks merge?
choices: The merge is allowed only after an administrator manually confirms the status name.
The merge goes through, because the protection rule automatically renames required checks to match the YAML.
The merge goes through, because a passing status from the pipeline is enough regardless of its name.
The merge stays blocked, because no passing status named unit-tests exists for the required check to read.
questions.why: A required check is matched by name, so a passing status under a different name does not satisfy the protection rule and the merge remains blocked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a single git hosting tool how a GitHub repository is connected to Azure Pipelines, what starts a run, and one limit or tradeoff of that connection.
lessons.modelAnswer: The repository stays on GitHub, and Azure Pipelines is granted permission to read it, usually through an installed app or an authorized connection. The pipeline definition is a YAML file in the repo, and a trigger, such as a push to a branch or a pull request, causes the service to fetch that exact commit and run the steps. The result comes back as a status check on the commit or pull request. The tradeoff is that the connection's authority depends on whoever set it up; if that person's account is removed, runs can break, so the grant should be tied to a shared or app identity. Another limit is that changes from outside forks may not get access to secrets, so a pipeline that needs secrets must be designed with that in mind. Finally, a passing status only means something if the check is marked required in branch protection.
rubricPoints: Describes the grant that lets the pipeline service read the repo and report status back
Explains that a trigger such as a push or pull request starts the run
Notes that the pipeline definition lives in the repo as YAML
States that a status check blocks merging only when marked as required
Names a limit such as dependence on one person's account or restricted secret access for forks

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix how a pipeline authenticates to an outside service without exposing the credential, which is the core skill behind the service connection.

lessons.plain: A trigger rule decides what automatically starts a pipeline run. Think of a mail sorter that only picks up certain letters. Some events, like someone saving new code to a shared repository, should start a build. Others, like a change to documentation only, may not need one. A few runs happen on a clock, such as a nightly check. Good trigger rules run the right checks at the right time without wasting machine time or hiding problems, so the team gets fast, trustworthy feedback.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's build runs for every change, including edits to the README, and takes 40 minutes, so the queue is always full. Without knowing any tool names, what rules would you write so that builds start only when they are useful, and what risk does each rule add?
lessons.teach:
A trigger is an event that starts a pipeline run. A trigger rule is the filter that says which events count. The common event types are: a push, where code lands on a branch; a pull request, where a proposed change to be reviewed and merged is opened or updated, so checks run before it lands; a schedule, a timed run defined with a cron expression (a short time pattern such as every night at 02:00); a tag, a named marker on a commit often used to mark a release; and a pipeline completion, where one pipeline starts when another finishes. A manual run is started by a person.

Most rules include or exclude specific branches and tags. Path filters look at which files changed, so a rule can ignore edits to a docs folder. Batching is another option: while one run is busy, further pushes are grouped so that only one new run starts after it finishes.

Why it works: the pipeline runs only when an event matches the rule. A documentation change can skip a 40-minute build, while a push to the main branch always gets the full build and deploy path.

Worked example: a repository has a main branch and feature branches. The rule triggers on pushes to main and on pull requests targeting main, with a path filter that excludes docs/. Step 1: a developer pushes to feature/login. That is not main, so no push run starts. Step 2: they open a pull request into main that changes src/auth.py. That matches, so validation runs. Step 3: they edit only docs/setup.md and push to main. The path filter excludes docs/, so no run starts.

Common mistake: a path filter that is too narrow, such as one that forgets a shared build script or a dependency lock file. A real change then merges without triggering any checks.

Consequence in a running system: a skipped run means that change has no recorded evidence of passing checks, so trigger rules must be reviewed whenever the repository layout changes.

questions.prompt: A team keeps a repository with a develop branch and a release branch named release/2.4. Their trigger rule starts a pipeline on pushes to release/* and on tags that match v*, and it has a path filter that excludes the images/ folder. Step 1: a developer pushes a commit to develop. That does not match release/*, so no run starts. Step 2: a developer pushes a commit to release/2.4 that changes only images/logo.png. The path filter excludes images/, so no run starts. Step 3: a developer pushes a commit to release/2.4 that changes both src/api.py and images/logo.png. Result: ?
choices: A run starts, because at least one changed file, src/api.py, is outside the excluded folder.
No run starts, because the commit touches a folder the path filter excludes.
No run starts, because a path filter drops the entire commit once any excluded file appears in it.
A run starts, because any push to a release branch always runs regardless of path filters.
questions.why: A path filter only removes events where every changed file is excluded, so the src/api.py change is enough to start a run.

questions.prompt: A team wants their security scan to run every weekday at 06:30 whether or not anyone has pushed code. Which trigger type fits, and how is the timing written?
choices: A tag trigger, written as the name of the release marker
A push trigger on every branch, with a path filter set to the scan folder
A schedule trigger, written as a cron expression for 06:30 on weekdays
A pipeline completion trigger that waits for the build pipeline to finish
questions.why: A schedule is the timed trigger type, and a cron expression is the time pattern that defines when it fires, so it runs at the set time without needing a code event.

questions.prompt: A monorepo pipeline has a path filter that lists only the services/billing/ folder. The build also reads a shared package-lock.json at the repository root. A developer merges a change that only edits package-lock.json. What is the most likely result?
choices: The pipeline does not run, so the dependency change lands with no recorded evidence of passing checks.
The pipeline runs but skips the build step because the changed file is outside the filter.
The pipeline runs the billing tests only and reports the lock file change as passing.
The pipeline runs on the merge because lock files are always included by default.
questions.why: Because the path filter is too narrow and omits the shared lock file, the change matches no rule, so no checks run and the merge has no recorded validation.

questions.prompt: A deployment pipeline has batching turned on. While one run is still in progress, three pushes arrive on the main branch. When the busy run finishes, how many new runs start?
choices: Three, one for each push, queued in the order they arrived.
One, which covers all three pushes that were grouped while the first run was busy.
Zero, because batching cancels pushes that arrive during an active run.
One for each push that changed a file, skipping the others.
questions.why: Batching groups the pushes that arrive while a run is busy so that only one new run starts after it finishes, rather than one run per push.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which events should start our build pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff of filtering runs by path or branch.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd start from what each event is for. Pushes to the main branch should always run the full build and deploy path, because that is what gets shipped. Pull requests into main should run the same checks before merge so problems are caught before they land. Feature-branch pushes can wait for a pull request, which saves minutes of compute. Scheduled runs suit slow checks like a nightly dependency scan. For path filters, I'd skip runs when only documentation changes. The tradeoff is risk: if a filter is too narrow, say it leaves out a shared build script or a lock file, a change can merge with no checks at all. So I'd keep a broad rule for anything that affects how the software is built, and review the filters whenever the repository layout changes.
rubricPoints: Matches each event type (push, pull request, schedule, tag, manual) to a clear purpose
Explains that branch and path filters save time but can skip checks that are needed
Names a concrete risk, such as a shared file that changes without triggering any checks
Recommends reviewing filters as the repository layout changes

suggested.rationale: Choosing which trigger fits a situation is a reasoning task that an exam-style scenario practises better than reading a list.

lessons.plain: A pipeline is an automated sequence of steps that takes code from a change to a built, tested and deployed result, so people do not have to run each step by hand. Writing the pipeline as a YAML file means describing those steps in a plain text file that sits next to the code. Think of it as a recipe card stored in the same folder as the ingredients. Anyone can read it, changes to it are reviewed like any other change, and the same card produces the same dish each time someone follows it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted every change to your application to be tested and built the same way every time, why might you store the list of steps as a file in the same repository as the code rather than clicking through a web form each time?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline is an automated sequence of steps that builds, tests and deploys code when something changes. In Azure Pipelines, a pipeline can be defined in a YAML file, a plain text format that uses indentation to show structure, stored in the same source repository as the code. Its main parts are: a trigger, which names the branch whose changes start a run; a stage, a major phase such as build or deploy; a job, a unit of work inside a stage that runs on one agent, meaning the machine that executes it; and a step, a single action inside a job, such as running a script or a built-in task. A pool setting chooses which group of agents may run a job.

Why it works: because the definition lives in source control, changes to the pipeline are reviewed and versioned like any other code, and the same file gives the same run each time. The service reads the file, schedules each job onto a free agent, and records the logs.

Worked example: a file says trigger on main, then has one stage called Build with one job called Compile. The job has three steps: install dependencies, run tests, publish output. When someone pushes to main, the service starts a run, assigns Compile to a free agent, runs the steps in order, and stops the job at the first failing step, so later stages do not run.

Common mistake: assuming that two jobs share files or variables. Jobs usually run on separate agents, so a file created in one job is absent in another unless it is published as an artifact and downloaded there.

Consequence: a pipeline that deploys from an unprotected branch lets any merged change reach production, so the trigger and branch rules decide what actually runs. The pipeline file is part of the release's design and deserves the same care as the application code.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a YAML pipeline on branch release-3. The Build stage has two jobs. Job Package runs on one agent (the machine that executes a job) and runs these steps: 1) restore packages, 2) compile the app into a folder called out/, 3) create out/fleet.zip. Job Scan is also in the Build stage and runs on a different agent, and its only step is to check the checksum of out/fleet.zip. When Scan runs, it fails with 'file not found'. The missing step is in Package: after step 3, the pipeline must publish out/fleet.zip as a named pipeline artifact (a file saved by the run so later jobs can download it). Scan then needs its own step to download that artifact before the checksum check.
choices: Increase the number of agents in the pool so Scan lands on the same machine as Package
Change the trigger from release-3 to main so both jobs see the same branch files
Move Scan into a separate Deploy stage so it runs after Build finishes
Publish out/fleet.zip as a pipeline artifact at the end of Package
questions.why: Jobs usually run on separate agents and do not share files, so the file must be published as an artifact in the producing job and downloaded in the consuming job.

questions.prompt: In a YAML pipeline, which part decides which group of agents is allowed to run a given job?
choices: The step list
The trigger
The pool setting
The stage name
questions.why: The pool setting chooses the group of agents that may run a job, while the trigger starts runs and steps are the individual actions inside a job.

questions.prompt: A job has five steps. Step 4 fails with a non-zero exit code. A later stage is set to run after this one. Which outcome matches how the service handles the run?
choices: Steps 1 to 3 run, step 4 fails, step 5 does not run, and the later stage does not run
Step 4 is retried automatically, then steps 5 onward run
Steps 1 to 5 all run, and the failure is only logged at the end
Steps 1 to 4 run in parallel on separate agents, and step 5 runs on a free agent
questions.why: The job stops at the first failing step, so later steps in that job are skipped, and a later stage does not run when an earlier one fails.

questions.prompt: A team lead asks why the build pipeline definition for a mobile app is kept as a YAML file inside the app's source repository instead of only being configured through a web form. Which answer best explains the benefit?
choices: Agents refuse to run jobs unless the definition is stored as a file in the repository
Storing the file in the repository makes each run faster because the logs are kept locally
The YAML file is reviewed and versioned like other code, so changes to the pipeline can be traced and reproduced
The web form cannot store a trigger, so the YAML file is the only way to start a run
questions.why: Because the definition lives in source control, its changes are reviewed and versioned, and the same file gives the same run each time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a YAML pipeline in Azure Pipelines is, how stages, jobs and steps relate, and one limit you should watch for when you split work across jobs.
lessons.modelAnswer: A YAML pipeline is a definition of our build and release process, kept as a text file in the same repository as the code, so changes to it get reviewed and versioned like code. The file nests three levels. A stage is a major phase such as build or deploy. A job inside a stage is a unit of work that runs on one agent, which is the machine that does the execution. A step inside a job is a single action, like running a script. The order and dependencies between stages and jobs decide what waits for what. The main limit to watch is that jobs normally run on different agents, so files and variables created in one job are not there in another unless we publish them as artifacts or pass them as outputs. If we forget this, a deploy job will fail because the build output it expects is missing.
rubricPoints: Defines a YAML pipeline as a definition kept in source control and versioned with the code
Explains that stages contain jobs and jobs contain steps, and that a job runs on one agent
States that jobs typically run on separate agents so files and variables do not carry over automatically
Names a practical way to pass work between jobs, such as publishing and downloading artifacts

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner read and correct the stage, job and step structure, which is the core of writing YAML pipelines.

lessons.plain: A pipeline is the automated assembly line that builds, tests and ships software. This objective is about deciding which of its pieces run one after another and which run side by side. Picture a kitchen: some dishes can be cooked at the same time, but plating only starts once every component is ready, and service opens only after the kitchen signs off. Getting that order right makes a pipeline faster without making it less safe. Getting it wrong either wastes time waiting on work that could have run together, or ships something before its checks have finished.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your pipeline has three test jobs that do not depend on each other and one deploy job that must wait for all three. Should the three test jobs run one after another or at the same time, and what would you need to decide before answering?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. A step is a single action, such as running a script. A job is a group of steps that runs on one agent, which is the machine or container that does the work. A stage is a named group of jobs, usually representing a phase such as build, test or production. A dependency is a rule that one unit must finish successfully before another starts; in Azure Pipelines YAML it is written with dependsOn. A condition decides whether a unit runs at all, for example only when the branch is main.

Why it works. Jobs with no dependency between them are eligible to run in parallel, limited by how many agents and parallel-job slots your organization has. The scheduler reads the dependency graph, starts every unit whose prerequisites are met, and holds the rest. Parallelism saves wall-clock time; dependencies protect correctness.

Worked example. Stage Build contains jobs LinuxTests and WindowsTests with no dependency between them. Step by step: both start together; each takes about six minutes, so the stage finishes in about six minutes instead of twelve; both succeed; job Package, which lists both test jobs in dependsOn, now starts; Package succeeds; stage Deploy, which depends on stage Build, starts.

Common mistake. Leaving out a dependency. If Package does not list the test jobs, it can start as soon as an agent is free and package output that has not been tested.

Consequence. In a running system, a missing dependency means an artifact can reach production before its tests report, and a failed test does not stop the deploy. Every ordering choice is a safety statement about what must be true before the next step is allowed to begin.

questions.prompt: A team has stage Scan with two jobs, Lint and Audit, that have no dependency between them. Lint takes 3 minutes and Audit takes 7 minutes. Job Publish lists only Lint in dependsOn and takes 2 minutes. Stage Release lists stage Scan in dependsOn. Trace it: both jobs start at minute 0. Lint succeeds at minute 3, so Publish starts and finishes at minute 5. Audit succeeds at minute 7. Stage Release starts at minute ___.
choices: Minute 5, when Publish finishes
Minute 7, when the slowest job in Scan finishes
Minute 10, after Publish and Audit each take a full extra run
Minute 3, as soon as Lint finishes
questions.why: A stage dependency waits for the whole stage to finish, so Release cannot start until every job in Scan, including the slower Audit job at minute 7, has completed successfully.

questions.prompt: A stage contains job Unit, which takes 5 minutes, and job Integration, which takes 8 minutes. There is no dependency between them and enough agents for both. Roughly how long does the stage take?
choices: 8 minutes, because the jobs run side by side and the stage ends with the slowest one
5 minutes, because the first job to finish ends the stage
13 minutes, because the jobs run one after the other
3 minutes, because the gap between the two times is the total saving
questions.why: Independent jobs run in parallel, so the stage's wall-clock time is set by its longest job, here 8 minutes.

questions.prompt: Job Package has no dependsOn entry, and job Tests in the same stage fails. What is the main risk?
choices: Package may run and produce output that was never tested, because the failed test does not stop it
Package is held back until Tests is fixed, so nothing is lost
Package runs only after Tests is retried and passes
Package is cancelled automatically whenever any job in the stage fails
questions.why: Without a dependency, Package is not waiting on Tests, so it can start as soon as an agent is free and package untested output, which is the missing-dependency failure the text describes.

questions.prompt: A team needs job Notify to start only after jobs BuildWin and BuildLinux both succeed. Which configuration is correct?
choices: dependsOn: BuildWin, then a second Notify entry for BuildLinux
dependsOn: [BuildWin, BuildLinux]
A condition that the branch is main, with no dependsOn entry
dependsOn: [BuildWin] only, because BuildLinux will finish first
questions.why: Listing both jobs in dependsOn makes Notify wait for each of them to succeed, whereas a condition only decides whether a unit runs at all and does not control what it waits for.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we split our pipeline into stages and parallel jobs instead of one long sequential job. Explain the tradeoff, and name one limit on how much parallelism you actually get.
lessons.modelAnswer: Splitting work into jobs that have no dependency on each other lets them run at once, so the total time approaches the length of the longest job instead of the sum of all of them. Stages add a clearer boundary: each stage can be an environment with its own approvals and conditions, so we can stop before production without re-running the build. The tradeoff is complexity. More dependencies mean more places to get the order wrong, and a job that is missing a dependsOn can run before its tests finish. The practical limit on parallelism is capacity: the organization has a fixed number of parallel job slots and agents, so if we queue many jobs at once, some will wait for a free agent and the speed-up disappears.
rubricPoints: Independent jobs run in parallel by default, which cuts wall-clock time.
Dependencies (dependsOn) and stages enforce that tested work is what gets deployed.
Stages give natural points for environment checks such as approvals.
Parallelism is capped by available agents and parallel-job slots.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline usually means finding a wrong dependency or ordering mistake, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: This is about running a team's automated build and release steps on the right kind of computer. A pipeline is a chain of automatic steps, such as compiling code, testing it and shipping it, that starts whenever code changes. Some of that work can run on machines the cloud vendor supplies and throws away afterwards. Other work needs a machine your team controls, such as one inside a private office network that can reach an internal database or a special device. Mixing these two kinds of machine, and preparing the team's machines from a saved template so they are all alike, is what complex pipeline setups are about. Think of a restaurant where head office plans the menu but some dishes must be cooked in your own kitchen.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your build runs fine on the cloud vendor's default machines, but the deploy step must reach a database that exists only inside your company network. Where would you expect that step to run, and what would you need to set up first?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline is an automated sequence of steps, such as build, test and deploy, that runs each time code changes. The machine that actually executes the steps is called a runner in GitHub or an agent in Azure Pipelines. A hosted runner or agent is supplied by the service and discarded after each job. A self-hosted one is a machine your team owns and registers with the service so it picks up jobs. A pool is a named group of agents that a job can be assigned to. A hybrid pipeline mixes the two kinds: the service schedules every stage, but some stages run on hosted machines and others on self-hosted machines inside your network. A VM template is a saved master image of a virtual machine with the operating system, SDKs and tools already installed, so every machine built from it starts identical.

Why it works: the service only needs to send instructions and receive results, so the machine doing the work can sit wherever the work needs to be. Self-hosted machines keep their state between jobs, which makes them useful but also means they can drift unless they are rebuilt from a template.

Worked example: a team deploys into a private network. Step 1, the build stage runs on a hosted agent, which cannot see the private network and does not need to, since it only compiles code. Step 2, the deploy stage is assigned to a pool named private-linux. Step 3, the service sends that job only to an online self-hosted agent registered in the pool. Step 4, that agent, built from a VM template, connects outward to the service, pulls the artifact and reaches the internal database. Step 5, when the team needs a fresh agent, it rebuilds from the template rather than patching the old one by hand.

Common mistake: assuming a self-hosted agent is simply a faster hosted one. It is not reset between jobs, so a leftover file or secret from one run can affect the next, and you are responsible for its patching and security.

Consequence: if a job's pool has no online agents, the job waits in a queue and the release stalls, even though the pipeline definition is correct.

questions.prompt: A retail firm called Brightwater runs its pipeline like this. A pool is a named group of agents that a job can be assigned to, and an agent is the machine that executes the steps. Step 1: the build stage runs on a hosted agent supplied by the service and produces a package. Step 2: the deploy stage is assigned to a pool named store-ops, which holds self-hosted agents inside the company's store network. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the agent that took the job connects outward to the service, downloads the package and writes it to the store's inventory server. Which step is missing between Step 2 and Step 4?
choices: The team opens inbound firewall ports from the internet so the service can push the job into the store network.
The deploy stage is moved into the build stage so it runs on the hosted agent instead.
A self-hosted agent in store-ops is registered with the service and is online, so the service can send it the deploy job.
The package is copied onto a hosted agent's disk so the store agent can read it without the service.
questions.why: The service only sends work to an agent that is registered in the pool and online, and that agent then connects outward to fetch the job and artifact.

questions.prompt: A fintech team wants to know what a self-hosted agent is. Which description is accurate?
choices: A saved disk image that holds the operating system and tools so new machines start identical.
A named group of agents that a job can be assigned to, rather than a single machine.
A machine the service supplies and discards after each job, so nothing carries over between runs.
A machine your team owns and registers with the service so it can pick up jobs from a pool.
questions.why: A self-hosted agent is a machine you own and register with the service; the other options describe a hosted agent, a VM template, and a pool.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's pipeline must run an integration test against a reporting database that can only be reached from its corporate network. The team currently uses a hosted agent for that stage. Which change fits the requirement?
choices: Use a second hosted agent in another region, which can reach the database through the internet.
Remove the test stage, because hosted agents cannot run any tests at all.
Keep the hosted agent and give the reporting database a public IP address.
Assign the test stage to a pool of self-hosted agents registered from inside the corporate network.
questions.why: Self-hosted agents inside the network can reach internal resources, while a hosted agent cannot see the private network and so cannot run this test.

questions.prompt: A payments firm has a pool named ledger-prod whose only self-hosted agent was switched off for maintenance. The pipeline YAML is valid and the deploy stage is now queued. What happens next?
choices: The job is discarded and the build stage is repeated automatically on a new agent.
The pipeline fails immediately with a syntax error about the missing agent.
The job stays queued and the release stalls until an online agent registers in ledger-prod, even though the definition is correct.
The service runs the deploy on a hosted agent instead, since no self-hosted agent is online.
questions.why: A job assigned to a pool with no online agents waits in the queue, so the release stalls even when the pipeline definition itself is correct.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should move every pipeline job onto self-hosted machines because they are faster and cheaper. Explain to them how hosted and self-hosted machines differ, when a hybrid pipeline makes sense, and one limit or tradeoff of self-hosted machines that we must manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: Hosted machines are supplied by the service and wiped after each job, so every run starts clean and the vendor handles their base upkeep. Self-hosted machines are ours: they stay registered to the service, keep their state between jobs, and can reach things a hosted machine cannot, such as an internal database. So they are not automatically faster or cheaper. Running everything on them means we pay for the machines, keep their operating system and tools patched, and risk leftover files or secrets carrying from one job into the next. A hybrid pipeline keeps the clean hosted machines for compiling and testing and uses a self-hosted machine only for the stage that needs private access. We build those machines from a VM template so they stay identical, and we rebuild rather than hand-patch them. The main tradeoff is that we take on security and maintenance in exchange for network reach.
rubricPoints: Hosted machines are supplied and reset by the service, while self-hosted machines are owned, kept between jobs and maintained by the team.
Self-hosted machines are needed when a job must reach private networks, on-premises resources or special hardware.
A hybrid pipeline mixes hosted and self-hosted stages, using each where it fits.
A VM template gives every self-hosted machine the same tools and configuration, and rebuilding is safer than hand-patching.
Tradeoff: self-hosted machines add patching, security and cost responsibility and can carry state between jobs.

suggested.rationale: Choosing hosted, self-hosted or hybrid for a given scenario is an exam-style judgement that a short situation to reason through teaches better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: When many projects need the same build or deploy steps, copying them into every project means fixing a bug in many places. Reusable pipeline pieces let you write a step list once and plug it in wherever it is needed, the way a function is written once and called from many places. You also pull settings such as a server name or a version number out of the steps into named values, so the same recipe can run for test or for production. This lesson covers the four common ways Azure DevOps does this: YAML templates, task groups, variables, and variable groups.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose ten repositories each have a copy of the same five build steps, and the team needs to add one new step to all of them. What would be the hard part, and how would you make the change once?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A pipeline is an automated sequence of build and release work. A step is one action inside it. A template is a separate YAML file holding steps, jobs or stages that other pipelines include by reference. A parameter is an input you pass into a template when it is included; it is fixed when the pipeline is expanded, before any job runs. A variable is a named value, such as an environment name, that steps read when they run. A variable group is a named set of variables stored centrally in the Azure DevOps library, which many pipelines can link to, and whose entries can be marked secret. A task group is a named bundle of tasks created in the web interface and reused across classic-style pipelines; it is an older mechanism than YAML templates, and new work usually favours templates.

Why it works: a reusable element is edited in one place, so a fix reaches every pipeline that includes it on its next run. Parameters and variables keep the reusable piece generic while each caller supplies the specifics.

Worked example. A template file build-steps.yml declares a parameter buildConfig with default Release, and contains a build step that uses that value. A pipeline includes it with a template reference and passes buildConfig set to Debug. Step by step: the service reads the calling pipeline, substitutes Debug into the template, expands the steps into the pipeline, and only then starts the run. The build runs in Debug.

Common mistake: storing a password as a plain value in a YAML file committed to source control. Anyone who can read the repository can read it, and it remains in the history even after deletion. Put secrets in a secret variable or in a variable group backed by a vault.

Consequence: a broken template breaks every pipeline that includes it on its next run, so changes to shared templates need the same review care as shipping application code.

questions.prompt: A team at Northwind Parcels has a pipeline named ingest-service that links the variable group ingest-settings. The group holds queueName set to ingest-q-07 and storageKey marked secret. A deploy step prints queueName when it runs. Here is the sequence so far: 1) A run is queued and the service attaches the linked group to it. 2) A maintainer edits queueName in the library to ingest-q-09 while no run is active. 3) [missing step] 4) The deploy step runs and prints ingest-q-09. Which statement correctly fills step 3?
choices: The next run's deploy step reads queueName from the library when it runs, so it gets ingest-q-09.
The storageKey secret is decrypted and written into the deploy step's log so the new queueName can be shown.
The service copies ingest-q-07 into the pipeline's YAML file so the old value stays fixed.
The already finished run is updated in place so that its deploy step prints ingest-q-09.
questions.why: Steps read variables when they run, and the variable group is central, so the next run picks up the current value rather than one saved earlier.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants one template that builds a container image, and each calling pipeline must choose the image tag before any job starts. Which mechanism should they use for the tag?
choices: A variable read by the build step at run time
A parameter passed in when the template is included
A task group edited in the web interface
A secret variable stored in a variable group
questions.why: A parameter is an input passed when the template is included and is fixed when the pipeline is expanded, which is before any job runs.

questions.prompt: A developer needs a database password available to several pipelines and wants to avoid exposing it in source control. Which approach fits?
choices: Paste it into each pipeline's step as a plain value so each pipeline is self-contained
Mark it secret in a variable group backed by a vault and link that group to each pipeline
Store it in a plain variable in the template's parameter default
Commit it to a YAML file in a private repository so that only the team can read it
questions.why: Secrets belong in a secret variable or a variable group backed by a vault, which keeps the value out of committed files and lets many pipelines share it.

questions.prompt: A team edits a shared template to add a step, and the edit contains a syntax error. What is the likely consequence?
choices: Only the template's own test pipeline fails, and calling pipelines keep using the previous version
Every pipeline that includes the template fails on its next run until the template is fixed
Pipelines already running are switched mid-run to the new template and fail there
Nothing happens until someone manually re-includes the template in each pipeline
questions.why: A template is expanded into each calling pipeline at its next run, so a broken template breaks all of them, which is why shared templates need the same review as application code.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would put a step in a YAML template instead of a variable group, and name one limit of the template approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A YAML template is for reusable structure: the steps, jobs or stages that should look the same across pipelines, with parameters for the parts that differ. A variable group is for reusable values: settings such as endpoints, feature switches or secrets that several pipelines need to read. So if three services all need the same test-and-package sequence, that goes in a template. If they all need the same staging database address, that goes in a variable group. The limit of templates is that parameters are fixed when the pipeline is expanded, so they cannot change based on a value that only appears during the run. A second limit is that a change to a shared template takes effect on every consumer at its next run, so a mistake spreads quickly.
rubricPoints: Templates hold reusable structure such as steps, jobs or stages, and groups hold reusable values
Parameters are fixed at expansion time, so they cannot depend on values produced during the run
A change to a shared template reaches every pipeline that includes it
Secrets belong in secret variables or vault-backed groups, never in committed YAML

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner read and change pipeline definitions, which is where templates and variables are used.

lessons.plain: When software is released to a live system, many teams want a person to say yes first, and want certain rules checked before anything is installed. In Azure Pipelines, an environment is a named place the software goes, such as test or production. You can attach checks to that place: people who must approve, times when deploys are allowed, and branches that are permitted to deploy. The pipeline file names the place it deploys to, and the place decides whether the deploy may go ahead. It is a bit like a building with a security desk: the visitor's badge alone does not open the door.
lessons.guessPrompt: If any developer can edit the pipeline file on a feature branch, what would stop that developer from pushing unreviewed code straight to production, and where would you put that protection?
lessons.teach:
An environment, in Azure Pipelines, is a named deployment target such as dev, test or production. A deployment job is a job in a YAML pipeline that declares which environment it deploys to, and it is the job type that gets gated. Checks are rules attached to an environment that must pass before any deployment job targeting it starts. An approval is one kind of check: named people must click approve. Other checks include branch control (only certain branches may deploy), business hours, an exclusive lock so only one run deploys at a time, and a call to an external service or REST endpoint that returns pass or fail.

Why it works: the gate lives with the target, not with the pipeline file. The YAML only says deploy here; the environment decides who may let it through. Because a run cannot skip the checks on the environment it targets, editing the YAML alone does not remove the approver.

Worked example: a pipeline has a build stage and a deploy stage. The deploy stage contains a deployment job whose environment is production. Step one: the build succeeds and publishes an artifact. Step two: the deploy stage is queued and the deployment job waits before running any step. Step three: the environment's checks run; branch control confirms the run came from the release branch. Step four: two approvers are asked and one approves before the timeout. Step five: the job starts and its steps run. If nobody approves before the timeout, the job fails and no deployment step ever runs.

Common mistake: assuming a deploy step is gated when it sits outside a deployment job that references an environment, or writing an approval into the YAML and expecting it to be enforced. Such steps run straight through.

Consequence: on a running system, an unguarded production environment lets a bad commit reach customers minutes after it is merged, which is why approvals and branch control belong on the environment.

questions.prompt: A payments company, Larkspur Pay, has a pipeline with a deploy stage. The stage contains a deployment job that targets an environment named staging-eu, which has an exclusive lock check attached. An exclusive lock is a check that lets only one run deploy to an environment at a time. Run 41 starts first. Step one: run 41's deployment job is queued and its environment checks run. Step two: the lock is free, so the check passes and run 41 acquires the lock. Step three: run 41's deployment job starts and its steps deploy the build. Step four (missing): run 42, triggered while run 41 is still deploying, reaches its own deployment job targeting staging-eu. Which outcome correctly completes step four?
choices: Run 42 deploys alongside run 41, because the exclusive lock only applies to approvals and not to deployments.
Run 42's deployment job starts at once and the lock check runs afterwards, once its steps have already begun.
Run 42's deployment job waits until run 41 releases the exclusive lock, and its steps run only after the lock check passes.
Run 42 skips the lock check, because its YAML file does not list the lock check itself.
questions.why: The exclusive lock is a check on the environment, so run 42's deployment job must wait for it to pass, which only happens once run 41 releases the lock.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a deployment job in an Azure Pipelines YAML file?
choices: A scheduled trigger that starts the pipeline every night regardless of what the environment's checks say.
A job that runs on the build agent and copies the artifact to a shared folder without naming any target.
A job that declares which named environment it deploys to, and is the job type that checks and approvals can gate.
A reusable template file that stores the approval list so several pipelines can share one set of names.
questions.why: A deployment job is defined by naming the environment it targets, and that link is what allows the environment's checks to gate it.

questions.prompt: A team at Quillfeather Labs writes an approval list into the YAML of a pipeline that deploys to a plain job, not a deployment job, with a script step that copies files to a server. The environment named prod-west has two approvers configured in the portal, but the script step is outside any deployment job. A run starts. What happens?
choices: The run fails at the start, because approvals written in YAML are rejected by the service.
The script step runs straight through, because no environment check is attached to a step outside a deployment job.
The approval list in the YAML pauses the script step until one named person clicks approve.
The two portal approvers are asked, and the script step waits until both of them approve.
questions.why: Checks are attached to environments and only gate deployment jobs that reference them, so a script step in a plain job runs without any gate, and an approval written in YAML is not enforced.

questions.prompt: A product team at Brightmoss Health attaches a REST check to an environment named billing-live. The check calls an external change-freeze service, which returns fail on Friday afternoons. A run is triggered on a Friday at 15:00 and its deployment job targets billing-live. What is the correct result?
choices: The deployment job starts immediately, because external checks only send warnings and never block a job.
The deployment job does not start and none of its deployment steps run, because the check did not pass.
Only the approval checks run, and the REST check is ignored because approvals take priority over it.
The deployment job starts, but the deploy steps are skipped and the run is marked as succeeded.
questions.why: A check must pass before any deployment job targeting its environment starts, so a failing REST check stops the job before any step runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an approval check on an environment differs from a condition written in the pipeline YAML, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on approvals.
lessons.modelAnswer: A condition in the YAML is part of the pipeline file, so whoever can edit that file on a branch can change or remove it. An approval check is attached to the environment that the deployment job targets, so the run has to pass it no matter what the YAML says, and the pipeline cannot skip it. The tradeoff is that approvals add waiting time: a deploy can sit until a person responds, and if the timeout passes the job fails and the release is delayed. Also, checks are only as strong as the permissions around them, since anyone allowed to change the environment's settings can change its checks. So I would pair approvals with branch control and restrict who can edit environment settings.
rubricPoints: An environment is a named deployment target, and checks such as approvals are attached to it rather than written in the pipeline YAML.
A deployment job that references the environment pauses until the checks pass, before any of its steps run.
Approvals add human waiting time and fail the job if they time out or are rejected.
Checks depend on who can edit the environment settings, so access control must also be restricted.

suggested.rationale: Environment checks are mostly configured through the Azure DevOps console and a YAML reference, so reading the setup steps and rules is the fastest way to learn them.

lessons.plain: A deployment strategy is the plan for how a new version of software replaces the old one in front of real users. Instead of switching everyone at once and hoping nothing breaks, you pick a pattern that limits how many people are affected if something goes wrong. Blue-green keeps two identical environments and moves all traffic at once. Canary sends a small slice of users to the new version first. Rings widen exposure in ordered groups. Feature flags switch a behavior on or off without redeploying. A/B testing compares two versions to see which one performs better. Each pattern trades speed, cost, and risk differently.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a new version of your app has a bug that only shows up under real traffic, would you rather send it to all users at once or to about 5% of users first? Why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment strategy is a chosen way of exposing a change to users, so that the blast radius of a bad release stays small and rollback stays quick. Blue-green deployment means running two production-like environments: blue serves live traffic, green holds the new version, you test green, then switch the router so traffic moves to green. Rollback is switching back to blue. A canary release routes a small share of traffic, such as 5%, to the new version, watches error rate and latency, and only increases the share if the signals stay healthy. Ring deployment releases to ordered groups, for example internal staff, then a beta group, then everyone.
