A feature flag is a runtime switch that lets code ship turned off and be enabled later for some users, which separates deployment from release. A/B testing splits users between two variants and compares a business metric, such as checkout completion, to pick a winner.

Worked example: a service gets 10,000 requests per minute. You send 5% (500 requests per minute) to the new version. Its error rate is 0.8% while the old version sits at 0.1%. Step one: the canary metrics breach the threshold you set in advance. Step two: you set the canary share to 0%, so all traffic returns to the old version. Step three: you fix and retry from a small share.

Common mistake: assuming a feature flag rolls back a database change. If the new code also altered the schema, turning the flag off does not undo that schema change, so the old code may fail. Another mistake is running a canary on too little traffic: 1% of 200 requests per minute is only two requests, which cannot reveal a 1% error rate.

A canary is only as trustworthy as the traffic and metrics behind it. Choose a strategy that matches how much signal you can actually observe.

questions.prompt: A payments API at a different company receives 4,000 requests per minute. The team routes 10% of traffic (400 requests per minute) to the new version. The new version's error rate is 0.2% and the old version's is 0.15%. The team set an alert threshold of 1.0% before the release. Step one: the canary receives 400 requests per minute. Step two: the canary's 0.2% error rate is below the 1.0% threshold, so its signals are healthy. Step three is missing and must be filled in: the team should ______.
choices: raise the canary share in controlled steps, such as 25% then 50%, while watching the same error and latency signals and keeping the old version available for rollback
switch all traffic to the new version at once, since the canary was healthy, and delete the old version immediately
turn the feature flag off, because a healthy canary means the change is unsafe to keep
keep the canary at 10% for the rest of the week and then call the release finished
questions.why: After healthy signals, the canary share is increased in controlled steps while the same metrics are watched, and the old version stays available so traffic can return to it quickly.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a ring deployment?
choices: Two identical production environments where live traffic is switched from one to the other through a router, with the previous one kept for rollback
Splitting users between two variants and comparing which one produces more completed purchases over time
A runtime switch that hides new code from users until someone enables it for a chosen group
Releasing a change to ordered groups of users, such as internal staff first, then a beta group, then everyone
questions.why: A ring deployment is defined by releasing to ordered groups that widen step by step, which is the only option describing that pattern.

questions.prompt: A team deploys new checkout code to production on Monday but keeps the new screen hidden. On Thursday they make it visible to everyone by changing one setting, without redeploying. Which technique makes this possible?
choices: A/B testing, which compares two variants on a sales metric before choosing one
Blue-green deployment, which needs a second environment that the router is switched to
Ring deployment, which moves a change through ordered groups of users one at a time
A feature flag: a runtime switch that separates deploying code from releasing it to users
questions.why: A feature flag lets code be deployed turned off and enabled later with a runtime setting, which is what separates deployment from release in this case.

questions.prompt: A team runs a canary on 0.5% of 300 requests per minute, expecting it to catch a 1% error rate. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: Only about 1.5 requests per minute reach the canary, too few to show a 1% error rate reliably
Canaries never work below 10% of traffic, so the team should use blue-green deployment instead
The canary is too large, which would slow the whole service down for every user across all regions at once
The 1% error rate is too high to be a realistic target for any canary to detect in production
questions.why: 0.5% of 300 requests is 1.5 requests per minute, and so few requests cannot reveal a 1% error rate with any reliability.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between blue-green and canary for a change to a payment service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from what can go wrong and how fast we need to undo it. For a payment service, a bad change can cost money quickly, so I want a small blast radius. A canary sends a few percent of real payments to the new version and compares error rates and latency against the old version before increasing the share. Blue-green is simpler to reason about and gives an instant full switch back, but it exposes every customer at the moment of the switch, and it doubles the environment cost. My tradeoff with canary is that it needs enough payment volume and good metrics to detect a problem in the small slice, and if the change alters a shared database, rolling back the traffic does not undo the data changes. So I would check the schema compatibility first, whichever strategy I pick.
rubricPoints: Defines blue-green as two environments with a traffic switch and instant rollback
Defines canary as a small traffic share widened only when metrics stay healthy
Links the choice to blast radius, cost, or speed of rollback
Names a real limit, such as cost of duplicate environments or needing enough traffic to see a signal
Notes that rolling back traffic does not undo shared data or schema changes

suggested.rationale: Choosing between strategies under specific risk constraints is best practised in the planned deployment strategies engine, which the listed missions do not cover.

lessons.plain: When one piece of software depends on another, the other must be in place first. Think of a new kitchen appliance that needs a power socket installed before anyone plugs it in. Deploying a system with several connected parts works the same way: a shared database schema, a library, or a backend service has to go live before the things that rely on it, or those things fail at start-up. A deployment pipeline is the automated line that moves changes into live environments, and designing it for ordering means deciding which steps wait for which, and checking that each one has actually finished well before the next one begins.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app and the database schema change it needs ship together in one release, and the pipeline starts both at the same moment. What can go wrong, and what single change to the pipeline would prevent it?
lessons.teach:
A dependency is anything a deployment needs to exist or be healthy before it can run correctly, such as a database schema, a shared package, a message queue, or another service's interface. A dependency deployment is the act of putting one of these into an environment. Ordering means making sure each dependency is deployed and verified before the things that rely on it. In a pipeline this is expressed as a directed graph: each step lists the steps it must wait for, and the system runs steps in an order that respects those links. The graph must contain no loops, because a loop means two steps each wait for the other and nothing ever starts. In Azure Pipelines YAML, the dependsOn keyword on stages and jobs declares these waits, and conditions decide whether a waiting step runs after an earlier failure. It works because a step that starts only after its prerequisite has succeeded can never read a half-written schema or call a service that is not yet listening.

Worked example: an order service needs a new column in its database. Step 1, the Database stage runs the schema migration. Step 2, a verification job checks that the column exists and that the migration is recorded as complete. Step 3, the Order service stage declares dependsOn Database and runs only if verification succeeded. Step 4, the Order service deploys and its health check passes. Step 5, the release is marked complete.

Common mistake: placing the database migration and the application in parallel stages because both appear in the same release, or treating 'job finished' as 'dependency ready'. A job can finish while the service it started is still warming up, so the pipeline should wait on a health check or another real readiness signal.

Consequence in a running system: if the application starts before the migration, requests fail with errors about missing columns until the migration completes, and rolling back the application alone may not restore order. Ordering the pipeline keeps the sequence of changes predictable.

questions.prompt: A team ships a shared logging package, version 2.4, to an internal feed, and a reporting service imports it. Their pipeline has these steps: 1) a Package stage publishes version 2.4 to the feed; 2) a smoke job installs 2.4 on a clean test agent and confirms the import resolves; 3) [NOT SHOWN: this is the one step you must supply]; 4) the Reporting stage deploys and its health check passes; 5) the change is marked complete. Which choice fills step 3 so the reporting service deploys only after the package is proven?
choices: The Reporting stage runs in parallel with the Package stage so that both finish inside the same release window and the team saves time.
The Reporting stage sets its condition to always() so it deploys even if the smoke job fails.
The Reporting stage declares dependsOn for the Package stage and runs only if the smoke job succeeded.
The Reporting stage declares dependsOn for itself so the version is locked before it deploys.
questions.why: A dependsOn declaration makes the Reporting stage wait for the Package stage, and the smoke job's success condition ensures it starts only after the package is verified.

questions.prompt: In Azure Pipelines YAML, what does a dependsOn keyword on a stage or job do?
choices: It declares which steps must succeed before this one starts, so the run is ordered.
It retries the named stage automatically whenever it fails, up to three times, without any logs being kept.
It assigns the stage to a specific agent pool for faster execution.
It copies the named stage's variables into the current stage at run time.
questions.why: dependsOn declares the waits in the directed graph, and the system runs each step only after the steps it lists have finished in the required way.

questions.prompt: A Search team stage rebuilds an index, and a Storefront API stage that queries that index is declared with no dependsOn, so the two run side by side. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The API may start serving queries before the index is rebuilt, so searches return empty or partial results until the rebuild finishes.
The pipeline refuses to start and reports a dependency loop between the two stages, so nothing deploys at all.
The API stage waits automatically until the index rebuild reports complete, so no bad results occur.
The index is deleted as soon as the API starts, which keeps both stages consistent.
questions.why: Without a dependsOn link the API stage is not forced to wait, so it can call an index that is not yet ready, which is the ordering failure the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A stage starts a message broker container with a job that finishes in 10 seconds, and the next stage depends on that job. The broker takes 40 seconds to accept connections. What should the pipeline wait on instead of the job finishing?
choices: A readiness check that confirms the broker accepts connections.
Whether the next stage's name is recorded in a variable.
A fixed one-hour sleep added to the job after it finishes, to be safe against slow starts.
The job's exit code of zero alone.
questions.why: A job finishing does not mean the service it started is ready, so the pipeline should wait on a real readiness signal such as a health check.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design a pipeline so that a shared library and two services that use it deploy in the right order, and name one limit or tradeoff of strict ordering.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would model the library as its own stage that publishes a versioned package, then give each service stage a dependsOn on that library stage so neither can start early. Each stage should end with a readiness check, not just a finished job, so the services only start once the library version they need is actually available. The tradeoff is speed: strict ordering serialises work that could otherwise run in parallel, so a slow library stage delays every service and lengthens the whole release. Parallel services can still run side by side after the library is ready. Ordering also does not fix a version mismatch on its own, so the services should pin the library version they were built against.
rubricPoints: Names the dependency as a stage or job that must finish and pass a readiness check first.
Explains that dependsOn or an equivalent declares the wait and that the graph must not contain cycles.
States a concrete tradeoff, such as added total duration from serialised steps.
Notes that a completed job is not the same as a dependency being ready for use.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style release where several dependent parts must deploy in order adds the most, since the skill is choosing the right ordering structure for a given situation.

lessons.plain: Downtime is the time users cannot use a service. When you ship a new version, the simplest approach stops the old copy and starts the new one, and users see errors in the gap. Minimizing downtime means changing software while still serving users. Three common techniques help: a load balancer, which spreads requests across several copies of an application and skips broken ones; a rolling deployment, which updates those copies a few at a time; and a deployment slot, which is a second, live-like copy of an app that you can prepare separately and then switch into the public address in one quick step.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app runs on two identical servers behind a load balancer. You want to ship a new version without users seeing errors. Would you update both servers at the same moment or one after the other, and why?
lessons.teach:
Terms first. A load balancer is a traffic distributor that sits in front of several copies of an application and sends each request to a healthy copy. A health check is a periodic probe that asks a copy whether it is responding correctly, and the balancer skips any copy that fails. A rolling deployment replaces copies a few at a time, so the rest keep serving. A deployment slot is a separate, live-like instance of an app with its own address, where you deploy the new version and warm it up, meaning let it start and load before it takes real traffic. A swap then exchanges which version holds the production address, usually within seconds.

Why it works: users only reach copies that are running and passing health checks, so a release never removes all capacity at once. Keeping the previous version intact is what makes rollback fast, because switching back is just another swap or another batch.

Worked example: four app servers sit behind a load balancer, and the rolling update uses batches of one. Step 1: the balancer stops sending traffic to server A. Step 2: A receives the new build and passes its health check. Step 3: A rejoins the pool. Step 4: the same steps repeat for B, C and D. At every moment three servers are serving traffic.

Common mistake: assuming a swap or rolling update is safe when the new version changes a database schema that the old code cannot read. Rolling back the code does not undo the data change, so the old version may fail.

Consequence: if a rollout skips health checks, a broken build joins the pool, and the balancer sends real users to it, turning a partial problem into a full outage.

Downtime is reduced by keeping healthy capacity serving while the new version comes in, and by keeping the old version ready to switch back to.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company keeps a live production slot and a preview slot. Step 1: the team deploys version 3.1 into the preview slot. Step 2: they warm up preview and confirm the seat map loads correctly. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: version 3.0 now sits in the preview slot, so switching back is simply another swap. Which completion fills the missing step 3?
choices: Delete version 3.0 from the production slot before anything else happens
Swap the preview and production slots so version 3.1 takes the production address
Scale the preview slot down to zero instances so it stops using memory
Restore the database from last week's backup so the old code can read it
questions.why: A swap exchanges which version holds the production address, so after step 3 version 3.1 serves users and version 3.0 moves to the preview slot, which is what step 4 describes.

questions.prompt: A team runs five instances behind a load balancer and performs a rolling update with batches of one. Which statement about capacity during the update is correct?
choices: At most one instance is out of rotation at a time, so four keep serving traffic
The balancer sends all traffic to the newest instance until the rollout finishes
Users see a pause of about ten minutes while each instance is updated in turn
All five instances are taken out of rotation at once and restarted together
questions.why: A rolling update replaces copies in small batches, so with batches of one the other four healthy copies keep serving while each one is updated.

questions.prompt: A rolling update across six instances skips health checks, and one instance receives a broken build. What is the most likely result?
choices: Only the deployment log shows an error, and the broken copy stays idle outside the pool
The old copies stop serving, so the rollout automatically reverts to the previous version
Users never reach the broken copy, because the balancer routes traffic at random and skips new builds
The broken copy joins the pool and real users reach it, turning a partial problem into a full outage
questions.why: Without health checks nothing stops a failing copy from rejoining the pool, so the balancer sends real traffic to it and a partial fault can spread to full outage.

questions.prompt: A team plans to warm up a staging slot and then swap it into production. The new release renamed a database column that the old code still reads. What is the main risk to rolling back?
choices: The swap will take several minutes because the slot address must be reassigned
Rolling back by swapping again may fail, because the old code cannot read the changed data
The health checks will pass, so the new version will be marked as safe to keep
The warm-up step will permanently delete the production address
questions.why: Swapping back restores the old code but not the old data layout, so a schema change the old code cannot read makes the rollback unsafe even though the swap itself is fast.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a rolling deployment and a slot swap each keep a service available during a release, and name one limit or tradeoff of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A rolling deployment updates instances in small batches behind a load balancer. The balancer takes one instance out, the instance gets the new build, it passes a health check, and then it returns to the pool, so the remaining instances keep serving users. The limit is that old and new versions run side by side during the rollout, so both must handle each other's requests and data formats. A slot swap works differently. The new version is deployed and warmed up in a separate slot that has its own address, so users are unaffected while it is prepared. Then the two slots exchange their production routing in a quick step. Rollback is another swap. The tradeoff is cost and configuration: you pay for a second copy of capacity during the release, and settings that should stay with a slot must be marked so they do not move during the swap.
rubricPoints: Explains that a load balancer sends traffic only to healthy instances
Describes a rolling deployment as updating a few instances at a time while others keep serving
Describes a slot swap as preparing the new version separately, then exchanging routing quickly
Names a real limit, such as mixed versions during rollout or the cost of a second copy
Notes that rollback is fast only if the previous version is still intact, and that schema changes can block a safe rollback

suggested.rationale: The deploy-shift engine teaches the strategies themselves, which is the decision-making this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A hotfix path is a pre-agreed route a team takes to ship an urgent fix to live software without waiting for the normal release cycle. Picture a bridge with a new crack: you do not wait for the next scheduled repair crew. Instead you follow a short, rehearsed plan to build a small patch, check it, install it quickly, and make sure the same crack is repaired in the master drawings too. Planning this path in advance means that under pressure the team follows steps it already agreed on rather than inventing them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Production is failing because of a bug that was already fixed on the main development branch, but main also contains several unfinished features. Where should the emergency fix branch start, and why?
lessons.teach:
A hotfix is a small, urgent change made to correct a defect that is already affecting users in production, the live environment. A hotfix path is the planned sequence of steps for moving that change from the faulty version to production safely and quickly. It works because the team agrees on the route before the emergency, so the only decisions left during the incident are about the specific fix.

The usual shape has four parts. First, start from the exact version running in production, usually marked by a tag, which is a fixed label on one commit, rather than from the newest development code, because that code contains unfinished work. Second, create a short-lived hotfix branch from that tag and apply the smallest fix possible. If the fix already exists elsewhere, copy that single commit across, a step called cherry-picking. Third, run the same build and test pipeline the normal path uses, and deploy through a production environment that has an expedited approval check, a gate where a named person signs off quickly. Fourth, merge the fix back into the main development branch so the bug does not return in the next scheduled release.

Worked example: production version 2.4.1 crashes on login. The team tags 2.4.1, branches hotfix 2.4.2 from that tag, copies a one-line null check from main, the pipeline passes, an on-call lead approves the production environment, version 2.4.2 deploys, and the change is merged back into main.

A common mistake is branching from main instead of the production tag, which ships untested features along with the fix. The consequence in a running system is that an unplanned release can surprise users, and skipping the merge-back means the next scheduled release silently reintroduces the bug.

A hotfix stays short, narrow, and still tested, and the path exists so that speed never removes the checks.

questions.prompt: Fleetwood Parcels runs production version 7.2.0, which is marked by the tag v7.2.0. Customers see the wrong weight printed on shipping labels. A developer has already written a one-line fix on a feature branch called feature/label-weight, but that branch also holds unfinished work. The team follows the hotfix path. Step 1: the production tag v7.2.0 already exists. Step 2: they create a short-lived branch called hotfix/7.2.1 from the tag v7.2.0. Step 3: they cherry-pick only the one fix commit from feature/label-weight onto hotfix/7.2.1. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: an on-call lead gives expedited approval on the production environment, version 7.2.1 deploys, and the fix is merged back into main.
choices: Run the same build and test pipeline the normal path uses on hotfix/7.2.1 before requesting production approval
Deploy 7.2.1 to production right after the cherry-pick, since the fix was already written and reviewed on the feature branch
Move the v7.2.0 tag to the cherry-picked commit so the production version label stays current
Rebase hotfix/7.2.1 onto the newest main so it includes the unfinished feature work
questions.why: The hotfix path keeps the same build and test pipeline as the normal path, so the missing step is running that pipeline on the hotfix branch before the expedited approval and deployment.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the starting point for a hotfix path?
choices: The newest commit on main, because it holds the latest fixes for every bug
The tag that marks the exact version currently running in production
The most recent release branch, whatever version number it carries
A fresh copy of the staging environment, which mirrors production
questions.why: A hotfix starts from the tag marking the exact production version, because main contains unfinished work that users have not seen.

questions.prompt: Corvane's payments team needs an urgent fix for version 4.9.0 in production. Their hotfix branch was created from main last Tuesday, and main now contains a new reporting feature. After the hotfix deploys, customers see the reporting feature appear in production along with the fix. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The cherry-pick step copied too many commits, which is why the reporting feature arrived
The merge back into main happened too early and pulled the reporting feature into the branch
The branch was started from main instead of from the production tag, so untested work came along
The expedited approval let the team skip the build and test pipeline for the hotfix
questions.why: Branching from main instead of the production tag ships whatever unfinished work main holds, which is the common mistake the hotfix path is designed to prevent.

questions.prompt: Corvane's hotfix fixes a crash and is deployed to production. The team forgets the final step of merging the fix back into main. The next scheduled release is three weeks away. What happens?
choices: The hotfix deployment is rolled back automatically once the scheduled release begins
The bug stays fixed in main, and nothing changes in the next scheduled release
The next scheduled release is built from main without the fix, so the crash silently returns
The production tag moves to the hotfix commit, so the bug is cleared from main's history
questions.why: If the fix is never merged back, main lacks it, so the next scheduled release built from main reintroduces the bug without any warning.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would plan a hotfix path for a production bug, and name one risk or tradeoff that the expedited route introduces and how you would limit it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start the hotfix from the tag of the version that is live, not from main, so the fix contains nothing else. I would make the change as small as possible, run the same build and test pipeline the normal release uses, and deploy through the production environment with an expedited approval from a named on-call owner. The tradeoff is that a shorter approval path means less review and less time for other teams to spot side effects. To limit that, I would keep the fix narrow, require the automated tests to pass before approval is possible, and monitor the error rate right after deployment with a rollback step ready. Finally I would merge the fix back into main, because a fix that exists only on the hotfix branch will be lost in the next release.
rubricPoints: Hotfix branches from the tag of the version running in production, not from the newest development branch
The fix is kept minimal and passes the same automated build and tests as a normal release
An expedited approval gate on the production environment replaces the slower standard approval
The fix is merged back into the main development branch so the defect does not return

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner rollback quickly and then fix forward, which exercises the same production-first, tested-patch reasoning that a hotfix path depends on.

lessons.plain: A resilient deployment is one that still works when something goes wrong during the release itself. Releases fail for ordinary reasons: a server restarts midway, a network call times out, or a new version crashes on startup. A resiliency strategy is the set of decisions you make in advance so those failures stay small and recoverable. You check that the new version is healthy before it receives traffic, limit how many machines change at once, retry only steps that are safe to repeat, and keep a fast way back to the last good version. It is like a train operator who checks the brakes before leaving the station and keeps a way to reverse if the track ahead is blocked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A release updates ten servers two at a time, and during the third batch one new server fails its health check. What should happen to the servers not yet updated, and why?
lessons.teach:
A health check is a quick test that asks a running instance whether it can serve real requests, usually by calling a status address and expecting a success answer. A rolling update replaces instances in small batches instead of all at once. A rollback returns instances to the previous known good version, using a stored copy of that version. Retry with backoff means repeating a failed step after a growing wait, so a brief network blip does not fail the whole release. Idempotent means that running a step twice leaves the system in the same state as running it once. A timeout is the longest a step may wait before it is treated as failed. The blast radius is how much of the system a bad change can damage before someone notices.

Worked example: a release of version 2 goes to ten instances in batches of two. Batch one updates and passes its health checks. In batch two, the first instance returns errors on its status address. The pipeline stops the rollout, so instances three through ten still run version 1 and keep serving users. The pipeline then rolls the failed instance and batch one back to version 1. At most four instances ever ran the bad version, and users saw errors on only part of the fleet for a short time.

A common mistake is treating a deployment script that exits successfully as proof that the release is healthy. A zero exit code only shows that the commands ran. Another mistake is retrying a step that is not idempotent, such as applying a database change or sending a payment, which can apply the change twice.

In a running system, a rollout with no health gate sends a broken version to every instance at once, so the blast radius equals the whole fleet. A resilient deployment limits that radius and makes rollback a routine action.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking firm releases version 7 of its tracking API to six instances in batches of two, and keeps version 6 stored as a known good copy. Step 1: batch one (instances A and B) moves to version 7 and both pass their health checks. Step 2: batch two (instances C and D) moves to version 7, and instance C returns errors on its status address. Step 3: the pipeline halts the rollout, so instances E and F still run version 6. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: the rolled-back instances pass their health checks on version 6. Which action fills the missing step 4?
choices: The pipeline rebuilds version 6 from current source code, since the stored copy is not trusted
The pipeline rolls instances C and D, plus batch one, back to version 6 using the stored copy
The pipeline marks the release successful because the rollout was halted before finishing
The pipeline deletes instance C and launches a fresh instance on version 7
questions.why: A rollback returns the affected instances to the stored known good version, so the pipeline restores the failed batch and the batch already updated to version 6 from that copy.

questions.prompt: A deployment step calls the status address on each instance and receives a success answer. What does that result most directly tell you?
choices: The new version is the same one stored as the rollback copy
The instance can currently serve real requests
Every batch in the rollout has finished updating
The instance has finished downloading all of its data files
questions.why: A health check asks a running instance whether it can serve real requests, usually by calling a status address and expecting success, so a success answer speaks to that and nothing more.

questions.prompt: A release script finishes with exit code 0, yet users report errors on the new version. Which statement best explains this?
choices: A zero exit code only shows the commands ran, not that the release is healthy
The script was run in a rolling update, which always hides errors
The rollback copy was overwritten during the script run
The timeout was set too long, so the script never noticed the failure
questions.why: A successful exit code only shows that the commands ran without an error; it does not prove the new version is healthy, which needs a health check.

questions.prompt: A pipeline step sets a counter in a stock table to the value 40 each time it runs. It times out, and the pipeline retries it. Which property makes this retry safe?
choices: The step has a longer timeout, so it never needs to be retried
The step adds a backoff, so it waits less before each retry
The step runs in a batch of one instance, so it cannot affect other instances
The step is idempotent, so running it twice leaves the table in the same state as running it once
questions.why: Setting the counter to a fixed value is idempotent: repeating it leaves the same result, whereas a step that adds to the counter would be doubled by a retry.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a rolling deployment with health checks limits the damage from a bad release, and name one tradeoff or limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A rolling deployment updates a small batch of instances, waits for each new instance to pass its health check, and only then moves on. If a check fails, the rollout stops, so the rest of the fleet keeps running the last good version. The rolled-out instances can be restored from the stored previous version. The main tradeoff is time: each batch waits for health checks, so a full rollout is slower than replacing everything at once. A second limit is that rollback is easy for code but hard for data. If the release changed a database schema in a way the old version cannot read, going back to the old code may fail. So the new schema must stay compatible with the previous version until the release is confirmed healthy.
rubricPoints: Health checks must confirm the new instance can serve real requests before the rollout continues.
Batching limits the blast radius, and a failed check halts the rollout before the rest of the fleet changes.
Rollback restores the last known good version from a stored artifact, and it must be fast.
Slower rollouts and data changes that cannot be undone are the main tradeoffs and limits.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner roll back a bad release quickly and then fix forward, which exercises the rollback and health-gating ideas taught here.

lessons.plain: A feature flag is a named on-or-off switch that a running program reads while it runs, so behaviour can change without shipping new code. Think of a light switch wired into a building: the wiring is installed once, and people flip the switch when they are ready. Teams use flags to put new code into production while keeping it hidden from users, then turn it on for a small group, then for everyone, and turn it off within moments if something goes wrong. Azure App Configuration is a managed service that keeps these switches in one central place. Its Feature Manager part is the piece application code uses to read flags and apply rules such as 'only for this group'. The idea transfers to any flag store.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team deploys a new checkout path to production but leaves it switched off for everyone. What does that change about the risk of the deployment, and what could they do later without redeploying?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A feature flag is a named setting, usually on or off, that application code checks before choosing which path to run. A feature flag store is a central service where flags are kept, so their values can change without a redeploy. A feature filter is a rule attached to a flag that decides, for a given request or user, whether the flag counts as on. Examples are a percentage of users, a named list of targets, or a time window. Azure App Configuration is Microsoft's managed store for such settings, and Feature Manager is the library your application uses to read flags and evaluate their filters.

Why it works. Deploying code (putting it on servers) and releasing a behaviour (letting users reach it) are separate events. The code ships with its flag off, so the new path is installed but dormant. Turning the flag on is a configuration change, which is fast and reversible, and it can reach a slice of traffic first.

Worked example. A team ships a new fare calculation behind a flag called fare-v2 with a percentage filter set to 0. Step 1: the deployment goes out and every request still uses the old path. Step 2: they set the filter to 10 percent, so about one in ten requests evaluates to on and takes the new path. Step 3: error rates stay flat, so they raise it to 100 percent. Step 4: a bug appears, so they switch the flag off. Within the cache refresh interval, all requests return to the old path, and no code was rolled back.

Common mistake. Teams leave flags in the code forever. Each stale flag doubles the paths that must be tested, and nobody remembers which branch is current. Remove a flag once its rollout is complete.

Consequence. If the application caches flag values, a change takes effect only after the cache refreshes, so a kill switch is quick but not instant. Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing it, but only when the team plans how each flag will be retired.

questions.prompt: Harbor Bikes runs a bike-share app. Their team adds a new dock-pricing path behind a flag called dock-price-v2, which starts with a percentage filter set to 0. Step 1: the release goes out to all app servers and every request still uses the old pricing path. Step 2: they change the filter to 5 percent, so about one in twenty requests takes the new path. Step 3: crash counts stay flat for two days, so they raise the filter to 100 percent. Step 4: the new path is now fully live, and the team needs to finish the lifecycle of this flag. Which step completes it?
choices: Leave the flag on permanently so no future configuration change is ever needed
Remove the old pricing branch and the dock-price-v2 flag in a later release, once the rollout is complete
Create a second flag named dock-price-v3 that wraps the same new path
Redeploy the old pricing code as a safety copy alongside the new path
questions.why: A flag should be retired once its rollout is complete, which means removing the dead branch and the flag itself, so the code does not keep two paths alive indefinitely.

questions.prompt: In a feature flag setup, what is a feature filter?
choices: The deployment step that copies new code onto application servers
A log of every time a flag was switched, kept for auditing
The cache that stores flag values so the application does not read the store on every request
A rule attached to a flag that decides, for a given request or user, whether the flag counts as on
questions.why: The teaching text defines a feature filter as a rule attached to a flag that decides whether the flag counts as on for a given request or user, with examples such as a percentage, a target list, or a time window.

questions.prompt: A payments team sets a flag called card-retry-v2 to off during a incident, expecting an instant switch to the old path. Their application caches flag values with a 30-second refresh. What should the team expect?
choices: The flag takes effect only after the next full deployment of the application
Only new users see the change, while existing sessions keep the new path until they sign out
Requests keep using the cached value until the cache refreshes, so the switch takes up to about 30 seconds to fully apply
The old path is used for all requests the moment the flag is saved, because the store pushes changes directly
questions.why: Because the application caches flag values, a change takes effect only after the cache refreshes, so the kill switch is quick but not instant, which is the wrong expectation described in the first option.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has nine feature flags that finished their rollouts a year ago but are still checked in the code. Why does the team's practice of leaving them in place cause problems?
choices: Each stale flag doubles the number of code paths that must be tested, and nobody can easily tell which branch is current
The store automatically turns off any flag that has not been changed in a year
Flags that are on cannot be read by Feature Manager, so the application fails to start
Old flags increase the cache refresh interval, which slows every request
questions.why: The teaching text warns that each stale flag doubles the paths to test and that teams lose track of the current branch, so flags should be removed once their rollout is complete.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used rollbacks why we would ship a risky change behind a feature flag instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: Feature flags separate deploying from releasing. The new code ships to production with its flag off, so it is installed but no user takes the new path yet. The team then turns the flag on for a percentage of users, or for a named group, through the flag store, without another deployment. If the new path misbehaves, switching the flag off is a configuration change that takes effect once the application's cached values refresh. That is usually quick but not instant, which is why it can be faster than a full rollback. The tradeoff is that every flag adds a branch that must be tested, and a flag left behind becomes stale code and confusing behaviour. So I would record an owner and a removal date for each flag. I would also not use a flag to hide a database schema change, since that needs its own migration plan, and I would check that the flag store is reachable, because the application's behaviour now depends on it.
rubricPoints: Explains that deploying code and releasing a behaviour are separated by a flag.
Describes gradual exposure, such as a percentage or named group, and reversal by switching the flag off.
Names a tradeoff such as extra code paths to test or stale flags left behind.
Notes that flag changes may take effect after a cache refresh, so they are not instant.

suggested.rationale: Feature flags are one of the deployment strategies that the planned deploy-shift engine would let the learner practise choosing between and sequencing.

lessons.plain: Shipping software means getting the program you built onto the machine where people will run it. There are three common ways to package what you ship. A container bundles the app together with everything it needs to run, like a sealed lunchbox that works the same in any kitchen. A binary is a compiled program, a single finished file you copy onto a server and start. A script is a text file of instructions that a tool runs step by step, such as copying files, changing settings, and restarting a service. The right choice depends on what the target machine can run and how much of the setup you need to repeat exactly every time.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you had to put a new version of a web API onto five servers that all run the same operating system, would you rather copy one finished program file to each server, or ship a sealed bundle that carries its own libraries, and why?
lessons.teach: A deployment is the act of putting a tested version of an application onto the place where it runs. Three common packaging forms are used. A container image is a sealed package holding the app and its libraries; a container is a running copy of that image, started by a container runtime, which is the software that runs containers on a host. An image is stored in a registry, a server that holds versioned images and hands them out on request. A binary is a compiled program: the build step has already turned source code into machine code, so the host needs no build tools, only the file and any operating system pieces it depends on. A script is a text file of commands run by an interpreter, such as a shell or PowerShell, which makes it flexible but leaves the steps to be re-run correctly by the script itself. Worked example: a pipeline builds image myapi with tag 2.4.1 and pushes it to the registry. The deploy stage tells the host to pull exactly myapi:2.4.1, starts a new container, checks a health endpoint, then shifts traffic to it. Common mistake: deploying with a moving tag such as latest. Next month the same name may point to a different image, so the version you tested is not the version you run, and a rollback cannot reproduce the old build. Consequence in a running system: a script that fails halfway can leave a service stopped with no record of which step failed. Pin every artifact to an exact, immutable version, and make scripts safe to run twice.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight's ledger team ships a Windows command-line tool called ledgerctl. The build stage compiles it, zips it as ledgerctl-3.2.0.zip, and writes its SHA-256 checksum (a fingerprint string computed from the file's contents, so any change to the file changes the string) into the build record. The deploy stage then runs these steps: 1) download exactly ledgerctl-3.2.0.zip from the artifact store to the host. 2) [step missing from this list] 3) extract the zip into C:\tools\ledgerctl\3.2.0. 4) point the folder link C:\tools\ledgerctl\current at 3.2.0. Which step belongs in the gap at position 2?
choices: Delete the previous version folder first so the disk has enough free space for the new extraction
Compare the downloaded file's checksum with the value recorded at build time and stop the deployment if they differ
Rename the zip to ledgerctl-latest.zip so the host's scheduled job can find it without an update to its configuration
Rebuild ledgerctl from the source code on the host so that the binary is compiled for that exact machine
questions.why: Checking the downloaded file against the checksum recorded at build time confirms the host is running the exact bytes that were built and tested, before anything is extracted or linked.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a container registry hold, and why does a deploy stage pull from it instead of copying files from the build machine?
choices: It holds versioned container images so any host can fetch the exact same image on request
It holds the operating system installer that the container runtime needs to start
It holds the source code so that the image can be rebuilt on demand
It holds running containers so that a host can attach to them after a reboot
questions.why: A registry is a server that stores versioned images and hands out copies on request, which lets many hosts get the same tested image without depending on the build machine.

questions.prompt: A team's deploy script at a logistics company runs these commands in order: create a database user, add a firewall rule, copy a config file, start a service. It fails after the firewall rule is added. The engineer reruns the script and it now fails at the first command with 'user already exists'. What change best makes the script safe to run twice?
choices: Move the service start command to the top so it runs before any failure can happen
Remove the config copy step so that fewer commands can fail in the middle of the run
Replace the script with a moving tag so every run picks up the newest settings
Add the firewall rule and the user creation with checks that skip each step if it is already in the desired state
questions.why: Making each step check whether its result already exists, and skip it if so, lets a rerun continue safely from a partial failure instead of stopping on the first leftover change.

questions.prompt: A binary release of a payroll calculator is copied to a server, and the server has no compiler installed. Which statement best explains why this deployment still works?
choices: The build step has already turned the source code into machine code, so the server only needs the file and any operating system pieces it depends on
The container runtime wraps the binary, so no operating system pieces are needed at all
The server recompiles the program the first time it runs, using the build tools on the server
The script interpreter on the server translates the binary into commands at each start
questions.why: A binary is already compiled, so the host needs only the file and the operating system components it relies on, not the tools that produced it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between packaging an application as a container image, a compiled binary, or a script for a deployment. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would be least comfortable using.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the target. If the hosts run a container runtime and we want the same environment everywhere, a container image is the strongest choice, because the app and its libraries travel together and the image tag gives us a version to roll back to. If the target is a set of servers with no container runtime, and the app is compiled, a binary copied into a versioned release folder is simpler and has fewer moving parts. A script is best for the surrounding steps, such as copying files or changing configuration, rather than for shipping the app itself. The tradeoff I would worry about with scripts is that they are only as repeatable as they are written; a script that fails halfway or appends settings on each run can leave a server in an unknown state. With containers, the cost is that someone has to run the registry and keep images patched.
rubricPoints: Defines a container image, a binary, and a script in plain terms
Explains that the choice depends on what the target host can run
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff for at least one option
Stresses using exact, immutable versions so rollback is possible

suggested.rationale: Choosing between packaging forms in a realistic release situation is best practiced by reasoning through the trade-offs, which an exam-style scenario supports better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Most applications keep their data in a database, and new versions of the app often need the database's structure changed too: a new column, a renamed table, a new index. Deploying that means running a set of database changes as part of the release, in the right order relative to the new app code. The hard part is that the old app version and the new one may both be running for a few minutes, so each database change has to work for both. Think of it like rewiring a building while people still live in it: you add the new wiring first, move everyone over, and only then remove the old wires.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your release updates the app and renames a database column the app reads. If you deploy the new app first, what could go wrong during the minutes when both old and new versions are running, and what order would you choose instead?
lessons.teach:
A database deployment is a release step that changes the database's structure or data, such as adding a column, creating a table, or filling in values for existing rows. Teams usually express these changes as migrations: small, versioned scripts that run in a fixed order and record which ones have already been applied. The schema is the structure of the database, meaning its tables, columns, and constraints. The migration tool keeps a history table so it knows what has already run. Some tools instead compare a packaged description of the target schema against the live database and generate the needed changes.

It is harder than deploying code, because code can be replaced in seconds but data already exists. A migration that drops a column loses that data, and rolling back the app cannot bring it back. For that reason many teams use the expand and contract pattern. In the expand step you add the new structure while keeping the old, so both old and new app versions still work. In the contract step, in a later release, you remove the old structure once nothing reads it.

Worked example. Release 2.4 renames customer_phone to contact_phone. Step 1: a migration adds contact_phone as a nullable column, and customer_phone stays. Step 2: app 2.4 writes both columns and reads contact_phone, falling back to customer_phone when it is empty. Step 3: a backfill job copies existing values across. It is idempotent, meaning running it twice gives the same result as running it once. Step 4: a later release, after every instance runs 2.4 and the rollback window has closed, drops customer_phone.

Common mistake: dropping the old column in the same release as the code change. If the rollout is partial or the release is rolled back, the old app now queries a column that no longer exists.

In a running system, the database stage must be ordered before the app stage in the pipeline, and each migration must be tracked so a retried deployment does not apply it twice.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app stores each agent's name in one column, full_name. The team wants separate first_name and last_name columns, and they will follow expand and contract. Release 3.1 goes as follows. Step 1: a migration adds first_name and last_name as nullable columns, and full_name stays. Step 2: app 3.1 writes all three columns and reads first_name and last_name, falling back to full_name when they are empty. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: in a later release, after every instance runs 3.1 and the rollback window has closed, a migration drops full_name.
choices: Mark the migration as applied by deleting the migration history table.
Run an idempotent backfill job that copies existing full_name values into first_name and last_name.
Make first_name and last_name NOT NULL immediately so the app never sees an empty value.
Drop full_name in the same release as step 1 so the table stays clean.
questions.why: The backfill fills in existing rows with the new structure, and because it is idempotent it can be re-run safely, which is the step that makes the fallback in step 2 rarely needed.

questions.prompt: What is the migration history table for in a database deployment tool?
choices: It stores a full copy of the database so a failed release can be undone.
It holds the list of application servers that are allowed to connect to the database.
It records which migrations have already been applied, so a retried deployment does not apply them again.
It keeps the compiled version of the application code that reads the database.
questions.why: The teaching text says the tool keeps a history table so it knows what has already run, which prevents a retry from applying the same migration twice.

questions.prompt: A team wants to rename an order_total column to total_cents across a release, with a rollback possible. Which first move keeps both the old and new app versions working?
choices: Delete all rows from the table, then recreate the table with total_cents.
Drop order_total and add total_cents in one migration, then deploy the new app.
Rename order_total to total_cents in place, since the old app will read the value anyway.
Add total_cents as a new column while keeping order_total, so both app versions still have a column they can use.
questions.why: The expand step adds the new structure while keeping the old, so old and new app versions both still work; dropping or renaming the old column first would break the old version if the release is rolled back.

questions.prompt: A pipeline has a database stage and an app stage. A team accidentally orders the app stage first, and the new app version reads a column that the database stage has not yet added. What is the most likely result, and what is the correct fix?
choices: Nothing happens, because the migration tool retries until the column appears.
The app will write to a backup table automatically, so the ordering only affects performance.
The database stage will drop the app's data, so the app stage must be ordered before the database stage.
The app will fail on reads of the missing column, so the database stage must be ordered before the app stage.
questions.why: The teaching text says the database stage must be ordered before the app stage, because the app needs the new structure to exist before it reads it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a release that changes the database and deploys new app code should not drop an old column in the same step, and name one limit or tradeoff of the expand and contract approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: If we drop the old column in the same release, we create a window where it is gone while old app instances are still running. During a rolling deployment those instances would query a missing column and fail, and rolling back the app cannot bring the column or its data back. So we expand first: add the new column, keep the old one, deploy code that works with both, and backfill existing rows. We only drop the old column in a later release, once nothing reads it and we are past the rollback window. The tradeoff is time and complexity. The schema holds two versions of the same data for a while, writes may have to go to both, and the cleanup release is easy to forget, so it needs a tracked follow-up task. The expanded design also costs extra storage and write work during that period.
rubricPoints: Database changes are versioned migrations ordered relative to the app deployment.
Old and new app versions can run together, so each change must be backward compatible.
Destructive changes such as dropping columns are deferred to a later release (expand and contract).
Migrations should be tracked or idempotent so retries and reruns do not apply them twice.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a mixed release where schema and app versions overlap teaches the ordering decision more than reading or a single existing mission, which covers rollback but not database migrations.

lessons.plain: Configuration management is keeping the software and settings on a fleet of machines the way you intend them to be, and putting them back when they drift away from that. Think of a kitchen where every cook must follow the same recipe card. You write down the wanted end state, such as this web server has this package installed, this service runs, and this file has these contents, and a tool checks each machine and fixes only what differs. Choosing the right technology means asking where the machines live, whether they can be reached, and how much drift matters, rather than picking the most popular tool.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have forty web servers that were set up by hand over two years and now differ slightly from one another. Before reading on, what kind of tool would you want to bring them all back to one agreed setup, and what should it do on a server that already matches the agreed setup?
lessons.teach:
Configuration management is the practice of describing the wanted state of machines (installed packages, running services, file contents, user accounts) in files, and using a tool to make each machine match that description. The idea is called desired state: you state the end result rather than a list of steps, and the tool works out what to change. Drift is the gap that builds up when someone edits a server by hand, and it is what configuration management exists to remove.

Why it works: the tool runs the same check again and again. If a machine already matches, nothing happens. If it has drifted, only the differing parts are corrected. Repeated runs are therefore safe, a property called idempotence.

Be careful to separate two jobs. Infrastructure as code (IaC) creates the cloud resources themselves, such as networks, virtual machines and databases; Bicep and Azure Resource Manager templates do this. Configuration management works inside those machines, setting packages, services and files. A common pattern is to use IaC to create the machine and a configuration tool to set it up, and to choose the configuration tool by where the nodes run and how they report back.

Worked example: a rule says nginx must be installed and running on 40 web nodes. The tool reads the rule, checks node 17, finds nginx stopped, starts it, and reports one change. The other 39 nodes already match and report no change.

Common mistake: treating the tool as a one-time script. If someone then edits a file by hand, the next scheduled run reverts it, which surprises people who did not know the rule existed. In a running production system this means an unmanaged change can be silently overwritten, so changes must go through the source-controlled configuration.

questions.prompt: A team runs 6 image-processing nodes in a private data centre that cannot accept connections from outside. They want a rule that the imagemagick package is installed and the watermark service is running on every node. The sequence is: (1) the rule is read from a source-controlled file; (2) each node checks in on a schedule; (3) ____; (4) each node reports its result back to the central service. Which step completes the sequence?
choices: A person logs into the node and adds the package by hand so the next run has less to do.
The tool removes every package on the node and reinstalls the full list from scratch on each run.
The tool creates six new virtual machines to replace the nodes that do not match the rule.
The node compares its current state with the rule and changes only the parts that differ.
questions.why: Step 3 is the comparison: the node checks its state against the desired state and corrects only the differences, which is what keeps repeated runs safe.

questions.prompt: A team must make sure a logging agent service is running on 25 existing virtual machines in a cloud subscription. The machines already exist. Which kind of tool fits this job?
choices: A configuration management tool that sets services, packages and files inside each machine
A database migration tool that versions the schema of the logging store
An infrastructure-as-code template that creates new virtual machines and networks
A manual runbook that engineers follow once per machine during business hours
questions.why: The machines already exist, so the need is to set state inside them, which is configuration management; infrastructure as code creates resources rather than configuring what runs inside them.

questions.prompt: An engineer fixes a misconfigured timeout by editing a file directly on one of 12 nodes. Two days later the timeout is back to the old value on that node, and nobody changed the source-controlled rule. What most likely happened?
choices: The tool detected the change and rolled back the whole cluster to its first state.
The scheduled configuration run reverted the hand edit because the rule still describes the old value.
The node's disk failed and the file was restored from a backup.
The network dropped the edit during transfer and the node never received it.
questions.why: Configuration management enforces the described state on each run, so an edit that is not made in the source-controlled rule gets overwritten, which is the drift-removal behaviour the tool is designed to produce.

questions.prompt: A team has 40 application nodes spread across two cloud regions and an isolated on-premises site. The on-premises nodes can only make outbound connections. What should decide which configuration management technology the team picks?
choices: Where the nodes run and how they report back to the central control point
Whether the tool's logo matches the colour scheme of the team's dashboard
The number of lines in the rule files, with the shortest tool always chosen
Which tool the team's most senior engineer used at their previous job
questions.why: The teaching text says to choose the configuration tool by where the nodes run and how they report back, so the network location and reporting path are the deciding factors.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Azure Automation State Configuration or Azure Machine Configuration and a tool such as Ansible for keeping web servers configured, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with where the machines are. If the servers are Azure virtual machines and we want Azure itself to check and enforce the configuration with compliance reporting in the portal, Azure Machine Configuration fits, since it evaluates desired state definitions and reports results. Azure Automation State Configuration uses PowerShell Desired State Configuration pulled from a central service, which suits a Windows-heavy estate already on Azure Automation. If the fleet spans clouds or includes on-premises Linux hosts reached over SSH, I would lean toward Ansible, because it connects without a permanent agent on each node. The tradeoff I would name is connectivity: a pull model needs each node to reach the central service and to keep its agent healthy, while a push tool needs the control machine to reach every node, so reachability often decides the choice as much as features do.
rubricPoints: Configuration management sets and maintains the state inside machines, which is separate from IaC that creates the cloud resources.
Desired state means declaring the end result and letting the tool correct drift safely on repeated runs.
The choice depends on where the nodes run, the operating system mix, and whether they can be reached pull-style or push-style.
A good answer names at least one tradeoff such as agent maintenance, outbound access, or reporting scope.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a configuration tool is a reasoning skill best shown by explaining the tradeoffs back, and no listed mission currently covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Configuration management is the habit of keeping the settings and setup of your application environments in a written, known state that you can rebuild on demand. Think of it as a recipe card for how each environment should look: which values it uses, which services it runs, and which secrets it needs. Instead of someone remembering how production was set up, the setup is recorded, reviewed like any other change, and applied the same way every time. Good configuration management makes environments predictable, and it makes a broken one easier to repair.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your test and production environments both run the same app, but production has been slow for a week and nobody remembers changing anything. What would you check first, and why would you suspect the settings rather than the code?
lessons.teach:
Configuration management is the practice of keeping the settings and setup of your application environments, such as the servers, containers, services and app settings they run with, in a known state that you can reproduce on demand. The strategy has three parts. First, configuration is stored in source control next to the code, so each change has an author, a review and a history. Second, values that differ between environments, such as the database address used in test versus production, are kept out of the code and supplied per environment. Secrets such as passwords go into a dedicated secret store, and the configuration only refers to them by name. Third, changes are applied by a pipeline rather than by hand, so the running system matches what is recorded.

Why it works: a pipeline that applies the same declared settings should reach the same result whether it runs once or ten times. That property, called idempotence, lets you re-run a deployment safely after a failure. Drift is the gap that appears when someone edits a live system by hand and the record no longer matches reality. You find drift by comparing the live state with the recorded one.

Worked example: a timeout is 5 seconds in test and must be 10 seconds in production. Step 1: the timeout is stored as a named setting with one value per environment, not hard-coded in the app. Step 2: the production change is a commit that goes through review. Step 3: the production stage of the pipeline reads that value and applies it. Step 4: a later check compares the live setting with the recorded one, and they match.

Common mistake: putting a production password into the repository, or editing production in a portal because it is quicker. The next rebuild then produces a different system, and the secret now sits in history where it is hard to remove.

Consequence: when drift exists, a redeploy can silently undo a manual hotfix or bring back an old value, which is a frequent cause of incidents after deployments.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a reporting service whose database password must not appear in its code. Its team follows a four-step path. Step 1: the password is stored in the team's secret store under the name rpt-db-pass, and the production configuration file holds only that name. Step 2: the production configuration change is committed through a pull request and approved by a reviewer. Step 3: [MISSING STEP]. Step 4: the production stage of the pipeline runs and the service starts, reading rpt-db-pass by name. Which action fills Step 3 so that Step 4 can succeed?
choices: Create a secret named rpt-db-pass in the production secret store before the stage runs, because the configuration only holds the name and the lookup must find something.
Edit the running service's environment variables by hand after the deploy so the password is set at runtime.
Paste the real password into the production configuration file so the pipeline can read it without a lookup.
Copy the password into the test environment's secret store so both environments share one value.
questions.why: The configuration refers to the secret only by name, so the named secret must exist in the production store before the pipeline stage tries to read it.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of storing configuration files in source control next to the application code?
choices: Each change gets an author, a review and a history, so you can see who changed what and when.
Passwords are encrypted automatically, so no separate secret store is needed.
Developers no longer need a pipeline, because the repository deploys changes on its own.
The configuration runs faster because the source control server is closer to the production servers.
questions.why: Keeping configuration in source control gives every change an author, a review and a recorded history, which the other options misstate or invent.

questions.prompt: A payment API allows a retry limit of 2 in staging and 6 in production. Which approach best fits the configuration management strategy?
choices: Set the limit once in a shared file that the team edits by hand on each server.
Store the limit as a named setting with one value per environment, and have the pipeline supply the right value at deploy time.
Change the number in the code on a release branch just before each production deploy.
Write an if-statement in the code that picks 6 when the app detects it is running in production.
questions.why: Values that differ between environments belong outside the code as per-environment settings that the pipeline applies, not hard-coded or hand-edited.

questions.prompt: A team added a firewall rule to a live server through the portal during an incident and never recorded it. After the next automated rebuild from the recorded configuration, the rule is gone and the service fails again. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Drift, meaning the live system was changed by hand and the record no longer matched it, so the rebuild restored the recorded state.
Idempotence failure, meaning the pipeline ran twice and applied the rule a second time with a different result.
A secret store outage that prevented the pipeline from reading the firewall rule value.
The pipeline ignored the commit history, so it applied an older version of the configuration.
questions.why: The manual change was never recorded, so the gap between live and recorded state (drift) caused the rebuild to undo it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what configuration management means for an application's environments, and name one limit or tradeoff of keeping all configuration in source control.
lessons.modelAnswer: Configuration management means the settings and setup of each environment are written down, versioned and applied by the pipeline, so any environment can be rebuilt to a known state. Environment-specific values such as addresses and timeouts are supplied per environment, and secrets live in a secret store that the configuration only references by name. The main tradeoff is that you get traceability and repeatability, but the record is only as good as the discipline behind it: anyone who edits a live system by hand creates drift, and a later redeploy can silently overwrite that change. Also, a secret that ever lands in the repository stays in the history even after deletion, so the rule of keeping secrets out has to be enforced, not just hoped for.
rubricPoints: Configuration is stored in source control and changed through reviewed commits and the pipeline
Environment-specific values are supplied per environment, not hard-coded in the code
Secrets are held in a secret store and referenced by name, never committed
Drift from manual edits is a risk, and a redeploy can silently overwrite a hand-made change

suggested.rationale: That mission practices supplying a deploy credential through configuration without exposing the secret, which is the secrets half of this strategy, though it does not cover the full strategy.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing the servers, networks and storage an application runs on as text files, written much like a program. Those files live in source control, a system that records every change, shows who made it, and lets a team review or undo it. A strategy for this answers a few practical questions: where the files are kept, what checks run automatically before any change is applied, and how changes reach real environments without anyone clicking through a web console. Think of it as a recipe card for a kitchen. Anyone can cook the same dish again, and any change to the recipe is visible to the whole team.
lessons.guessPrompt: If someone changed a server's settings by hand in a web console last Tuesday and nobody wrote it down, what problems would you expect when you try to rebuild that environment next month?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing infrastructure, such as virtual machines, networks and storage, in files that a tool can read and apply. A declarative template states the wanted end result, and the tool works out the steps to reach it. Source control is a system, such as git, that stores every version of those files, records who changed what, and lets a team review a change before it is merged. An IaC strategy is the set of decisions that connects these pieces: which repository holds the files, which branch may deploy, what checks run automatically, and which environments are updated and in what order.

It works because a file in source control becomes the single record of what should exist. A change arrives as a pull request, so reviewers see the exact difference. An automated pipeline then runs three kinds of checks before anything touches a real environment: a syntax and style check (linting), a preview of what would change, and tests that confirm the result behaves as expected. Only after those pass does a deployment stage apply the change, first to a test environment and later to production, usually after an approval.

Worked example. A team keeps a template for a storage account and a network subnet. An engineer opens a pull request that changes the subnet's address range. Step 1: the pipeline lints the template and fails on a typo. Step 2: the preview shows the subnet will be replaced rather than resized, which the reviewer rejects in favour of a different design. Step 3: the revised change deploys to the test environment, and a test confirms the subnet exists with the expected range. Step 4: after approval, production receives the same change.

Common mistake: someone edits production in a web console, or runs the template from a laptop with no review. The running system now differs from the file, which is called drift. The next automated deployment may silently revert the manual change, or a rebuild from the files may produce an environment that does not match the one customers use.

The strategy is only as good as the discipline behind it. If changes bypass the repository, the files stop being the truth.

questions.prompt: A pull request (a proposed change that reviewers examine before it is merged into the main code) is worked through here for a different team. A payments company keeps a template for a key vault and a firewall rule that allows one app server to reach it. Someone logged into the cloud portal and widened the firewall rule to allow a whole subnet, and the team discovers the file no longer matches production. Step 1: the engineer copies the portal's rule into the template in a new pull request, so the file describes what is actually running. Step 2: the pipeline lints the template and passes. Step 3: the preview shows that production would not change, because the file now matches it. Step 4 is left blank on purpose: it is the one step needed to bring the team back to its strategy. Which choice completes Step 4?
choices: Leave the template as it is, since the wider rule is working and nobody has complained.
Merge the pull request after review, then let the pipeline deploy it through test and on to production after approval.
Delete the portal change by hand so production matches the old file again.
Run the template from a laptop directly against production to confirm the rule is set correctly.
questions.why: Merging after review and deploying through the pipeline keeps the file as the single record and prevents the drift from being reverted or repeated by hand.

questions.prompt: A team describes a storage account in a file and says the template is declarative. Which statement best explains what that means?
choices: The file states the wanted end result, and the tool works out the steps needed to reach it.
The file is a snapshot of the running environment taken at the moment someone exported it.
The file records every person who has ever edited it, along with the date of each edit.
The file lists each command the tool must run, in the exact order it should run them.
questions.why: A declarative template describes the desired end state and leaves the tool to work out the steps, which is what distinguishes it from a list of commands.
