Maintain adds most project management without the most sensitive actions. Admin can change everything, including repository settings and who has access. An organization is the shared account that holds many repositories, and a team is a group of organization members. You can give a team a role on a repository, and every member inherits it. A person can reach a repository through several paths: a direct grant, a team grant, or an organization base permission that applies to all repositories. GitHub uses the highest role across these paths, so a team with only Read does not cancel a direct Write grant. Worked example: Priya belongs to the team billing-devs, which has Write on the repo billing-api. She also has a direct Read grant on the same repo from an earlier project. Step one, list the paths: Read from the direct grant, Write from the team. Step two, take the highest: Write. Step three, conclude: Priya can push branches. Common mistake: setting the organization base permission to Write or Admin to save time. Every new member then gets that role on every repository, including ones they should not change. Consequence in a running system: a CI bot or deploy account given Admin can change branch protection rules and delete the repository, so a leaked token does far more harm than one limited to Write. Least privilege means granting the lowest role that does the job and reviewing team membership regularly.

questions.prompt: Tomas works in the northwind-labs organization. He has a direct Triage grant on the repository ledger-sync from an old review, a team grant of Maintain on the same repository through the qa-reviewers team, and the organization base permission is Read. Step one lists the three paths: Triage from the direct grant, Maintain from the team, and Read from the base permission. Step two is missing. Step three: Tomas can manage issues and most project work on ledger-sync but cannot take the most sensitive repository actions.
choices: Take the highest role across the paths, which is Maintain.
Use only the direct grant, Triage, because it was set on the repository itself.
Add the three roles together, which gives Admin.
Pick the lowest of the three, Read, so the most restrictive grant wins.
questions.why: GitHub uses the highest role across all paths a person has to a repository, and Maintain is higher than Triage and Read, so it is the one that applies.

questions.prompt: Which built-in repository role lets someone push branches to a repository without being able to change the repository's settings or who has access?
choices: Read
Maintain
Write
Admin
questions.why: Write adds pushing branches, while Maintain and Admin reach further into project management and settings, and Read and Triage do not allow pushing.

questions.prompt: A new hire at a different company is added to a fresh organization, and the owner sets the organization base permission to Admin to avoid making individual grants. What is the main risk?
choices: The new hire loses access to any team they are later added to.
The new hire can only see repositories they were explicitly granted.
Every member gets Admin on every repository, including ones they should not be able to change.
The new hire can read code but cannot push branches anywhere.
questions.why: The organization base permission applies to all repositories, so setting it to Admin hands every member full control everywhere, which is the opposite of least privilege.

questions.prompt: A deploy token used by a CI job on the mobile-app repository is granted only the Write role. Which action is outside what that token can do?
choices: Open a pull request
Read the source code
Delete the repository
Push a branch
questions.why: Write covers pushing branches and similar work, but deleting a repository is among the sensitive actions reserved for Admin, which is why a Write-only token limits the damage if it leaks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how GitHub works out what a person can do in a repository when their access comes from more than one place, and name one tradeoff of giving a team a broad role.
lessons.modelAnswer: GitHub looks at every route a person has to a repository: a direct grant on that repository, membership in a team that has a role on it, and the organization's base permission that applies to all its repositories. It takes the highest role across those routes, and that is what the person gets. So a Read team membership does not cancel a direct Write grant. The tradeoff is convenience against exposure. A broad role on a team is quick to set up and lets new members start work immediately, but every member can then change code or settings beyond what some of them need. A narrower role takes more deliberate setup, but it limits the damage from one compromised account. A good answer picks the lowest role that does the job and reviews it when people change roles or leave the team.
rubricPoints: Names the built-in repository roles and what the broader ones can change.
Explains that direct grants, team grants and organization base permissions combine, and the highest role applies.
States the tradeoff between broad team roles and least privilege.
Gives a concrete example of an account, such as a bot or deploy user, that should not hold Admin.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right role for a scenario with several access paths is best practised by reasoning through situations, and no listed mission covers GitHub roles.

lessons.plain: Azure DevOps is where a team keeps its code, work items, and pipelines. Permissions decide who can read, change, or run each of those things. Instead of handing out rights one person at a time, you place people in groups, such as readers or contributors, and grant each group a set of rights. A security group is a named bucket of people who share the same rights. Done well, a new engineer joins a group and immediately gets the access the job needs, and nothing more. Done badly, rights pile up on individuals, nobody remembers why they exist, and one leaked account can change production.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer belongs to two groups. One group allows deleting a branch, and the other group explicitly denies deleting that branch. What do you expect the developer's effective access to be, and why might a team want the rule to work that way?
lessons.teach:
A security group is a named set of identities, such as users or other groups, that shares permissions. A permission is a single right on a single object, such as Contribute on a repository or Edit on a pipeline. For each permission, a group can be set to Allow, Deny, or Not set. Groups exist at the organization level and at the project level. Project groups such as Readers, Contributors, and Project Administrators come with preset rights, and you can create your own groups for narrower jobs.

Why it works: permissions are inherited. Rights set on a project flow down to its repositories and pipelines unless a lower-level setting overrides them. When a user belongs to several groups, Azure DevOps combines them, and an explicit Deny beats any Allow for the same permission, no matter which group the Allow comes from.

Worked example: Priya is in Contributors, which allows Contribute on a repository. She is also in a Contractors group where Contribute on that same repository is set to Deny. Step 1: Azure DevOps collects every setting that applies to her for Contribute on that repository. Step 2: it finds an Allow from Contributors and a Deny from Contractors. Step 3: the Deny wins. Priya can read the repository but cannot push to it.

Common mistake: granting Allow to individual people, or to a broad group such as all valid users, then being surprised by how wide the access is. The opposite mistake is a Deny placed high in the hierarchy, which silently blocks a team that needs the work.

Consequence: an Allow on a production deployment environment, granted to a group with many members, lets every one of them start a release to production. Permissions are the first line of control, so the group design decides who can cause a change.

questions.prompt: A consultancy has a project called Harbor-Billing with a repository called invoice-core. Tomas belongs to two groups. The Field-Engineers group has Contribute set to Allow on invoice-core. The Client-Guests group has Contribute set to Deny on the whole Harbor-Billing project, which flows down to invoice-core. Work through it. Step 1: Azure DevOps collects every setting that applies to Tomas for Contribute on invoice-core, including the Allow from Field-Engineers and the Deny inherited from Client-Guests. Step 2: it finds an Allow and a Deny for the same permission on the same object. Step 3 is the one you must complete: state what Tomas can do with Contribute on invoice-core and why.
choices: Tomas can push to invoice-core, because the Allow from Field-Engineers is on the repository itself, which is closer to the object than the project-level Deny.
Tomas can push to invoice-core only if the Client-Guests group has at least as many members as Field-Engineers, since membership count decides ties.
Tomas cannot push to invoice-core, because the explicit Deny from Client-Guests beats the Allow from Field-Engineers no matter which group it comes from.
Tomas gets a Not set result for Contribute, so the system falls back to the default Allow for project members.
questions.why: An explicit Deny wins over any Allow for the same permission, and the inherited project-level Deny applies to invoice-core, so Tomas cannot push.

questions.prompt: In Azure DevOps permissions, what does the setting Not set mean for a group and a permission?
choices: The group has no explicit rule for that permission, so the group neither grants nor blocks it.
The permission is removed from the object and cannot be granted again by any group.
The group has been granted that permission across all projects in the organization.
The group is explicitly blocked from that permission, which is the same as Deny.
questions.why: Not set means there is no explicit Allow or Deny for that group on that permission, so the group contributes nothing to the decision either way.

questions.prompt: A team lead at a logistics firm sets Allow on Manage variable groups for the group All valid users, so that anyone can edit the shared variable group holding a deployment password. Which change best fits the control this situation calls for?
choices: Move the variable group into a different project so that the inherited permissions no longer apply.
Leave the settings unchanged and rely on the team's shared understanding of who should edit it.
Keep the Allow on All valid users and add a Deny on Manage for the Interns group so they are blocked.
Set the Allow on Manage to Not set for All valid users and grant it only to a small custom group made for the people who maintain that variable group.
questions.why: Granting to a narrow custom group limits who can change the secret, while removing the broad Allow stops the wide access that comes from granting to all valid users.

questions.prompt: A project administrator at a retail company puts a Deny on Create pipeline for the Project Valid Users group at the project level, intending to restrict one contractor. Now the internal delivery team, who need to create pipelines, are blocked. What is the most accurate explanation and fix?
choices: The Deny is set high in the hierarchy and flows down to the pipelines, so the fix is to move the restriction to a narrower group or object instead of the project-wide level.
Pipeline creation is a repository permission, so the Deny must be removed from the repository only, leaving the project setting alone.
The delivery team needs to be removed from the organization and re-added so their group memberships reset.
The delivery team is blocked because Azure DevOps counts the number of Deny entries, and one more Allow would outweigh them.
questions.why: Permissions inherit downward, so a Deny at the project level silently blocks every team beneath it; the correct fix is to scope the restriction to the contractor's own group.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how permissions are assigned and combined in Azure DevOps, and name one limit or tradeoff of controlling access mainly through group membership.
lessons.modelAnswer: Permissions in Azure DevOps are set on objects like repositories, pipelines, and environments, and they can be Allow, Deny, or not set. We put people in groups, such as Contributors or Readers, rather than granting rights to each person, because groups are easier to audit and change when someone joins or leaves. A user's effective rights come from all the groups they belong to, and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow for the same permission. The tradeoff is that broad groups are convenient but give more access than a specific job needs, so a large group with one Allow can unlock a sensitive pipeline for everyone in it. Another tradeoff is that a Deny buried in a parent group can block people in ways that are hard to spot, so I check the effective permissions on the object before assuming a group works.
rubricPoints: Permissions are Allow, Deny, or not set, and each applies to one object.
Users get rights through group membership, and rights are inherited down the hierarchy.
An explicit Deny overrides an Allow for the same permission, even across groups.
A tradeoff exists: broad groups are convenient but can grant more access than the job needs.

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace Allow, Deny, and inherited permissions to a final decision, which is the core reasoning in this objective.

lessons.plain: When people outside your core engineering team need to use your DevOps tools, you decide how much they can do. Too little and they cannot help; too much and they can change things they should not. The skill is choosing the smallest set of permissions that still lets the person do their job. Azure DevOps offers a free stakeholder level for people who only need to follow and comment on planned work. GitHub lets you invite someone from outside your organization as an outside collaborator, with rights limited to the specific repositories you choose. Both are about giving people the right door, not the master key.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor needs to see the sprint board and comment on bugs, but must never change any code. Which access level would you give them in Azure DevOps and in GitHub, and why?
lessons.teach: Access level is the amount of a DevOps tool a person may use. Least privilege means giving each person only what their job requires, and no more. In Azure DevOps, an access level is a tier attached to a user account. Stakeholder is the tier meant for people who track work but do not build: by default they can view and contribute to work items, boards and dashboards, but they do not get the full set of repository and pipeline features a developer gets. Basic is the tier for members who write code and run pipelines. Access level is separate from permission. A permission such as editing a pipeline is granted through a security group, which is a different decision. In GitHub, an outside collaborator is a person who is not a member of your organization but has been given access to one or more specific repositories. Repository roles, from least to most powerful, are read, triage, write, maintain and admin. Read lets someone view and clone. Triage lets them manage issues and pull requests without changing code. Write allows pushing branches. Worked example: the contractor must comment on bugs and see progress, but must never change code. Step 1: list the actions needed, which are viewing and commenting on work items. Step 2: match them to the lowest tier, which is Azure DevOps Stakeholder. Step 3: in GitHub, if they need to triage issues in one repository, invite them as an outside collaborator with triage on that repository only, not as an organization member and not with write. Common mistake: granting Basic or write access just to be safe, or adding the person to the organization so they can see everything. The consequence in a running system is that a write-level account can push to any branch the rules allow, so a leaked credential carries that power into your code. Least privilege limits the damage from both honest error and compromise. Grant narrowly, and review every external grant when the contract ends.

questions.prompt: A compliance auditor at Harbor Dental needs to review test results and comment on quality-related work items in Azure DevOps, and needs to read the source code of one GitHub repository, without changing anything. Step 1: the Azure DevOps actions are viewing and commenting on work items, so the lowest matching tier is Stakeholder. Step 2: the GitHub need is reading one repository. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it: choose the GitHub grant for that auditor, which is to invite them as an outside collaborator with the role that lets them view and clone that one repository.
choices: Give the auditor the admin role on the repository so they can review settings
Add the auditor to the organization as a member with the maintain role on all repositories
Invite the auditor as an outside collaborator with the write role on every repository in the organization
Invite the auditor as an outside collaborator with the read role on that one repository only
questions.why: Read is the lowest GitHub repository role that lets an outside collaborator view and clone, and limiting the grant to one repository as an outside collaborator follows least privilege.

questions.prompt: In Azure DevOps, which access level is meant for people who track work and view boards and dashboards but do not build software?
choices: Basic
Project owner
Stakeholder
Basic plus a pipeline-editing security group
questions.why: Stakeholder is the tier designed for people who track work but do not build, while Basic is for members who write code and run pipelines.

questions.prompt: A team member already has Basic access in Azure DevOps but cannot edit a pipeline definition. Which check is the most appropriate first step?
choices: Check whether the security group that grants the pipeline-editing permission includes them
Raise their access level to a higher tier than Basic
Remove and re-add their user account to reset the access level
Downgrade them to Stakeholder so the access level is cleaner
questions.why: Access level and permission are separate decisions, so a Basic user who lacks a pipeline permission needs the security group grant checked rather than a change to the access tier.

questions.prompt: A reviewer from outside your company needs to close stale issues and apply labels to pull requests in one GitHub repository, but must never push a branch. Which repository role fits?
choices: Write
Triage
Maintain
Admin
questions.why: Triage lets a person manage issues and pull requests without changing code, and it does not allow pushing branches the way write does.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not simply make the new contractor a regular team member so they stop asking for access. Explain how you would choose the access level for an external stakeholder in Azure DevOps and an outside collaborator in GitHub, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from what the contractor actually needs to do, then choose the lowest tier that allows it. In Azure DevOps, a Stakeholder account can follow and comment on work items and boards without the code and pipeline features that a Basic member gets. In GitHub, I would invite them as an outside collaborator on only the repository they need, with triage rather than write, so they can manage issues without pushing code. Making them a full organization member would give them reach into repositories nobody asked them to touch. The tradeoff is friction: a stakeholder cannot see everything, so they may need a developer to share a build result or attach a file, and every external grant needs a reminder to review and remove it when the contract ends.
rubricPoints: Chooses the lowest access tier that matches the actual tasks, not the most convenient one
Explains that Azure DevOps Stakeholder limits access to tracking work rather than code and pipelines
Explains that a GitHub outside collaborator is scoped to chosen repositories and is not an organization member
Names a real tradeoff, such as limited visibility or the need to review and remove access later

suggested.rationale: Deciding which principal gets which level of access against a stated need is the same reasoning a planned authorization policy evaluator would exercise.

lessons.plain: A team's project setup decides where its work lives and who sees it. Think of a company's filing system: one cabinet for the whole department, a folder for each group, and labels that say which group owns each file. In Azure DevOps, Microsoft's tool for planning work, building code and shipping releases, a project is the container for one body of work, and teams are groups inside it that each get their own backlog, board and schedule. Configuring projects and teams means deciding how work is labelled and routed, so each piece of work lands on the right board and shows up in the right reports.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company has three engineering groups sharing one big to-do list with no labels, what problems would you expect within a month, and what would you add to fix them?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A project in Azure DevOps is a container that holds the repositories, pipelines, boards and other tools for one body of work. A team is a named group of people inside a project who share a backlog, which is the ordered list of work waiting to be done, and a board that shows that work as columns. An area path is a hierarchical label on a work item that says which part of the product or which group owns it. An iteration path is a label for a time window, such as a sprint, that says when the work is planned. Each team claims the area paths it owns and chooses the iterations it uses, and its default area path is the label that new items receive when they are created from that team's board.

Why it works. Labels are how the system decides what appears where. A team's board only displays items whose area path falls under an area that team has claimed, so the labels act as the routing rule, not decoration.

Worked example. A project called Payments has two teams, Checkout and Ledger. Under the project you create the area paths Payments\Checkout and Payments\Ledger, plus the iteration path Payments\Sprint 12. You set Checkout's default area to Payments\Checkout and claim that area for the team. A tester on the Checkout board files a bug. Step one: the new item opens with the area Payments\Checkout because that is the team default. Step two: the item appears on Checkout's backlog because its area falls under a claimed path. Step three: it does not appear on Ledger's board, so Ledger's sprint load stays accurate.

Common mistake. Teams often leave every default on the project root or leave some area paths claimed by no team. Then items show up on everyone's board or on nobody's, and capacity figures and queries stop meaning anything.

Consequence. When routing is wrong, an urgent bug can sit unowned because no board shows it, and sprint reports quietly count the wrong team's effort against their plan.

questions.prompt: Northwind's Storefront project has two teams, Web and Mobile. The area paths Storefront\Web and Storefront\Mobile exist, and each team claims its own. Mobile's default area is Storefront\Mobile. Trace a crash report a tester files from the Mobile board. Step 1: the new item opens with the area Storefront\Mobile, because that is Mobile's default. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Mobile's sprint load includes the item, while Web's load does not.
choices: The item is copied to the project root so that every team can see it on its own board.
The item is hidden from all boards until a project administrator approves its iteration path.
The system reassigns the item to Web because Web is the first team listed in the project.
It appears on Mobile's backlog, since its area falls under a path Mobile claims.
questions.why: A team's board shows only items whose area path falls under an area that team has claimed, so the crash report appears on Mobile's backlog because Mobile claims Storefront\Mobile.

questions.prompt: What does a team's default area path control?
choices: It is the label new items receive when created from that team's board.
It sets the sprint dates the team's work is planned against.
It caps how many items the team can hold on its board at once.
It lists the people who are allowed to edit the team's backlog.
questions.why: The default area path is the label automatically applied to new items created from a team's board; it does not control dates, limits, or permissions.

questions.prompt: Contoso's area path Contoso\Billing is not claimed by any team. A customer's payment failure is filed under that area. What is the most likely result?
choices: The item appears on no team's board, so it can go unowned.
The item is automatically assigned to the project's first team.
The item appears on every team's board so someone will notice it.
The item moves to the iteration with the most open capacity.
questions.why: A board only displays items whose area falls under a path a team has claimed, so an unclaimed area appears on no board and the urgent bug can sit unowned.

questions.prompt: A project has teams Atlas and Beacon. Beacon's sprint load is inflated by Atlas's work. Which configuration corrects this?
choices: Set Beacon's default area to the project root so its items are easier to find.
Delete all area paths so every item is labelled by iteration instead.
Give both teams the same iteration path so their load is pooled.
Give each team its own claimed area path and set each team's default to its own path.
questions.why: Separate claimed area paths with matching defaults keep each team's items on its own board and in its own load figures, which stops Atlas's work from counting against Beacon.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how area paths and a team's default area decide which board a new work item appears on, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on area paths for routing.
lessons.modelAnswer: A work item has an area path, which is a label saying which part of the product owns it. Each team in an Azure DevOps project claims one or more area paths, and its board shows only items whose area falls under those claims. The team's default area is the label automatically applied to items created from that board, so most items land correctly without anyone thinking about it. Iteration paths work the same way for time: they say which sprint the item is planned for. The main limit is that routing depends on people and defaults being right. If someone files an item under the parent area, or two teams claim overlapping paths, the item can show up on the wrong board or on several boards at once. Nothing stops that automatically, so the team has to review area assignments, and reports built on those labels are only as accurate as that review.
rubricPoints: Area paths label items by owning part of the product, and iteration paths label them by time window.
A team claims area paths, and its board shows items under those claimed paths.
The team's default area sets the label on items created from that board.
A limit: routing is only as good as how labels are applied, so misfiled or overlapping items land on the wrong board.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly settings and structure rather than a skill a listed mission drills, so reading the concepts and then checking them in a sandbox project is the efficient route.

lessons.plain: Azure Key Vault is a managed safe that a cloud provider runs for you. It holds the sensitive things your software needs but should never write into code: passwords and connection strings, the cryptographic keys used to lock and unlock data, and digital certificates that prove who a server is. Your applications and pipelines ask the vault for these items when they run, after proving who they are, instead of carrying copies around. Access is granted by permission rules, reads can be logged, and saving a new value creates a new version so you can rotate credentials without rewriting every tool that uses them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your deployment needs a database password. Where should that password live so the pipeline can use it, without the password appearing in the source repository or in build logs?
lessons.teach:
A vault is a managed service that stores three kinds of sensitive item. A secret is any text value you must keep private, such as a password, an API token or a connection string. A key is a cryptographic key that stays inside the vault: you ask the vault to encrypt, decrypt or sign something with it, and the key material is never handed back to you. A certificate is an X.509 certificate, a document that binds a public key to an identity, packaged with its private key so a server can use it for HTTPS. Each item has a name and a version history.

Why it works: the sensitive value lives in one place with one set of access rules, so you do not scatter copies through repositories, pipeline definitions and servers. A caller authenticates with an identity, and the vault checks whether that identity holds a permission such as reading secrets, using keys or managing certificates. Access can be granted through Azure role-based access control (RBAC), the modern model, or through older vault access policies. Either way the principle is least privilege: each caller gets only the actions it needs.

Worked example. A deployment needs a database password stored as a secret called db-password. Step 1: an administrator saves the value in the vault as db-password. Step 2: the deployment's identity is granted a read-only secret role on that vault. Step 3: when the pipeline runs, it asks the vault for db-password and receives the current version. Step 4: the password is rotated by saving a new value, which creates version two. The next fetch returns version two, and no file or pipeline definition changed.

Common mistake: pasting the secret into a pipeline variable or configuration file 'just this once'. That copy outlives the vault, can appear in logs and history, and never rotates. Another mistake is giving owner rights to everyone who needs to read one value.

Consequence: a leaked secret stays usable until it is rotated, so the vault only helps if rotation is practiced. Soft delete and purge protection keep deleted items recoverable for a set period, which guards against accidental loss.

Vault access is the control point for every secret, key and certificate the vault holds.

questions.prompt: A payments team keeps a card-processor API token in a vault named kv-shop-prod, under the item name payments-api-token. Step 1: the team saves the token value in the vault. Step 2: the payments service's identity is granted a read-only secret role on kv-shop-prod. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the processor issues a new token, and the team saves it under the same name, which creates version two, with no change to the service's code. Which entry correctly fills Step 3?
choices: When the service runs, it asks the vault for payments-api-token and receives the current version.
The administrator turns off purge protection so the old token is removed at once.
The service's configuration file is updated to hold the token value for faster startup.
The team emails the token to the on-call engineer so they can keep a local backup.
questions.why: At run time the service requests the item from the vault and gets the current version, so the value is never copied into code, files or messages.

questions.prompt: A team needs a certificate for HTTPS on its public website. Which vault item type fits, and why?
choices: A secret, because a certificate is simply a text password stored for safekeeping.
A certificate, because it binds a public key to an identity and is packaged with its private key for server use.
A key used only to sign build artifacts, because keys are what HTTPS uses.
A connection string, because it tells the browser where the website lives.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a certificate as an X.509 document binding a public key to an identity, packaged with its private key so a server can use it for HTTPS.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to copy a vault key's material onto a build server so the build can encrypt files offline. What is the problem with this plan?
choices: Keys are not a vault item type, so the developer should store the key as a secret instead.
Keys never leave the vault; the build should ask the vault to encrypt, decrypt or sign instead of copying key material.
Keys can be exported after encryption as long as the build server is trusted, so the plan is fine.
The vault returns key material only once, at creation, so the developer should copy it then.
questions.why: The teaching text states the key stays inside the vault and the material is never handed back; callers request operations such as encrypt, decrypt or sign.

questions.prompt: A pipeline secret was printed in a build log two days ago, and the team has since saved a new value. Why does the team still need to act on the leak?
choices: Soft delete removes the leaked value from logs as soon as the new value is saved.
A leaked secret stays usable until rotated, so rotation must be practiced to close that window.
The vault automatically revokes any value that has appeared in a log.
Only the team lead can use a value that appeared in a log, so the risk is small.
questions.why: The teaching text says a leaked secret remains usable until it is rotated, and that the vault only helps if rotation is practiced.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we keep a deployment's database password in Azure Key Vault instead of a pipeline variable, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a vault.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pipeline variable is a copy. The value sits in the pipeline definition, can show up in logs, and every place holding it must be changed when the password rotates. Key Vault keeps one authoritative copy with its own access rules. The pipeline's identity is granted read access to that one secret, fetches the current version at run time, and nothing sensitive is committed to source. Rotation becomes saving a new version. The tradeoff is that the vault becomes a dependency: if the identity loses access or the vault is unreachable, the deployment fails, so access must be granted deliberately and tested. The vault also cannot stop an authorized caller from printing the value, so pipelines still need masking and careful logging.
rubricPoints: A pipeline variable or file is a copy that is hard to rotate and easy to leak
Key Vault keeps one authoritative copy with access rules and versioning
Callers fetch the current value at run time under least-privilege permissions
A real limit: the vault becomes a dependency, and authorized callers can still expose values

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix how a deploy receives a credential without exposing it, which is the core Key Vault retrieval skill.

lessons.plain: A secret is any value that proves who you are, such as a password, an access key, or a token. Anyone holding it can act as you. Build and deploy pipelines usually need secrets to reach cloud accounts, and the old habit was to paste one into the pipeline settings and hope it never leaked. Secretless authentication changes that. The pipeline presents a signed statement from its own host, such as GitHub or Azure DevOps, saying which repository and branch is running. The cloud checks that statement against a trust rule you wrote in advance and hands back a short-lived pass. Nothing long-lived is stored, so there is little to steal.
lessons.guessPrompt: A deploy job must log into a cloud account. Option A stores a password in the CI settings. Option B lets the CI system prove its identity at run time and receive a short-lived pass. Which option leaves less to steal if a log file leaks, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A secret is a credential stored somewhere a program can read it. A federated credential is a trust rule you configure on the cloud identity, saying which external identity provider may use it and which exact caller is accepted. OpenID Connect, or OIDC, is a standard way for one system to hand a signed identity token to another. A workload identity is the identity given to a running job rather than to a person.

Why it works. GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines can each issue an OIDC token to a running job. The token carries claims, which are facts such as the organisation, repository, branch or environment, together with the issuer that signed it. The cloud side compares those claims with the federated credential. If they match, it issues a short-lived access token that expires within about an hour. The pipeline never stores a password.

Worked example. A deploy job runs on the main branch of the repository contoso/shop. Step 1: the CI host signs a token whose subject says repo contoso/shop, branch main. Step 2: the job sends that token to the cloud sign-in endpoint. Step 3: the cloud checks that the issuer is the expected CI host and that the subject matches the federated credential exactly. Step 4: it returns a short-lived token, the job deploys, and the token expires.

Common mistake. Writing the subject loosely, for example with a wildcard that accepts any branch or pull request, so untrusted code can obtain deploy rights. Keeping an old client secret in repository settings as a fallback brings back the leak risk you were removing.

Consequence. A leaked stored secret keeps working until someone rotates it, often weeks later. With a tight federated rule, a leaked log line reveals nothing reusable, and a job from a fork cannot match the rule. The safe pattern is a narrow trust rule with no stored secret at all.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's billing team runs a nightly deploy job in Azure Pipelines for the project fabrikam/billing-svc, on the branch release/2.4. The job is set up with OpenID Connect and no stored secret. Here are the steps in order. Step 1: Azure Pipelines signs an OIDC token that carries claims for the organisation, project and branch, plus the issuer that signed it. Step 2: the job sends that token to the cloud sign-in endpoint. Step 3: [MISSING STEP: the cloud checks the issuer and compares the token's subject with the federated credential, and it issues a token only if they match exactly.] Step 4: the cloud returns a short-lived access token, the job deploys, and the token expires. Which option correctly fills in the missing step 3?
choices: The cloud copies the signed token into the pipeline variable group so the next night's run can reuse it.
The cloud checks the issuer and compares the token's subject with the federated credential exactly, and it issues a token only if both match.
The cloud accepts any subject that begins with fabrikam/billing-svc, so every branch in the project can deploy.
The cloud issues a token valid for 90 days so the nightly job does not have to sign in again.
questions.why: Step 3 is the trust check: the cloud confirms the expected issuer and an exact subject match against the federated credential before it returns a short-lived token.

questions.prompt: In the sense used in this course, what is a federated credential?
choices: A saved copy of an OIDC token that a job reuses on later runs.
A list of every person allowed to sign in to the cloud subscription.
A trust rule set on the cloud identity that names which external identity provider may use it and which exact caller is accepted.
A password that the pipeline reads from a protected variable at the start of each run.
questions.why: The course defines a federated credential as a trust rule on the cloud identity that names the external provider and the exact accepted caller, not as a password or a saved token.

questions.prompt: A team sets the federated credential subject to the pattern northwind/web:* so that every branch and pull request can deploy to production without changing settings. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: The cloud will refuse all deploys because wildcards are never permitted in OIDC subjects.
Untrusted code from any branch or pull request can match the broad subject and obtain deploy rights.
Tokens will stay valid for longer than the usual short lifetime of about an hour.
The pipeline will have to store a client secret before the wildcard pattern can match.
questions.why: A loose subject lets code the owner never reviewed, including code from pull requests, match the rule and receive a short-lived deploy token, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: An engineer on the inventory-api job in the northwind organisation, which already uses a tight OIDC rule for the main branch, keeps the old client secret in repository settings as a backup in case OIDC fails. What is the consequence the teaching text points to?
choices: The backup secret would expire within an hour, so it is harmless to keep in repository settings.
A leaked stored secret would keep working until someone rotates it, often weeks later, so the backup reintroduces the leak risk.
The secret would work only from forks, so the main branch would stay safe.
The cloud would reject the OIDC tokens while the secret exists, so the backup would have to be removed first.
questions.why: The teaching text says a leaked stored secret keeps working until rotated, often for weeks, and that keeping one as a fallback brings back the leak risk the OIDC setup removed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a pipeline can deploy to the cloud without a stored password or key. Name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The pipeline asks its CI host for a short-lived, signed identity token for that specific run. That token says which repository, branch or environment is running. The cloud has a federated credential that lists the exact subject it trusts, and it checks the token's issuer and subject against that rule. If both match, the cloud returns a temporary access token that expires within about an hour. Nothing long-lived is stored in the repository, so a leaked log has nothing reusable. The main tradeoff is that the protection depends entirely on how precise the trust rule is. A wildcard subject can let an unintended branch or fork match. Setup is also more involved than pasting a secret, and some tools or older pipeline steps may still need a stored credential, which then has to be rotated and guarded.
rubricPoints: Defines the pipeline's signed identity token and what its claims describe
Explains that the cloud matches the issuer and subject against a federated credential before issuing a short-lived token
States that no long-lived secret is stored, so a leak yields nothing reusable
Names a tradeoff, such as the risk of loose subject matching or extra setup effort

suggested.rationale: The mission has the learner fix a deploy's authentication wiring without exposing the secret, which practises the same reasoning about where credentials live and how they are trusted.

lessons.plain: When a program is released to a server, it often needs a private file along with it, such as a signing certificate, a key file that proves identity, or a configuration file holding a login. Those files should not sit in the project's source code, where anyone with read access could copy them. A secure file store is a locked cabinet inside the delivery tool. You place the file there once, decide which automated pipelines may open it, and the delivery job borrows a copy only while it runs. This objective is about choosing that pattern on purpose and knowing what it does not protect.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your deployment script needs a signing certificate file to run. Where would you keep that file so the automated build can use it unattended, but the file is not visible to every developer who can read the code repository? Name one place and say why it is better than committing the file to the repo.
lessons.teach:
A secure file is a file you upload once into a protected store instead of committing it to source control. In Azure Pipelines, that store is part of the Azure DevOps project's Library, and the file is kept encrypted at rest. Encrypted at rest means it is scrambled on the storage disk, so someone who obtains the raw storage cannot read it directly. Pipeline authorization is the setting that says which pipelines are allowed to request a given file. Roles such as reader, user, creator and administrator control who can view, use, change or authorize the file.

Why it works: the file never lives in the repository, so clones, forks and past commits do not contain it. At run time, a task named DownloadSecureFile fetches the file onto the build agent, which is the virtual machine or container that runs the job. The task exposes the file's location through a variable, so later steps work with a path rather than the contents. When the job ends, the temporary copy on the agent is removed, which limits how long it exists.

Worked example: a release needs a certificate called deploy-signing.pfx. Step 1: an administrator uploads the file to the secure file store and authorizes only the release pipeline. Step 2: the pipeline runs a DownloadSecureFile step with a name such as cert. Step 3: a later step signs the package using the path held in the variable for cert. Step 4: the job finishes and the temporary copy is cleaned up. The repository never held the certificate.

Common mistake: a step that echoes the file's contents, or copies the file into a build artifact that is published. That republishes the secret into a place with wider access. The store protects the file at rest, not after a script prints it.

Consequence: if the certificate is committed to the repo, anyone who can clone it, and every old commit, holds a copy, and rotating it means rewriting history and reissuing the certificate. With a secure file, you replace it in one place and the pipelines pick up the new version.

questions.prompt: A mobile team builds an Android app in Azure Pipelines and needs a signing keystore named release.jks. Their steps so far: (1) an administrator uploads release.jks to the project's secure file store, the Library, and authorizes only the Android release pipeline; (2) the job starts on the build agent, the virtual machine that runs the job. (3) This step is missing. (4) A signing step reads the file's location from the variable the download task created and signs the app. Which step belongs in place of (3)?
choices: The team commits release.jks to a hidden folder in the repository so the agent can find it on checkout.
The job runs a DownloadSecureFile task, given a name such as keystore, which copies release.jks onto the agent and sets the variable.
The signing step prints the keystore contents to the job log so reviewers can confirm the right key was used.
An administrator grants the Android pipeline the Administrator role on the file so it can read the contents directly.
questions.why: DownloadSecureFile is the task that fetches the protected file onto the agent and exposes its path through a variable, which is what step (4) depends on.

questions.prompt: In this teaching text, what does 'encrypted at rest' mean for a secure file?
choices: The file is hashed so its contents can be checked for changes but never recovered.
The file is protected by a password that each pipeline author must type before running a job.
The file is scrambled on the storage disk, so someone who gets the raw storage cannot read it directly.
The file is encrypted only while the agent downloads it over the network.
questions.why: Encrypted at rest means the stored copy is scrambled on disk, which is the protection the secure file store provides for the file while it sits in storage.

questions.prompt: A payments team needs a private key for a test certificate authority to sign nightly test certificates. Which approach best keeps the key out of source control while letting only the nightly deploy pipeline use it?
choices: Upload the key to secure files, authorize only the nightly deploy pipeline, and have that pipeline download it at run time.
Paste the key into the pipeline YAML as a plain-text value so every run has it without a download step.
Copy the key into the published build artifact so the release stage can use it without a separate download.
Commit the key to a private branch that only the payments engineers can clone, and reference the branch from the pipeline.
questions.why: Secure files keep the key out of the repository, and pipeline authorization limits which pipeline can request it, which matches the requirement exactly.

questions.prompt: A job step runs a command that prints the contents of a downloaded secure file to the job log, so a developer can debug a certificate problem. What is the main risk?
choices: Secure files are encrypted in transit, so anything written to the job log stays protected.
The contents are copied into the job log, where people with log access may have wider permissions than the file store allowed, so the protection no longer applies.
The variable holds only a path, so printing it shows a location and exposes nothing secret.
The agent deletes the file when the job starts, so there is nothing left to print by the time the step runs.
questions.why: The secure file store protects the file at rest, but once a script prints the contents, the secret sits in a log that can be read more widely than the store.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just commit the production signing certificate to the repo in a private folder, since the repo is already private. Explain to them, in your own words, why a secure file store is still the better choice, and name one limit of the approach you are recommending.
lessons.modelAnswer: A private repo does not limit access well enough. Everyone with read access, every fork or clone, and every past commit would hold the certificate, and I could not revoke those copies without rewriting history and reissuing the certificate. With a secure file, the certificate sits in the pipeline library, encrypted at rest and open only to pipelines we authorize. The job copies it to the build agent only while it runs, and the copy is removed when the job ends. The limit is that this protects the file at rest, not after the job uses it. If a script prints it or we publish it as an artifact, the secret escapes, so the signing step still has to be written so it never echoes the contents. This store also belongs to this Azure DevOps project, so other systems need their own approach.
rubricPoints: The file lives in a protected store, not in source control, so clones and history do not hold it.
Only authorized pipelines can request the file, and roles limit who can view or change it.
The pipeline fetches a temporary copy onto the build agent at run time, and that copy is removed after the job.
The approach protects the file at rest but not if a step prints or publishes it.
Rotating the file means replacing it in one place rather than rewriting repository history.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you fix how a deploy gets its credential without leaking it, which uses the same reasoning as keeping sensitive files out of the repo and handing them over only at run time.

lessons.plain: Sensitive information is any value that would hurt you if a stranger saw it, such as passwords, access keys, tokens, certificates, and private customer data. A delivery pipeline is the automated line that builds and ships software, and it handles these values constantly. Leakage happens when one escapes somewhere it should never reach, like the saved history of a code repository, a build log that many people can read, a packaged output file, or a public copy of the project. Designing a pipeline to prevent leakage means deciding where secrets may live, who and what can read them, and how you catch mistakes before they spread.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate's build log shows the line 'Connecting with password abc123' because a script printed its settings. Before reading on, list two places besides the log where that password could now be exposed, and say what you would do first.
lessons.teach:
A secret is any value that proves identity or grants access, such as a password, an API token, a signing key, or a connection string. A pipeline is the automated sequence of steps that builds, tests, and deploys software. It runs with copies of secrets so it can log in to other systems. Leakage happens when a secret is written somewhere that more people or systems can read than should. The main routes are source code, logs, artifacts (the packaged output a build produces), and forks (independent copies of a repository, which may be controlled by outsiders).

Each route has a matching defense. Keep secrets out of source code, because history is permanent and every clone keeps a copy. Store them in a dedicated secret store and inject them at run time as secret variables. The runner then masks those values in logs, meaning it replaces a known secret value with asterisks if it appears in output. Use secret scanning, which searches commits for patterns that look like keys, and push protection, which blocks a push that contains one before it lands. Limit who can read secrets: deployment secrets should be available only to the protected main branch and approved environments, never to a pull request from a fork, because that code is written by someone you may not trust.

Worked example: a script prints the database password variable to debug a failure. Step 1: the variable holds the real secret. Step 2: the print writes that value to standard output. Step 3: the runner recognizes the exact value and masks it in the log. Step 4: but if the script encodes the value first, or splits it across lines, the masking no longer matches and the secret appears in plain text. The reliable fix is that no script prints secret values at all.

Common mistake: assuming that deleting a secret in a later commit removes it. Git history keeps the old commit, so the secret must be revoked and rotated, meaning disabled and replaced with a new value.

Consequence: a leaked deployment key lets anyone who finds it deploy to production until it is rotated. The response order is revoke first, rotate second, and clean up history last.

Treat every secret as exposed the moment it reaches a place it should not, and design the pipeline so that it never does.

questions.prompt: A retail company's build script writes its storage account access key into an appsettings.json file so the app can read it at startup. Step 1: the script writes the real key into that file. Step 2: the file is zipped into the build artifact. Step 3: the artifact is published to an internal package feed that about 400 staff can read. The security team finds the key in the feed. Step 4 is still missing: what must the team do first, before any other cleanup?
choices: Revoke the exposed storage key so it stops working, then issue a replacement key
Turn on secret scanning so the leak is flagged the next time it happens
Add appsettings.json to the ignore list so future builds skip that file
Delete the artifact from the feed and wait for download caches to clear
questions.why: The exposed key is still valid until it is revoked, so revoking it comes first and replacing it second, while cleanup of copies comes last.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean that a pipeline secret has 'leaked'?
choices: The build ran slower than its usual time because a step failed and retried
A pipeline stage was approved by someone outside the release team
A value that proves identity or grants access was written where more readers can see it than should
The runner's log grew past its storage limit and older lines were removed
questions.why: Leakage is defined in the teaching text as a secret being written somewhere that more people or systems can read than should, which matches the third choice in plain words.

questions.prompt: A build script prints a connection string after reversing its characters. The runner normally masks secrets in logs by replacing the exact known value with asterisks. Why is the reversed string likely to appear in the log in plain text?
choices: The masking only applies to values stored in the repository, not in a secret store
Reversed text is too short for the runner to treat as a secret
Runners never mask anything that is printed to standard error
The runner's masking matches the exact stored value, so a transformed copy is not recognised
questions.why: Masking depends on recognising the exact secret value, so any changed form of that value can slip through, which is why scripts should not print secrets at all.

questions.prompt: A contributor opens a pull request from a personal fork of a team's repository, and the pipeline runs automatically for that pull request. Which control best limits the risk to deployment secrets?
choices: Keep deployment secrets available to every pull request so tests can reach the staging service
Make deployment secrets available only to the protected main branch and approved environments, not to fork pull requests
Store the deployment secrets in the source code with a note asking people not to read them
Rename the deployment secrets each week so forked code cannot use old names
questions.why: Deployment secrets should be scoped to the protected main branch and approved environments, because code from a fork is written by someone the team may not trust.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would stop a deployment password from leaking through a pipeline. Name one control that catches mistakes and one limit of log masking.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the password out of the repository and load it at run time from a secret store into the pipeline as a secret variable, so the runner masks it in logs. I would scope that variable to the protected main branch and the production environment, so a pull request from a fork cannot read it. For mistakes, secret scanning and push protection search commits for key-shaped strings and block a push before it lands. The limit of masking is that it only hides exact values the runner knows about. A script that encodes or splits the value can still expose it, so the rule is that scripts never print secrets. If something has leaked, I revoke the secret first and rotate it, because deleting the line does not remove it from history.
rubricPoints: Secrets stay out of source code and are injected at run time from a secret store.
Log masking hides only exact known values, so transformed or split secrets can still leak.
Scope secrets to protected branches and approved environments so forks cannot read them.
Secret scanning and push protection catch key-shaped strings before they land in the repository.
A leaked secret must be revoked and rotated; deleting it from history is not enough.

suggested.rationale: This mission has you fix a deploy's secret wiring without exposing the secret, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Security and compliance scanning means running automated checks on your software before it reaches users. Think of inspectors on an assembly line, each looking for a different kind of defect. One reads your own code for risky patterns. One checks the third-party libraries you pulled in for known weaknesses. One hunts for passwords or keys that were pasted where they should not be. One checks that the licence terms of every component allow how you plan to ship the product. Designing the strategy means deciding which inspector runs, at which point in the delivery process, and whether a failed check stops the release or only raises a warning.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's pipeline already runs unit tests. One developer commits a database password into a config file, and separately the project pulls in a library version that has a published security flaw. Which kind of check would catch each problem, and at what point in the delivery process should each check run?
lessons.teach:
A scanner is an automated tool that inspects software for a specific kind of problem. Four kinds matter here. Static code analysis (sometimes called SAST) reads your source code without running it and flags risky patterns, such as building a database query by joining user input into the text. Dependency scanning, also called software composition analysis, lists the third-party libraries your build uses, including the versions, and compares them against databases of published vulnerabilities. Secret scanning looks for text that matches the shape of a credential, such as a key format or a long random-looking string, in files and in commit history. Licence scanning identifies the licence attached to each component and checks it against the rules your organisation has set.

Why this works: each scanner only knows its own kind of problem, so a strategy combines several, and each one runs where its input exists. Dependency scanning needs the dependency list, so it runs after the build resolves it. Secret scanning can run on every commit because it only needs the text.

Worked example. A developer updates a library to version 2.1.0. The dependency scan reads the lock file, matches 2.1.0 against an advisory that says 2.1.4 fixes a high-severity flaw, and the policy says high findings block merges. The pipeline fails. The developer updates to 2.1.4, the scan passes, and the merge proceeds.

Common mistake: running scans on a weekly schedule, or only producing reports. Findings then pile up, nobody owns them, and the risk ships anyway. Another mistake is treating secret scanning as a cure. A secret that has already been pushed must be treated as compromised and rotated, because removing it from the latest file does not remove it from history.

Consequence: a blocking gate stops a bad release, but a gate tuned too strictly produces false positives, and teams then disable it. Good strategy sets gates by severity, allows documented exceptions with an expiry date, and reviews them regularly.

questions.prompt: A payments team's pipeline runs dependency scanning after the restore step, because the scanner needs the resolved list of library versions. The scanner reads the lock file and finds a parser library at version 4.2.0. An advisory matches that version and says 4.2.3 fixes a medium-severity flaw. The team's policy says medium findings produce a warning but do not block the merge. Steps 1 to 3 are done: (1) the scanner reads the resolved versions and matches 4.2.0 to the advisory; (2) the policy compares the severity, medium, with the blocking threshold and records a warning instead of failing the build; (3) the warning is assigned to a named owner with a target date for the upgrade. Step 4 is the only one not yet written, and it is what closes the finding. Which choice correctly completes step 4?
choices: Block the merge until the scanner has been run once a week for a month.
Once the owner upgrades to 4.2.3, the next scan confirms the finding is gone and the warning is closed.
Turn off dependency scanning for this library, because medium findings never block.
Upgrade to 4.2.3 straight away, with no owner, since the fix is known.
questions.why: The finding is closed only when the fix is applied and a fresh scan no longer reports the vulnerable version, which is what the correct choice describes.

questions.prompt: A developer accidentally pastes a cloud storage access key into a configuration file and commits it. Which kind of scanner is most likely to catch this before the code is merged?
choices: Secret scanning, because it looks for text that matches the shape of a credential
Static code analysis, because it runs the code and watches what the key does
Licence scanning, because it checks the key against the organisation's licence rules
Dependency scanning, because it compares the key against published vulnerability databases
questions.why: Secret scanning looks for credential-shaped text in files and commits, which is exactly what a pasted access key is.

questions.prompt: A team finds a database password in a commit from last month. A later commit removes the password from the current file, and the secret scan now passes. What is the correct response?
choices: Nothing is needed, because the latest file is clean and the risk is gone.
Add the password to the scanner's exception list so the old finding stops appearing.
Rotate the password, because the earlier commit still exposes it in history.
Ask the scanner to run weekly until the old finding ages out of its report.
questions.why: Removing a secret from the latest file does not remove it from history, so a pushed secret must be treated as compromised and rotated.

questions.prompt: A team's build gate blocks the merge on every scanner finding, regardless of severity. Developers are now turning the gate off to get work done. What is the better design?
choices: Keep blocking on every finding so that no risk can slip through the pipeline.
Remove the gate entirely and rely on developers to check findings during code review.
Run all scans on a weekly schedule and produce reports for the security team to read.
Set gates by severity, allow documented exceptions with an expiry date, and review them regularly.
questions.why: A gate tuned too strictly causes false positives and gets disabled, so good strategy sets thresholds by severity and manages exceptions with expiry dates and regular review.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a security scan that only produces a report is not the same as a security gate, and name one limit of automated scanning that the team should still plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A report records findings, but nothing stops the change, so a risky library or a leaked key can still reach production if someone does not read the report in time. A gate is a stage in the pipeline that fails when findings cross an agreed severity threshold, so the change cannot move forward until it is fixed or formally excepted. The gate is only as good as its tuning. If it blocks too much, people will work around it, so the team should set thresholds by severity and record exceptions with an expiry date. The main limit of automated scanning is that each tool only detects the patterns it knows about. A static analysis tool will miss a logic flaw that does not match a known pattern, and a dependency scanner cannot see a vulnerability that has not yet been published. So the team should still plan for code review and periodic manual testing.
rubricPoints: A report alone does not stop a change, while a gate fails the pipeline at a set threshold.
Gates need severity thresholds and documented exceptions so they stay usable.
Each scanner only detects the kinds of problem it is built to recognise.
Automated scanning must be complemented by human review and manual testing.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which scan to place where, and whether it blocks, is best practised by reasoning through a realistic situation.

lessons.plain: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a security service that watches your cloud resources and reports weaknesses. Its DevOps part connects to the places where software is built and shipped, such as GitHub organizations and Azure DevOps organizations, and reads their repositories and pipelines to find security problems. Think of it as a building inspector who walks the site, lists what is unsafe, and ranks the problems. The inspector reports; the team still has to change the code and settings itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your company links its code hosting to one central security dashboard. What do you think the dashboard can do on its own, and what still needs a person to act?
lessons.teach:
A connector is the link you create between Defender for Cloud and a source of DevOps work, here a GitHub organization or an Azure DevOps organization. Once connected, Defender reads what exists there, such as repositories and pipelines, and builds an inventory of them. A recommendation is a finding that says a specific setting or artifact is weaker than it should be, and it carries a severity. Posture means the overall state of your security settings across everything in the inventory.

Why it works: the connector is authorized through a permission grant that an administrator approves, so Defender can read configuration and security alerts without holding anyone's personal password. It then compares the inventory against security checks and shows the results in one place, so a security owner does not have to sign in to every repository to see the state of things.

Worked example. A team connects its GitHub organization. Step 1: an administrator approves the connector with read access to the repositories. Step 2: Defender lists the repositories it can see. Step 3: one repository has a secret-scanning alert open, meaning a credential string was found in committed code. Step 4: Defender raises a high-severity recommendation against that repository. Step 5: the owner revokes the credential, removes it from the code, and fixes the source. Step 6: at a later assessment the recommendation clears.

Common mistake: treating the dashboard as enforcement. Connecting the service does not block a merge or stop a pipeline by itself; it reports. Blocking needs separate controls in the source host or the pipeline.

Consequence: a recommendation nobody owns can sit for months while an exposed credential stays valid. A connection without a named owner and a remediation route gives false comfort.

Defender for Cloud reports posture; your team owns the fix.

questions.prompt: A team connects its Azure DevOps organization, named Harbor Labs, to Defender for Cloud. Step 1: an administrator approves the connector with read access to the projects. Step 2: Defender builds an inventory of 14 repositories and 6 pipelines. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: Defender raises a medium-severity recommendation against the pipeline that holds the plaintext value. Step 5: the pipeline team moves the value into a secure store and removes the plaintext. Step 6: at the next assessment the recommendation clears. Which statement correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The administrator revokes the connector so Defender stops reading the pipeline definitions
Defender blocks the next pipeline run that references the plaintext value, so the team cannot merge until it is fixed
Defender edits the pipeline file in the repository to read the value from a secure store automatically
Defender compares the inventory against its security checks and finds the weak setting on the pipeline that holds the plaintext value
questions.why: Defender compares the inventory against security checks and reports weaknesses as recommendations; it does not block runs, revoke access, or edit files, so the detection itself is the missing step.

questions.prompt: A security lead at a retail company asks what a connector means in Defender for Cloud for DevOps. Which description is accurate?
choices: A personal access token that a developer saves in the pipeline so Defender can sign in as that developer
A rule in the source host that blocks merges whenever a recommendation is open
A pipeline step that runs security scans during each build and stores the results
The link between Defender for Cloud and a DevOps source, such as a GitHub or Azure DevOps organization, through which Defender reads repositories and pipelines
questions.why: A connector is the link you create to a DevOps source so Defender can read its repositories and pipelines and build an inventory from them.

questions.prompt: A team connected its Azure DevOps organization to Defender for Cloud six months ago. Open recommendations have piled up, and merges still go through unchecked. What best explains this?
choices: The connector grants read access to personal passwords, so merges are exempt from review
The connection reports posture only; blocking needs separate controls in the source host or pipeline, and no named owner is acting on the findings
Defender blocks merges only for personal accounts, so shared accounts are never checked
The connector was never approved, so Defender is not running any checks at all
questions.why: Defender reports posture and does not enforce by itself, and unowned recommendations sit open, which is why the team sees findings without any blocking or fixing.

questions.prompt: A new Azure DevOps organization shows a high-severity recommendation: a credential string was found in committed code in one repository. Which response fits?
choices: The repository owner revokes the credential, removes it from the code, and fixes the source; the recommendation should clear at a later assessment
The team waits for the next quarterly audit before touching the repository
Defender automatically deletes the commit from history, so no action is needed from the team
The administrator removes Defender's connector, which deletes the recommendation and secures the credential
questions.why: The exposed credential must be revoked and removed by the owner, and the recommendation clears only after the source is fixed and reassessed, since Defender reports and the team fixes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what connecting Microsoft Defender for Cloud to our GitHub and Azure DevOps organizations does and does not do. Name at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Connecting Defender for Cloud gives us a connector that reads our repositories and pipelines, builds an inventory, and raises recommendations when a setting or artifact looks weak, such as an exposed secret. It is authorized with a permission grant an admin approves, so it does not need anyone's password. The limit is that it reports and ranks findings; it does not block a merge or stop a pipeline on its own. Blocking needs controls in GitHub or Azure DevOps. The tradeoff is that every recommendation needs a named owner and a fix route, or the dashboard becomes a list nobody acts on. Findings also only update after the next assessment, so a fixed issue may still show for a while.
rubricPoints: Defines the connector as the link that lets Defender read GitHub or Azure DevOps configuration
Says it reports and recommends, and does not enforce or block on its own
Names the need for an owner and remediation for each recommendation
Notes that results update on a later assessment rather than instantly

suggested.rationale: This is console setup and product behavior, so reading the product facts and then checking the connector steps in the console fits best.

lessons.plain: GitHub Advanced Security is a licensed set of automated checks that look at your code and repository while you work. It has three main parts: a scanner that reads source code for common bugs and risky patterns, a scanner that hunts for passwords and keys accidentally saved in the repository, and a check that flags libraries with known problems. Setting it up means choosing which repositories get these checks, deciding who reviews the results, and making the important checks block a merge. It exists for GitHub and for Azure DevOps, with similar ideas and different screens on each.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer accidentally commits a live cloud access key to a shared repository. Which control would you want to stop it earlier, and what would you still have to do afterwards?
lessons.teach:
Start with the named parts. Code scanning is static analysis: it reads source code without running it, looking for patterns such as user input reaching a database query unsafely. On GitHub the engine is CodeQL, which builds a searchable model of your code and runs security queries against it. Secret scanning looks for credentials that match known formats, such as cloud access keys and API tokens. Push protection is the blocking part: it refuses a push that contains a recognized secret before the secret reaches the repository. A required status check is a branch rule saying a named check must pass before a pull request can merge. Azure DevOps offers the same kinds of scanning as a licensed add-on that you switch on per organization and project, so the names differ but the decisions are the same.

Why it works: the cheapest place to stop a mistake is before it is merged or pushed, and scanners give a fast, repeatable answer on every change.

Worked example. A developer adds a config file containing a storage key and runs git push. With push protection on, the server reports that a secret was detected and refuses the push. The developer moves the value into the pipeline's secret store, removes it from the file, and pushes again. Nothing sensitive reached the shared branch.

Common mistake: treating the setting as the finish line. Enabling scanning does not stop anyone merging with open alerts unless a required check is configured. And a secret that already reached the history must be revoked and rotated, because deleting the commit does not make the old value safe.

Consequence: automated bots scan public and leaked material for keys and can use one within minutes, so a scanner that only runs after the push is a detector, not a shield.

questions.prompt: A logistics team turned on push protection on Monday. On the previous Friday, a developer had already pushed a config file containing an API token in a recognized format to the main branch, before the setting existed. On Monday a second developer cleans it up. Step 1: she removes the token line and commits the change, and the push succeeds. Step 2: she confirms the latest version of the file has no token. Step 3: she marks the scanner alert as fixed. What is the missing step that completes the response?
choices: She checks the commit history to confirm the Friday commit was the only copy of the file.
She turns on a required status check so that future merges are blocked while alerts are open.
She asks the owner of the token to revoke it and issue a new one, because the old value is still in the repository history.
She force-pushes to rewrite main so the Friday commit no longer appears in the history.
questions.why: Deleting the line in a new commit does not make the old value safe, because it remains in the history, so the credential must be revoked and rotated.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is push protection in GitHub's secret scanning feature?
choices: A rule that requires a named check to pass before a pull request can merge.
A block that refuses a push containing a recognized secret before the secret reaches the repository.
A background process that rotates credentials automatically whenever a key appears in the code.
A report that lists every secret found in a repository after it has been merged.
questions.why: The teaching text defines push protection as the blocking part that refuses a push containing a recognized secret before it reaches the repository.

questions.prompt: A team has code scanning enabled and many open alerts on a branch. A developer opens a pull request and merges it without any warning, because the branch has no required status check for the scanner. What is the best description of the gap?
choices: The scanner has not been turned on for the organization, so no alerts are generated at all.
Code scanning only reads compiled binaries, so it cannot evaluate changes in a pull request.
