The alerts were generated after the merge, so the scanner can only detect problems and cannot stop them.
Scanning is on, but nothing in the branch rule requires a passing check before merging, so open alerts do not block the merge.
questions.why: Enabling scanning does not stop merges unless a required check is configured, so open alerts alone leave the merge unblocked.

questions.prompt: A payments team wants to stop a risky code pattern, where user input is passed unsafely into a database query, from ever being merged into the main branch. Which combination of controls fits this requirement best?
choices: Rotating the database password every day, so a stolen query cannot be used for long.
Secret scanning with push protection, because it blocks suspicious database queries from being pushed.
Code scanning, which reads the source without running it, plus a required status check on the main branch so a failing result blocks the merge.
A nightly report that lists any database queries changed in the last week for manual review.
questions.why: Code scanning is the static analysis that detects this pattern, and a required status check is the branch rule that stops a merge when that check fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what turning on GitHub Advanced Security does for a repository, and name one limit of secret scanning that they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: It adds automated checks to the repository. Code scanning reads our source for risky patterns, secret scanning looks for credentials that match known formats, and push protection can stop a push that contains one. These checks only protect us if something depends on them, so I would make the scanner a required status check on the main branch. The limit I would flag is that secret scanning recognizes known formats. A custom internal password or an unusual token can get past it, so it does not replace code review, and it does not clean up a secret that has already leaked. If a key was pushed, the fix is to revoke and rotate it, then check access logs for misuse. Findings also need someone to triage them, or the alerts just pile up unread.
rubricPoints: Names the parts: code scanning, secret scanning and push protection, and what each one checks
Explains that blocking only works when a required status check or branch rule enforces it
States a real limit, such as unknown secret formats or false positives needing triage
Says a leaked secret must be revoked and rotated, not just removed from the history

suggested.rationale: Choosing which scanner fits a repository situation and where it must block is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: Modern code hosting services can check your code for security problems automatically, and a cloud security tool can collect those results in one place. GitHub Advanced Security is the checking part that runs on your code repositories: it looks for risky code patterns, leaked passwords and keys, and vulnerable libraries. Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a security dashboard for your cloud environment. Connecting the two lets a security team see the findings from many code projects next to their cloud warnings, in one list. The checks still run where the code lives. The dashboard only gathers and organises what those checks report, so it is only as complete as the checks that were switched on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A security lead wants one list of every leaked password and risky code finding across 40 code repositories. Where would you expect those findings to be produced, and what would have to connect them to a single list?
lessons.teach:
GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS) is a set of security checks built into GitHub. Code scanning reads source code without running it, using static analysis, which means it looks for patterns that suggest bugs or vulnerabilities. GitHub's code scanning uses CodeQL, a query engine that treats code as data you can search. Secret scanning looks for credentials such as access keys and tokens that were committed to a repository. Each result is an alert, and each alert belongs to one repository. Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud security posture service: it scores your environment against recommendations and shows warnings in one place. Its DevOps security capability uses a connector to link a GitHub organisation or Azure DevOps organisation, so repository alerts appear alongside cloud findings.

The connector does not replace the scanning. It reads findings that GHAS has already produced and maps them into the posture view. A finding must exist in the repository before Defender can show it, and the connector must be authorised with permission to read security alerts.

Worked example: a developer commits a cloud access key into a configuration file. Step one, secret scanning detects the key's pattern and raises an alert in that repository. Step two, the Defender connector for the organisation pulls that alert into the DevOps security view. Step three, the security team sees it in the shared list, assigns it, revokes the key so it stops working, and removes it from the file's history.

Common mistake: assuming that connecting Defender turns scanning on. If code scanning or secret scanning is disabled on a repository, nothing appears for it, and the dashboard looks clean when it is actually blind to that project.

Consequence: a leaked credential stays usable until it is revoked, so a missing scan creates a silent exposure window that no dashboard will warn you about. The connector gives you one view; the scanners are what find the problems.

questions.prompt: A team at Northwind Freight enables code scanning on their route-planning repository. A scan on the main branch finds a database query built by joining user-typed text directly into the SQL string, which is a pattern that lets an attacker change the query. The team wants this finding to appear in the Defender for Cloud DevOps security view for their organisation. Step one: code scanning runs on the repository and raises an alert in that repository. Step two: [missing step]. Step three: the security lead sees the finding in the shared DevOps security list and assigns it to a developer.
choices: The Defender connector for the organisation, authorised to read security alerts, pulls the repository alert into the DevOps security view.
Defender re-runs CodeQL on the repository to confirm the query pattern before it shows anything.
Defender turns on secret scanning for the repository so that the code finding is cross-checked against it.
The team copies the alert text into a spreadsheet and uploads it to Defender each week.
questions.why: Defender does not scan code itself; the connector, which must be authorised to read security alerts, reads the alert GHAS already produced and maps it into the posture view.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the Defender for Cloud connector for a GitHub organisation do?
choices: It encrypts repository alerts so that only the security team can read them.
It replaces secret scanning with checks that run only in the cloud.
It runs code scanning on every commit so that new alerts are created as code is pushed.
It reads alerts that GHAS has already produced and maps them into the posture view.
questions.why: The connector is a link that reads existing findings; it does not create findings, replace scanners, or encrypt anything.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight connected its GitHub organisation to Defender. The DevOps view shows zero alerts for its billing-api repository, but a teammate says the repository has never been scanned. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Code scanning and secret scanning are disabled on billing-api, so no findings exist for the connector to read.
The connector only shows alerts raised within the previous hour.
Defender cannot display alerts from private repositories at all.
The dashboard is clean because the repository contains no secrets.
questions.why: The connector can only show findings that GHAS has produced, so a repository with scanning turned off appears clean even though it is unchecked.

questions.prompt: Secret scanning raises an alert saying a storage account access key was committed to a repository three weeks ago. The key has not been revoked yet. What should the team do first?
choices: Delete the file in a new commit, close the alert, and assume the problem is solved.
Revoke the key so it stops working, because a leaked credential stays usable until it is revoked.
Disable secret scanning on the repository so that no further alerts are raised for it.
Wait for the next weekly Defender report to confirm whether the key was used.
questions.why: A leaked credential remains usable until revoked, so revoking it is the first action; removing it from the file or history does not stop someone who already copied it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what GitHub Advanced Security does, what connecting it to Microsoft Defender for Cloud adds, and name one limit of this integration.
lessons.modelAnswer: GitHub Advanced Security runs the checks inside each GitHub repository. Code scanning looks for risky code patterns, secret scanning looks for committed keys and tokens, and dependency alerts flag libraries with known vulnerabilities. Each finding is created in the repository where it was found. Connecting the GitHub organisation to Defender for Cloud through a connector does not run new scans. It pulls those findings into one posture view with cloud recommendations, so a security team can triage across many repositories in one list. The limit is that the view is only as complete as the scanning. If secret scanning or code scanning is off for a repository, that project will look clean in the dashboard while still being unchecked. Teams should confirm coverage per repository, not assume it from the dashboard.
rubricPoints: GHAS performs the scanning inside each repository, such as code, secret, and dependency checks
Defender for Cloud connects to the organisation and gathers existing findings into one posture view
The connector does not turn scanning on, so unscanned repositories show no findings
Coverage must be checked per repository, since a clean dashboard can hide gaps

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and console integration steps, which no current mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: Container scanning means checking the packaged parts of an application for known security problems before it ships. A container image is a sealed bundle holding an application plus the operating system pieces and libraries it depends on. Scanning an image compares those pieces against lists of known vulnerabilities. Code scanning is different: it reads your own source code looking for risky patterns. Automating both means the checks run on every build, so a problem is caught while the fix is still cheap, not after customers are affected.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's application is packaged as a container image and its source code passes a code scanner with no findings. Would that code scanner tell you whether the base operating system inside the image has a publicly known flaw? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A container image is a read-only package built from stacked layers: a base operating system layer, installed packages, and your application. A vulnerability is a publicly catalogued weakness with its own identifier. Image scanning lists every installed package in each layer and matches each package name and version against vulnerability databases. Static analysis means examining code without running it. CodeQL is a static analysis tool: it builds a database from your source code and runs queries that look for patterns such as untrusted input reaching a dangerous call. CodeQL never inspects the packages baked into an image, and image scanning never reads your application logic. You need both because they see different things.

Why it works: each scanner needs an inventory. For images, the inventory comes from package metadata stored in each layer. For CodeQL, it comes from the code itself. In GitHub Actions, a job can run inside a container image, so CodeQL analysis uses the same toolchain the project builds with.

Worked example: a pipeline builds image web:1.4. Step 1, the image is built. Step 2, the scanner lists packages and finds an openssl version with a published flaw and a fixed release. Step 3, a gate, meaning a pipeline check that stops promotion when it fails, blocks the push because the severity is high. Step 4, the developer rebuilds on a patched base image, the scan passes, and the image is pushed.

Common mistake: treating a passing CodeQL run as proof the image is safe. CodeQL can pass while the base image carries a known library flaw.

Consequence: without the gate, the vulnerable image reaches the registry and then production, and every running replica carries the flaw until it is redeployed.

questions.prompt: A bank's payments team adds a container job to its GitHub Actions workflow so that CodeQL runs inside the image payroll-build:5.0, the same image the service is built with. Step 1: the job starts inside that container. Step 2: CodeQL builds a database from the Python source code. Step 3 is the step you must supply: what CodeQL does with that database next. Step 4: the findings appear as code scanning alerts for developers to review.
choices: The scanner lists every package in each layer of the image and matches each version against vulnerability databases.
The base layer is rebuilt on a patched release so the packages inside it are newer.
A gate checks that every finding is low severity before the image is pushed to the registry.
CodeQL runs its queries against the database, looking for risky input patterns.
questions.why: CodeQL is a static analysis tool, so after building its database from the source code it runs queries against that database to find patterns such as untrusted input reaching a dangerous call.

questions.prompt: A team asks which tool would flag a library version with a published identifier and a fixed release sitting in the base layer of their container image. Which answer is correct?
choices: CodeQL, because it reads the package metadata stored in each layer of the image before it analyses any source code.
Image scanning, because it lists the packages in each layer and matches their names and versions against vulnerability databases.
CodeQL, because it builds a database that includes every package installed in the image as well as the application code.
Neither tool, because published flaws in installed packages only show up once the container is running in production.
questions.why: Image scanning is the control that inventories installed packages in each layer and matches them to catalogued vulnerabilities, while CodeQL only analyses source code and never inspects the packages in an image.

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs a CodeQL analysis job on an application and the job passes. Which statement is true?
choices: The image is proven free of known flaws because static analysis covered the whole container.
Packages baked into the image were confirmed safe by the code analysis that just passed.
CodeQL also inspected the base layer, so the package versions in it were checked and cleared.
The pass covers the application source code only, so packages in the base image may still carry known flaws.
questions.why: CodeQL inspects application source code and never reads the packages baked into an image, so a passing CodeQL run says nothing about known flaws in base-layer packages.

questions.prompt: A gate blocks promotion of an image because a scan found a high-severity flaw. A developer wants to push the image anyway, arguing the flawed library is barely used by the app. What is the right response?
choices: Hold the push, rebuild on a fixed version, and rescan before promoting.
Remove the scanner from the pipeline so the gate never runs again.
Push it now and rescan after the next production deployment.
Push it, since an unused library cannot be exploited.
questions.why: The gate exists to stop promotion of high-severity findings, and the fix is to rebuild with a patched version and pass a fresh scan, because every replica deployed from a flawed image carries the flaw until it is redeployed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a pipeline needs both CodeQL analysis and container image scanning, and name one limit of image scanning that you would tell them to plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: CodeQL and image scanning check different things, so one cannot replace the other. CodeQL reads our own source for risky patterns, such as input that reaches a database query without checking, and it has to run on code built with the same toolchain as the build, which is why we run it inside a container matching that toolchain. Image scanning lists the packages in the built image and matches them against known vulnerability records, which catches flaws in the operating system and third-party libraries that our own code never touches. The limit to plan around is that image scanning only knows about vulnerabilities already catalogued. A package with no published record passes, and a newly disclosed flaw can make an image that passed yesterday fail today, so we rescan on a schedule as well as on each build.
rubricPoints: CodeQL analyzes your own source code for risky patterns and does not inspect packages inside an image.
Image scanning matches installed packages in each layer against known vulnerability records.
Running CodeQL in a container job makes the analysis use the same toolchain the build uses.
Image scanning only catches catalogued vulnerabilities, so rescanning on a schedule matters.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which scan answers a given risk is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission or planned engine practises container or code scanning directly.

lessons.plain: Open-source libraries are ready-made code written by others that your project borrows, such as a web framework or a date-parsing library. Each one can contain security flaws, and those flaws are often reported publicly once they are found. Dependabot is a GitHub service that watches the list of libraries your project uses, compares each version against a database of known flaws, and raises an alert when one of your versions is affected. The purpose is to learn about a known weakness in code you depend on without checking by hand, and then decide how to fix it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service uses a library that someone else wrote, and a security researcher publishes a flaw affecting the exact version you use. How would you learn about this without reading every security bulletin yourself, and what would you still have to do yourself?
lessons.teach:
A dependency is a library your code uses but did not write. Your project lists these in a manifest file, such as package.json for JavaScript or requirements.txt for Python, and often in a lock file that pins the exact version installed. A vulnerability is a known security flaw in a specific range of versions. An advisory is the published record that describes the flaw, which versions are affected, and which version fixes it. GitHub maintains an advisory database of these records.

Dependabot alerts work by reading your dependency graph, the map GitHub builds from your manifests and lock files, and matching every listed package and version against the advisories. When a match appears, GitHub creates an alert in the repository's Security tab and can notify people with access to it. The alert names the package, the severity, the affected range, and the first patched version. An alert is a detection step. It does not change your code by itself.

Worked example: your service pins examplelib at version 1.4.2. An advisory says versions below 1.4.5 let a crafted input crash the parser, and 1.4.5 contains the fix. The dependency graph lists examplelib 1.4.2. The advisory's affected range includes 1.4.2, so Dependabot raises an alert naming 1.4.5 as the fixed version. A security update can then open a pull request, a proposed code change for review, that changes the pin to 1.4.5. The test suite runs on that change, a reviewer checks it, and it is merged.

Common mistake: treating an alert as handled because someone dismissed it, or assuming a transitive dependency, meaning one pulled in by another library you did not choose directly, is not your problem. Transitive packages appear in the graph too and can still be flagged.

Consequence: until the pinned version changes, the vulnerable code keeps running in production on every deploy, so an alert that sits unread is a live risk, not paperwork.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company keeps its Node service's dependencies in package-lock.json. The service directly uses reportkit 3.0.0, which itself depends on tinyxml-helper 0.8.1. A published advisory says tinyxml-helper versions below 0.8.3 can be tricked into reading past a buffer, and 0.8.3 contains the fix. The team's dependency graph lists tinyxml-helper 0.8.1, the advisory's affected range includes it, and Dependabot raises an alert naming 0.8.3 as the first patched version. So far the steps are: the graph lists the installed version, the advisory range matches it, and the alert is raised. The one missing step is the one that changes the version the running service actually loads. What is that step?
choices: Wait for the advisory to be withdrawn, which removes the alert and the risk
Dismiss the alert in the Security tab, since the package was never a direct choice
Make the installed version reach 0.8.3 or later through a tested change that is merged and deployed
Delete the lock file so the tool rebuilds the graph and the alert clears
questions.why: The alert is only a detection step, so the vulnerable code keeps running until a change that moves the loaded version to 0.8.3 or later is merged and deployed, and a transitive package still counts.

questions.prompt: In the teaching model, what is the dependency graph?
choices: A diagram of your team's sprint and ticket dependencies
The map built from your manifests and lock files, which alerts are matched against
A security policy file that tells Dependabot which severities to ignore
A list of advisories GitHub publishes for each language ecosystem
questions.why: The teaching text defines the dependency graph as the map GitHub builds from manifests and lock files, and Dependabot matches listed packages and versions against advisories using that map.

questions.prompt: A team dismisses a Dependabot alert because their code never calls the vulnerable function. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: The alert will reappear on every commit, slowing the build
Nothing, because a dismissed alert is always safe to ignore
The vulnerable package version keeps being installed and run on every deploy until it changes
Dismissing the alert deletes the advisory from GitHub's database
questions.why: Until the pinned version changes, the vulnerable code keeps running in production on every deploy, so dismissing the alert alone leaves the live risk in place.

questions.prompt: An alert says the affected range is below 2.1.0 and the first patched version is 2.1.0. Your project pins 2.0.9. Which statement is correct?
choices: The project is affected only if the lock file is missing
The project is affected, and the fix is to move the pin to 2.1.0 or later
The project is safe because 2.0.9 is close to 2.1.0
The project is affected, but only the direct use of the library needs fixing, not any transitive copies
questions.why: 2.0.9 falls inside the affected range below 2.1.0, so the project is vulnerable and the remedy is a pin at the first patched version or later.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Dependabot alert tells you, what it does not do for you, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Dependabot alert means GitHub compared the libraries listed in our manifest and lock files, which it calls the dependency graph, against its advisory database and found a version we use that has a publicly known security flaw. The alert names the package, the severity, the affected versions and the first fixed version. It tells us about the risk but does not fix anything. We still need to upgrade the pinned version, run the tests, and merge a change. The main limit is coverage: Dependabot only knows about flaws that have been published as advisories, so a new unreported bug will not show up, and it only sees packages declared in files it can read. Also, dismissing an alert hides the warning but leaves the vulnerable code in place, so dismissals should have a stated reason and be reviewed.
rubricPoints: An alert is produced by matching the dependency graph against published advisories
An alert identifies the package, affected versions and fixed version but does not patch the code
Upgrading, testing and merging are still required after an alert
Limit: only published advisories and readable manifests are covered, and dismissing hides rather than fixes

suggested.rationale: Triaging a real alert means reasoning through affected versions, fixed versions and tradeoffs, which a situation-based exercise builds better than memorizing a list.

lessons.plain: Think of the security cameras in a large building. Each one records something, but the footage only helps when it is gathered into one room where someone can search it. Azure Monitor is Microsoft's set of tools for watching how cloud systems behave. Azure Monitor Logs is the part that stores text records, such as events and errors, in one searchable store called a Log Analytics workspace. Integrating DevOps tools means connecting the places where your team builds, tests, and changes software, so that their activity also lands in that same store. Then one question can span code changes, pipeline runs, and production errors, instead of checking several separate screens.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's builds run in one tool, your application's errors show up in another, and a release went out at 09:00. Without looking anything up, what would you want to be able to ask that is hard to answer when these records live in separate places?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. Azure Monitor is the umbrella service for collecting metrics and logs from Azure resources and applications. Azure Monitor Logs is the log side of it: records are stored in a Log Analytics workspace, which is a database you query with Kusto Query Language (KQL), a read-only language for searching tables of records. A DevOps tool integration is a configured connection that exports a tool's activity records, such as pipeline runs, approvals, or audit events, into a workspace. An integration is a setting you turn on, not code your application writes.

Why it works. Each DevOps tool keeps its own history. Once the records share one workspace and a common timestamp, you can join a release event with a spike in error logs from the same minute. Retention and access can also be managed in one place.

Worked example. A release pipeline finishes at 09:02. Step 1: the pipeline's run records flow into the workspace through the integration. Step 2: the application's error records flow into the same workspace from its monitoring. Step 3: you query for errors between 09:00 and 09:30 and compare them with the release's run time. Step 4: the errors begin at 09:03, one minute after the deploy step, so the release is the likely cause. The query only works because both kinds of record landed in the same workspace.

Common mistake. Assuming that turning on an integration fills in old history, or that the workspace holds everything the tool's own screen shows. Integrations usually capture events from the moment they are enabled, so earlier records may be missing, and the workspace may hold only the event types you chose to export.

Consequence. If the integration is missing or misconfigured, responders see errors but cannot line them up with deployments, and alert rules built on those records stay silent when they should fire.

The real value of this setup is correlation: one query can connect a change, a run, and a failure.

questions.prompt: A retail team at a different company enables an integration that exports its build tool's approval records into a Log Analytics workspace. Their storefront's error records already flow into the same workspace. Step 1: the approval at 14:03 is recorded in the workspace through the integration. Step 2: the storefront's error records arrive in that workspace from its monitoring. Step 3: missing, to be filled in by you. Step 4: the first error is at 14:07, four minutes after the approval, so the approved deployment is the likely cause. Which action is step 3?
choices: Query errors in a window around the deploy time and compare the first error's timestamp with the deploy time
Delete approval records older than the deploy to speed up queries
Send the storefront's error records to a separate workspace to keep them apart
Turn the integration on again so older approval records are backfilled into the workspace
questions.why: Step 3 is the query over a time window that compares the error timestamps with the deployment time, which is what lets the correlation in step 4 happen.

questions.prompt: In this teaching context, what is a DevOps tool integration?
choices: Code your application writes to push its own log lines to a store
A dashboard that shows live pipeline status and nothing else
A configured connection that exports a tool's activity records, such as runs and approvals, into a workspace
A rule that automatically deletes workspace records after a set period
questions.why: An integration is a setting that exports a DevOps tool's activity records into a workspace; it is not application code, a dashboard, or a retention rule.

questions.prompt: A team turned on their pipeline integration on Monday and now asks why the failed release from last Friday does not appear in the workspace. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The integration captures events from the moment it was enabled, so Friday's records were never exported
The Friday release must be rerun before the integration can see it
The workspace is corrupted and must be rebuilt from scratch
KQL cannot read records that are more than seven days old
questions.why: Integrations usually capture events only from the point they are enabled, so earlier records may be absent from the workspace.

questions.prompt: An on-call engineer has an alert rule based on application error records, but the pipeline integration was never enabled. A deployment fails and the alert never fires. Why?
choices: Without the pipeline records in the workspace, a rule that needs both the change and the errors cannot connect them, so it can stay silent
The error records alone are enough to link the failure to the deployment through their timestamps
Enabling the integration now will make the earlier failed deployment appear in the workspace
Azure Monitor reads the pipeline's screen directly, so the alert should have fired anyway
questions.why: Alert rules built on records that need the missing pipeline data cannot correlate the change with the failure, so they can stay silent when they should fire.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we bother sending our pipeline and repository activity into an Azure Monitor Logs workspace when the DevOps tool already shows its own history. Explain what the workspace gives us that the tool's own screens do not, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing this.
lessons.modelAnswer: The DevOps tool's screens show its own history, but each tool only knows about itself. The Log Analytics workspace gathers pipeline runs, deployment records, and application errors into one place with shared timestamps, so we can write one KQL query that asks, for example, whether errors rose right after a particular release. That correlation is the main gain. The tradeoff is that the integration only captures events from the time it is enabled, so older history may be missing, and we may only export the event types we configured. There is also a cost: workspace storage and query usage are billed, and retention settings decide how long the records stay available. We should decide up front which events matter and how long to keep them.
rubricPoints: The workspace joins records from several tools and the application on a shared timeline, which separate screens cannot do.
An integration is a configured export, so it captures events from the point it is enabled and may not include older history.
Only the event types we chose to export appear in the workspace, so coverage must be checked.
Storage and query costs and retention settings need deliberate choices.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about which records each tool can export and how the connection is set up, which is best learned by reading the concepts and then checking them against the console.

lessons.plain: Telemetry is the stream of measurements and records a running system produces: how long requests take, how busy a machine is, which errors happen. Azure's monitoring tools each collect a different slice of that stream. Application Insights watches the application code itself, VM Insights watches virtual machines, Container Insights watches the container clusters that run apps, and the storage and network monitoring views watch those resources. Knowing which slice you need is the first step, because a tool only shows what it was set up to collect.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer says the checkout page feels slow, but the servers' CPU graphs look normal. Which kind of telemetry would you collect first to find the slow step, and why might CPU graphs alone miss it?
lessons.teach:
Telemetry collection means setting up a tool so that measurements and records from a system are gathered and stored where you can query them later. In Azure, many of these tools write into a Log Analytics workspace, a central store for log and metric data that you query with the Kusto Query Language (KQL), a query language for log data.

Application Insights is Azure Monitor's application performance feature. It collects requests, dependency calls (such as database or HTTP calls made by your code), exceptions and custom events from the application. You add it with an SDK or an auto-instrumentation agent. It answers the question: what did this request do inside the app?

VM Insights, Container Insights, Azure Monitor for Storage and Azure Monitor for Networks are resource-focused. VM Insights collects performance counters and, optionally, the processes and connections on virtual machines. Container Insights collects node and container metrics and logs from Kubernetes clusters, including AKS. The storage and network views read platform metrics and diagnostic logs that Azure already emits for those resources, so they need little or no agent setup.

Why it works: each tool sees one layer. A resource metric tells you a machine is busy. Only application telemetry tells you which call inside a request is slow.

Worked example: checkout is slow. First, Application Insights shows POST /pay requests averaging 4 seconds. Second, its dependency view shows 3.8 seconds spent in one call to a payment database. Third, VM Insights shows the database VM's CPU is normal, which points to waiting on disk. Each tool narrowed the cause.

Common mistake: enabling VM Insights and assuming slow application requests are now visible. VM Insights does not record your application's requests; that needs Application Insights.

Consequence: without application telemetry, the team sees healthy servers while customers see timeouts, and the fix is delayed. Each control should be chosen by the layer where the answer is most likely to be.

questions.prompt: A logistics team runs a label-printing API. Its POST /labels requests average 3 seconds. Step 1: Application Insights shows the requests averaging 3 seconds. Step 2: its dependency view shows 2.7 seconds spent in one HTTP call to a rate-limited carrier service. Step 3 is missing from the trace: before blaming the carrier, the team needs to check whether the print service's virtual machine is short on CPU or memory. Which control fills that missing step?
choices: Azure Monitor for Storage, to read the storage account's metrics
Container Insights, to read the metrics of the cluster's containers
Application Insights, to view the requests again
VM Insights, to read the virtual machine's performance counters
questions.why: VM Insights collects performance counters from virtual machines, so it is the resource-level control that shows whether the machine itself is the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Which Azure Monitor feature records the requests your application handles, the dependency calls its code makes, and its exceptions?
choices: Container Insights
VM Insights
Application Insights
Azure Monitor for Networks
questions.why: Application Insights is the application performance feature that collects requests, dependency calls, exceptions and custom events from inside the app.

questions.prompt: A team enabled Container Insights on its Kubernetes cluster. Now it wants to know how long one SQL call inside each web request took. Which control answers this?
choices: Application Insights, because it records dependency calls made by the application code
Container Insights, because it already covers every call the containers make
Azure Monitor for Storage, because the SQL server keeps its data in storage
VM Insights, because it lists the processes running on the nodes
questions.why: Container Insights shows node and container metrics and logs, not what happens inside individual application requests, so the dependency timing must come from Application Insights.

questions.prompt: A storage team wants a view of request latency and throttling for its blob service, using metrics that Azure already emits for the account. Which control fits?
choices: Azure Monitor for Storage
Container Insights
VM Insights
Application Insights
questions.why: Azure Monitor for Storage reads the platform metrics and diagnostic logs that Azure already emits for storage resources, so it needs little or no agent setup.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Application Insights, VM Insights and Container Insights for a slow API running in AKS. Name one limit of the tool you did not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with Application Insights, because the symptom is slow API requests. It records each request, its duration and the dependency calls it makes, so we can see whether the time goes to our code or to a downstream service. Container Insights comes next, since the API runs in AKS. It shows node and container CPU, memory and restarts, which tells us whether pods are starved or being killed. VM Insights is the wrong first pick here. AKS nodes are managed for us, and VM Insights is built for virtual machine performance and process or connection data, not per-request timing. The limit of Container Insights is that it cannot explain why one specific request was slow. For that, we need the application telemetry from Application Insights.
rubricPoints: Application Insights shows request timing and dependency calls inside the app.
Container Insights covers cluster, node and container metrics and logs.
VM Insights targets virtual machine performance and processes, not per-request app timing.
Each tool sees one layer, so the choice depends on where the answer is likely to be.
Names a real limit of the tool that was not chosen first.

suggested.rationale: Picking the right control from a scenario builds more skill than reading the catalogue, and no listed mission covers Azure Monitor collection directly.

lessons.plain: Instrumentation means recording measurements about how your work and software behave, so you can see trends instead of guessing. In GitHub, this mostly means two kinds of view: built-in insight pages that summarise activity for a repository or organisation, and charts that plot one measurement over time, such as how long a build takes each week or how many issues were closed. Think of it like a car dashboard. The gauges only help if you know which one to read and what a normal reading looks like.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team says the build feels slower lately. Before looking anything up, what single measurement over time would you plot to test that claim, and why would one day's result not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Telemetry means data a system emits about itself, such as durations, counts and pass or fail results. Monitoring is the habit of collecting that data and reviewing it on a schedule. In GitHub, you configure monitoring mainly through insights, which are built-in views that summarise activity for a repository or organisation, and through usage data for Actions, GitHub's automation service that runs workflows. A chart is a view that plots one measurement against time, so a trend becomes visible instead of being buried in a list of single runs.

Why it works: one value tells you what happened once, while a series tells you whether something is changing. Comparing the same measurement across equal time windows, such as weekly medians, smooths out a single unusually slow run.

Worked example. The question is whether a workflow called build has slowed down. Step 1: open the run history for that workflow in the repository. Step 2: set the window to the last eight weeks. Step 3: read the duration of each run, or the usage figures Actions reports. Step 4: group the runs by week and take the median duration for each week. Step 5: if the median rises from about six minutes to about eleven minutes in the week a large new test suite was merged, the chart points at that change, and you can investigate it.

Common mistake: judging from the latest run, or averaging across different workflows, which mixes slow and fast jobs together. Compare like with like.

Consequence: a slow pipeline delays every merge, so a trend you spot early is far cheaper to fix than one discovered during an incident.

questions.prompt: A team's repository named orders-service has a workflow called release-check. The learner has completed three of the five steps. Step 1 opened that workflow's run history. Step 2 set the window to the last six weeks. Step 3 read the duration of each run. Step 4 is blank and must be filled before step 5 can be read. Step 5 reads: the weekly median rose from about four minutes in week one to about nine minutes in week five, after a new integration test set was merged in week four. Which step 4 completes the method?
choices: Delete the runs that took longer than five minutes so the chart looks steadier.
Use only the single most recent run to confirm the slowdown.
Average the durations of release-check together with the durations of the lint workflow, to get one figure.
Group the runs of release-check by week and take the median duration for each week.
questions.why: Grouping runs by week and taking each week's median is the step that produces the weekly series the trend in step 5 depends on, while the other choices either use one run or mix workflows together.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines telemetry as this unit uses the word?
choices: A written approval record that a change was reviewed before release, kept for audit purposes.
Data a system emits about itself, such as durations and counts.
A built-in view that summarises activity for a repository.
The automation service that runs workflows.
questions.why: Telemetry is data a system emits about itself, such as durations, counts and pass or fail results; the other choices describe an approval record, a service and a view, which are different things.

questions.prompt: A developer says a workflow got slower because yesterday's run took fourteen minutes, while its usual run takes about five. What is the main problem with that conclusion?
choices: A single run can be unusual, so the conclusion needs a series of runs compared across equal time windows.
Durations should never be read in minutes; seconds are required.
The developer should have averaged all workflows in the repository together instead.
Nothing is wrong; one slow run always proves a trend.
questions.why: One run is a single value that says what happened once, and only a series compared across equal windows shows whether something is changing.

questions.prompt: A repository runs two workflows, unit-tests and docs-build. The owner wants to know whether unit-tests has slowed over six weeks. Which approach fits the method in this unit?
choices: Chart unit-tests alone by week, using the median duration for each week over six weeks.
Check only the most recent unit-tests run and decide from its result.
Plot unit-tests and docs-build together on one line so the overall pipeline health is visible.
Average the two workflows' durations each week to get a single repository figure.
questions.why: The method compares like with like, so the chart should track one workflow across equal weekly windows using a weekly median, not mix it with other workflows or rely on a single run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use GitHub's built-in insights and a chart to check whether the team's build has got slower. Name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the workflow's run history for the last several weeks, because a trend needs a series of values, not one run. I would group the runs by week and look at the median duration, since the median is less distorted by one unusually slow run than the average is. If the median rises in a particular week, I check what was merged then. The limit is that these views show what GitHub recorded: they tell me the build got slower, not why. Runner changes, cache misses, or a slow external service can also change durations, so before blaming the new test suite I would open the logs of a slow run and confirm the cause. Older history may also no longer be kept under the retention settings, so the chart may not reach back as far as I would like.
rubricPoints: Explains that a trend needs a series of measurements over equal time windows, not a single run
Uses a robust summary such as the median and says why it is preferred over a single latest run
Names a limit: insights show that something changed, not the cause
Mentions checking history retention or confirming the cause in run logs

suggested.rationale: This objective mostly involves current GitHub insight views and console steps that the learner should read in the live product, so reading with a short explanation fits best.

lessons.plain: When an automated build or deployment runs, the system records events such as a run starting, passing, or failing. An alert is a rule that watches for a chosen event, lets through only the cases you care about, and sends a message to a place someone will see, such as an email inbox, a chat channel, or a webhook. The skill is choosing the event, the filter, and the destination. Think of a smoke detector wired to the one room that matters, not a siren that goes off for every kettle.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has 40 pipeline runs a day across many branches. If you want to hear within minutes when a run on the main branch fails, and nothing else, what would you need to decide before you set anything up?
lessons.teach:
An event is a moment the CI/CD system records, such as a workflow run finishing or a pipeline run completing with a result. An alert, also called a notification, is a rule that watches for a chosen event, checks its details against a filter, and sends a message to a destination. A filter narrows the event, for example to only failed results or only the main branch. A webhook is a URL that accepts an automatic message over HTTP, which lets one tool post into another, such as a chat channel.

Why it works: the platform already knows the outcome of every run. An alert reads that outcome and forwards it, so nobody has to keep checking the run page.

Worked example in Azure Pipelines. A team wants to hear when a build on main fails. They create a service hook (or a notification subscription) that listens for the build-completed event. Step 1: the event fires when a run finishes. Step 2: the filters check the result, which must be failed, and the branch, which must be main. A failed run on a feature branch is dropped here. Step 3: the hook posts the run name, branch, and link to the team channel's webhook. In GitHub Actions the same idea can be built with a workflow triggered by workflow_run, which starts after another workflow completes. A step checks that the other run's conclusion is failure, then sends the message.

Common mistake: alerting on every completed run with no filter. The channel gets noisy, people mute it within a week, and the real failure is lost.

Consequence: if a failed main build alerts nobody, a broken build or bad deploy can sit unnoticed while other changes keep merging on top of it.

An alert tells you that a run happened and what it reported. It does not tell you that the running service is healthy.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lane Logistics runs a GitHub Actions workflow named deploy-staging. They want a message in their ops chat when a deploy-staging run fails on the branch release/2.4. They build a second workflow triggered by workflow_run, which starts after deploy-staging completes. Step 1: the workflow_run event fires when deploy-staging finishes. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the notification step posts the run name, the branch, and the run link to the ops chat's webhook URL. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Check that the deploy-staging conclusion is failure and that the branch is release/2.4, and stop if either check does not match
Send a request to the staging server's health endpoint and post whether it returns HTTP 200
Confirm that the deploy-staging run started within the last hour, so stale runs are skipped
Post a message for every completed deploy-staging run so the team sees both successes and failures
questions.why: The filter in Step 2 must check the run's conclusion and branch so that only failed release/2.4 runs continue to the webhook post, which is the purpose of a filter in this kind of alert.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a webhook in the context of CI/CD alerts?
choices: A URL that accepts an automatic message over HTTP, letting the CI tool post into another tool such as a chat channel
A branch protection rule that blocks merges until a build passes
A saved password that gives a pipeline access to a secrets vault
A scheduled job that asks the CI server every few minutes whether any run has failed
questions.why: A webhook is defined as a URL that accepts an automatic HTTP message, which is what lets one tool post results into another.

questions.prompt: Bluewater Labs uses Azure Pipelines. Their hotfix/* branches go straight to production, and they want to hear immediately when a run on any hotfix branch fails, but not about routine feature-branch runs. Which alert setup fits this requirement?
choices: A notification for the pipeline-started event with no filters, so the team sees every new run
A weekly summary email listing all runs across every branch in the project
A notification for the build-completed event filtered to result succeeded, so the team knows what shipped
A notification for the build-completed event filtered to result failed and to branches matching hotfix/*
questions.why: Filtering the build-completed event on failed results and hotfix/* branches matches the requirement, while the other options either ignore the result, ignore the branch, or do not alert on failures in time.

questions.prompt: Ridgeline Freight's alert channel has been silent for nine days, and a team lead concludes the production API is healthy. What is the most accurate response?
choices: The silence means the notification subscription was deleted, so the team should restart the pipelines
The silence proves the API is healthy because any outage would have produced a failed pipeline alert
The silence means no completed run matched the alert filters, but it does not confirm the running service is healthy, since alerts report run outcomes rather than service state
The silence means the webhook is broken and the API should be assumed down until the channel is tested
questions.why: An alert reports what a run recorded, not whether the running service is healthy, so a quiet channel only means no matching run results were reported.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure the team hears about a failed build on the main branch in Azure Pipelines or GitHub Actions. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on these alerts.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick the completion event for the pipeline, then add two filters: the result must be failed and the branch must be main. That sends one clear message per real failure to the team channel, through a webhook or a notification subscription. In GitHub Actions I would use a workflow triggered by workflow_run, check that its conclusion is failure, and post the message from a step. The main tradeoff is that the alert only reports what the CI system recorded. If the message is filtered wrongly, or the channel is muted, the failure can still go unseen. Also, a passing build alert does not prove the deployed service works, so we still need monitoring on the running system.
rubricPoints: Names the completion event and filters on result and branch
Explains the destination, such as a webhook or notification subscription
Names a real limit: alerts report recorded outcomes, not live service health
Notes the risk of noise or missed messages when filters or destinations are wrong

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through which event, filter, and destination fit a stated team need builds the selection skill this objective tests, and no listed mission covers CI event alerts directly.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure performance indicators are the numbers that show how hard a server or network connection is working. The four main ones are CPU, which is how busy the processor is; memory, which is how much working space programs have left; disk, which covers how fast data is read and written and how full storage is; and network, which is how much data moves in and out. Engineers watch these numbers to spot a machine that is struggling before users notice. Think of a car dashboard: speed, fuel, temperature, and tyre pressure each tell you something different, and a warning on one gauge rarely explains the whole problem alone.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server's CPU graph sits at 30 percent all day, yet users say pages are very slow. Name one other indicator you would check first and say why.
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A metric is a number recorded repeatedly over time, such as CPU percentage sampled every minute. A platform metric is one the cloud provider collects from outside the virtual machine, at the hypervisor level, with no software installed inside it. A guest metric is one collected from inside the operating system by an agent, which is a small program installed on the machine. Azure Monitor is the Azure service that stores and charts these metrics. VM Insights is a feature that turns on richer guest data.

Why it works. Platform metrics include Percentage CPU, network bytes in and out, and disk read and write bytes or operations. They need no setup, so they are the first place to look. Memory is different: the host cannot see how much RAM the guest operating system is using, so available memory normally comes from a guest metric collected by an agent. Without that agent, a memory problem can be invisible in the default charts.

Worked example. A web VM shows Percentage CPU at 35 percent, but users report timeouts. Step 1: open the platform metrics and check CPU, which looks normal. Step 2: check network out, which is flat. Step 3: check disk write bytes, which spikes every few minutes. Step 4: conclude the disk is the likely bottleneck, then confirm with a guest memory or disk metric if the agent is installed.

Common mistake. Reading only the average. Averages hide spikes; a CPU average of 40 percent can hide five minutes at 100 percent. Check the maximum and the time window you are looking at.

Consequence. An alert on CPU alone stays silent while memory runs out, the operating system starts swapping to disk, and response times climb sharply. Covering all four indicators is what makes the diagnosis reliable.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a nightly reporting VM, which is a virtual machine, a computer simulated in the cloud. The operators see Percentage CPU peak at 22 percent all night, yet the job finishes three hours late. Step 1: they check platform network out, which is a steady low line. Step 2: they check the maximum of disk read bytes, which shows long flat stretches at zero with short bursts. Step 3: they find no guest available memory chart, because no monitoring agent is installed. Step 4: the team installs the agent and reviews available memory across the job window, looking at the lowest value rather than the average. Which conclusion should the team draw from Step 4?
choices: The average CPU of the whole day is low, so the job delay is caused by the network and nothing else needs checking.
Memory can only be read by the host, so the agent adds no information and the team should wait for a platform memory metric.
If available memory drops near zero during the job, RAM shortage is a likely cause, and the team should confirm it against disk and CPU readings before changing the VM size.
The CPU is the bottleneck, so the VM should be resized to a larger size with more processors.
questions.why: Platform metrics cannot see guest RAM, so the agent supplies available memory, and the lowest value over the job window shows whether memory is running short, with other indicators used to confirm the cause.

questions.prompt: A team has a VM with no monitoring agent installed. Which of these can Azure Monitor still show without any extra setup?
choices: Available memory in megabytes reported from inside the operating system.
The number of running processes listed inside the guest operating system.
Network bytes sent out of the VM, collected at the hypervisor level.
Free space on the data volume reported by an installed agent.
questions.why: Platform metrics such as network bytes are collected outside the VM by the cloud host and need no agent, while memory, process counts and free disk space are guest metrics that require an agent.

questions.prompt: A VM's Percentage CPU averages 28 percent over 24 hours. Its maximum over the same window reaches 100 percent for about 40 minutes each day. Which reading is best?
choices: The daily average is hiding a 40-minute period at full CPU that could cause slow responses during that window.
The VM is healthy, because the average is well under 50 percent.
The VM is idle most of the day, so no investigation is needed.
CPU is not the concern, and the team should only check memory because CPU metrics never spike.
questions.why: Averages smooth out short spikes, so checking the maximum and the time window reveals the saturation that the average conceals.

questions.prompt: An operator sets an alert that fires when Percentage CPU exceeds 80 percent on a VM. Memory on the same VM runs out every night, but the alert never fires. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The CPU alert is fine, but it must be set to 0 percent to catch memory problems.
The CPU alert only watches processor usage, and available memory needs a guest metric from an installed agent before an alert can watch it.
The network is too slow to send the alert, so the alert is delayed.
The alert was set on a platform metric, and platform metrics always include guest memory.
questions.why: An alert can only watch the metric it is attached to, and memory is a guest metric that is invisible to the host unless an agent collects it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a slow virtual machine is short on CPU, memory, disk, or network, and name one limit of the default data you would have to account for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the platform metrics that come free with the VM: Percentage CPU, network in and out, and disk read and write. I would look at the maximum and the time of the slowdown, not just the average, because short spikes are often the cause. If CPU and network are flat but disk writes spike, disk is the likely bottleneck. The limit is memory. The platform cannot see RAM use inside the guest, so available memory only appears if an agent such as VM Insights is installed and collecting guest data. Until I confirm that agent exists, I cannot rule memory out, so I would say so in the report rather than claim the machine is healthy.
rubricPoints: Names the four indicators (CPU, memory, disk, network) and what each measures
States that default platform metrics do not show guest memory use
Explains that averages can hide spikes, so maximum and time window matter
Gives a reasoned next step, such as installing an agent or checking disk metrics

suggested.rationale: Choosing which indicator to read from a symptom is an exam-style reasoning skill, and an incident-style situation adds more than a listing would.

lessons.plain: A metric is a number recorded again and again over time, such as how many requests a web service handled each minute or how long each request took. Analyzing metrics means turning that stream of numbers into answers: is the service busy, is it fast, is it failing, and did something change? Usage metrics show how much the system is used. Performance metrics show how well it responds. The key skill is choosing the right summary, because a summary can look calm while some real users are having a bad time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service handled 1,000 requests in one minute. Nine hundred were answered in 0.1 seconds and one hundred took 10 seconds. Would the average response time alone tell you whether users are having a bad time? Why or why not?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number recorded at regular times, so it becomes a time series: a list of time and value pairs. Analyzing metrics means choosing an aggregation, which is a rule that combines many raw values into one summary, such as a count, a sum, an average, a rate, or a percentile. A percentile such as the 95th (p95) is the value that 95 percent of samples are at or below. A dimension is a label that splits a metric into groups, such as region or API route. Usage metrics answer how much the system is used, for example requests or active users. Performance metrics answer how well it responds, for example latency, error rate, or dependency duration. This works because every aggregation throws information away, so your choice decides what you can see. Worked example: one minute holds 1,000 requests, 900 taking 0.1 s and 100 taking 10 s. Step 1: the mean is (900 x 0.1 + 100 x 10) / 1000 = 1.09 s. Step 2: sort the 1,000 durations; the 95th percentile sits at rank 0.95 x 1,000 = 950, which is 10 s. Step 3: the mean looks only mildly slow, while p95 shows that one request in ten waits ten seconds. Common mistake: averaging percentiles, such as averaging five per-minute p95 values to get an hour's p95. That result is not the true hour p95, so compute percentiles from the underlying samples over the full window. Consequence: an alert on the mean above 2 s stays silent during this minute, while a p95 alert fires. Usage context matters too: a traffic spike with rising latency points to capacity, while flat load with rising latency points to a code or dependency change.

questions.prompt: A file-upload API handled 500 uploads in one minute. 450 finished in 0.3 s and 50 took 4 s. Step 1: the mean is (450 x 0.3 + 50 x 4) / 500 = 0.67 s. Step 2: sort the 500 durations and find the 95th percentile rank, which is 0.95 x 500 = 475. Missing step: state the duration at sorted position 475. Ranks 1 to 450 are the fast uploads and ranks 451 to 500 are the slow ones, so the p95 value is the one you must name.
choices: 0.67 s, because the p95 equals the mean
2.2 s, because it is halfway between the two groups
0.3 s, because most uploads are fast
4 s, because rank 475 falls in the slow group
questions.why: Rank 475 is past the 450 fast values, so it lands in the slow group, and the slow group's duration is 4 s.

questions.prompt: A search service reports a p95 latency of 620 ms for one hour. Which statement describes what that number means?
choices: Only 5 percent of requests were faster than 620 ms.
The average request took 620 ms during the hour.
The slowest request in the hour took 620 ms.
95 percent of the samples in that hour were at or below 620 ms.
questions.why: A p95 is the value that 95 percent of samples are at or below, so it is neither the mean nor the maximum.

questions.prompt: A billing API's request count rose 40 percent over the same hour that its p95 latency rose from 300 ms to 900 ms, and its dependency call durations stayed flat. Which conclusion does the usage context support best?
choices: A code change or a slower dependency is the most likely cause, since load alone would not explain it.
Nothing can be concluded because percentiles cannot be compared across hours.
The metric pipeline is broken and the latency numbers should be discarded.
The service is probably under capacity pressure, so adding instances is the first thing to check.
questions.why: Rising load with rising latency points toward capacity, and flat dependency durations make a dependency cause less likely.

questions.prompt: A payments API has a global mean latency of 180 ms, which looks healthy on the main dashboard. When the same metric is split by the payment provider dimension, one provider shows a p95 of 2.4 s while the others stay under 200 ms. What does this show?
choices: Dimensions cannot be used with latency metrics, only with usage counts.
The provider with 2.4 s is a measurement error and should be excluded.
The dimension split reveals a slow group that the single aggregate hides.
The global mean is wrong and should be recalculated from the raw logs.
questions.why: A dimension separates the metric into groups, and an aggregate across all groups can look healthy while one group is clearly slow.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says latency is fine because the dashboard shows a 200 ms average. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would check whether users really get a good experience, and name one limit of the method you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not trust the average alone, because an average can hide a slow tail. I would look at the 95th percentile of request duration over the same window, split by route or region, and compare it against the error rate and request volume. If p95 is high while the average looks fine, a minority of requests are slow, which the average smooths over. I would also check whether load rose at the same time, since that separates a capacity problem from a code or dependency change. The limit of this method is that percentiles must be computed from the raw samples over the full window; averaging stored per-minute percentiles gives a misleading number. Also, a percentile says nothing about which users were affected, so I would confirm with a route-level breakdown before drawing conclusions.
rubricPoints: Says that an average can hide slow requests, so a percentile such as p95 is needed.
Notes that usage and performance metrics should be read together, for example load against latency.
Names a limit: percentiles must be computed over the full window from raw samples, not averaged from summaries.
Explains that grouping by dimension, such as route or region, narrows where the problem is.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where the learner must choose which metric summary fits a usage or latency question adds the most to reading the definitions alone.

lessons.plain: Distributed tracing is a way of following one user request as it hops across several services, so you can see where the time went. Imagine a parcel that gets scanned at a sorting office, a van and a depot. The scans show exactly which stop was slow. In Azure, the Application Insights feature of Azure Monitor records these scans for web apps and services and links them under one shared ID. This objective is about reading those linked records to find which step in a request caused a delay or failure, instead of guessing from averages.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout takes 4 seconds for one customer, yet the average response time for the API this month looks normal. What might explain that gap, and how would you find the slow part of that one request?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A trace is the full record of one request as it passes through your system. A span is one timed step inside that trace, such as an incoming web call, a call from your API to a database, or a call to another service. Each span records a start time, a duration, a success or failure result, and a shared operation ID that ties it to the others. Distributed means the spans come from several separate services, possibly on different machines.

Why it works: instrumentation, meaning the SDK or agent you add to each application, stamps outgoing calls with the operation ID and the calling span's ID. The next service reads those values and records its own span as a child of the earlier one. Application Insights collects the spans, and its end-to-end transaction view rebuilds the parent and child tree so you can see the timings together.

Worked example: a checkout request takes 4 seconds. First, open that slow request and its end-to-end view. Second, the root span is the web request, lasting 4.0 seconds. Third, its child is the API call, lasting 3.8 seconds. Fourth, under that, the database call lasts 3.6 seconds. The database query is the cost; the layers above it are only waiting on it.

Common mistake: reading only average response times. An average can look healthy while a few requests spend seconds inside one dependency. Sampling, where the SDK keeps only a percentage of traces to control cost, is another trap, because a rare slow request may not be stored at all unless you check the sampling settings.

Consequence: if one service does not pass the operation ID along, its spans appear as a disconnected trace, and the chain you need to follow breaks at that hop.

Tracing answers where one request spent its time, while metrics answer how often something happens.

questions.prompt: A mobile banking app's transfer request takes 2.5 seconds. Work through it with one step left blank. (1) Open the slow request's end-to-end transaction view in Application Insights. (2) The root span is the gateway request, lasting 2.5 seconds. (3) Its child span is the fraud-check call, lasting 2.1 seconds. (4) Missing step: ______. Which completion correctly fills the blank?
choices: Conclude the gateway is the cause because it is the root span and therefore the slowest component.
Raise the sampling rate to 100 percent and restart the gateway so that every future trace is stored.
Average the gateway's response times across the whole day to see whether 2.5 seconds is normal.
Find the deepest child span under the fraud-check call, a rules-store lookup lasting 1.9 seconds, since that leaf is where the time is actually spent.
questions.why: Following the parent-child tree down to the deepest span that does the real work identifies the cost, because the layers above it are only waiting on it.

questions.prompt: In Application Insights distributed tracing, what does the shared operation ID do?
choices: It counts how many times a dependency was called per minute, for use on dashboards.
It decides which spans are kept when sampling is turned on and which are discarded.
It sets the maximum duration a span is allowed to record before it is cut off.
It ties together the spans from different services that belong to the same request, so they can be grouped into one trace.
questions.why: The operation ID is the shared value stamped on outgoing calls that links every span of one request into a single trace.

questions.prompt: A payments service calls an inventory service, but the payments service's SDK is not configured to pass the operation ID on outgoing calls. What will a learner see when they open the end-to-end view of a checkout request?
choices: Spans from the inventory service that appear disconnected, so the chain of calls breaks at that hop.
No spans at all for the checkout request, because the whole trace is discarded when one hop is missing.
A complete trace with the inventory timings averaged into the payments span.
A single trace where the inventory span appears as a child of the payments span with the correct timing.
questions.why: Without the operation ID and parent span ID being passed along, the receiving service cannot attach its span to the earlier one, so the chain breaks at that hop.

questions.prompt: A team sees that the number of failed sign-in requests per minute has roughly doubled since yesterday's release. They want to know both how often this happens over time and where a single slow failing sign-in spent its time. Which instrumentation fits each part of the question?
choices: Use the end-to-end trace view for the frequency over time, and an average response time chart for the single slow request.
Use metrics for how often the failures happen over time, and distributed tracing to see where one request spent its time.
Use sampling settings to count the failures, and distributed tracing to produce the per-minute failure rate.
Use a single span's start time to measure frequency, and metrics to see the internal steps of one request.
questions.why: Metrics answer how often something happens, while tracing answers where one request spent its time, so the two parts of the question map to these two tools.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what distributed tracing in Application Insights shows that averaged response-time metrics do not, and name one limit of tracing that they should keep in mind when relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Averages tell you how the system behaves overall, but they hide the story of any single request. Distributed tracing links the timed steps of one request across services under a shared operation ID, so you can open a slow checkout and see that the database call took most of the time. That tells you where to look next. The main limit is sampling. The SDK often keeps only a percentage of traces to control cost, so a rare slow request may not be stored at all. Another limit is propagation: if one service does not pass the operation ID onward, the trace breaks at that hop and the chain looks incomplete. So before trusting a trace view, I would check the sampling rate and confirm that every service in the path is instrumented.
rubricPoints: Tracing follows one request across services using a shared operation ID and timed spans
Averages can hide rare slow requests that a single trace reveals
Sampling can mean some requests are never recorded
A service that does not propagate the ID breaks the trace

suggested.rationale: Choosing which trace view or sampling setting fits a slow-request situation is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario.

lessons.plain: Logs are the written record a running system leaves behind. Every request, error and deployment adds a line with a time stamp and some details. When there are millions of lines, you need a way to ask questions of them, such as how many errors happened in the last hour or which service fails most often. Kusto Query Language, usually shortened to KQL, is the question language used by Azure Monitor Logs, Microsoft's central store for this kind of record. You write a query as a chain of small steps. Each step narrows or reshapes the data, and the result comes back as a table you can read or chart. Learning the basics is mostly learning a handful of these steps and the habit of limiting the time window first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A log table holds a month of records, but you only care about errors from the last ten minutes. Which condition would you apply first, and why would that choice matter for how much data the system has to read?
lessons.teach:
A table is a named set of rows, and each row has columns, such as a time stamp, a name and a result code. KQL queries start from a table and pass its rows through a series of steps. The vertical bar, called the pipe, hands the output of one step to the next. The where step keeps only rows that match a condition. The project step chooses which columns to show. The extend step adds a computed column. The summarize step groups rows and calculates a value for each group, such as a count. The order by step sorts results, and take returns only a few rows for a quick look. The function ago() means a time offset counted back from now, so ago(1h) means one hour ago.

Worked example, using a table of web requests named AppRequests: AppRequests | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | where ResultCode >= 500 | summarize Failures = count() by Name | order by Failures desc. Step one starts with every row in the table. Step two keeps only rows from the last hour. Step three keeps only server-error responses, those with a code of 500 or higher. Step four groups the remaining rows by endpoint name and counts each group. Step five sorts the groups so the endpoint with the most failures appears first.

The common mistake is leaving out the time filter. Without it, the query scans the whole table, which is slow and costs more, and a dashboard or alert built on it may time out and show stale data. Filtering by time first keeps each step small. In a running system, an alert that depends on an unbounded query can fail quietly, so the team stops seeing errors they expected to be warned about.

questions.prompt: A team keeps a table named StorageOps with columns Timestamp, Region and LatencyMs. They want the 20 slowest recent requests in the West Europe region, with the slowest first. Their query is: StorageOps | where Timestamp > ago(6h) | where Region == 'westeu' | extend LatencySec = LatencyMs / 1000.0 | ___ | take 20. The blank is the one step that sorts rows by LatencySec from largest to smallest, so the slowest rows come first before take keeps 20. Which step fills the blank?
choices: project LatencyMs
order by LatencySec desc
summarize count() by Region
where Timestamp > ago(6h)
questions.why: Order by sorts results and must come before take, so that take keeps the 20 slowest rows rather than 20 arbitrary ones, and desc puts the largest latency first.

questions.prompt: In a KQL query, what does the pipe character (the vertical bar) do?
choices: It hands the output of one step to the next step in the query
It saves the query result to a file for later reading
It joins two tables together by a shared column name
It deletes rows that fail a condition from the original table
questions.why: The pipe passes the rows produced by one step into the following step, which is how a query is built as a chain of steps.

questions.prompt: A table named SignInLog has columns TimeGenerated, UserPrincipal and Result. Which query returns the number of failed sign-ins per user over the last 15 minutes, highest count first?
choices: SignInLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | where Result == 'Failure' | summarize Failed = count() by UserPrincipal | order by Failed desc
