SignInLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | where Result == 'Failure' | project UserPrincipal | order by UserPrincipal asc
SignInLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | where Result == 'Failure' | summarize Failed = count() by UserPrincipal | order by Failed asc
SignInLog | where Result == 'Failure' | summarize Failed = count() by UserPrincipal | order by Failed desc
questions.why: The query needs a time filter, a filter for failures, a count grouped by user, and a descending sort, which is the only option containing all four steps in that order.

questions.prompt: A team's alert query starts from a table of job runs and has no time filter. It returns rows from months ago when the team only wants the last 2 hours, and it slows down badly on the full table. Which change most directly keeps the query to recent rows?
choices: Add extend Age = now() - TimeGenerated before the summary
Add a where step that keeps rows with TimeGenerated later than ago(2h)
Add take 5 at the end so only five rows are shown
Change the final sort from desc to asc
questions.why: A where step comparing TimeGenerated to ago(2h) removes older rows early, which keeps each later step small, whereas take only limits what is displayed after the work is done.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the dashboard shows zero errors, but users are reporting failures. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would check the logs with a basic KQL query, and name one limit of this approach that they should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not trust the dashboard alone. I would open the log table for the requests and run a query that filters to the time window when users reported problems, then keeps only responses with server-error codes, and groups them by endpoint. That shows whether failures exist and where they cluster. The main limit is that the query only sees what was logged. If an application crashes before writing a log line, or the logging is switched off for that service, the failures will not appear, so zero rows does not prove zero errors. I would also check that the time window and the table are the right ones before drawing a conclusion. The result is only as complete as the telemetry feeding the table.
rubricPoints: KQL queries are a chain of steps that pass rows from one stage to the next.
Filtering by a time window first keeps queries fast and cheap.
where selects rows, summarize groups and counts, and order by sorts results.
Query results are only as complete as the logs that were actually collected.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning about which query fits a logging situation adds the most here, and linux-02-log-detective builds the habit of reading logs to find a failing service.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Logistics: Linking Work, Releases, and Alerts
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Logistics is a fictional company that runs a small web app for tracking delivery trucks. Its engineers use GitHub to store code and Azure Boards, the work-tracking part of Azure DevOps, to hold work items (each one is a single tracked piece of work, such as a bug or a user story). The team follows GitHub Flow, which means each change is made on a short-lived branch, reviewed through a pull request (a request to merge a branch into the main code line, with a review step), merged into main, and then deployed. The team lead, Priya, has asked you to set up three things this sprint. 1. Explain how you would connect Azure Boards to the GitHub repository so that a commit or pull request that mentions a work item gets linked to it automatically, and name the exact text pattern a developer would type to create that link. 2. The leadership group wants a dashboard showing lead time (the time from a change being committed until it runs in production) and time to recovery (the time from when an outage starts until service is restored). Name the Azure Boards or Analytics-based metric you would use for each, and say what data each one depends on. 3. The on-call channel in Microsoft Teams (a group chat tool) should post a message whenever a production deployment fails. Describe how you would send those events from GitHub into Teams, and state what kind of event mechanism you would use and why.
subParts: Connecting Azure Boards to GitHub and the link text
Lead time and time to recovery metrics
Deployment failure alerts into Microsoft Teams
modelAnswer: Connect the Azure Boards project to the GitHub repository using the GitHub connection in the Azure Boards project settings, which authorizes Azure Boards to read the repository and its pull requests. After that, a developer adds the text AB# followed by the work item number (for example AB#214) to a commit message or to the pull request title or description. Azure Boards reads that text and shows the commit or pull request as a linked development item on the work item, so the link exists without anyone editing the work item by hand. The common mistake is writing the number without the AB# prefix, which creates no link, or assuming the connection works without first authorizing the repository.

Lead time is the elapsed time from a change being committed to it reaching production. To measure it, you need the commit timestamp from GitHub and the production deployment timestamp, so the metric depends on linked build and deployment data being recorded for each change. Time to recovery is the elapsed time from the start of an incident to the moment service is restored. You measure it from an incident work item or alert record, where the start time and the resolved time are both captured, so it depends on incidents being logged consistently. A common mistake is building a lead time chart from work item creation dates instead of commit and deployment dates, which measures planning time rather than delivery time. Charts built from inconsistent incident timestamps will also give misleading recovery times.

Send the failures from GitHub to Teams using a webhook, which is an automatic HTTP message that GitHub sends to a URL you specify whenever a chosen event happens, such as a deployment status change. Create an incoming webhook or a connector in the Teams on-call channel to receive those messages, then configure the GitHub deployment or workflow event to post to it when the status is failure. The reason to use a webhook rather than polling is that the message is pushed the moment the event occurs, so the on-call engineer sees the failure without anyone checking a dashboard. Teams can also receive the Azure Boards app for work item notifications, but for deployment status the event-driven webhook is the direct fit. A common mistake is filtering only on pipeline start events and missing the failure status, so failures never reach the channel.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Cargo: release branches, large video files and a leaked password
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Cargo Systems is a fictional company that runs a parcel-tracking web app. Its engineers keep the app in one Git repository hosted on Azure Repos. Git is a version control system that stores every change to files as a series of commits, and a branch is a movable label that points at one commit so that work can proceed in parallel. The team ships a customer release once a month from a branch named release/2024-06, and occasionally needs an urgent fix for a bug that is live in production. Three problems arrived this week. First, the engineering lead wants a branching model that keeps the main branch always deployable while still allowing monthly releases and hotfixes. Second, the design team committed about 900 MB of promotional video files straight into the repository, so every clone takes many minutes. Third, a developer pushed a commit three days ago that contains a database password in a configuration file. That commit reached the shared develop branch. The same developer then accidentally deleted a feature branch named feature/returns-api that still had unmerged work. Answer the following. 1. Recommend a branch strategy for the monthly release and hotfix flow. Say where each branch type is created from and where it merges to, and describe one branch policy that protects main. 2. Explain how Git Large File Storage, called Git LFS, would handle the video files from now on, and what it does and does not change about the existing history. 3. Explain how to recover the deleted feature branch, and how to remove the leaked password from the repository history, including what teammates must do afterwards.
subParts: Branch strategy for monthly releases and hotfixes
Handling large video files with Git LFS
Recovering the deleted branch and removing the leaked password
modelAnswer: A trunk-based model keeps one main branch that all work merges into in small pieces. A feature branch is a short-lived branch made for one piece of work and merged back through a pull request, which is a request to merge that triggers code review. For monthly releases, create a release branch such as release/2024-06 from main on release day. It is frozen to stabilise one version and receives only bug fixes. A hotfix is a small urgent fix for a live version; it starts from the release branch that is live, is merged into that release branch, and is then merged back into main so the fix is not lost. Worked example: main is at commit C10 and is cut as release/2024-06 at C10. A price bug is fixed on hotfix/2024-06-price branched from C10, merged into release/2024-06 and then into main, so the next release includes it. A branch policy protecting main is a rule that blocks a merge until conditions are met. For example, require at least one approving review and a passing build before a pull request can complete, and block direct pushes to main. Common mistake: fixing a hotfix only on main. The next release gets the fix, but the live version does not. The reverse mistake, fixing only on the release branch, means the fix disappears in the following release. Consequence: customers keep seeing the bug until the fix reaches the version they are running.

Git LFS, Large File Storage, is an extension that replaces large files in the repository with small text pointers. The real file contents are stored on a separate LFS server. You tell Git which file patterns to track, such as *.mp4, by recording them in a file named .gitattributes, which is committed like any other file. Worked example: the team runs the tracking command for *.mp4, commits the .gitattributes file, then adds promo-spring.mp4. Git stores a small pointer file in the commit, and uploads the 900 MB of video to LFS storage. A new clone downloads the pointers and only the LFS files needed for the current checkout, so clones become small. It does not change existing history. The 900 MB of video already stored in past commits remains in the repository's history, so clones that fetch full history still download it. Removing it requires a separate history rewrite, which changes commit IDs and must be agreed with the whole team. Common mistake: adding the tracking rule after the files are committed and expecting old commits to shrink. They do not. Consequence: the repository stays large for anyone cloning full history until history is rewritten or the content is migrated, and everyone who holds the old history must re-clone or reset after a rewrite.

Git keeps a reflog, a local record of where branch tips and HEAD (the pointer to your current branch or commit) were recently. Commits that no longer belong to any branch stay in the repository until Git's cleanup process removes them after a grace period. To recover the deleted branch, look through the reflog for the last commit that was on feature/returns-api, or use git fsck to list unreachable commits, then recreate the branch at that commit. Worked example: the reflog shows the last commit on the deleted branch was 4f2a9c. Run git branch feature/returns-api 4f2a9c to recreate the branch, check it with git log, then push it back to the server. To remove the password, first rotate it, meaning replace it with a new password in the database and in the secret store, because any secret that was pushed must be treated as exposed even after the history is cleaned. Then rewrite history with a tool such as git filter-repo, which removes or replaces the password string in every commit that touched the configuration file. Force-push the rewritten branches, after temporarily allowing it if branch policies block forced pushes and having an administrator approve the change. Every teammate must then re-clone the repository or reset their local branches to the rewritten history, so the old commits are not pushed back. Common mistake: deleting the password in a new commit, or rewriting history without rotating the password. In both cases the password remains readable in old commits. Consequence: anyone with repository access can still find the password, and a teammate who pushes from an old local copy can restore the secret into the shared history.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern routekit versioning and feeds
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional company. Its platform team maintains routekit, an internal library that three services use, and a web service called order-api. Two problems came up this month. First, a build broke overnight because a public open-source package that routekit depends on published a new version with a breaking change, and nothing pinned the older version. Second, the pipeline storage bill grew fast because every build keeps its output forever. Your lead asks you to answer three items. 1. Recommend how to host routekit and the public packages it depends on. Name the feed and view approach you would use, and explain what an upstream source does for the team. 2. Choose a versioning scheme for routekit and a different one for order-api. Justify each choice using semantic versioning (SemVer, a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH number that signals breaking changes) or date-based versioning (CalVer, a number built from dates). 3. Propose a retention strategy for pipeline artifacts (the files a build produces, such as packages or compiled binaries) and package versions, and state what a quality gate (an automated check that must pass before a build can move forward) should verify before a build is promoted to production.
modelAnswer: Use an Azure Artifacts feed, which is a managed package store inside Azure DevOps, for routekit's own packages. Create a package view, a named read-only subset of a feed that consumers point to, such as a view called stable that only exposes versions that passed the release checks. Turn on an upstream source on the same feed so that requests for public packages are fetched through the feed and cached there. An upstream source is a configured link to an external registry; it means the team pulls public packages through one controlled place, so a new upstream release does not reach a build until someone allows it. Worked example: the build asks the feed for the dependency at version 2.4.1. The feed already holds a cached copy from the last approved fetch, so the build gets exactly that version and the overnight release is not picked up. Common mistake: pointing builds straight at the public registry, which lets any new upstream release change the build without warning. Consequence: the broken overnight build in this scenario would have been avoided by pinning the exact version and caching it through the feed. GitHub Packages is an alternative if the code and packages already live in GitHub; the choice should follow where the team's source and permissions already sit.

Use SemVer for routekit because other teams import it as a library, and they need the number to tell them whether an upgrade is safe. Format is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase PATCH for bug fixes that keep the public interface the same, MINOR for new features that remain compatible, and MAJOR for any breaking change. Worked example: routekit 3.2.0 changes the signature of one public function, so the release becomes 4.0.0. A consumer on 3.x sees the major jump and knows to test before upgrading. Use CalVer for order-api because it is a deployed web service that the business tracks by release date, not by a compatibility contract with other code. A format such as 2024.06.3 shows when it shipped and the third build or release of that month. Common mistake: using SemVer on a service that nobody imports, which creates version numbers that mean nothing to anyone, or using CalVer on a shared library, which hides breaking changes from consumers. Consequence: with the wrong scheme, a consumer may upgrade a library across a breaking change without warning and break at runtime.

Retention means the rule that decides how long artifacts and package versions are kept before automatic deletion. A reasonable policy keeps all versions of routekit that are referenced by a stable view or a production deployment, keeps the most recent 10 pipeline runs for feature branches, and deletes unreferenced prerelease packages after 30 days. The reason is that storage cost grows with every kept file, while deleting a package still in use breaks a deployment that depends on it. Worked example: a prerelease build from a feature branch from 45 days ago is not in any view and not deployed, so the policy removes it; the 4.0.0 release stays because the stable view references it. Common mistake: setting a single blanket age limit that also deletes versions a production rollback might need. Consequence: a rollback to the previous version fails if that package was deleted. A quality gate for promotion to production should verify that unit tests and integration tests passed, that code coverage (the percentage of code exercised by tests) meets the agreed threshold, that a security scan reports no new high-severity findings, and that the approval record exists from a named owner. The gate should block promotion and report which check failed, rather than letting the build continue with a warning.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Logistics: securing a nightly deploy and a contractor's access
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional freight company with a small engineering team. Its web app source code lives in GitHub, its work items and boards live in Azure DevOps, and the app runs in Azure App Service, which is Azure's managed hosting service for web apps. A GitHub Actions workflow, meaning an automated pipeline defined in a file inside the repository, deploys the app every night. The workflow currently signs in to Azure using a long-lived client secret, a password-style credential for a service principal (an identity that an application uses to sign in to Azure), stored as a GitHub secret. A contractor, Dana, is joining to build reporting features. Dana needs to read one repository and see the Azure DevOps boards, but must not change pipelines or push code. Imani, the product manager, only needs to view and comment on work items. Two problems have also appeared. A secret scanner flagged an old personal access token (a token a person creates to act on their own behalf against an API) in an earlier commit, and Dependabot (GitHub's automated checker for vulnerable open-source libraries) raised an alert about a logging library the app uses. Complete the following: 1. Recommend the identity the nightly workflow should use to sign in to Azure, and explain why it beats the alternative. 2. Recommend the access level for Dana in GitHub and the access level for Imani in Azure DevOps, and explain why each one fits. 3. Describe your immediate response to the leaked token, the steps that stop a repeat, and what you do about the Dependabot alert.
subParts: Identity for the nightly workflow to sign in to Azure
Access levels for Dana in GitHub and Imani in Azure DevOps
Response to the leaked token and the Dependabot alert
modelAnswer: Use a service principal with workload identity federation, also called OpenID Connect (OIDC). Federation means Azure is configured to trust tokens that GitHub issues for a specific workflow run, so no password is stored anywhere. GitHub hands the workflow a short-lived signed token, and Microsoft Entra ID (the Azure identity service) exchanges it for an Azure access token. Add a federated credential on the app registration's service principal that matches only this repository and the main branch, then delete the stored client secret from GitHub. Grant the service principal the narrowest role that still works, such as Contributor scoped to the App Service resource group. The alternative is a managed identity, which is an identity Azure creates and attaches to an Azure resource such as an App Service or a virtual machine. A managed identity suits code running inside Azure. A GitHub-hosted runner runs outside your Azure resources, so a managed identity does not fit this workflow directly. A common mistake is to keep the old client secret as a fallback, which leaves a long-lived credential that can leak.

Dana should be an outside collaborator in GitHub, added to that one repository only, with Read permission. Read lets Dana view and clone the code and open issues, but not push, merge, or edit workflow files. Do not add Dana to the organization or give Write access, because that would reach other repositories and the pipeline definitions. Imani should get stakeholder access in Azure DevOps. Stakeholder is a limited access level for people who need to see and collaborate on work items and boards without a full paid contributor license, and it does not allow editing pipelines or repositories. Give Imani access through the project, not through an administrator group. The mistake to avoid is granting a broad group such as Contributors to a non-engineer because it is the quickest way to make things visible. Check the current feature list for each access level before you finalise, since vendors change these.

Treat the personal access token as compromised immediately. Revoke it in the owner's GitHub settings, even though it sits in old history, because anyone who saw the commit can still use it. Check the audit log for any use since the commit date, and rotate any other credential that token could reach. Rewriting history to remove the value is a cleanup step only, because copies may already exist, so it does not replace revocation. To prevent a repeat, turn on secret scanning with push protection so that GitHub blocks pushes that contain recognised credential patterns. Move the remaining secrets into GitHub encrypted secrets or Azure Key Vault (a service for storing and controlling access to secrets, keys, and certificates), and have the workflow read them from there. For the Dependabot alert, look at which version of the logging library is affected and whether the app actually calls the vulnerable code path. Accept Dependabot's pull request that upgrades to a patched version, let the tests run, and merge it. Dismiss an alert only with a written reason, such as the vulnerable code not being reachable, and record that reason in the alert.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Logistics: Finding Out Why Checkout Got Slow
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Logistics is a fictional company that sells packaged coffee online. Its engineering team runs a checkout web app on Azure, deployed from GitHub Actions workflows and an Azure Pipelines release. The app sends telemetry (the measurements and logs a running system produces, such as request timings and error counts) to Azure Monitor, Microsoft's shared place for collecting and analysing that data. Application Insights is the part of Azure Monitor that watches a web application's requests, failures, and dependencies, and it stores its records in a Log Analytics workspace, which is a database you query with Kusto Query Language (KQL, a read-only query language for log tables). Distributed tracing means following one user request as it hops across several services, so you can see which step took the time. Yesterday, customers reported slow checkouts after a release. You are the new DevOps engineer on call, and your lead asks you to do three things. 1. Name the Application Insights feature you would open to follow one slow checkout request across the web app, the payment service, and the database, and explain what it shows you that a single average response time does not. 2. Name the alerting approach you would configure so the team is told when a GitHub Actions deployment workflow fails or an Azure Pipelines release stage fails, and say what event the alert reacts to. 3. Write a basic KQL query against the requests table that counts failed requests in the last 60 minutes, grouped by request name, and explain what each part of the query does.
subParts: Name the Application Insights feature for following one slow request across services, and say what it reveals.
Name the alerting approach for failed GitHub Actions workflow runs and failed Azure Pipelines release stages, and the event it reacts to.
Write a basic KQL query that counts failed requests in the last 60 minutes grouped by request name, and explain each part.
modelAnswer: The feature is distributed tracing, viewed in Application Insights as the end-to-end transaction view for a request. It follows one user request through each component it touched, showing the time spent in the web app, each downstream call such as the payment service, and each database call. A single average response time only tells you that the system is slow overall; the trace tells you which hop was slow for that specific request, so you can focus the investigation.

Use an alert rule that reacts to run or stage completion events with a failed outcome. For GitHub Actions, configure monitoring of workflow runs in the repository so that a run finishing with a failure conclusion raises a notification or action. For Azure Pipelines, configure an alert on the release or stage failure event in the project. In both cases the alert fires on the event of a finished run or stage with a failed result, not on a metric average, so the team hears about a broken deployment as soon as it happens. A common mistake is alerting on every run start, which floods the team with noise and hides real failures.

A query that works is: requests | where timestamp > ago(60m) and success == false | summarize FailedCount = count() by name. Step by step: requests is the table of incoming request records; where timestamp > ago(60m) keeps only rows from the last 60 minutes; and success == false keeps only failed requests, since success is a true/false field on each row; summarize FailedCount = count() by name counts the remaining rows and groups the counts by the request name, so you see which endpoint fails most. A common mistake is writing success = false with one equals sign, which is an assignment rather than a comparison, or forgetting the time filter, which makes the count cover all stored history and hides what changed after the release.
